# Can an AI-Powered Tutor Produce Meaningful Results?

![Image 2: Author](https://www.aei.org/wp-content/themes/aei-2025/assets/img/icons/avatar.svg?x46528)by[Frederick M. Hess](https://www.aei.org/profile/frederick-m-hess/)

![Image 3: Date](https://www.aei.org/wp-content/themes/aei-2025/assets/img/icons/calendar.svg?x46528)July 30, 2025

![Image 4: Publisher](https://www.aei.org/wp-content/themes/aei-2025/assets/img/icons/category.svg?x46528)[Education Week](https://www.edweek.org/technology/opinion-can-an-ai-powered-tutor-produce-meaningful-results/2025/07)

![Image 5: facebook sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/facebook.svg)

![Image 6: twitter sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/twitter.svg)

![Image 7: linkedin sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/linkedin.svg)

![Image 8: bluesky sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/bluesky.svg)

![Image 9: email sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/email.svg)

_As regular readers know, I’ve long held that American education is overdue for a_[_rethink_](https://www.aei.org/research-products/book/the-great-school-rethink/)_but also that most “reform” is_[_oversold_](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED426168)_. Finding the sweet spot, as Michael Horn, Julie Squire, and I note in our new book,_[School Rethink 2.0](https://www.aei.org/research-products/book/school-rethink-2-0-putting-reinvention-into-practice/)_, requires focusing on rubber-meets-road change._ Rethink 2.0 _offers accounts from leaders doing that work, and I’m delighted to speak with one of them today._ _Kristen DiCerbo is the_ _chief learning officer at the acclaimed Khan Academy, where she oversaw development of Khan’s AI-powered tutor Khanmigo and was named to_[_Time Magazine’s AI 100 in 2024_](https://time.com/7012801/kristen-dicerbo/)_. Khanmigo has been described as a “personal tutor and teaching assistant” and is designed to support users with mathematics, science, humanities, and coding questions. Here’s what she had to say._

_—Rick_

**Rick:**In _School Rethink 2.0_, you write about developing the Khan Academy’s AI tutor Khanmigo. How did that come about?

**Kristen:**Our initial impetus was a 2022 meeting where leadership from OpenAI demonstrated a new model they had just finished training, which we now know as GPT-4, and gave us the chance to interact with it. After a few days of doing all the things everyone probably did when they first got access to a large language model—writing poems for our partners and asking it all kinds of questions—we started thinking about whether it could help address some of the persistent problems we have in education. We decided that it could have a significant impact on the ways students get support as they learn, so we threw away our road map for what we thought we would be working on and started building Khanmigo.

**Rick:**So you quietly started designing Khanmigo even before ChatGPT was released. What was it that grabbed your imagination?

**Kristen:**Our first lesson in prompting was what initially amazed me. We could provide it with some basic instructions, in English rather than code, and change the kinds of output it gave. If we said, “You are a Socratic tutor. I am a student. Don’t give me answers to my questions but lead me to get to them myself,” it returned different responses from what it returned when we asked it a question without those instructions. It started doing some of the things good tutors do. We spent September and October 2022 deciding what we were going to build and doing basic prototyping. We then started seriously designing and building in November and launched in March 2023, so it took seven months to develop Khanmigo.

**Rick:**What were some early lessons you learned while designing Khanmigo?

**Kristen:**Consistently getting the AI to do what we wanted was not as easy as giving it three sentences of instructions! Even when given the same prompt and set of instructions, the model provides a different answer every time. You can’t just test a prompt once and call it a day. We had to set up evaluation systems to repeatedly run each prompt and check the results of those tests. Then, we had to keep track of the most recent version of each prompt since we were constantly tweaking the language. We also learned that when prompts get to be too long, the model starts randomly ignoring different parts of the instructions. What kept us motivated was remembering our core goal: giving students better support and feedback as they practice.

**Rick:**Have there been any surprises about how educators or students are using Khanmigo?

**Kristen:**I have been designing and researching educational technology for 20 years, and the first thing that surprised me was how quickly AI has been adopted. We went from about 68,000 Khanmigo student and teacher users in our partner school districts in 2023-24 to more than 700,000 in the 2024-25 school year, expanding from 45 to more than 380 district partners. In total, Khan Academy partners with around 450 districts in the U.S., meaning that most of our partner districts have decided to use Khanmigo. I was also surprised by the number of students and teachers raving about Khanmigo as a tool for English-language learners to get support in their native language since it can answer students’ questions in many languages. I was also surprised by the number of teachers using Khanmigo to refresh their _own_ knowledge. However, I’m a little disheartened by how often some teachers would primarily use our AI to generate multiple-choice questions. I’d love to see students engage much more deeply with content through AI, something that multiple-choice questions rarely encourage. I would like to see greater usage of Khanmigo activities like Ignite My Curiosity, which allows students to engage in conversations around interesting ideas in domains they may not be familiar with.

**Rick:**As you know, there are concerns that students are spending too much time on devices. What’s that mean for AI tutoring?

**Kristen:**Prior to generative AI, our efficacy research showed that students who used Khan Academy for an average of 30 minutes of additional math practice per week throughout the school year saw greater-than-expected gains on standardized assessments. Incorporating AI is not meant to add even more time on top of that but to make students even more productive with the time they have by providing active support and feedback during study sessions. We in no way envision a classroom where students spend all of their time individually working on screens.

**Rick:**What are some of the practical challenges when it comes to AI tutoring?

**Kristen:**The biggest challenge we are facing with Khanmigo is the same challenge we have seen historically with educational technology: achieving meaningful student engagement. We know tools like Khan Academy will work … if students use them correctly. When I review student chats with Khanmigo, I see some conversations where students are doing exactly what we would hope by answering questions and then posing their own to deepen their understanding. I also see a lot of chats where students are responding, “I don’t know,” or, my recent favorite, “Bro, IDK.” If students are not putting forth cognitive effort in their interactions, there is no reason to expect that they will learn from them. In some cases, we also see that students don’t actually have the skills to recognize what they know, what they need to get support on, and how to write good questions to address their weaknesses.

**Rick:**What helps students figure out the right questions to ask?

**Kristen:**The teacher is the most powerful tool to address this. For example, one science teacher worked with her students to come up with good question stems to start questions for Khanmigo. She then printed them out on 3×5 cards to put on their desks. It was quite a surprise to enter the classroom and witness students referencing cards on their desks, just like I had in the 1980s, to teach them how to interact with this new technology. The broader lesson is that students and teachers need the skills and the motivation to use AI well.

**Rick:**What do people get wrong about AI and tutoring?

**Kristen:**AI doesn’t change the fundamentals of how kids learn. When we learn new things, we need practice with support and feedback to master them. In too many cases, students just don’t get enough opportunities, whether in math, writing, or other domains, to effectively practice these skills. AI tutoring makes it easier for every student to get that practice.

**Rick:**AI is developing at a breakneck pace. What does that mean for your efforts?

**Kristen:**In the near term, Sal Khan is still on the hook for a good number of videos for new courses we’re launching. We have found that AI dubbing of his voice into other languages has gotten very good. We will be launching that soon, with appropriate labeling. We are continuing to work on bringing new AI technology to the tutoring experience. For instance, we just launched image inputs. Now, Khanmigo can interact with students about an image they share. This is critical for domains that rely on visual representation, like geometry. We are inching closer to the place where the model can collaborate in real-time with students about work done on a scratchpad. Finally, we’re interested in how AI might impact assessment, ranging from developing more authentic kinds of assessment activities to helping teachers, parents, and students better understand their scores.

**Rick**: As educators get more comfortable with AI, do you have any advice on how to best ensure they’re making sound decisions for learners?

**Kristen:**Always focus on what problems you are trying to solve, not the technology you have available. Then, ask whether the technology will help solve that problem, and if so, how it can help. Finally, develop a method for measuring progress—ask how you will know if that new technology is working. We are in the early days of the journey with AI in classrooms, so there isn’t a lot of high-quality data to rely on. This means teachers and schools may want to start slowly and gather their own evidence about what works with AI. But I would echo advice I heard Rebecca Winthrop of the Brookings Institution[give recently](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/13/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-rebecca-winthrop.html): Don’t let FOMO drive your decisions.

This is a Q&A interview published in Education Week on July 30, 2025, hosted by Frederick M. Hess (Senior Fellow at AEI) with Kristen DiCerbo, Chief Learning Officer at Khan Academy and a member of Time Magazine's AI 100 in 2024. The discussion centers on Khan Academy's AI-powered tutor, Khanmigo, which was developed after OpenAI demonstrated GPT-4 to Khan Academy leadership in 2022. The interview covers the development process, lessons learned, adoption rates, and challenges facing AI tutoring.

Key points include:
- Khanmigo was developed in just seven months (from November 2022 to March 2023) after Khan Academy abandoned its existing roadmap.
- The AI tutor was designed as a Socratic tutor that guides students rather than giving them answers.
- Adoption grew rapidly: from 68,000 users in 2023-24 to more than 700,000 in 2024-25, expanding from 45 to over 380 district partners.
- A surprising use case emerged for English-language learners seeking support in their native languages, and for teachers refreshing their own knowledge.
- DiCerbo expressed disappointment that some teachers primarily use the AI to generate multiple-choice questions rather than deeper engagement activities.
- The biggest challenge is achieving meaningful student engagement, as many students respond with "I don't know" or don't put forth sufficient cognitive effort.
- DiCerbo emphasizes that AI doesn't change the fundamentals of how kids learn—they still need practice with support and feedback.
- Advice for educators: focus on the problems to solve, not the technology; start slowly; gather evidence about what works; and don't let FOMO drive decisions.

### AI in K–12 Education (2022–2025): A Comprehensive Landscape Scan

# AI in K–12 Education (2022–2025): A Comprehensive Landscape Scan

## Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a key theme in K–12 education from 2022 through 2025. The late-2022 debut of advanced generative AI (e.g. OpenAI’s ChatGPT) **sparked fundamental questions about AI’s role in schools**[edweek.org](https://www.edweek.org/technology/schools-are-taking-too-long-to-craft-ai-policy-why-thats-a-problem/2024/02#:~:text=It%E2%80%99s%20been%20more%20than%20a,12%20education). Educators and policymakers are exploring AI-driven personalized learning tools, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, and even administrative AI assistants. This report provides an in-depth overview of the U.S. K–12 EdTech landscape involving AI, including government initiatives, industry developments, school implementations, equity considerations, ethical concerns, and early evidence of impact.

## Government Policies, Strategies, and Funding for AI in K–12

**Federal Initiatives:** The U.S. government has taken active steps to support AI in education. In May 2023, the Department of Education’s Office of Educational Technology released *“Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning”*, outlining a vision for **safe, effective, and equitable AI use in schools**[ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/ai-report/ai-report.pdf#:~:text=%E2%97%8F%20Recommendations%3A%20Use%20of%20AI,protections%2C%20protect%20data%20privacy%2C%20provide)[ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/ai-report/ai-report.pdf#:~:text=%E2%97%8F%20About%20AI%3A%20AI%20systems,our%20collective%20vision%20for%20high). The report emphasizes that AI tools should have *“algorithmic discrimination protections, protect data privacy, provide notice and explanation, and provide recourse to humans when problems arise.”*[ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/ai-report/ai-report.pdf#:~:text=match%20at%20L868%20They%20must,to%20humans%20when%20problems%20arise) These principles align with the White House’s *Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights* (Oct. 2022), which calls for safe and transparent AI systems in all sectors, including education. In practical terms, federal agencies are reviewing laws like FERPA and COPPA to ensure **student data privacy and safety** in an AI-driven era[ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/ai-report/ai-report.pdf#:~:text=Regulations%20related%20to%20key%20student,CIPA%29%2C%20and%20the%20Children%E2%80%99s)[ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/ai-report/ai-report.pdf#:~:text=also%20passed%20privacy%20laws%20that,for%20responsible%20AI%20in%20parallel).

In April 2025, a presidential executive order established a national *“Artificial Intelligence Education”* Task Force and set an explicit **policy to promote AI literacy and integration in K–12**[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=Sec,ready%20workforce). This order directs federal efforts toward: integrating AI into curricula and classroom practice, providing professional development on AI for educators, and encouraging early exposure to AI concepts[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=youth%20with%20opportunities%20to%20cultivate,of%20scientific%20and%20economic%20achievement)[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=Sec,generation%20of%20American%20AI%20innovators). It also launched a *Presidential AI Educator Challenge* to spur collaboration among government, academia, and industry on AI solutions for education[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=Within%2090%20days%20of%20the,national%20challenges%20with%20AI%20solutions). Within 90–120 days of the order, the Department of Education was instructed to issue guidance on using federal funds for AI-based instructional resources (e.g. AI-driven tutoring) and to leverage existing research programs to improve student outcomes with AI[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=,student%20achievement%2C%20attainment%2C%20and%20mobility)[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=improve%20education%20outcomes%20using%20AI%2C,student%20achievement%2C%20attainment%2C%20and%20mobility). Similarly, NSF was directed to **prioritize AI-in-education research** and expand teacher training in AI tools[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=Sec,all%20educators%2C%20so%20they%20can)[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=and%20other%20relevant%20courses,H%20and%20the%20Cooperative%20Extension). These moves signal strong federal support for integrating AI innovations in K–12 teaching and learning.

Federal funding programs have also targeted AI in education. In late 2023, the Department of Education awarded $277 million in innovation grants (Education Innovation and Research program) focusing on academic recovery and transformative strategies – explicitly citing the **“rapid ascendance of artificial intelligence”** as a driver for new interventions[edweek.org](https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/heres-how-the-feds-are-spending-277m-for-academic-recovery/2023/12#:~:text=Amid%20a%20youth%20mental%20health,Education%20Department%20news%20release%20said)[edweek.org](https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/heres-how-the-feds-are-spending-277m-for-academic-recovery/2023/12#:~:text=rapid%20ascendance%20of%20artificial%20intelligence%2C,Education%20Department%20news%20release%20said). Meanwhile, the National Science Foundation has established multi-institution **AI research centers** relevant to K–12. For example, the NSF *AI Institute for Student-AI Teaming* (launched 2020) unites universities, school districts, and industry partners to develop AI that can facilitate collaborative learning and support teachers[cra.org](https://cra.org/crn/2020/09/nsf-advances-artificial-intelligence-research-with-new-nationwide-institutes/#:~:text=NSF%20Advances%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Research,both%20students%20and%20teachers). In December 2023, NSF also announced the *EducateAI initiative* to boost AI education nationwide, including grants for AI curriculum innovation in high schools and professional development for teachers in under-resourced areas[nsf.gov](https://www.nsf.gov/news/nsf-launches-educateai-initiative#:~:text=The%20U,in%20formal%20training%20in%20AI)[nsf.gov](https://www.nsf.gov/news/nsf-launches-educateai-initiative#:~:text=To%20ensure%20that%20educators%20are,serving%20institutions%20and%20emerging%20research). This focus on AI literacy complements the use of AI as a learning tool.

**State Policies and Pilots:** State governments have been increasingly proactive. As of March 2025, **28 U.S. states have published or adopted K–12 AI education guidance**[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=As%20of%20March%202025%2C%2028,12), signaling broad recognition of AI’s importance. Many states initially issued high-level guidelines (e.g. ethical use policies or AI curriculum standards) and are now moving toward concrete classroom integration and pilots[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=As%20of%20March%202025%2C%2028,12)[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=specific%20instructional%20and%20support,and%20support%20services%20so%20far). For example, **Connecticut** launched a pilot in spring 2025 across seven districts to give grades 7–12 students hands-on experience with state-approved AI tools, alongside teacher training in AI integration[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=At%20least%20five%20states%20have,develop%20and%20implement%20the%20program)[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=spring%202025%2C%20Connecticut%20launched%20an,develop%20and%20implement%20the%20program). This program was mandated by state legislation (Public Act 24-151) and is aimed at *“responsible use”* of AI in the classroom. **Indiana** ran an *AI-Powered Platform Pilot Grant* in the 2023–24 school year, investing $2 million of federal relief funds to provide an AI tutoring platform and training for one year[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=Similarly%2C%20during%20the%202023,schools%20have%20chosen%20to%20continue)[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=launched%20the%20AI,the%20state%E2%80%99s%20Digital%20Learning%20Grant). The goal was high-dosage tutoring to boost student learning and reduce teacher workload. **53% of participating teachers reported a positive experience** with the AI tool, and even after the grant ended, some schools chose to continue via other state ed-tech funding streams[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=subscription%20fees%20and%20professional%20development,the%20state%E2%80%99s%20Digital%20Learning%20Grant)[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=the%20teachers%20who%20participated%2C%2053,schools%20have%20chosen%20to%20continue). Likewise, **Iowa**’s state education department is rolling out an AI **reading tutor platform to all public and private elementary schools** (starting summer 2025) backed by a $3 million investment[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=their%20programs%20via%20the%20state%E2%80%99s,Digital%20Learning%20Grant)[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=The%20Iowa%20Department%20of%20Education,begin%20in%20the%20summer%202025). This intelligent tutor listens to children read aloud (using voice recognition) and provides immediate corrective feedback in phonics, decoding, and comprehension – an approach Iowa sees as a scalable way to strengthen early literacy[educate.iowa.gov](https://educate.iowa.gov/press-release/2024-08-27/iowa-department-education-launches-new-personalized-reading-tutor-iowa-schools-builds-upon-prior#:~:text=To%20further%20support%20summer%20and,through%20the%20summer%20of%202025)[educate.iowa.gov](https://educate.iowa.gov/press-release/2024-08-27/iowa-department-education-launches-new-personalized-reading-tutor-iowa-schools-builds-upon-prior#:~:text=reading%20tutor%20as%20part%20of,based%20programming). These state pilots illustrate targeted uses of AI: Connecticut focusing on student-facing AI apps, Indiana on AI tutoring for learning recovery, and Iowa on AI for foundational reading practice.

Some states have also adopted AI for **education management and student support**. For instance, **Kentucky** offers all districts an AI-driven *Early Warning Tool* that mines student data (attendance, grades, etc.) to identify those at risk of dropping out[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=Some%20states%20have%20implemented%20AI,generative%20AI%20platforms%20like%20ChatGPT). Each student receives a predictive “graduation risk” score accessible to teachers on a dashboard. (Notably, such predictive systems predate the latest AI wave and raise concerns about accuracy and bias, discussed later.) In another novel use, four districts in **New Mexico** are piloting *Edia*, an AI platform to automate attendance tracking and parent outreach[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=Four%20school%20districts%20in%20New,high%20rates%20of%20chronic%20absenteeism). When a student is marked absent, a chatbot auto-messages the parent to collect absence reasons, handling a task typically done by school staff[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=Four%20school%20districts%20in%20New,high%20rates%20of%20chronic%20absenteeism). This illustrates AI streamlining an administrative process (addressing the surge in chronic absenteeism) so that humans can focus on more complex family interventions. Overall, **federal relief funds (e.g. ESSER) and state budgets have been tapped to fund these AI initiatives**, underscoring that post-pandemic recovery efforts are intertwined with adopting new AI tools.

**Legislative and Regulatory Developments:** Policymakers are grappling with how to regulate AI in education. In mid-2024, a bipartisan bill (the *NSF AI Education Act of 2024*) was introduced in the U.S. Senate to significantly boost AI education and guidance nationwide[commerce.senate.gov](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/2024/5/cantwell-moran-introduce-bill-to-boost-ai-education#:~:text=Bill%20would%20create%20student%20scholarships%2C,education%20hubs%20at%20community%20colleges)[commerce.senate.gov](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/2024/5/cantwell-moran-introduce-bill-to-boost-ai-education#:~:text=The%20NSF%20AI%20Education%20Act,and%20the%20Cooperative%20Extension%20Service). This proposed law would authorize NSF to fund scholarships and fellowships to grow an AI-skilled workforce (including training K–12 educators in AI), create **“AI education hubs”** at community colleges, and crucially require NSF to develop **guidance for K–12 teachers on using AI tools in classrooms**[commerce.senate.gov](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/2024/5/cantwell-moran-introduce-bill-to-boost-ai-education#:~:text=The%20NSF%20AI%20Education%20Act,and%20the%20Cooperative%20Extension%20Service)[commerce.senate.gov](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/2024/5/cantwell-moran-introduce-bill-to-boost-ai-education#:~:text=and%20training.%20~~~~%20,income%2C%20rural%20and%20tribal%20students). It also calls for research into classroom AI applications with a focus on tools for **low-income, rural, and underserved students**[commerce.senate.gov](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/2024/5/cantwell-moran-introduce-bill-to-boost-ai-education#:~:text=and%20training.%20~~~~%20,income%2C%20rural%20and%20tribal%20students). This indicates Congress’s recognition of both the opportunities and equity challenges of AI in K–12.

At the state level, some are formalizing local AI policies. **Tennessee** passed a law in 2024 requiring every school district to **draft and submit an AI policy** by the 2024–25 school year, detailing how AI will be used and governed in instruction[tnfirefly.com](https://www.tnfirefly.com/news/20240618/ai-policies-are-still-a-work-in-progress-for-several-tennessee-school-districts-ahead-of-2024-25-school-year#:~:text=Legislation%20passed%20in%20February%20requires,ahead%20of%20next%20month%27s%20deadline). By July 2024, public districts and charters must report their plans to the state DOE[tnfirefly.com](https://www.tnfirefly.com/news/20240618/ai-policies-are-still-a-work-in-progress-for-several-tennessee-school-districts-ahead-of-2024-25-school-year#:~:text=Legislation%20passed%20in%20February%20requires,ahead%20of%20next%20month%27s%20deadline). This came as districts nationwide began confronting issues of AI-assisted student work (“AI plagiarism”) and the need for teacher guidance. Tennessee’s approach pushes schools from ad-hoc responses toward a *“proactive, balanced approach”* in the words of one district leader[tnfirefly.com](https://www.tnfirefly.com/news/20240618/ai-policies-are-still-a-work-in-progress-for-several-tennessee-school-districts-ahead-of-2024-25-school-year#:~:text=While%20the%20district%E2%80%99s%20AI%20guidelines,more%20experience%20with%20the%20technology). In these local policies, educators are considering guidelines to prevent misuse (cheating), ensure **equitable access to AI tools**, address AI biases/hallucinations, and define acceptable use for students[tnfirefly.com](https://www.tnfirefly.com/news/20240618/ai-policies-are-still-a-work-in-progress-for-several-tennessee-school-districts-ahead-of-2024-25-school-year#:~:text=According%20to%20a%20report%20by,to%20close%20the%20digital%20divide)[tnfirefly.com](https://www.tnfirefly.com/news/20240618/ai-policies-are-still-a-work-in-progress-for-several-tennessee-school-districts-ahead-of-2024-25-school-year#:~:text=%E2%80%9CIn%20July%2C%20our%20policy%20committee,%E2%80%9D). We see a shift from initial bans on AI toward constructive engagement: by mid-2024, many districts that once blocked student use of tools like ChatGPT are instead developing frameworks to *teach* responsible use while providing teacher training[edweek.org](https://www.edweek.org/technology/schools-are-taking-too-long-to-craft-ai-policy-why-thats-a-problem/2024/02#:~:text=More%20than%20three,conducted%20in%20November%20and%20December)[crpe.org](https://crpe.org/ai-is-coming-to-u-s-classrooms-but-who-will-benefit/#:~:text=,policy%2C%20but%20existential%20concerns%20loom).

On the **funding** front, public-private partnerships are being encouraged at the highest levels. In 2025, the White House secured a *“Pledge to America’s Youth”* from **67 companies and organizations** to invest in AI education for K–12[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=,year%20moratorium%20on%20states)[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=The%20%E2%80%9CPledge%20to%20America%E2%80%99s%20Youth%3A,Software%20%26%20Information%20Industry%20Association). Tech giants (Google, IBM, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA, etc.) and ed-tech firms (e.g. MagicSchool, Varsity Tutors) committed to *“provide resources that foster early interest in AI, promote AI literacy, and enable AI training for educators.”*[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=,year%20moratorium%20on%20states). This pledge accompanies the executive order and is aimed at mobilizing industry support (cloud services, content, tools) to **democratize AI access for all students**[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=The%20%E2%80%9CPledge%20to%20America%E2%80%99s%20Youth%3A,Software%20%26%20Information%20Industry%20Association). At the same time, policymakers are debating regulatory guardrails: a controversial proposal in Congress to impose a **10-year moratorium on state AI regulations** (to preempt a patchwork of laws) was met with strong opposition from education groups, who argued it would *“wipe out virtually all existing and future state AI laws”* and leave students vulnerable[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=,would%20threaten%20children%E2%80%99s%20safety%20online)[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=In%20a%20Monday%20statement%2C%20AASA,%E2%80%9D). By mid-2025 the Senate removed this moratorium provision[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20senators%20voted%20overwhelmingly%20%E2%80%94,breaking%20vote), affirming that states can continue to enact AI protections (such as student data privacy enhancements or algorithm transparency requirements). The regulatory landscape is thus evolving, with a balancing act between innovation and protection.

## AI-Powered EdTech Products and Companies in K–12

In recent years, a wave of **AI-driven educational products** has entered U.S. classrooms, offered by both established companies and new startups. These tools leverage techniques from machine learning and natural language processing to personalize learning, tutor students, assist teachers, and automate routine tasks. Below is a summary of notable AI EdTech products (commercial and nonprofit) making an impact in K–12:

| **AI Tool/Initiative** | **Description & Use Case** | **Organization/Sector** | **Launch/Pilot** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Khanmigo (Khan Academy)** | GPT-4-powered *AI tutor and teaching assistant*. Provides students with personalized tutoring in various subjects and supports teachers with lesson planning and grading feedback. Piloted in >50 districts in 2023, it expanded to **266 school districts by late 2024**[cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/video/khanmigo-ai-tutor-60-minutes-video-2024-12-08/#:~:text=Meet%20Khanmigo%3A%20the%20student%20tutor,60%20Minutes). In 2024, Microsoft partnered with Khan Academy to donate Azure cloud access, enabling Khanmigo to be offered **free to all K–12 teachers in the U.S.**[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/khan-academy-and-microsoft-partner-to-expand-access-to-ai-tools/#:~:text=Today%20at%20Microsoft%20Build%2C%20Microsoft,powered%20by%20Azure%20OpenAI%20Service)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/khan-academy-and-microsoft-partner-to-expand-access-to-ai-tools/#:~:text=partnership%20aka,powered%20by%20Azure%20OpenAI%20Service). Teachers use Khanmigo via a dashboard to generate lesson ideas, adapt texts to different reading levels, and even group students, reportedly saving *~5 hours per week* of planning time[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/khan-academy-and-microsoft-partner-to-expand-access-to-ai-tools/#:~:text=Besides%20offering%20creative%20lesson%20plans%2C,five%20working%20hours%20each%20week). For students, Khanmigo can simulate a Socratic tutor or debate partner, making learning interactive. | *Nonprofit* – Khan Academy (with Microsoft as cloud partner) | Piloted 2023; expanded 2024 |
| **Quizlet “Q-Chat”** | An AI-powered tutor chatbot built on OpenAI’s language model, launched by Quizlet in March 2023. **Q-Chat** draws on Quizlet’s vast flashcard/Q&A database and ChatGPT to quiz students in a conversational format[prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlet-launches-q-chat-ai-tutor-built-with-openai-api-301759014.html#:~:text=Quizlet%20first%20in%20education%20space,with%20access%20to%20ChatGPT%27s%20API). It adapts to the user’s level, asking questions, providing hints, and adjusting difficulty – essentially a *fully adaptive study coach*. Quizlet had been using AI for years (its *Learn Mode* and grading features), but Q-Chat was the first to use generative AI for open-ended tutoring. (Initially it was offered to users 18+ in beta for safety[prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlet-launches-q-chat-ai-tutor-built-with-openai-api-301759014.html#:~:text=they%27re%20learning.), but it signaled a trend of mainstream study platforms embedding AI.) | *For-profit* – Quizlet, Inc. (in collaboration with OpenAI) | Launched 2023 (beta) |

Duolingo Max offers two major AI features: *Roleplay*, where learners have interactive conversations with AI characters to practice real-life dialogue (like ordering coffee in French)[techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/03/14/duolingo-launches-new-subscription-tier-with-access-to-ai-tutor-powered-by-gpt-4/#:~:text=The%20Roleplay%20feature%20unlocks%20an,of%20their%20responses%2C%20as%20well); and *Explain My Answer*, an AI tutor that gives instant detailed explanations of why a user’s answer was right or wrong and clarifies language concepts[techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/03/14/duolingo-launches-new-subscription-tier-with-access-to-ai-tutor-powered-by-gpt-4/#:~:text=Duolingo%20says%20human%20experts%20write,where%20to%20take%20the%20conversation). These features bring human tutor-like feedback into the app. While Duolingo is used by a broad age range, many K–12 students use it for supplemental language practice; Duolingo’s CEO has described the company’s vision of an **“AI tutor for every student”** to replicate 1:1 tutoring at scale. | *For-profit* – Duolingo (EdTech company) | Launched 2023 |

Funded by federal COVID relief (ARP ESSER) money, Iowa’s rollout of Amira aims to help educators address reading gaps and personalize practice for struggling readers[educate.iowa.gov](https://educate.iowa.gov/press-release/2024-08-27/iowa-department-education-launches-new-personalized-reading-tutor-iowa-schools-builds-upon-prior#:~:text=Funds%20for%20the%20Summer%20Reading,level%20educational%20efforts). By streamlining the attendance communication loop, the districts hope to free up staff time and identify attendance issues faster. This reflects a broader trend of AI chatbots being used in districts for parent communication and front-office queries (e.g. answering common questions on school websites), extending AI’s reach to *school operations*. | *For-profit* – Edia (startup) in partnership with *New Mexico public school districts* | Pilot launched 2025 |

This tool uses a generative AI model during tutoring sessions to suggest next steps or probing questions when a student is stuck. This human+AI model (AI as a tutor’s aide rather than a standalone tutor) is an emerging product category. It also includes communication aids like a parent email writer, a student feedback generator, and even lighthearted tools (a “teacher joke generator” for morale)[avidopenaccess.org](https://avidopenaccess.org/resource/227-magicschool-an-ai-tool-for-educators/#:~:text=This%20section%20includes%20tools%20to,and%20refine%20the%20communication%20process)[avidopenaccess.org](https://avidopenaccess.org/resource/227-magicschool-an-ai-tool-for-educators/#:~:text=This%20section%20includes%20tools%20to,both%20teacher%20and%20student%20communities). The aim is to save teachers precious time on planning and paperwork by automating tedious writing tasks – an AI “copilot” for the classroom. Its popularity signals that **AI is not just for students, but also a game-changer for teacher workflow**, helping address burnout by reclaiming hours each week. | *For-profit* – MagicSchool (startup, SIIA member) | Launched 2023 |
| **Early Warning & Analytics Systems** | A category of AI use in K–12 involves **learning analytics** and predictive modeling to identify student needs. For example, Kentucky’s statewide Early Warning System uses AI/ML to analyze data and flag at-risk students (attendance issues, failing grades, etc.), giving each a “Graduation Likelihood” score for educators to monitor[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=Some%20states%20have%20implemented%20AI,generative%20AI%20platforms%20like%20ChatGPT). Many districts also use AI-based analytics within platforms like Illuminate, PowerSchool, or Canvas to spot patterns (e.g. disengagement, content mastery gaps) and personalize interventions. While these tools can help allocate support resources, they carry risks of *algorithmic bias* and false positives. A revealing analysis of one such system in Wisconsin found it was **wrong nearly 75% of the time in identifying potential dropouts**, and it disproportionately misidentified Black and Hispanic students[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=analysis%20of%20data%20from%20the,by%20AI%2C%20it%20is%20important)[ecs.org](https://www.ecs.org/ai-artificial-intelligence-pilots-k12-schools/#:~:text=barriers%20to%20access,and%20opportunity%20for%20all%20students). *Table: Notable AI-driven tools and initiatives in U.S. K–12 education (2022–2025).*

As seen above, AI is being applied across a spectrum of educational needs: **personalized learning** (adaptive practice, chatbots like Khanmigo and Q-Chat), **intelligent tutoring** (one-on-one in subjects like math or language, via Khanmigo, Duolingo, FEV Tutor, etc.), **assessment and feedback** (AI graders, Duolingo’s explanation bot, MagicSchool’s quiz generators), **specialized skills tutoring** (reading fluency with Amira, conversational skills with role-play bots), and **teacher/admin support** (planning, communication, analytics). Established education companies (e.g. Pearson, McGraw Hill) are also embedding AI quietly – for instance, adaptive learning systems like *McGraw Hill ALEKS* or *Curriculum Associates i-Ready* use AI algorithms to adjust to student performance. Likewise, learning management systems and classroom apps are adding AI features: by 2023, **50% of teachers using AI reported employing generative AI chatbots like ChatGPT** in some capacity[crpe.org](https://crpe.org/ai-is-coming-to-u-s-classrooms-but-who-will-benefit/#:~:text=Teachers%20report%20using%20AI%20primarily,coaching%20and%20feedback%20to%20teachers)[crpe.org](https://crpe.org/ai-is-coming-to-u-s-classrooms-but-who-will-benefit/#:~:text=IXL.%20However%2C%2050,coaching%20and%20feedback%20to%20teachers) (often to generate materials), and major platforms like Google Classroom and Microsoft Teams began integrating AI to help create practice questions or reading passages. This proliferation of AI products has created a dynamic ed-tech market, with **reputable ed-tech media (EdSurge, EdWeek)** regularly profiling new AI tools and their classroom impact.

It’s worth noting that nonprofits and academia also play a role: beyond Khan Academy, organizations like **Carnegie Learning** (with roots in Carnegie Mellon University’s AI research) offer AI-based math curricula, and projects like **ASSISTments** (WPI/NSF-backed) provide AI-supported homework feedback for free. In sum, the K–12 AI ed-tech ecosystem from 2022–2025 is vibrant and growing, characterized by a mix of **commercial innovation and mission-driven efforts** to leverage AI for better learning outcomes.

## Collaborations Between Government, Industry, and Academia

AI in education is a multidisciplinary frontier, and the period 2022–2025 saw many **collaborative efforts** bringing together public agencies, private tech firms, and research institutions:

**Public-Private Partnerships:** The federal government explicitly prioritized partnerships. The White House Task Force on AI Education (2025) was charged with forming public-private partnerships with *“leading AI industry organizations, academic institutions, [and] nonprofit entities”* to develop K–12 AI resources[whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/#:~:text=Sec,basis%20as%20they%20are%20formed). The *Pledge to America’s Youth* (2025) that 60+ companies signed (Google, Microsoft, IBM, Meta, NVIDIA, educational startups, etc.) is a direct outcome – each company is contributing in its domain, for example: Google expanding free AI curriculum content, Microsoft providing cloud credits and AI training (as it did with Khan Academy’s Khanmigo)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/khan-academy-and-microsoft-partner-to-expand-access-to-ai-tools/#:~:text=Today%20at%20Microsoft%20Build%2C%20Microsoft,powered%20by%20Azure%20OpenAI%20Service)[k12dive.com](https://www.k12dive.com/news/over-60-organizations-sign-white-house-pledge-to-invest-in-ai-education/752139/#:~:text=Companies%20that%20signed%20the%20pledge%2C,throughout%20this%20week%2C%20Kloek%20said), NVIDIA possibly donating AI hardware or expertise to schools, and nonprofits like Code.org working on AI-literacy lessons. These collaborations are meant to **accelerate AI adoption in an equitable way** by pooling resources and expertise from all sectors.

**Tech Industry and Schools:** Aside from broad pledges, individual partnerships bloomed. We saw **Microsoft partner with Khan Academy** to scale Khanmigo nationwide (contributing Azure computing to reduce costs)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/khan-academy-and-microsoft-partner-to-expand-access-to-ai-tools/#:~:text=partnership%20aka,powered%20by%20Azure%20OpenAI%20Service)[news.microsoft.com](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/khan-academy-and-microsoft-partner-to-expand-access-to-ai-tools/#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20new,at%20no%20cost). **Meta (Facebook)** in 2023 open-sourced large language models (like Llama 2) which some districts and researchers have experimented with as a basis for custom tutor chatbots, potentially reducing reliance on closed systems. The **NSF AI Institutes** are prime examples – the *AI Institute for Student-AI Teaming* (led by University of Colorado Boulder) includes not only university researchers in AI and education, but also a network of K–12 school districts and science museums[par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10499524-from-learning-optimization-learner-flourishing-reimagining-ai-education-institute-studentai-teaming-isat#:~:text=,science%20museums%2C%20and%20nonprofit%20partners). They collaborate to design AI that can operate in classrooms to facilitate group work and dialogue, effectively **treating AI as a new member of the class** (one tagline is developing AI partners that help students learn collaboratively). Such institutes produce prototypes (like the Stanford TutorCoPilot) and test them in schools, often via controlled studies. The *Learning Engineering* community also sponsored trials – e.g. the *EF+Math program* and others funded by NSF or philanthropy have tested AI-guided math tutoring in public schools.

In 2022 the DOE’s *Office of EdTech* held listening sessions with ed-tech developers, educators, and privacy experts to develop its 2023 AI report. In summary, **multi-sector collaboration is recognized as essential** to bring AI safely and effectively into K–12. Research on Khan Academy makes it extremely clear that AI tutors will not transform education. The study noted that without teacher or parental encouragement, usage dropped sharply, suggesting intrinsic motivation is low for many. Khan Academy's 2024 efficacy report (350,000 students) found that only ~9% of students met the recommended dosage of 18+ hours/year (~30 minutes/week). While those who did saw ~20% greater-than-expected MAP Growth gains (0.36 SD), the vast majority didn’t engage enough to benefit, pointing to a scalability issue in unsupervised settings. A 2016 UC Berkeley RCT (103 middle schoolers) explicitly tested parental encouragement and found that without it, students’ usage plummeted, and short-term score gains (10-16%) vanished within a week. This underscores that engagement often depends on external nudging, not the platform itself

This is an important insight, Jamie. Too often the conversation assumes AI tutors, or any edtech, will work the same way everywhere. But motivation and engagement aren’t just individual traits, they’re deeply shaped by community context. Affluent schools often have kids who can lean into asynchronous and self-guided models because they’ve been primed to trust school as a system that works for them. In working class and urban communities, where school has often been a site of frustration or exclusion, students need a bridge to engagement before the tool even matters. Same with parents, if their own experiences with school were negative, they’re less likely to encourage their child’s use of something that feels like “more school.” Which makes me wonder: instead of chasing “universal” solutions, shouldn’t AI implementation strategies be designed explicitly for community context, with different pathways for different student realities?

  AI Literacy ≠ How to Type a Prompt According to College Board’s latest research brief, more students and educators are using GenAI for schoolwork. But, just because “everyone’s using it” doesn’t mean it is best practice. Their presented findings show that students are still using GenAI largely for obtaining information, do "research", and find sources. In other words, they are still using it superficially like a search engine. GenAI/LLMs are predictive machines trained to output plausible sounding content, not verified information. They sound fluent, they sound smart, but they do not understand the truth. And students recognize this with the College Board reporting that 60% of students are worried about GenAI spreading wrong information. An ethical issue for students? Or are students worried that they will submit an assignment with more errors? Meanwhile, the College Board shows that the majority of school networks aren’t blocking GenAI tools. Let’s be real... if these are Google schools, Gemini is baked into Docs and Slides, and the "decision" to allow GenAI wasn't really a decision at all. Nowhere in the brief do we get a working definition of AI literacy. Is AI literacy just teaching kids to write prompts like “Act as an expert historian”? Or is it understanding what these models are and how they produce outputs? If we’re serious about closing the “AI literacy gap,” let’s teach students: -What predictive language models are… -Why GenAI can’t cite sources reliably… -How algorithmic bias enters LLMs… -What fabrications (hallucinations) are... -Why good sounding outputs ≠ as factual accuracy. As a Social Studies educator, I can’t help but ask: if students are using GenAI for writing, research, and analysis do they know how that output is generated? Do they know what might be missing? For those pushing GenAI for efficiencies’ sake, do you care?   This school just “replaced” teachers with AI. In Austin, an entire school now runs on artificial intelligence. Kids spend their mornings learning math, science, and reading through AI-driven platforms. The adults in the classroom aren’t called teachers anymore... they’re “guides.” Their role isn’t to stand at the board and lecture, but to motivate, connect, correct, and guide students on how to actually use AI in their learning. Each child gets focused one-on-one time, then afternoons shift to projects: financial literacy, public speaking, team challenges, real-world skills that matter as work changes. From my perspective I don’t believe AI will replace teaching. But I do see the problem: our current curriculum, across the world, struggles to keep up with how fast technology is moving. Regulations, systems, approvals - they move slowly. And while that’s necessary to keep education safe and responsible, it also leaves little room for flexibility. What excites me is how AI can make learning more personalized and tailored to each student. Not one program for every single child, but an adaptive system that adjusts to the individual. That’s where I think AI in education has the most potential - not replacing teachers, but transforming how they teach and how students learn. Would you trust AI to guide your child’s education? args.summary:
This LinkedIn post by Jamie Martin argues that AI tutors will not transform education, citing research on Khan Academy. Key findings from multiple studies:

1. **2024 University of Toronto RCT (10,979 students)**: Only grades 3-6 students who used Khan Academy ~35 min/week saw math gains (0.12-0.17 SD). Grades 7-8 averaged ~10 min/week with no significant improvement. Usage dropped sharply without teacher/parental encouragement.

2. **Khan Academy 2024 efficacy report (350,000 students)**: Only ~9% met the recommended dosage of 18+ hours/year (~30 min/week). Those who did saw ~20% greater-than-expected MAP Growth gains (0.36 SD), but the vast majority didn't engage enough.

3. **2016 UC Berkeley RCT (103 middle schoolers)**: Without parental encouragement, usage plummeted, and short-term score gains (10-16%) vanished within a week.

The post concludes that engagement depends on external nudging, not the platform itself. Commenters largely agree, noting that intrinsic motivation, human connection, community context, and supportive environments are critical for effective learning. Additional related posts in the feed discuss AI literacy, China mandating AI education in schools, and examples of AI-powered schools (like Alpha School in Austin) where teachers become "guides."

**Other notable posts in the feed:**
- A post about AI literacy arguing students use GenAI superficially like a search engine, with 60% worried about misinformation.
- China mandating AI education in all primary/secondary schools starting September 2025.
- An Oxford University Press survey of 2,000 students (13-18) finding 8 in 10 use AI for schoolwork, but 6 in 10 say it negatively affected learning.
- Coverage of Alpha School in San Francisco/Austin where AI guides learning and teachers act as "guides."

Education, like many fields, is not immune to fads. Methods and policies wax and wane in popularity, often promising revolutionary change yet delivering mixed results. Amid this ebb and flow of trends, however, the primary goal of educators remains constant: to engage students in meaningful learning experiences. The rapid growth of AI tools in education presents both opportunities and challenges to achieve this goal.

It’s tempting to be taken with promises of AI-powered planning sessions, personalized feedback, and intelligent tutors. Yet to reject the technology outright may be easier still. Instead, let's consider how Generative AI may support principles of good teaching. Our tools may amplify our capabilities, but principles guide our actions. When considering AI tools, teachers should focus on how these technologies can support specific instructional goals rather than adopting them for their novelty or for vague promises of "improving learning" or "saving time."

### Foundations

Before diving into specific AI platforms, let's review some of those principles of good teaching:

**Prior knowledge mediates all learning.** In other words, we learn in relation to what we already know.

**Learning requires active engagement**. Or, actively processing information leads to deeper understanding and retention.

**Learning is more effective when directed toward clear, meaningful goals**. That is to say, students learn best when they understand the purpose and relevance of what they’re learning.

**Effective learning involves practices like spacing out study sessions and asking why questions**. To put it more formally, techniques like distributed practice and elaborative interrogation can assist in reinforcing and deepening understanding.

**Timely and constructive feedback is crucial for learning**. In other words, students need specific, actionable feedback to understand their progress and how to improve.

These principles assume a certain level of skill with classroom management and relationship-building, as learning takes place within a community context. Moreover, this is not an exhaustive list but rather a sampling of things to keep in mind and items to look for in AI responses.

I've compiled a list of five AI tools that seem promising. These are not miracles, mind you, but rather potential aids in our noble profession. I offer them not as endorsements but as starting points for your exploration.

So, let us proceed with open minds and steady hands, ready to embrace innovation where it serves us well, but always grounded in the fundamental principles of our craft. For in the end, it is not the tool that makes the teacher, but the teacher who makes the tool worthwhile.

## Eduaide.Ai

**What It Does:** Eduaide.Ai provides teachers with a workspace for lesson planning, resource generation, and instructional design. It offers an array of customizable tools for creating and revising educational materials.

### **Cognitive Science Insight**

One of the fundamental principles of effective teaching is scaffolding—building on students’ prior knowledge and gradually introducing new concepts in reference to that previous knowledge. In other words, the [curriculum should be logically sequenced](https://www.deansforimpact.org/files/assets/thescienceoflearning.pdf) and progressively built based on prior knowledge.

### **Practical Use Case**

Use [Eduaide.Ai](http://Eduaide.Ai) to generate differentiated instructional materials that cater to the diverse needs of your students. Start by identifying gaps in student understanding, and use the tool to create resources that explicitly address these areas, ensuring that new content is both accessible and challenging.

### Considerations

Curipod’s interactive features can be used to foster such engagement by encouraging students to collaborate with peers in controlled environments peppered throughout multimedia-based direct instruction.

### **Practical Use Case**

Incorporate Curipod into lessons where students can interact with the content in real-time, such as during a Socratic seminar or group discussion. This tool can help structure these interactions, prompting students to engage with the material and with each other in a way that deepens their understanding.

## Flint

**What It Does:** Flint is an AI-powered tutoring platform that personalizes learning experiences based on individual student needs.

### **Cognitive Science Insight**

Personalized learning, when properly understood and done correctly, aligns instruction to the learner’s current level of understanding. This means a meaningful interplay of the process, path, and product of learning beyond a mere passing mention of student’s interest in their math problem set. Flint’s AI capabilities can help provide this personalized approach, ensuring that students receive the right level of challenge and support.

### **Practical Use Case**

Integrate Flint into your classroom for students who need additional support in specific areas. For example, if a student struggles with a particular math concept, use Flint to provide targeted practice and actionable feedback to assist the student on the path to mastery before moving on.

**What It Does:** Quizizz is an interactive quiz platform that gamifies learning, making it fun and engaging for students.

### **Cognitive Science Insight**

Spaced retrieval practice—recalling information from memory—is a well-established method for reinforcing learning. Quizizz can be used to implement this practice in a way that is both effective and enjoyable for students. Moreover, you can use Quizizz to create regular practice sessions by interleaving in new concepts with persistent reviews of prior knowledge.

### **Practical Use Case**

Use Quizizz to create formative assessments that help students consolidate their learning. Regular low-stakes quizzing can help reinforce content, identify areas where students are struggling, and provide immediate feedback, all of which are key to long-term retention.

Lesson Planning Revolution: "The teachers are innovating," according to [Andrea Malek Ash](https://www.gallup.com/analytics/659819/k-12-teacher-research.aspx), lead author of the Walton Family Foundation report and senior research consultant at Gallup. Administrative Task Automation: A 2024 Salesforce education industry report found that 23% of tertiary education institutions have integrated AI chatbots for student services. Beyond chatbots, teachers are using AI to automate attendance notes, parent update emails, and curriculum documentation.

The real impact: teachers consistently report three benefits, getting their evenings back, providing better feedback to students, and having more energy for actual teaching. The key isn't replacing teacher expertise; it's eliminating the time-consuming busywork.

The biggest mistake teachers make is trying to use every AI tool at once. Instead, start with your biggest pain point and find one tool that solves it well.

* ChatGPT: Handles most basic teaching tasks and has the largest community of educators sharing prompts. The free version works fine for lesson planning, discussion questions, and email templates. ChatGPT Plus ($20/month) adds faster responses and file upload support.
* Claude AI: Excels at longer, more detailed tasks like unit planning and curriculum development. Maintains context better across lengthy conversations, making it ideal for complex educational projects.
* Google Gemini: Free with any Google account and integrates seamlessly with Google Workspace. If your district runs Google Classroom, Docs, and Sheets, Gemini is the most natural fit for daily workflow.

### Why GCC Schools Need Different Tools

* Multi-language support (English/Arabic).
* British curriculum alignment (EYFS, Key Stages, GCSE, A-Levels).

2. Diffit, Excellent for EAL (English as an Additional Language) students.

### What Dubai and Riyadh Teachers Report

Teachers at British schools in Dubai and Saudi Arabia report saving several hours a week using AI tools (based on TRT client observations), with the biggest gains in:

* Creating differentiated materials for diverse classrooms.
* Generating parent communications in multiple languages.
* Building curriculum-aligned assessments for British qualification frameworks.

When not to use AI, and the risks to watch

* Student data: never paste pupil names or personal details into general tools like ChatGPT. Use education platforms covered by a data agreement with your school.
* Grading judgement: AI is strong on structured, right-or-wrong answers and weaker on nuanced essays. Review every grade before it is final.
* Hallucinated content: AI can invent facts, citations or quiz answers. Check anything that reaches students.
* Over-reliance: AI should remove busywork, not replace your subject expertise or your relationships with pupils.

## Abstract

Students with special needs often require more assistance and attention to meet their educational needs. However, schools frequently grapple with a critical shortage of special education teachers and support staff. This shortage of special education teachers can result in limited resources for general and subject teachers (e.g., math, science), making it challenging to provide individualized support to students with special needs. Specifically, subject teachers may struggle to design effective curricular content modifications and accommodations for such students without the guidance and suggestions of special education teachers. Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies can provide some support for teachers and schools in meeting the needs of students with special needs. Also, AI may help reduce teachers’ workload. In this technology review, we assess the capabilities of Magic School AI (MSAI) in providing accommodations and modifications to assist teachers in streamlining their workload and fostering inclusivity in their classrooms. We examined five functions: text leveler, text scaffolders, assignment scaffolder, exemplar and non-examples, and sentence starters. Additionally, we discuss the limitations of MSAI and conclude by suggesting potential improvements for the system.

## 2. Introduction

Education equity and equality, particularly in the context of special education, remain a critical concern for schools, teachers, and parents. The pursuit of educational equity strives to ensure all students, especially those with Individual Education Plans (IEPs) due to disabilities such as learning disabilities and concentration deficits, receive the necessary resources ([McCabe & Ruppar, 2023](#B25-education-15-00963)). The range of disabilities students may have is extensive. The range of disabilities includes 13 categories: specific learning disability (SLD); other health impairment (OHI); Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); emotional disturbance; speech or language impairment; visual impairment; hearing impairment; deafness; deaf-blindness; orthopedic impairment; intellectual disability; traumatic brain injury; and multiple disabilities. These varied needs necessitate collaboration between special and general education teachers or subject teachers to support the development of tailored learning objectives and approaches for students with IEPs.

A major challenge in achieving this collaboration is the understaffing prevalent in schools, significantly affecting special education ([Jameson & Huefner, 2006](#B16-education-15-00963); [Nichols et al., 2008](#B29-education-15-00963); [The Children’s Guild, 2024](#B34-education-15-00963)). Moreover, 40% of special education teachers leave the field within the first five years, which results in a high turnover rate ([Jameson & Huefner, 2006](#B16-education-15-00963)). In addition, special education teachers, specialists in their field of education, are vital for supporting and co-teaching with colleagues in core subjects like English Literature, Math, and Science ([Vannest & Hagan-Burke, 2010](#B36-education-15-00963)). However, they often find themselves overextended ([Eisenman et al., 2011](#B11-education-15-00963); [Morgan, 2016](#B27-education-15-00963)). This overextension leads to insufficient support for teachers, especially those of non-core subjects (e.g., foreign languages, music, PE, etc.), resulting in increased workload and stress for general and subject teachers and less inclusive classrooms. Teachers without specialized training often fail to provide appropriate accommodations and modifications ([Chu et al., 2020](#B7-education-15-00963); [Cutanda-López & Alfageme-González, 2022](#B10-education-15-00963)), potentially hindering students’ academic engagement and growth ([Gesel et al., 2021](#B12-education-15-00963)). Recognizing these challenges underscores the need for broader teacher training in special education and a more equitable distribution of resources across all subjects ([Ballhysa & Flagler, 2011](#B3-education-15-00963); [Cooc, 2019](#B8-education-15-00963)).

Amid these challenges, emerging technologies offer innovative solutions. [Carr](#B6-education-15-00963) ([2023](#B6-education-15-00963)) indicated that Artificial Intelligence (AI) could support teachers to create inclusive lessons by tailoring the content to address the learning gap. In addition, [Petera](#B32-education-15-00963) ([2023](#B32-education-15-00963)) demonstrates that AI can recognize students’ potential misconceptions and provide teachers with an alternative instructional approach. However, specific applications in the field of special education have not been thoroughly explored.

Magic School AI (MSAI) is a breakthrough AI tool that can be applied to special education. Both general teachers and special education teachers can benefit from using it. It can provide modification and accommodation suggestions for general teachers to promote an inclusive teaching and learning environment. Besides, it can reduce the workload of special education teachers and directors by generating comprehensive reports.

In addition, MSAI is an affordable support tool for subject teachers who do not receive adequate special education resources. The researchers chose MSAI because of its practical value in aiding general education teachers in effectively providing appropriate support for special education students in their students, especially in content areas such as science, social studies, arts, PE, etc., who may lack both previous formal special education training ([Begeske et al., 2023](#B4-education-15-00963)) or ongoing structured teaching support ([Özgüç & Cavkaytar, 2015](#B30-education-15-00963)). As a free and easy-to-operate platform, MSAI requires minimal training for practical usage.

The features of MSAI are intuitively organized within an accessible portal, allowing teachers to quickly locate the correct tools based on their teaching goals and meet diverse student needs through lesson planning, differentiation, and individualized content creation. The evaluation focused on effectively using the app to bridge the gap by developing differentiated teaching materials, adapting accessible class instructions, and brainstorming inclusive teaching strategies.

Therefore, in this technology review, the researchers critically examine how MSAI can aid teachers in providing modifications and accommodations so that students with IEPs can access instructional content and be included in the classroom. The researchers also assess how MSAI can help special education teachers and directors reduce workload. Our assessment focuses on the tool’s effectiveness and practicality, considering broader systemic changes necessary for addressing the overarching challenges in special education.

## 3. Literature Review

The lesson planning process is a critical aspect of educational pedagogy, serving as a detailed guide for educators to outline objectives, activities, and expected outcomes for each lesson ([Hall, 2019](#B14-education-15-00963)). Lesson planning is a key tool in ensuring a well-balanced and time-managed approach to teaching and facilitates the effective use of resources, including technology. Lesson plans also function as a communicative tool, helping teachers address various teaching challenges and assumptions ([Janssen & Lazonder, 2015](#B17-education-15-00963); [Y. Lee & Takahashi, 2011](#B21-education-15-00963)). An essential component of lesson planning is considering the diverse needs of all students, including those with Individual Education Plans (IEPs), and integrating appropriate accommodations and modifications.

[Harrison et al.](#B15-education-15-00963) ([2013](#B15-education-15-00963)) provide a helpful set of definitions for the types of supports that an IEP may include: (1) modifications, which are “practices that alter expectations to compensate for a disability”; (2) accommodations, which are “changes that maintain the expectations for the child, but provide a differential support to help in the meeting of the standards”; and (3) interventions, “changes made through a systematic process to develop or improve knowledge, skills, behaviors, cognitions, or emotions” (p. 556).

Accommodations are supportive measures provided to students, especially those with special needs, to ensure equal access to the curriculum without altering its content or expected outcomes. Examples include extended test times and the use of assistive technology. To aid teachers in conceptualizing suitable accommodations, models such as preexisting lesson plans are recommended ([Martínez & Porter, 2018](#B24-education-15-00963)). On the other hand, modifications refer to changes made to the curriculum or assessment methods to assist students with special needs, potentially altering assignment content, complexity, or expectations. These modifications can assist in ensuring that educational content is accessible and beneficial to all students ([Lim et al., 2018](#B23-education-15-00963)).

Teachers, however, often encounter difficulties in providing these accommodations and modifications for these students due to limited access to instructional materials, resources, and support ([Cuñado & Abocejo, 2019](#B9-education-15-00963)). Art teachers interviewed reported having limited professional development opportunities to collaborate with special education personnel ([Burdick & Causton-Theoharis, 2012](#B5-education-15-00963); [Guay, 2003](#B13-education-15-00963)). Students with special needs constantly meet challenges in reading and writing, which limit their academic development and, therefore, cause lower performance in other subjects. [Villanueva et al.](#B37-education-15-00963)’s ([2012](#B37-education-15-00963)) comprehensive meta-analysis showed that inquiry-based instruction, especially when paired with appropriate scaffolding and support, can significantly enhance science achievement for these students. Yet, a four-month study observing a middle school science and technology class that included students with mild intellectual disabilities also revealed a contradiction between the need for differentiated and adapted instruction and the teacher’s lack of resources to enhance teaching effectiveness ([Özgüç & Cavkaytar, 2015](#B30-education-15-00963)).

In this context, integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education, particularly in providing accommodations and modifications, emerges as a promising solution. AI has the potential to streamline the lesson planning process by leveraging data analysis to offer tailored recommendations for individual student needs ([Paiz et al., 2025](#B31-education-15-00963); [Nguyen et al., 2023](#B28-education-15-00963)). Research showed that preservice teachers who incorporated AI-driven modifications into pre-existing lesson plans produced more effective and inclusive lesson plans while gaining increased confidence in their teaching abilities ([Lim et al., 2018](#B23-education-15-00963); [Kehoe, 2023](#B18-education-15-00963); [Acquah et al., 2024](#B1-education-15-00963)). [Lampou](#B19-education-15-00963) ([2023](#B19-education-15-00963)) and [Mollick and Mollick](#B26-education-15-00963) ([2023](#B26-education-15-00963)) also show that AI infused in lesson planning can make learning more accessible by providing multiple explanations, solving students’ misconceptions, and offering additional scaffolding to students with special needs and language barriers.

AI’s application in accommodations and modifications extends to providing personalized learning experiences and adapting content to individual student needs ([Amzil et al., 2023](#B2-education-15-00963)). It also offers predictive analytics to assist educators in making informed instructional decisions. However, despite these advances, there are still significant research gaps in exploring the full potential of AI in aiding teachers in providing modifications and accommodations.

## 4. Results

### 4.1. Potential Benefits and Implications of Magic School AI

Magic School AI (MSAI) represents a transformative tool for teachers, simplifying the design of lesson plans, rubrics, assignments, assessments, and even editing class-appropriate videos. Its diverse functionalities promise a more inclusive class by providing accommodations and modifications. In this technology review, we focus on the functions of subject teachers to include students with special needs, which is under the student support category. These functions include Exemplar and Non-exemplar, Text Levelers, Assignment Scaffolders, Text Scaffolders, and Sentence Starters to evaluate and understand how MSAI facilitates the creation of inclusive learning and enhances teaching effectiveness. We categorize all the functions through three perspectives: support modification, assignment scaffolder, and workload reduction.

### 4.2. Support Modification

#### Text Levelers

Modification aims to modify the task and make it aligned with students’ levels. Students with ADHD or reading disabilities cannot read for long due to their attention deficit ([Toplak et al., 2003](#B35-education-15-00963)). Most special education students’ reading levels are also behind their counterparts ([Lewandowski et al., 2015](#B22-education-15-00963)). Teachers can use text levelers to adapt the text to their reading levels or grade levels.

In [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_education-15-00963-f001), teachers can upload any documents to the MSAI and choose the appropriate levels they want the text to be. I used a text from the CommonLit Website. This is a 9th-grade level with Lexile: 1140 news.

### 4.3. Support Scaffolding and Access

#### Assignment Scaffolder

Students who have IEPs need scaffolding and support for their assignments. Teachers can use the assignment scaffolder function, which will be broken down into multiple steps and made manageable and understandable for students. This not only reduces teachers’ workload through generating step-by-step scaffolding but also benefits students who need assistance to process the multiple-step task.

[Figure 4](#fig_body_display_education-15-00963-f004) shows the assignment prompt, which is long and contains multiple questions. We chose the 9th grade as the grade level to ask MSAI scaffolding questions for students.

![Education 15 00963 g004](/education/education-15-00963/article_deploy/html/images/education-15-00963-g004-550.jpg)

**Figure 4.**
Assignment Scaffolder Prompt.

[Figure 5](#fig_body_display_education-15-00963-f005) indicates that MSAI breaks down the task into seven steps. Each step starts with clearly telling the audience what to do, with two bullet points. For example, MSAI asked the students to “write down their impression of ‘story-teller’ in each work” in Step 4. This visualization and simplification essentially help special education students to process the information effectively. Afterward, MSAI continued to deepen students’ understanding by prompting them to compare the similarities and differences in how they convey stories.

#### 4.4.2. Text Scaffolder

Most special education students may be behind grade level compared to their counterparts. Text scaffolders modify the complexity and length of the text. This enables students to get access to the content. In addition, this function provides teachers with some level-appropriate questions to check students’ understanding.

Researchers adopted a time machine story ([ReadingVine, 2022](#B33-education-15-00963)) as an example. This text is appropriate for the 7th-grade level and has 451 words. Researchers imputed the grade level, the vocabulary that they wanted to define, and the questions they wanted to ask ([Figure 9](#fig_body_display_education-15-00963-f009)). The maximum vocabulary that can be defined is 7, and the maximum number of literal questions that can be generated is 7. Researchers chose seven vocabulary words to define and three literal questions to ask ([Figure 10](#fig_body_display_education-15-00963-f010)). It can accurately define the Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary words. It also provides three questions for teachers to assess readers’ comprehension.

### 4.5. Supports Access and Comprehension

#### 4.5.1. Exemplar & Non-Exemplar

The exemplar and non-exemplar functions provided by MSAI serve as valuable tools for teachers working with special education students. The exemplar sets clear expectations and serves as a model for special education students to finish their assignments effectively. In addition, all students, regardless of their educational needs, can benefit from the clarity provided by exemplars and non-exemplars as they embark on their assignments.

To illustrate, we chose a Common Core State Standard (CCSS) for 9th grade: ELA.RL.9-10.1: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support explicit analysis of what the text says and inferences drawn from the text. The text the researchers chose was To Kill a Monckingbird ([H. Lee, 2010, p. 119](#B20-education-15-00963)). By specifying the grade level, CCSS standards, length, and prompt (as shown in [Figure 11](#fig_body_display_education-15-00963-f011)), MSAI generated an exemplar and a non-example (as depicted in [Figure 12](#fig_body_display_education-15-00963-f012)). Besides, it also provides explanations for the errors made by non-exemplars.
