# Australian and New Zealand Students Receive Free, Curriculum-Aligned AI Literacy Through Tailored Local Programs

Day of AI Australia and Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand launch to help students understand how AI works and use the technology responsibly.

* [News and Impact](/about-us/news-and-impact)
* News

* [(opens in a new tab/window)](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://dayofai.org/news/australian-and-new-zealand-students-receive-free-curriculum-aligned-ai-literacy-through-tailored-local-programs)
* [(opens in a new tab/window)](https://www.twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://dayofai.org/news/australian-and-new-zealand-students-receive-free-curriculum-aligned-ai-literacy-through-tailored-local-programs&text=Australian and New Zealand Students Receive Free, Curriculum-Aligned AI Literacy Through Tailored Local Programs)
* [(opens in a new tab/window)](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://dayofai.org/news/australian-and-new-zealand-students-receive-free-curriculum-aligned-ai-literacy-through-tailored-local-programs)

   ![Doai aus2 crop](https://deadpan-dragonfly.transforms.svdcdn.com/production/assets/doai-aus2-crop.jpg?w=1200&q=85&auto=format&fit=crop&crop=top&dm=1773093099&s=77da596d1ea138dcfcc546204c4f5ae9)  

Day of AI Australia and Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand today announced the launch of free, country-specific AI literacy programs tailored to local curriculum and classroom contexts. These innovative programs give teachers across both countries access to high-quality resources that help students understand, question, and use artificial intelligence responsibly.

From 9 March on, teachers across Australia and New Zealand will be able to deliver curriculum-aligned, classroom-ready lessons designed to demystify AI through interactive activities, educational games, and guided classroom discussion. Students will explore how AI systems work, where they are used in real life, and the opportunities and limitations of the technology, with a particularly strong focus on ethics, safety, and critical thinking.

The launch comes as AI use among students continues to rise rapidly, while understanding and guidance have not kept pace.

* In Australia, 84% of young people aged 15 to 24 have used generative AI, yet only 27% say they have an “excellent” or “very good” understanding of it (per Year13, 2025).
* 69% of Australian high school students say they want more training on using AI responsibly and effectively (Elevate Education, 2025).
* In New Zealand, the Day of AI pilot found that while 92% of students were already using AI, few understood how it works.
* After the pilot, understanding increased from 20% to 64%.”

## Day of AI Australia: 2026 marks its most comprehensive program yet

For Day of AI Australia, 2026 is its most engaging and comprehensive program yet, building on four years of national delivery. Since launching in 2022, Day of AI Australia has reached more than 340,000 students nationwide, with a strong focus on reaching students in government schools, those in regional areas, First Nations students, and girls. A core part of its impact model is the Classroom Champions program, which places trained STEM ambassadors in classrooms across the country to help deliver the program.

The 2026 Australian program includes:

* New expert-developed educational games, including Inky’s Great Experiment, which explores the ethics of AI, and Pyramid Puzzle, which helps students understand how machines “learn” and “understand.”
* Classroom incursions for government, regional, and lower-ICSEA schools.
* A Student Challenge in which students design AI-powered solutions aligned to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, running across Terms 1-3 and culminating in the Dolphin Tank showcase, where finalists work with expert mentors to refine and present their ideas.
* Expanded teacher professional learning across the year.
* A continued focus on ethics, safety, and real-world application.

![Natasha Banks headshot square](https://deadpan-dragonfly.transforms.svdcdn.com/production/assets/Natasha-Banks_headshot_square.jpg?w=415&h=436&q=85&auto=format&fit=crop&crop=top&dm=1773093453&s=ddf5cf78864504521da1683091775bd2)

“AI is increasingly embedded in everyday life, whether that is in social media, study, or work. Ensuring all young Australians can recognize AI, understand its limitations, and use it responsibly is really important. Equipping all Aussie students with the skills they need to be informed, discerning, and empowered digital citizens is vital in 2026.”

— Natasha Banks, Program Director at Day of AI Australia

## Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand: built for the New Zealand school context

Day of AI New Zealand is the first nationally designed, scalable AI literacy program created specifically for New Zealand’s school context. First piloted with 10 schools in 2025, the program provides curriculum-aligned learning resources for Years 5–10 that will be freely available to all schools across Aotearoa from 2026. Developed in partnership with Day of AI’s United States team, MIT’s RAISE (“Responsible AI for Social Empowerment and Education”) initiative, Day of AI Australia, and in collaboration with the Education Partnership & Innovation Trust (EPIT), Technology Education New Zealand (TENZ), Westlake Girls’ High School, and the New Zealand Council for Educational Research (NZCER), this initiative aims to ensure every learner can develop the knowledge and critical understanding needed to navigate AI responsibly.

Evaluation of the 2025 pilot found strong shifts in both student understanding and teacher confidence. Students moved from viewing AI as a “magic helper” to recognising it as a system that can be questioned, checked, and critically evaluated, while teachers reported greater confidence leading discussions about AI, ethics and responsible use. The program’s culturally grounded approach - incorporating Aotearoa-specific contexts and Māori concepts such as whakapapa, data sovereignty, tikanga, and kaitiakitanga - also supported deeper engagement and ethical understanding. Building on strong pilot results and interest from more than 100 schools ahead of launch, the next phase will scale nationally while expanding resources for classrooms and whānau and strengthening partnerships across education and industry.

![Susana Tomaz headshot square](https://deadpan-dragonfly.transforms.svdcdn.com/production/assets/Susana-Tomaz_headshot_square.jpg?w=415&h=436&q=85&auto=format&fit=crop&crop=top&dm=1773093623&s=f75ecad18fb088635c2c541073a27ae3)

"Young people across Aotearoa New Zealand are already using AI every day, but understanding hasn’t kept pace with access. In the absence of a formal national framework for generative AI in schools, many schools recognize the urgency of AI literacy but lack clear, coherent guidance on how to approach it. Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand is about closing that gap by giving schools free, high-quality, culturally grounded resources that empower teachers to model and build ethical and responsible use of AI, and to develop strong critical thinking habits in students.

— Susana Tomaz, Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand Coordinator

## Ensuring Access…Powered by Best-in-Class Collaborators

Day of AI Australia and Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand prioritize students in low-ICSEA government schools, regional and remote communities, and schools serving higher proportions of First Nations students, helping ensure access to high-quality AI education regardless of postcode.

Day of AI Australia is delivered in partnership with UNSW Sydney. The program is backed by partners including Microsoft, Rokt, Commonwealth Bank, CDC Data Centres, and Officeworks Education, with support from Google.org and philanthropic contributions from TDM Foundation, P & S Bassat Foundation, and Square Peg. The program is also underpinned by ongoing research into student perceptions, confidence, and understanding of AI, ensuring continuous improvement and evidence-informed delivery.

In Aotearoa New Zealand, the initiative is now seeking partners and funding to support the next phase of development. Phase 3 will expand the program from Years 5-10 to Years 11-13 and support the development of additional resources for schools, school leaders, and parents.

Day of AI Australia and Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand have launched free, country-specific AI literacy programs tailored to local curricula. Available from March 9, these programs provide teachers with classroom-ready lessons, interactive activities, games, and guided discussions to help students understand AI, with a strong focus on ethics, safety, and critical thinking.

The launch addresses a growing gap: in Australia, 84% of young people aged 15-24 have used generative AI, but only 27% have a strong understanding of it; 69% of high school students want more training on responsible AI use. In New Zealand, a pilot found 92% of students were already using AI, but understanding rose from 20% to 64% after the program.

Day of AI Australia (reaching 340,000+ students since 2022) will offer its most comprehensive program in 2026, including new educational games (Inky's Great Experiment, Pyramid Puzzle), classroom incursions for disadvantaged schools, a Student Challenge aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals culminating in a "Dolphin Tank" showcase, expanded teacher training, and continued focus on ethics and real-world application. The program is delivered in partnership with UNSW Sydney and backed by Microsoft, Rokt, Commonwealth Bank, and others.

Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand (piloted with 10 schools in 2025) is the first nationally designed AI literacy program for New Zealand's school context, targeting Years 5-10. It incorporates Māori concepts such as whakapapa, data sovereignty, tikanga, and kaitiakitanga. Developed with MIT's RAISE initiative, EPIT, TENZ, and NZCER, the program saw strong pilot results: students moved from viewing AI as a "magic helper" to critically evaluating it, and teachers reported greater confidence. The program is now seeking partners to expand to Years 11-13.

# AI in Education: Guide for Schools in Australia & New Zealand

TABLE OF CONTENTS

[Toggle](#)

## **Introduction**

Across schools and universities, conversations about how to teach, learn, and assess are increasingly shaped by Artificial Intelligence. Instead of being a distant concept, AI is showing up in everyday tasks to help teachers reduce administrative workload, support students with personalized study tools, and prompt governments to rethink policies for the digital era.

In Australia and New Zealand, the adoption of AI in education is moving quickly, guided by new national frameworks and local initiatives that focus on ethics, privacy, and equity. At [**SotaTek ANZ**](https://www.linkedin.com/company/sotatek-anz/), with years of experience implementing EdTech solutions for schools and enterprises, we’ve learned that only a strategic approach can ensure AI in Education delivers long-term impact and measurable results.

## **What is AI in Education?**

Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education refers to technology that helps machines perform tasks traditionally requiring human intelligence, such as learning, adapting, making decisions, and providing feedback. In educational settings, AI is commonly used to personalise student experiences, automate repetitive administrative tasks, and enhance teaching effectiveness through adaptive learning systems.

The integration of AI tools, particularly generative AI, has rapidly expanded, allowing educators to automate content creation, grading, and lesson planning, freeing up valuable time. According to recent studies, approximately 65% of educators now see AI as critical for improving student outcomes, and educators could potentially save up to 13 hours per week through AI-assisted automation of routine tasks.

![Impacts of AI in Education](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%201608%201052%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Statistics to demonstrate the usage and impacts of AI in Education

In Australia and New Zealand, the adoption of AI in education is particularly driven by a need to maintain robust privacy standards and educational equity. Organisations and governments have issued specific guidelines, such as Australia’s Generative AI in Schools Framework and New Zealand’s guidelines for using AI within the NCEA framework, reinforcing the importance of a structured, ethical approach to implementing these powerful technologies.

Read more: [Top AI trends in Australia 2025](https://sotatek.com.au/blogs/ai-trends-in-australia-2025/)

## **Benefits of AI in Education**

### **Personalised and Adaptive Learning**

AI can tailor lessons to each student’s level and pace. Intelligent tutoring systems track progress in real time, offering extra explanations or new challenges when needed. How do Australian schools use AI? One common way is through adaptive learning platforms that adjust tasks automatically and give instant feedback. In New Zealand, for example, EdTech providers use AI-generated hints and adaptive tasks, and trials show higher engagement and stronger understanding. This personalized approach helps students learn more effectively and stay motivated.

### **Reduced Teacher Workload and Smarter Use of Time**

AI can take over repetitive tasks like grading quizzes, generating practice questions, or answering common student queries. Examples of AI in education New Zealand include chatbots that handle routine questions and free up staff for deeper support. Many Australian schools are also piloting AI tools for marking and scheduling. By cutting administrative work, teachers gain more time for creative lesson planning and individual guidance, improving the quality of teaching and relationships with students.

Related: [AI for Teachers: Top 5 Roles & Use Cases](https://sotatek.com.au/blogs/ai-for-teachers/)

### **Early Intervention and Data-Driven Insights**

AI analytics quickly identify patterns that signal when a student may be struggling or disengaged. By spotting these signs early, schools can step in with targeted tutoring, counselling, or adjustments before small issues become major setbacks. Leaders can also use real-time data to improve resource planning, curriculum design, and overall school performance.

### **Greater Accessibility and Inclusion**

AI tools can translate materials, give instant feedback, and adapt content for learners with different abilities or language backgrounds. For example, AI-powered writing assistants help bilingual students or those with limited literacy receive immediate, constructive feedback. This makes education more inclusive and ensures all students, regardless of learning style, language, or location, have equal opportunities to succeed.

### **Preparing Students for an AI-Driven Future**

Introducing AI into everyday learning helps students build the skills they will need in a technology-rich society. By using and questioning AI tools, they develop digital literacy, critical thinking, and ethical understanding. In both Australia and New Zealand, education leaders highlight AI literacy as a core skill for future careers, making AI-supported classrooms an investment in the workforce of tomorrow.

![Benefits of AI in Education](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%201920%201080%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Benefits of AI in Education

## **Challenges and Risks of AI in Education**

While AI offers major opportunities, schools need to address its downsides to keep learning safe, fair, and effective. The following points highlight key issues every Australian and New Zealand school should plan for:

* **Data privacy and security** are at risk when AI tools collect and store sensitive student information, requiring strict protection and compliance with privacy laws.
* Algorithmic bias can produce **unfair outcomes** or reinforce inequalities if AI models are not carefully designed, tested, and updated.
* **Over-reliance on technology** may reduce human interaction, weaken critical thinking, and create problems if systems fail or go offline.
* **Limited teacher training and support** can lead to poor implementation and ethical mistakes, so continuous professional development is essential.
* **High costs and uneven infrastructure** can widen the digital divide, leaving some schools or communities behind.
* **Content inaccuracy or misuse** can occur when generative AI produces incorrect or inappropriate material without proper monitoring.

By anticipating these challenges, schools can adopt AI technology more responsibly and protect both students and educators.

## **AI Policy and Compliance in Australia & New Zealand**

Schools that introduce AI must follow local regulations and best-practice guidelines to protect students and ensure responsible use. **In Australia,** the federal Department of Education has released the *Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Schools*. This framework sets out principles for safe and ethical AI adoption, covering areas such as privacy, consent, data security, transparency, and the need for teacher and parent involvement. States and territories also apply their own privacy and child-safety rules, so schools must check both national and local requirements.

**In New Zealand,** education providers are governed by the *Education and Training Act,* as well as the *Privacy Act 2020*. The Ministry of Education encourages schools to conduct privacy impact assessments before deploying [AI solutions in New Zealand](https://sotatek.com.au/blogs/ai-solutions-new-zealand/) and to ensure that any data stored or processed overseas complies with New Zealand's privacy standards. Guidelines highlight the need for clear consent from parents or guardians when collecting student data and for ongoing monitoring of AI systems to keep them accurate and fair.

Both countries stress **transparency, explainability, and human oversight.** Schools are expected to keep records of how AI systems are used, make decision processes understandable to students and families, and provide alternatives when AI-generated outcomes are disputed. Regular reviews, staff training, and documented risk assessments are recommended to maintain compliance and public trust.

By following these national and local rules, schools in Australia and New Zealand can harness AI’s benefits while meeting their legal and ethical responsibilities.

## **Case study: AI Tools for Smart Note Management by SotaTek ANZ**

Developed by SotaTek ANZ, one of the [best technology companies for Australian and New Zealand businesses](https://sotatek.com.au/blogs/ai-solutions-in-australia/), this case study shows how locally built AI can support modern classrooms. Our AI Tools for Smart Note Management, often called NoteX, demonstrate how **affordable AI tools for schools in Australia and New Zealand** can transform everyday teaching and learning.

![Smart Note Apps NoteX by SotaTekANZ](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%201758%202000%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Smart Note Apps, NoteX by SotaTekANZ

For students, the tool captures lectures in real time, transcribes them with high accuracy, and instantly creates clear summaries, flashcards, quizzes, and mind maps. Translation features help multilingual learners, while cloud syncing means notes are always available across devices. These functions make the study more efficient and inclusive.

For teachers, [NoteX](https://sotatek.com.au/portfolio/ai-tools-for-smart-note-management/) removes time-consuming tasks such as summarising lessons, preparing revision quizzes, or creating alternative materials for diverse learners. Educators can upload lesson recordings and receive ready-to-use study aids and insights on where students may need extra help, freeing them to focus on deeper instruction and personal guidance.

By delivering advanced note-taking, content organisation, and learning analytics in one platform, SotaTek ANZ shows how home-grown solutions can give schools powerful, practical, and cost-effective ways to integrate AI. It helps both educators and students work smarter and learn better.

## **Implementation Roadmap for Schools & Universities**

Introducing AI in education works best when done in well-defined stages. The roadmap below outlines key phases, main actions, and practical tips for schools and universities in Australia and New Zealand.

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Phase** | **Key Actions** | **Practical Tips** |
| **1. Strategy & Needs Assessment** | Define learning goals and problems AI should solve; review curriculum priorities and student needs; check budgets and infrastructure. | Involve teachers, IT staff, and student representatives early to align goals with real classroom challenges. |
| **2. Policy & Compliance Check** | Map requirements against national frameworks;  run privacy impact assessments. | Document data flows, consent processes, and risk assessments before any purchase. |
| **3. Tool Selection & Pilot Design** | Compare solutions, focusing on affordable AI tools for schools in Australia and New Zealand; set clear pilot objectives and success metrics. | Choose a small set of classes or departments to test first; include accessibility and multi-device checks. |
| **4. Training & Change Management** | Provide professional development for teachers and administrators; create student and parent guides on responsible AI use. | Offer short, hands-on sessions and ongoing support to build confidence and address concerns. |
| **5. Pilot Implementation** | Deploy selected tools with a limited group; monitor performance, data security, and learning impact. | Collect feedback weekly and adjust settings or teaching methods quickly. |
| **6. Evaluation & Scaling** | Review pilot outcomes against success metrics; refine policies and rollout plans. | Share results with the wider school community; budget for long-term maintenance and updates. |
| **7. Continuous Improvement** | Schedule regular reviews of AI performance, content accuracy, and privacy compliance. | Keep a feedback loop with teachers and students; update training as tools evolve. |

## **Conclusion**

AI is reshaping education across Australia and New Zealand, offering personalised learning, streamlined administration, and new opportunities for both teachers and students. By following clear policies, addressing privacy and fairness concerns, and implementing AI step by step, schools and universities can harness these benefits safely and effectively. With thoughtful planning and affordable AI tools, educators can create more engaging, inclusive, and future-ready learning environments.

With years of experience delivering custom AI solutions for education and enterprise, SotaTek ANZ provides trusted local expertise to help schools and universities adopt AI responsibly and cost-effectively. #### [What is AI in education?](#faq_tab_1)

AI in education refers to the use of machine learning, natural language processing, and generative models to personalize learning, automate routine tasks (e.g., grading and feedback), enhance accessibility, and provide data-driven insights that support teachers and students.

#### [What are the benefits of AI in education?](#faq_tab_2)

* Personalized learning paths and pacing
* Instant feedback and formative assessment
* Accessibility (speech-to-text, captions, translation)
* Time savings for teachers (rubrics, quiz/item creation)
* Learning analytics to spot gaps and at-risk students

#### [What are the advantages and disadvantages of AI in education?](#faq_tab_3)

*Advantages:* scalability, personalization, consistency, inclusion, data-informed decisions.  
  *Disadvantages:* bias and hallucinations, privacy and safety risks, overreliance/cheating, uneven access, and potential deskilling. Always pair AI with clear policies and human oversight.

#### [What are real-world examples of AI in the classroom?](#faq_tab_4)

* Intelligent tutoring/chatbots aligned to the syllabus
* Adaptive practice and spaced-repetition quiz engines
* AI-assisted grading and feedback on writing/code
* Early-warning dashboards from LMS data
* Language-learning conversation partners
* Accessibility tools (reading support, captioning)

#### [What is the future of AI in education?](#faq_tab_5)

Expect multimodal tutors (text, voice, vision), classroom-aware agents that respect privacy, better alignment to curricula/standards, offline/edge models for equity, and stronger governance on data protection and academic integrity.

#### [Will AI replace teachers?](#faq_tab_6)

No. AI augments teachers by handling routine tasks and providing insights; pedagogy, motivation, and pastoral care remain human-led. The best results are achieved through “human-in-the-loop” designs.

#### [How can schools implement AI responsibly?](#faq_tab_7)

Start with clear goals, a procurement and privacy checklist, teacher training, age-appropriate guardrails, transparent use policies, and continuous evaluation (learning outcomes, equity, time saved).

args.summary:
This webpage from SotaTek ANZ (dated September 30, 2025) is a comprehensive guide on AI in Education for schools in Australia and New Zealand. It defines AI in education as technology that personalizes learning, automates administrative tasks, and enhances teaching. Key statistics note that 65% of educators see AI as critical for improving student outcomes, and teachers could save up to 13 hours per week through AI automation.

**Benefits** include personalized and adaptive learning, reduced teacher workload, early intervention through data-driven insights, greater accessibility and inclusion, and preparing students for an AI-driven future.

**Challenges and risks** include data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, over-reliance on technology, limited teacher training, high costs widening the digital divide, and content inaccuracy.

**Policy and compliance** are covered: Australia follows the *Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Schools*, while New Zealand operates under the *Education and Training Act* and *Privacy Act 2020*, both emphasizing transparency, human oversight, and privacy impact assessments.

**Case study**: SotaTek ANZ's NoteX (AI Tools for Smart Note Management) is presented as an affordable solution that transcribes lectures, creates summaries/flashcards/quizzes, and supports multilingual learners and teachers.

**Implementation roadmap** includes seven phases: Strategy & Needs Assessment, Policy & Compliance Check, Tool Selection & Pilot Design, Training & Change Management, Pilot Implementation, Evaluation & Scaling, and Continuous Improvement.

The page concludes with an FAQ section addressing common questions about AI in education.

# Shaping the future of AI in schools: new roadmap for participatory approaches to AI in education

* News

![](https://simplepixels.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/appi/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/AdobeStock_1478961982-1024x683.jpeg)

**Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming educational systems worldwide. In December 2025, the Australian Government released its National AI Plan that calls for greater community and industry engagement to explore practical ways to support responsible deployment. New research on governing AI in education, supported by an APPI Policy Challenge Grant, offers practical examples for supporting responsible deployment and equitable use of AI in education.**

A multiuniversity team from the University of Sydney, University of Technology Sydney and the University of Bergen in Norway – led by **Professor Kalervo Gulson** and supported through an APPI Policy Challenge Grant – conducted a study within the NSW EdTech ecosystem, testing two participatory methods to inform AI policy in school education.

Working with students, teachers, policymakers, and technologists, [**this report**](https://appi.org.au/report/governing-ai-in-education-policy-opportunities-for-building-participatory-and-equitable-futures/) identified opportunities to enhance the use of AI in Australian education through participatory approaches and tools that engage educators, students, and communities. This includes innovative, non-regulatory mechanisms to guide the responsible evolution of its use.

Key findings have been translated into policy opportunities for the Australian Government, state and territory governments, and education sectors, to improve governance, strengthen oversight and develop policy capability. They include operationalising local engagement to identify AI risks and benefits, establishing a permanent Advisory Council for AI in Education, and strengthening equity and inclusion in EdTech procurement.

This study highlights policy opportunities that the Australian Government can seize to proactively navigate the complex landscape of AI in education, supporting both educational outcomes and equity. “With the global AI education market forecasted to reach US$22 billion by 2028, proactive governance and policy tools to ensure safety and equity have become more critical. Participatory methods elevate critical implementation issues, equity considerations, and broaden participation of groups often left out of decision-making, to ensure AI is leveraged with the chance of being effective and fair,” noted Professor Kalervo Gulson, the lead author.

“The opportunities outlined in this report provide a roadmap of actionable, participatory strategies to take advantage of the benefits that AI can bring to classrooms,” added **Isabella Whealing**, Head of Social Policy at the Australian Public Policy Institute. “The APPI Policy Challenge Grants program supports timely, policy-relevant issues such as these, outlining practical steps that are front-of-mind for policymakers today.”

# Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Schools

The Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools (the Framework) seeks to guide the responsible and ethical use of generative AI tools in ways that benefit students, schools, and society. In June 2025, Education Ministers endorsed the 2024 Framework Review, undertaken by the National AI in Schools Taskforce (the Taskforce) in consultation with representatives of all jurisdictions, school sectors and national agencies.

# Generative AI

Guidance and resources for education professionals on the use of artificial intelligence in schools.

Last updated: 22 May 2026

![](/_next/static/media/icon_clock.d2701c3d.svg)6 mins to read

On this page

* [What generative AI is](#what-generative-ai-is-1)
* [What to think about when using AI tools](#what-to-think-about-when-using-ai-tools-1)
* [Talk about it and make a policy](#talk-about-it-and-make-a-policy-1)
* [Teachers using AI](#teachers-using-ai-1)
* [Students using AI](#students-using-ai-1)
* [GenAI in NCEA](#genai-in-ncea-1)
* [Frequently asked questions about GenAI in NCEA assessment](#frequently-asked-questions-about-genai-in-ncea-assessment-1)
* [GenAI case studies](#genai-case-studies-1)

## What generative AI is[#](#what-generative-ai-is-1)

'Generative artificial intelligence' is a term that covers a range of tools that have been trained using huge sets of data to create new content. It is also called 'AI' and 'GenAI'.

Artificial intelligence has been around for a while, powering technology like predictive text. It is quickly becoming more widely available to more people, in both free-to-use and paid tools and services.

### Resources[#](#resources-1)

These resources from trusted sources can help you learn more about GenAI.

[Introduction to artificial intelligence – Tāhūrangi](https://newzealandcurriculum.tahurangi.education.govt.nz/introduction-to-artificial-intelligence/5637235331.p)

[He Kōrero Whakataki ki te Atamai Rorohiko – Tāhurangi](https://kauwhatareo.tahurangi.education.govt.nz/mi/he-k-rero-whakataki-ki-te-atamai-rorohiko/5637236082.p)

[Exploring generative AI in a NZ classroom – Netsafe](https://education.netsafe.org.nz/tools/exploring-generative-ai-in-a-nz-classroom-environment)

## What to think about when using AI tools[#](#what-to-think-about-when-using-ai-tools-1)

### Check the output[#](#check-the-output-1)

AI can create content that seems plausible but contains nonsensical or incorrect detail. Whenever you use AI, make sure that you are reviewing and checking the outputs.

[An introduction to the role of Artificial Intelligence in classrooms and schools – The Education Hub](https://theeducationhub.org.nz/an-introduction-to-the-role-of-artificial-intelligence-in-classrooms-and-schools/)

### Don’t use personal data[#](#don-t-use-personal-data-2)

Most free AI tools use the prompts you put in to continue to train the model. Don’t use personal data when you use AI tools – what you put in may be reused.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner has guidelines about AI and privacy that principals and teachers should keep in mind.

[Artificial intelligence and the information privacy principles – Office of the Privacy Commissioner](https://www.privacy.org.nz/resources-and-learning/a-z-topics/ai/)

### Cultural bias[#](#cultural-bias-3)

AI models are trained on huge amounts of data from different countries and cultures. This means most AI models are built on dominant cultures and languages, and the tools may not accurately reflect indigenous knowledge.

For a New Zealand context, AI models are likely to be weak on mātauranga and te reo Māori, as well as Pacific languages and Polynesian cultures.

### Read terms and conditions[#](#read-terms-and-conditions-4)

Carefully read the terms and conditions of use.

Many AI models will reuse your prompts and the data you provide it to continue to learn and train. Make sure you do not enter copyright, confidential, personal, or sensitive information into these models.

## Talk about it and make a policy[#](#talk-about-it-and-make-a-policy-1)

Discuss with your staff how AI is used at your school and what rules and guidance you need to put in place for different contexts. It is best to adopt a practical, educative approach to AI and its uses.

Consider structuring your school AI policy to include guidance on:

* purpose and scope
* principles
* guidelines for external and internal
* risk mitigation
* professional development for teachers
* data privacy
* review.

### GenAI and assessment[#](#genai-and-assessment-1)

Schools with consent to assess listed standards are required to have an authenticity policy to support assessment practice. This policy must include the acceptable use of GenAI.

Assessment is authentic when it affirms the skills, knowledge and competencies acquired by ākonga | students and reflects real world contexts and/or meaningful contexts.

Things to be aware of:

* valid assessment evidence must be the student’s own work. Similarly to plagiarism or over-scaffolding, if GenAI is used to produce evidence that is assessed as the student’s work, then the assessment is invalid
* the possible uses of GenAI in assessment contexts are therefore more limited than in teaching and learning contexts.

For NCEA internal assessments, teachers must be aware of any specific requirements of the achievement standard being assessed and its conditions of assessment.

[NCEA – NCEA Education](https://ncea.education.govt.nz/)

For NCEA external assessments, the use of GenAI is not permitted. The New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) has more information.

[Guidance on the acceptable use of artificial intelligence – NZQA](https://www2.nzqa.govt.nz/ncea/ncea-for-teachers-and-schools/managing-national-assessment-in-schools/ai-guidance/)

### Questions to consider[#](#questions-to-consider-2)

When writing assessment policy that includes GenAI you should consider:

* how you promote academic integrity
  + what is academic integrity?
  + how does the use of GenAI relate to academic integrity?
  + what are the responsibilities for ensuring academic integrity for stakeholders? (students, teachers, whānau | families)?
  + does your school’s operational policy (for example, an ‘assessment handbook’ for students and families) outline the responsibilities of each group, and have a clear process to follow when these may not have been met?
* whether your school policy outlines your preferred approach to referencing source material, including referencing GenAI
* whether your school policy warns about bias and inaccurate information being generated by GenAI.

Log in to Netsafe's Kete for further guidance that may be useful.

[AI policy – Netsafe Kete](https://education.netsafe.org.nz/sign-in)

## Teachers using AI[#](#teachers-using-ai-1)

AI in education should improve teaching and learning, supporting knowledgeable and skilled teachers.

Human teachers must:

* remain central in students’ education
* take responsibility for students’ learning.

### AI tools for marking[#](#ai-tools-for-marking-1)

Our guidance for schools and teachers on the use of AI for marking has been updated. The guidance follows and promotes a principles-based approach centred on:

* teacher responsibility and professional judgement
* human oversight
* appropriate use cases.

The guidance affirms that teacher-student relationship remains central. The use of AI tools for marking should support, not replace, the professional judgement of teachers.

We have worked with NZQA to develop this update.

## Students using AI[#](#students-using-ai-1)

GenAI can be used to enhance teaching and learning, but it needs to be restricted to make sure each student’s work is their own.

### Age restrictions on use of AI[#](#age-restrictions-on-use-of-ai-1)

Teachers and students must abide by the terms and conditions of the tools they’re using. Several AI tools have age restrictions on their use.

To use ChatGPT you must:

* be at least 13 years old
* have your parent or legal guardian’s permission if you are under 18.

Never send any AI tool the personal information of anyone under the age of 13.

## GenAI in NCEA[#](#genai-in-ncea-1)

Schools must have a policy on the acceptable use of GenAI. This policy should guide teachers’ and students’ NCEA assessment practice.

The principle of authenticity means that students are required to demonstrate their own knowledge, understanding, and skills in NCEA assessment events. Any evidence submitted for assessment must be their own work.

Another way of thinking about a student’s ‘own work’ is that it presents evidence of the knowledge and skills being assessed against the standard that the student has independently demonstrated and that they could repeat in a different context.

The use of GenAI is not permitted in NCEA external assessment.

### AI in assessment[#](#ai-in-assessment-1)

As students move into the senior secondary years, summative assessments become increasingly important markers of students' progress and achievement.

When, why and how students use AI and GenAI tools needs careful consideration and should be informed by school policy. The guidance below aims to assist teachers with designing summative assessment activities for students that are clear, authentic and robust.

args.summary:
This is a New Zealand Ministry of Education webpage providing guidance and resources for education professionals on the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in schools. Last updated 22 May 2026.

Key points include:

- **What GenAI is**: A range of tools trained on large datasets to create new content, becoming widely available in free and paid forms.

- **Considerations when using AI**: Check outputs for accuracy as AI can produce plausible but incorrect content; avoid using personal data as free tools use prompts for training; be aware of cultural bias (models are weak on mātauranga Māori, te reo Māori, and Pacific languages); read terms and conditions carefully.

- **School policy**: Schools should discuss AI use and develop policies covering purpose, principles, risk mitigation, professional development, data privacy, and review. Schools with consent to assess NCEA standards must have an authenticity policy including acceptable GenAI use.

- **Teachers using AI**: Human teachers must remain central and responsible for student learning. AI marking tools should support, not replace, teacher professional judgement. A principles-based approach is promoted with human oversight.

- **Students using AI**: GenAI can enhance learning but must be restricted to ensure students' work is their own. Age restrictions apply (e.g., ChatGPT requires age 13+ with parental permission for under 18). Never input personal information of anyone under 13.

- **GenAI in NCEA**: Schools must have a GenAI policy. Authenticity requires students to demonstrate their own knowledge. GenAI is not permitted in NCEA external assessments. For internal assessments, teachers must be aware of specific standard requirements.

- **Resources**: Links to Tāhūrangi curriculum materials, Netsafe guidance, Privacy Commissioner guidelines, NZQA AI guidance, and downloadable PDFs including case studies from Aotea College and Hobsonville Point Secondary School.

--- SOURCE 1: How AI Is Reshaping K-12 & Higher Education in the USA 2026 ---
URL: https://www.thirdrocktechkno.com/blog/how-ai-is-reshaping-the-future-of-k-12-and-higher-education-in-the-usa

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Third Rock Techkno, published February 3, 2026 and updated August 3, 2026, examines how AI is reshaping K-12 and higher education in the USA. The central finding is that AI adoption has surged dramatically—student usage jumped from 66% in 2024 to 92% in 2025, with 83% of K-12 teachers now using generative AI tools. The U.S. AI-in-education market is projected to grow from $2.01 billion in 2025 to $32.64 billion by 2034.

**Key Evidence:**
- A June 2025 Harvard study found that students using a well-designed AI tutor (PS2 Pal) learned more than twice as much in less time compared to active-learning classrooms.
- Teachers using AI weekly save an average of 5.9 hours per week.
- Georgia State University reduced summer melt from 19% to 9% using an AI chatbot, achieving a 3.3% increase in enrollment.

**Policy Landscape:**
- April 2025: President Trump signed an Executive Order establishing a White House Task Force on AI Education.
- Ohio and Tennessee enacted laws requiring school districts to develop AI policies; New York banned facial recognition in schools.
- As of May 2026, the USA has zero binding federal AI curriculum standards—policy remains fragmented across states.

**Risks and Concerns:**
- A University of Pennsylvania study found that unguided AI access harmed learning outcomes in high school mathematics.
- Over 30% of students risk becoming overly dependent on AI tools.
- 68%+ of urban teachers have received no AI training.
- Equity gaps persist as under-resourced schools struggle to implement AI effectively.

**Success Patterns:**
- Intentional design over default tools (the Harvard study succeeded due to pedagogical guardrails, not the underlying GPT-4 technology).
- Clear policies, professional development, and student AI literacy programs.
- AI literacy is expected to become a core competency embedded across disciplines by end of 2026.

**Higher Education Trends:**
- ~90% of college students use AI as their primary research tool (2026 estimate).
- University of Wisconsin-Madison approved a standalone College of Computing and AI (first new academic college since 1983).
- Assessment is shifting toward process-over-product, oral defenses, and AI-co-authored work with transparent attribution.

The article concludes that well-designed AI can double learning outcomes, but poorly implemented AI harms learning. The difference lies in intentionality, and institutions that approach AI as a tool for achieving their educational mission—with clear policies, trained educators, and thoughtful design—are seeing genuine results.
</summary>

Student AI usage in the USA jumped from 66% to 92% in a single year — this is not gradual adoption, it's a wholesale classroom transformation., A Harvard 2025 study found AI tutors produce 2x learning gains vs. active learning classrooms — but only when designed with pedagogical guardrails., The #1 failure pattern: institutions adopt AI tools without intentional design, which can harm learning outcomes rather than improve them., USA has zero binding federal AI curriculum standards as of May 2026 — policy is fragmented across states, creating uneven adoption., The AI in education market in the USA is projected to grow from $2.01 billion in 2025 to $32.64 billion by 2034.

--- SOURCE 2: Factors Influencing Preschool Teachers’ Continuous Intention to Use AI Generated Content in Education | Open Praxis ---
URL: https://openpraxis.org/articles/10.55982/openpraxis.18.1.1010

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article, published in Open Praxis (Volume 18, Issue 1, 2026), investigates factors influencing preschool teachers' continuous intention to use Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) in education. The study integrates three theoretical models—Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM), and Flow Theory—into a unified framework. Data were collected through a questionnaire survey of 433 preschool teachers in China and analyzed using both PLS-SEM and fsQCA methods.

Key findings from PLS-SEM analysis show that all 11 hypotheses were supported. Confirmation had the strongest effect on perceived usefulness (β=0.505) and satisfaction (β=0.349). Perceived usefulness strongly influenced attitude (β=0.530) and satisfaction (β=0.309). Flow experience positively impacted continuous intention (β=0.223) and attitude (β=0.220). Satisfaction (β=0.280) and attitude (β=0.262) also significantly predicted continuance intention. Perceived ease of use had comparatively smaller effects.

The fsQCA analysis revealed three equifinal configurations leading to high continuance intention, with overall consistency of 0.918 and coverage of 0.764. Two configurations for low continuance intention were also identified.

The study found that the model explains 51.8% of variance in continuance intention. Notably, the stronger influence of flow experience and satisfaction over perceived usefulness challenges the rational evaluation assumption of classic technology adoption models, suggesting that affective engagement plays a critical role in shaping long-term adoption. The authors recommend differentiated support strategies, real-time feedback, targeted training, gamified interaction, and adaptive content creation to promote AIGC integration in preschool contexts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The stronger influence of flow experience and satisfaction over perceived usefulness challenges the rational evaluation assumption of classic technology adoption models. This underscores that affective engagement, not rational utility, plays the critical role in shaping long-term adoption.", "To promote the effective integration of AIGC in preschool contexts, administrators could adopt differentiated support strategies tailored to teachers' motivational profiles. They should strengthen confirmation through real-time feedback and targeted training that aligns with expectations.", "Results indicate that confirmation and perceived usefulness are robust predictors of continuance, whereas perceived ease of use exerts a comparatively smaller effect.", "The fsQCA uncovers three equifinal configurations that lead to high continuance intention, highlighting complementary pathways that combine confirmation, usefulness, attitude, satisfaction, and flow experience.", "The R2 value of continuous intention to use (CITU) indicates that the predictors in the model explain approximately 51.8% of the variance in continued use intention, demonstrating strong explanatory power."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Artificial Intelligence in K–12 Schools ---
URL: https://livehandbook.org/k-12-education/miscellaneous/k-12-education/school-resources/artificial-intelligence-in-k%E2%80%9312-schools

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage, titled "Artificial Intelligence in K–12 Schools" (last updated August 2026), is a chapter in the Live Handbook of Education Policy Research by Cristina Barnard, Lily Fesler, and Susanna Loeb. It provides a comprehensive review of the evidence on AI in K-12 education, focusing on how AI tools affect student learning.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Thin evidence base:** The causal evidence on AI in K-12 education is limited but growing. A recent review identified over 800 relevant papers but only 20 high-quality causal studies, with none conducted in U.S. K-12 schools on student-facing AI tools. Most studies examine short-term performance rather than durable learning.

2. **AI influences learning through experiences:** AI tools shape student learning by affecting access to personalized instruction, complex problem-solving, meaningful collaboration, substantive discussion, and sustained relationships with educators.

3. **Performance vs. proficiency:** AI tools often improve performance during use, but these gains do not consistently reflect independent proficiency. A study of high school math students found that those using a general-purpose chatbot performed worse on a subsequent closed-book exam than students who practiced with no AI support, despite having higher practice performance.

4. **Design choices matter:** Systems that prompt students to explain reasoning and engage actively tend to support learning, while systems that generate complete answers reduce cognitive work and learning. Tutoring-style AI with hints and guided reasoning shows more promise than general-purpose chatbots.

5. **Educator capacity:** Generative AI can reduce time educators spend on routine preparation and grading without reducing quality. Tools that provide instructional feedback to teachers and tutors show early promise, but whether this benefits learning depends on how freed-up time is redirected.

**Introduction:** The chapter notes that 54% of middle and high school students and 53% of teachers reported using AI for school (2025 RAND survey). It argues that educators need a framework for evaluating AI grounded in learning science rather than relying on product-specific studies.

**Areas for future research** include: longer-term student learning outcomes, equity and student experiences, system-level applications (scheduling, tutoring coordination), assessment, and research priorities such as tracking durable learning outcomes and studying implementation across diverse contexts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The evidence base on AI in K-12 education—especially causal evidence on U.S. schools—is thin but growing., AI tools often improve performance during use, but these gains do not consistently reflect independent proficiency., Systems that prompt students to explain their reasoning, engage actively with problems, and revise their understanding tend to reinforce the cognitive work associated with deeper learning. Systems that generate complete answers tend to reduce cognitive work and learning., Students using general-purpose AI systems frequently complete tasks more successfully when assisted, but may show weaker performance on unassisted assessments than students who did not have access to AI., In a nationally representative 2025 RAND survey, 54% of middle and high school students reported using AI for school, and 53% of English language arts (ELA), math, and science teachers reported using AI in instructional tasks.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article provides a comprehensive analysis of AI integration in K-12 education globally since 2025, covering policy developments, empirical evidence, risks, stakeholder perspectives, and best practices.

**Regulatory Landscape:** The post-2025 period has seen accelerated but fragmented regulation. In the U.S., an April 2025 executive order established a national K-12 AI literacy strategy, and by early 2026, over half of states had enacted AI policy guidance. COPPA rules were updated in 2025 to strengthen children's data protections. China leads with the world's most comprehensive mandatory national AI curriculum. South Korea rolls out AI-enabled homework tutors. The EU AI Act remains under debate. No national bans on AI in K-12 have been enacted.

**Empirical Evidence:** Evidence is strong for short-term benefits but lacking for long-term impact. 85% of U.S. K-12 teachers and students report using AI, primarily for lesson planning, feedback, and data analysis. Over two-thirds endorse AI's benefits for personalized learning. Up to 75% of students report higher motivation in AI-enhanced settings. However, there are no recent longitudinal studies tracking sustained impact on higher-order cognitive skills. Quasi-experimental studies show 15-35% academic improvements, but effects vary greatly. Without human guidance, some studies report declines or no effect.

**Risks:** Only 11% of U.S. districts rigorously evaluate AI tools for privacy compliance. AI-generated deepfakes targeting students have emerged in Australia. 72% of students would use generative AI for assignments, but only 17-22% are taught about responsible use. Over 70% of teachers express concern about skill erosion. AI adoption remains below 15% in most African and Latin American systems.

**Key Pilots:** Iceland launched a national pilot with Anthropic in 2025. China's mandatory AI curriculum is the world's largest. Penn GSE and Digital Promise distributed $26 million to U.S. district-level programs.

**Best Practices:** Recommendations include targeted professional development, ethical guidelines with consent and transparency, digital infrastructure investment in under-resourced regions, and institutional oversight on procurement and algorithmic impact.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This podcast episode (Tech Talk For Teachers, #463, January 20, 2026) hosted by Paul Beckermann reviews deep research results from both ChatGPT and Gemini that identify the top 10 most popular and effective strategies for using generative AI in K-12 classrooms. The research was conducted using the prompt: "Act as a K–12 educational research expert. Research best practices in using generative AI in K–12 schools, focus on U.S. schools during the past two years, generate a list of top 10 most popular and effective strategies."

Key context: Generative AI adoption in schools has outpaced the development of both school policies and best-practice research. The highest area of teacher use is time-saving tasks. A Cengage report found that 52% of teachers used AI to create course content, 71% for lesson planning, and 68% for quizzes and assessments. The "human-AI-human" model (Washington State) emphasizes that generative AI engagement should start with human inquiry and end with human reflection and insight.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Technology Review of Magic School AI: An Intelligent Way for Education Inclusivity and Teacher Workload Reduction

## Overview
This technical note (published July 25, 2025 in *Education Sciences*, Vol. 15, Issue 8) by Li et al. (Fordham University and Purdue University) reviews **Magic School AI (MSAI)**, an AI tool designed to help teachers provide accommodations and modifications for students with special needs, particularly those with Individual Education Plans (IEPs), while reducing teacher workload.

## Key Problem Addressed
- Schools face a critical shortage of special education teachers, with 40% leaving within the first five years
- General/subject teachers often lack training in special education and struggle to design appropriate content modifications
- Students with disabilities span 13 categories (e.g., SLD, ASD, ADHD, speech/language impairment)

## MSAI Features Evaluated (Five Functions)
1. **Text Leveler** – Modifies text to different reading/grade levels (e.g., adjusting a 9th-grade text to 7th or 11th grade level)
2. **Text Scaffolder** – Modifies complexity and length of text; provides vocabulary definitions and comprehension questions
3. **Assignment Scaffolder** – Breaks multi-step assignments into manageable steps for special education students
4. **Exemplar & Non-Examples** – Provides model answers and incorrect examples with explanations of errors
5. **Sentence Starters** – Provides writing scaffolds for students (e.g., describing mitosis phases)

## Key Benefits
- Free and easy-to-operate platform requiring minimal training
- Helps teachers create inclusive lessons by tailoring content
- Can generate follow-up questions and suggest visual aids
- Particularly valuable for teachers of non-core subjects (e.g., foreign languages, music, PE) who lack special education support

## Limitations
- No ability to offer detailed, specific feedback on teachers' lesson plans
- Teachers must manually revise their own lesson plans based on general suggestions
- Lack of adequate technological training for teachers may hinder effective use
- Falls short of providing direct, actionable activities ready for classroom implementation

## Suggested Improvements
1. Categorize functions by subject area (Special Education, Math, ELA, etc.) for easier navigation
2. Create tutorial videos as mini-professional development for teachers
3. Develop a more intelligent lesson plan modification system that allows teachers to upload lesson plans and receive direct feedback, modifications, and accommodations
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the **"Guidance for the Use of AI in the K-12 Classroom"** published by the Southern Regional Education Board (SREB) in **April 2025**. It provides a comprehensive framework for integrating AI into K-12 education, focusing on four main pillars:

**PILLAR #1: Use AI to develop more cognitively demanding tasks.** AI should be used as a tool to enhance student engagement with creative problem-solving and innovative thinking, not as a final product. Teachers can use AI as a lesson planning partner, for project-based learning, interactive simulations, and to help students explore counter perspectives. Cautions include recognizing AI's inherent bias and ensuring students master underlying concepts first.

**PILLAR #2: Use AI to streamline teacher administrative and planning work.** AI can serve as a planning partner, help improve assignments, assist with grading and feedback, draft communications, provide behavioral insights, and support English language learners. Cautions include protecting student data privacy (never input personally identifiable information), avoiding over-reliance on AI, and the need for continuous teacher training.

**PILLAR #3: Use AI to support personalized learning.** AI can analyze student data to create individualized learning experiences, support students with special needs (text-to-speech, speech recognition), provide intelligent tutoring systems, predictive analytics, automated feedback, and adaptive learning platforms. Cautions include data privacy/security (FERPA compliance), algorithmic bias, the digital divide (unequal access to technology), and balancing screen time.

**PILLAR #4: Develop students as ethical and proficient AI users.** Students need to understand ethical implications including data privacy, bias, transparency, and academic integrity. Opportunities include using AI for brainstorming/outlining, developing critical media literacy, cross-disciplinary learning, and student-led AI ethics committees. Cautions include cheating, deepfakes, AI hallucinations, and data security concerns.

The appendix includes an **Artificial Intelligence Literacy for Educators** framework outlining skills and aptitudes needed for teachers and school/district leaders, and **Hess' Cognitive Rigor Matrix** for classifying cognitive demand of student assignments.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review article published in Frontiers in Education on September 23, 2025, authored by Abdullah Alfarwan from Najran University, Saudi Arabia. The study systematically reviews empirical research on the use of Generative AI (GenAI) in K-12 education, analyzing 30 papers retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and snowballing techniques.

**Key Findings:**
- **Publication Timeline:** Most papers (19 of 30) were published in 2024, with 6 from 2025 and 5 from 2023.
- **Educational Levels:** High school students and pre-service teachers were most represented. In-service teachers, elementary, primary, and vocational education were underrepresented. No studies focused on early childhood education (ECE).
- **Subject Domains:** Mathematics was the most common subject (5 papers), followed by Physics (4). The majority focused on STEM-related subjects. Non-STEM subjects included History, Writing, and English Language.
- **Geographic Representation:** Most studies were conducted in Taiwan and China (4 each), followed by the US and Germany (3 each). No studies from Africa were included.
- **GenAI Tools:** ChatGPT was used in 21 of 30 papers. Other tools included Copilot, DALL-E, Midjourney, and others.
- **Study Design:** Quasi-experimental design was most common (30% of papers), followed by descriptive and mixed-method approaches (20% each).
- **Measures:** Primarily psychological variables (attitudes, self-efficacy, trust, motivation, critical thinking, self-regulated learning). Only two studies examined self-regulated learning specifically. Objective measures (standardized tests) were largely absent.
- **Recommendations:** 90% of papers emphasized the need for teacher professional development for AI-integrated classrooms. Future research should explore longitudinal studies, true experimental designs, objective learning measures, parental involvement, diverse GenAI tools, and under-researched contexts (ECE, special needs, rural settings).

**Limitations:** The search only covered English-language publications and specific GenAI tools (ChatGPT, Google Bard, Copilot, Midjourney). There is a lack of representation from Africa, the Middle East, and South America.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Generative artificial intelligence in K-12 education: A systematic review | Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning ---
URL: https://rptel.apsce.net/index.php/RPTEL/article/view/2026-21034

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an academic article titled "Generative artificial intelligence in K-12 education: A systematic review," published in Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning (RPTEL), Vol. 21, 2026. Authored by Tianyu Zhang, Yiu Chi Lai, and Philip Leung Ho Yu (The Education University of Hong Kong), the study systematically reviews 45 studies published between 2020 and 2024 on the application of Generative AI (GenAI) in K-12 education. Key findings include: (1) GenAI tools significantly improve students' academic performance, cognitive abilities, and learning motivation, promoting personalized learning; (2) challenges include misleading or erroneous content generation, difficulty in understanding technology, student dependence on technology, and privacy infringement; (3) educators demonstrate shortcomings in AI literacy, highlighting the need for targeted training; and (4) most existing empirical research focuses on short-term impacts, with future research needing more longitudinal studies to evaluate long-term implications of GenAI in education.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
GenAI tools can significantly improve students' academic performance and cognitive abilities, enhance their learning motivation, and thus promote the development of personalized learning, Using these tools also brings a series of challenges, including misleading or erroneous content generation, difficulty in understanding technology, students' dependence on technology, and privacy infringement, The shortcomings demonstrated by educators in terms of AI literacy emphasize the necessity for relevant educational institutions to organize targeted AI literacy training, Most existing empirical research has focused on the short-term impact of GenAI tools on K-12 education. Future research will incorporate more longitudinal studies to systematically evaluate the long-term and deep implications of GenAI in education

--- SOURCE 2: AI in Education: Use Cases and Real Examples | 2026 ---
URL: https://www.thirdrocktechkno.com/blog/ai-in-education-top-use-cases-and-real-examples

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published December 24, 2025, updated August 3, 2026) by Tapan Patel of Third Rock Techkno provides a comprehensive overview of AI in education, covering the nine highest-impact use cases with real-world examples.

**Key Statistics:**
- 86% of education organizations use generative AI (highest adoption rate of any industry, per Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education Report)
- The global AI in education market reached $7.57 billion in 2025, projected to hit $112 billion by 2034
- Teachers using AI tools report reclaiming 5–10 hours per week for instruction
- A 2025 randomized controlled trial in Nature Scientific Reports found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning

**The Nine Core AI in Education Use Cases:**

1. **Personalized Learning** – Adaptive platforms analyze student performance in real-time, adjusting content difficulty and pacing. Example: Sourcebook (built by TRT) turns documents into interactive, adaptive learning experiences.

2. **Automated Content Creation** – Generative AI produces quizzes, lesson plans, and learning modules at scale. Example: Squirrel AI generates tailored textbooks and materials.

3. **Intelligent Tutoring** – AI tutors use NLP to guide students through problem-solving. Example: Khan Academy's Khanmigo (built on GPT-4) asks guiding questions rather than giving answers.

4. **Enhanced Student Engagement** – AI-driven gamification and interactive simulations maintain student interest. Example: Duolingo uses AI to personalize lesson difficulty and spaced-repetition algorithms.

5. **Teacher Assistance & Administrative Automation** – Automated grading, scheduling, and chatbots handle routine tasks. Example: Gradescope uses AI to evaluate handwritten math, coding, and essays.

6. **Language Learning & Translation** – NLP provides personalized vocabulary, grammar practice, and pronunciation feedback. Example: Duolingo's AI optimizes review timing and lesson difficulty.

7. **Predictive Analytics** – ML models identify at-risk students before they fail. Example: IBM Watson Education reported 20% improvements in student performance through early intervention.

8. **Accessibility & Inclusivity** – Text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and translation tools remove barriers. Example: Microsoft Immersive Reader reads aloud, translates, and adjusts formatting for students with dyslexia or visual impairments.

9. **Collaborative Learning** – AI helps form study groups, moderate discussions, and track projects. Example: Kiddom manages virtual study groups and peer collaboration.

**Limitations & Considerations:**
- Student data privacy under FERPA must be protected
- Bias in training data can widen inequities; regular bias testing is essential
- AI should support, not replace, teachers; deep critical thinking still requires human instruction

**Recommendation:** Start with one high-value use case, pilot with real students, and expand based on evidence rather than hype.
</summary>

86% of education organizations now use generative AI, the highest adoption rate of any industry (Microsoft, 2025), Teachers using AI tools report reclaiming 5 to 10 hours a week for actual instruction, A 2025 randomized controlled trial in Nature Scientific Reports found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning on measured outcomes, The global AI in education market reached $7.57 billion in 2025 and is projected to hit $112 billion by 2034, The platforms that win use AI to support teachers, protect student data under FERPA, and watch for bias, rather than chasing novelty.

--- SOURCE 3: Artificial Intelligence in K–12 Schools ---
URL: https://livehandbook.org/k-12-education/miscellaneous/k-12-education/school-resources/artificial-intelligence-in-k%E2%80%9312-schools

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the AEFP Live Handbook (last updated August 2026) by Barnard, Fesler, and Loeb examines the state of AI in K-12 education. It argues that the most useful way to evaluate AI is to ask whether tools expand students' access to proven learning experiences—personalized instruction, complex problem-solving, meaningful collaboration, substantive discussion, and sustained relationships with educators.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Thin evidence base:** Of 800+ academic papers on AI in K-12 education, only 20 meet standards for strong causal inference. No high-quality causal studies exist on student-facing AI tools in U.S. K-12 classrooms. Most studies examine short-term performance rather than durable learning.

2. **AI as a mediator of learning experiences:** AI shapes learning through three pathways—student-facing interactions, educator support, and system-level organization. The central evaluative question is whether tools expand access to experiences that research identifies as important for development.

3. **Performance vs. proficiency gap:** A randomized study of high school math students found that those using a general-purpose chatbot performed worse on subsequent closed-book exams than students who practiced with no AI support, despite higher performance during practice. Students using a tutoring-style system (hints and guided reasoning) showed no difference on exams. Similar patterns appear across subjects.

4. **Design choices matter:** Systems that prompt explanation, reflection, and revision reinforce cognitive work for deeper learning. Systems that generate complete answers reduce cognitive work and learning. Guided reasoning tools improve independent problem-solving performance.

5. **Educator capacity:** A randomized experiment found teachers with ChatGPT spent less time preparing lessons while maintaining quality. AI tools that provide instructional feedback to teachers and tutors show early promise, with largest gains for lower-performing tutors.

**Research Priorities:** Long-term studies on durable learning outcomes, equity implications, system-level applications (scheduling, tutoring coordination), and AI-based assessment validity are needed. The article emphasizes that the evidence base is too thin to draw definitive conclusions, especially for U.S. K-12 settings.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from FifthRow Blog (published April 9, 2026) provides a comprehensive overview of AI integration in K-12 education globally since 2025. It covers regulatory developments, empirical evidence, risks, stakeholder perspectives, and best practices.

**Regulatory Landscape:** In the U.S., an April 2025 executive order established a national K-12 AI literacy strategy; by early 2026, over half of U.S. states had enacted AI policy guidance. China leads with a mandatory national AI curriculum. South Korea rolled out AI-enabled tutors. Europe's EU AI Act is still being debated with unclear practical impacts. Iceland launched a first-of-its-kind national AI pilot with Anthropic. No national bans on AI in K-12 education have been enacted since 2025.

**Empirical Evidence:** 85% of U.S. K-12 teachers and students report using AI, primarily for lesson planning, feedback, and data analysis. Two-thirds endorse AI's benefits for personalized learning and administrative tasks. Up to 75% of students report higher motivation in AI-enhanced settings. Academic improvements of 15–35% have been recorded in some studies. However, no long-term longitudinal studies exist on sustained impacts on higher-order cognitive skills. Most evidence comes from short-term interventions.

**Key Risks:** Privacy and security concerns are significant—only 11% of U.S. districts rigorously vet AI tools for data privacy. AI-generated deepfakes and false cheating accusations have caused harm. 72% of students would use generative AI for assignments, but only 17–22% receive instruction on responsible use. The digital divide persists, with AI adoption below 15% in most African and Latin American systems.

**Stakeholder Views:** Teacher attitudes are polarized—25% believe AI causes more harm than good, while 6% see clear net gains. Student enthusiasm (39%) lags behind teacher enthusiasm. Parent engagement is growing but under-researched.

**Best Practices:** Recommendations include targeted ongoing professional development, ethical/privacy guidelines that evolve with technology, digital infrastructure investment in under-resourced regions, institutional oversight on procurement, and maintaining human-in-the-loop approaches for high-stakes decisions.
</summary>

Written By [Rachel Lawler](/?author=680907fec74e1b63b898e333)

#### **The** [**Education Endowment Foundation**](/news/tag/EEF) **(EEF) is recruiting 450 primary school teachers to try out** [**Oak National Academy**](https://www.thenational.academy/)**’s artificial intelligence (AI)-powered lesson planning assistant.**

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/65a69e0c110a6977ead9741c/7a71cced-2500-42fc-ac80-13acdf4c4a81/Lesson+plan+Aila+EEF+Oak.jpg)

The new trial of Aila, Oak Academy’s [AI](/news/tag/AI)-powered lesson planning assistant, will be independently evaluated by the National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) and is expected to report in autumn 2026.

NFER is recruiting 450 Key Stage 2 teachers from 86 primary schools. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: one will be asked to use Aila for planning their lessons across all subjects and the other will be asked to continue with their lesson planning as standard.

The [trial](https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/projects-and-evaluation/projects/aila-teacher-choices-trial) will consider teacher workload, measuring the average time spent planning in one term and lesson quality, which will be assessed by an independent panel. The panel will not be told whether Aila was used in the lesson planning.

John Roberts, Interim CEO at Oak National Academy, explains: “AI has real potential to support in this area. But we only save teachers time if what it produces is reliable, safe and high-quality. Aila, our AI-powered lesson assistant, was purpose built by a team of expert teachers and engineers to help tackle this challenge.

“We’re really excited to put Aila to the test in this EEF trial, and learn what’s working and what could make it even more impactful for our teachers.”

Launched in 2024, Aila supports teachers to create personalized lesson plans and teaching resources tailored to the needs of their pupils. Aila aims to save time whilst supporting high-quality lesson planning and can cater to different literacy levels, or incorporate local examples depending on teacher needs.

The trial comes shortly after the [EEF shared research into teacher use of ChatGPT](/news/education-endowment-foundation-trials-chatgpt), which found a potential 31 percent reduction in lesson planning time for those using the software. The EEF also highlighted the need for additional research into how AI can be used to support teachers without lowering quality.

Emily Yeomans, co-CEO at The Education Endowment Foundation, says: “Our latest trial is an exciting opportunity to explore if generative AI tools like Aila can genuinely reduce workload without compromising the quality of teaching. As interest in AI continues to grow, it’s vital that we continue to build a clear and rigorous evidence base to guide how it’s used in classrooms.”

**How to use Aila**

Getting started with Aila is easy. By the end of the process, you’ll have created a lesson plan with teaching slides, quizzes, worksheets with practice tasks and more.

**Step one**

Visit [labs.thenational.academy](https://labs.thenational.academy/) to log in or create an account.

**Step two**

Tell Aila what you want to plan a lesson on. For example, you could try ‘key stage 3 history - the end of Roman Britain’ or ‘KS2 geography - features of a volcano’.

**Step three**

You’ll be guided through an intuitive step-by-step process to build your lesson plan and resources. Throughout this, you can ask Aila to adapt them to suit your needs. Aila can add additional case studies, make keywords easier or more challenging, change the context of your lesson, and so much more. **Step four**

Download the lesson plan and resources in editable formats. After you’ve downloaded them, you can continue to tweak the resources if you wish to, as you plan how you’ll deliver the lesson, with more time to focus here, thanks to Aila.
