args.summary:
This webpage from Panorama Education provides a comprehensive guide titled "AI in Education: The Ultimate Guide for K-12 District Leaders," authored by Sam DeFlitch. The guide addresses how artificial intelligence has shifted from experimental to essential in K-12 education, with the classroom of 2025 looking fundamentally different due to AI's integration into student learning and teacher planning.

Key statistics highlighted include: more than half of educators are incorporating AI into their work, nearly 60% of K-12 teachers now use AI tools (up significantly in the past year), student adoption among high school students jumped from 58% to 70% in one year, 81% of teachers believe AI should be part of basic education but fewer than half feel equipped to teach it, 54% of students use AI tools regularly, 96% of teachers report receiving no professional development on AI, and only 5% of superintendents have formal AI policies in place. Harvard experts have called AI "the biggest change to education in a thousand years."

The guide outlines benefits for three stakeholder groups: Students (personalized learning, real-time feedback, improved engagement, and digital literacy development), Teachers (more time for meaningful work, data clarity, creativity, and sustainable workloads), and Administrators (smarter resource allocation, consistent communication, strategic decision-making data, and streamlined reporting).

The content details AI use cases including lesson planning, MTSS and student support, feedback, attendance and early intervention, and family/staff communication. It presents a 9-step AI implementation strategy for districts: 1) Vision and Strategy, 2) Leadership and Support, 3) Infrastructure and Technology, 4) Data Privacy and Security (emphasizing FERPA and COPPA compliance), 5) Teacher Readiness and Professional Learning, 6) District Materials Integration, 7) Budget and Sustainability, 8) Community Engagement, and 9) Evaluation and Continuous Improvement.

The page promotes Panorama's own AI products (Panorama Solara, Solara with Class Companion, and Panorama Student Success) and offers a free "AI Roadmap for District Leaders" resource containing a buyer's guide, 100+ AI prompts for K-12, and an implementation infographic. Related articles cover the future of AI tutors, Panorama's acquisition of Class Companion, and how AI inspires student writing.

# Building AI Literacy in Pre-Service Teacher Education in Canada: A Case Study of Two Cohorts

## Authors

* Mohammed Estaiteyeh   Brock University   <https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8925-3108>
* Michael Mindzak   Brock University   <https://orcid.org/0009-0000-3186-0845>

## DOI:

 <https://doi.org/10.22329/jtl.v19i4.10041>

## Keywords:

 AI Literacy, Pre-Service Teachers

## Abstract

Preparing new teachers for the reality of artificial intelligence in education (AIEd) has become a pressing issue. This study was conducted in a Canadian teacher education program that offers a course on digital technologies incorporating a module on AIEd. This paper addresses two research questions: 1) What were teacher candidates’ (TCs’) experiences with the module on AIEd? and 2) What were TCs’ views on the use of AI by themselves and their students? The study employed an explanatory mixed methods design, combining quantitative and qualitative data gathered via a survey administered to TCs directly following their module completion. Participants were two cohorts of TCs (108 TCs in 2024 and 104 TCs in 2025). Findings show TCs’ satisfaction with the module as they highlighted three major benefits: offering useful teaching resources; more acceptance to explore the technology and embrace it critically; and promoting AI literacy. TCs expressed an inclination to use AI as teachers. However, they expressed negative views toward their students’ use of AI. Additionally, most TCs demonstrated developing levels of critical AI literacy, especially among the most recent cohort. This research offers insights into promoting TCs’ AI literacy and presents implications for teacher education research, practice, and policy.

## Author Biographies

### Mohammed Estaiteyeh, Brock University

**Mohammed Estaiteyeh, PhD** is an assistant professor of Digital Pedagogies and Technology Literacies in the Faculty of Education at Brock University, Canada. He is also the subject team leader for digital technology courses in the Teacher Education program. Dr. Estaiteyeh’s research focuses on educational technologies, teacher education, STEM education, and differentiated instruction.

### Michael Mindzak, Brock University

**Michael Mindzak, PhD** is an assistant professor in the Faculty of Education at Brock University, Canada. His research focuses on educational leadership and policy issues, the sociology of work and labour, as well as technology and education-futures in the contemporary period.

args.summary:
This academic article, published in the Journal of Teaching and Learning (Vol. 19 No. 4, 2025, Special Issue: AI and Machine Learning Intensifies Digital Transformation of Higher Education), examines AI literacy development in Canadian pre-service teacher education. Authors Mohammed Estaiteyeh and Michael Mindzak (both from Brock University) conducted a case study of two cohorts of teacher candidates (TCs) in a Canadian teacher education program offering a digital technologies course with an AI in education (AIEd) module.

The study addressed two research questions: 1) What were teacher candidates' experiences with the AIEd module? and 2) What were TCs' views on the use of AI by themselves and their students? Using an explanatory mixed methods design (quantitative and qualitative survey data collected immediately after module completion), the researchers surveyed 108 TCs in 2024 and 104 TCs in 2025 (212 total participants).

Key findings include: TCs expressed satisfaction with the module, highlighting three major benefits: (1) offering useful teaching resources, (2) increasing acceptance to explore the technology and embrace it critically, and (3) promoting AI literacy. TCs expressed an inclination to use AI as teachers but held negative views toward their students' use of AI. Most TCs demonstrated developing levels of critical AI literacy, particularly in the most recent (2025) cohort. The research offers insights into promoting TCs' AI literacy with implications for teacher education research, practice, and policy.

Author backgrounds: Dr. Estaiteyeh is an assistant professor of Digital Pedagogies and Technology Literacies, subject team leader for digital technology courses in the Teacher Education program, researching educational technologies, teacher education, STEM education, and differentiated instruction. Dr. Mindzak is an assistant professor researching educational leadership, policy, sociology of work, technology and education-futures.

The article includes an extensive reference list (80+ sources) covering AI literacy frameworks, generative AI in education, teacher AI competence, and related topics. Published October 22, 2025, the article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License (DOI: 10.22329/jtl.v19i4.10041).

# AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review

###### Abstract.

Even though AI literacy has emerged as a prominent education topic in the wake of generative AI, its definition remains vague. There is little consensus among researchers and practitioners on how to discuss and design AI literacy interventions.
The term has been used to describe both learning activities that train undergraduate students to use ChatGPT effectively and having kindergarten children interact with social robots. This paper applies an integrative review method to examine empirical and theoretical AI literacy studies published since 2020. In synthesizing the 124 reviewed studies, three ways to conceptualize literacy—functional, critical, and indirectly beneficial—and three perspectives on AI—technical detail, tool, and sociocultural—were identified, forming a framework that reflects the spectrum of how AI literacy is approached in practice. The framework highlights the need for more specialized terms within AI literacy discourse and indicates research gaps in certain AI literacy objectives.

###### Keywords:

## 1. Introduction

The rapid development of AI-based technologies brings about promising potentials and risks. Accordingly, education researchers and practitioners have increasingly turned to AI literacy as a promising learning objective. As AI would become more important, as the reasoning goes, people will need to be AI literate in order to adapt and participate. However, the definition of AI literacy remains vague. Researchers have used the term to describe learning interventions that are distinct in educational contexts, learning objectives, and types of AI technologies they use. Furthermore, the research of AI literacy is shifting significantly in the wake of generative AI. Thus, it is crucial to review the field and develop a conceptual framework that captures the diverse conceptualizations of AI literacy.

Indeed, the concept of AI literacy and recognition of its potential significance are well-established ([Touretzky et al. 2019](#bib.bib130); [Long and Magerko 2020](#bib.bib77)). One of the pioneering works by Touretzky et al. in 2019 laid out ‘five big ideas’ for the AI4K12 initiative: “computers perceive the world using sensors”, “agents maintain models/representations of the world and use them for reasoning”, “computers can learn from data”, “making agents interact with humans is a substantial challenge for AI developers”, and “AI applications can impact society in both positive and negative ways” ([Touretzky et al. 2019](#bib.bib130)). This paper had a major influence on subsequent AI literacy curriculum design. The next year, another prominent work by Long and Magerko defined AI literacy as “a set of competencies that enables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies; communicate and collaborate effectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace” ([Long and Magerko 2020](#bib.bib77)). However, even among these early definitions, there already were some differences, such as whether AI literacy is more about understanding the technical foundations of AI, the use of AI tools, or about critical evaluation of AI.

Further complicating the concept of AI literacy, the rise of publicly available generative AI tools shifted the landscape of AI almost overnight. The vast increase in ability of LLMs to perform a wide range of tasks, coupled with lowered barriers of access given their natural language interface, prompted researchers to rethink what future students could do with the help of AI ([Denny et al. 2023](#bib.bib27); [Finnie-Ansley et al. 2023](#bib.bib38); [Phung et al. 2023](#bib.bib96); [Prather et al. 2023](#bib.bib97); [Joshi et al. 2024](#bib.bib51)). Amidst reflections on how generative AI tools could reshape education objectives ([Kamoun et al. 2024](#bib.bib53); [Lau and Guo 2023](#bib.bib66); [Rahman and Watanobe 2023](#bib.bib99)), teaching AI literacy emerged as a potential path forward. The resulting proliferation of AI literacy research brought greater diversity to the field, resulting in a wide range of definitions of AI literacy.

AI has always been loosely defined, due to its history as a Computer Science branch that explored many different paradigms over time ([Haenlein and Kaplan 2019](#bib.bib42)). AI researchers have used AI to refer to search algorithms in the 50s, expert systems with symbolic knowledge representation and logical reasoning in the 80s, machine learning models trained on big data in the early 21st century, and now large language models ([Haenlein and Kaplan 2019](#bib.bib42)). Beyond its technical definitions, AI is applied in many technologies across different contexts. Thus, it cannot be understood merely as a technical discipline, but as sociotechnical systems ([Winner 1985](#bib.bib143)). When evaluated in this way, the use of AI has raised ethical concerns, including AI accountability for its decisions, latent biases, environmental costs, and privacy intrusions during training data collection ([Awad et al. 2018](#bib.bib7); [Buolamwini and Gebru 2018](#bib.bib16); [Selinger and Leong 2021](#bib.bib109)). Crucially, these sociocultural effects of AI are connected to, but distinct from understanding AI’s underlying technical mechanisms. Lastly, there are debates regarding the necessity of learning to use LLM-based generative AI tools, and their broader educational and labor implications ([Noy and Zhang 2023](#bib.bib92); [Peres et al. 2023](#bib.bib95)).

Literacy, while originally referring to the ability to read and write, has been adopted to describe various technology-related skill sets, including digital literacy, computational literacy, data literacy, among others ([Eshet 2004](#bib.bib34); [Gummer and Mandinach 2015](#bib.bib40); [diSessa 2018](#bib.bib29)). The usage of the term “literacy” comes with its own ambiguity. Even in the original context of reading and writing, there exists diverse perspectives and approaches. Some view literacy as a utilitarian labor skill while others emphasize its role in organizing political power ([Scribner 1984](#bib.bib107)). When applied to technological domains, “literacy” similarly entails contrasting ideas. For instance, Selber theorized that digital literacy is comprised of functional literacy, critical literacy, and rhetorical literacy (the ability to self-express using digital technologies), together forming digital multiliteracies ([Selber 2004](#bib.bib108)). Extending these ideas to AI technologies, researchers have considered both the skills of using AI technologies and understanding their broader sociocultural implications as literacy.

AI literacy is thus an umbrella term that can encompass very dissimilar interpretations that are equally valid.
Educators and scholars have labeled initiatives that have completely different pedagogical approaches and objectives as ‘AI literacy’, ranging from having kindergarteners interact with social robots to helping CS major undergraduate students practice prompt engineering for LLMs ([Su and Yang 2024](#bib.bib122); [Denny et al. 2024](#bib.bib28)). It is thus necessary to create a framework to organize the work, in order to create more precise terms and facilitate more effective and clear communications among researchers and practitioners.

This study aims to identify the connections across the seemingly distinct studies and construct a framework that can coherently capture the diversity of the field while remaining concise and legible. To achieve that, it includes an integrative review of 124 studies published between 2020 and 2024. By analyzing what forms of AI the studies address and what capabilities they seek to promote in students, this review derives common conceptualizations of AI literacy and presents them under a unified framework. The review includes AI literacy studies that both involve and do not involve generative AI technologies, so that it can identify emerging trends in the field. It is guided by the following research questions:

RQ1: How do researchers conceptualize and approach AI literacy in K-12 and higher education?

RQ2: What new trends have emerged in AI literacy research in K-12 and higher education in the wake of generative AI?

This study contributes to existing AI literacy work in three ways. 1) It updates prior AI literacy reviews and definitions by including new AI literacy studies published since the introduction of generative AI, 2) it delineates the boundaries of AI literacy to highlight the need for more precise and informative terms, and 3) by adapting established theories in digital literacy, it builds a unifying framework for AI literacy. This framework does not seek to supplant prior lists of competencies, but situates them in a broader theoretical landscape, so they can be in conversations with each other.
By capturing the current AI literacy discourse in a consistent framework, this paper seeks to promote more effective communication among researchers and practitioners by advocating for terms that can better describe their objectives and approaches than generic ‘AI literacy’.

## 2. Prior Work

### 2.1. AI literacy Frameworks and Reviews

Long and Magerko created the most influential framework by describing a set of seventeen competencies related to AI, ranging from understanding the steps in machine learning to critically interpreting data ([Long and Magerko 2020](#bib.bib77)). Their definition of AI literacy as “a set of competencies that enables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies; communicate and collaborate effectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace” is widely cited in empirical work on AI literacy interventions ([Long and Magerko 2020](#bib.bib77)). However, given that the work’s publication happened prior to the mainstream introduction of generative AI, it is in need of an update to reflect the current landscape.

Another set of reviews that are highly cited among AI literacy studies were conducted by a group of University of Hong Kong researchers. Their work included both high-level overviews of the conceptualization of AI literacy ([Ng et al. 2021a](#bib.bib86); [Ng et al. 2021b](#bib.bib87)) and reviews of empirical studies within various contexts, including K-12 education in the Asia-Pacific region ([Su et al. 2022](#bib.bib124)), early childhood ([Su et al. 2023](#bib.bib120)), and secondary education ([Ng et al. 2024a](#bib.bib89)). They proposed four aspects of AI literacy, “know and understand, use and apply, evaluate and create, and ethical issues”, define AI literacy as a series of competencies similar to those of Long and Magerko ([Long and Magerko 2020](#bib.bib77); [Ng et al. 2021b](#bib.bib87)). Their work on defining AI literacy was also conducted before the introduction of generative AI. This review seeks to augment their work by expanding our understanding of AI literacy beyond technical competencies and include interventions that emphasize empowerment and critical awareness surrounding AI.

There are several other review studies published since 2020 that examined AI literacy. Several reviews explicitly acknowledged the nascent and changing nature of AI literacy and the resulting difficulty in defining it ([Laupichler et al. 2022](#bib.bib69); [Benvenuti et al. 2023](#bib.bib11); [Tenório et al. 2023](#bib.bib127); [Lee and Kwon 2024](#bib.bib73)). Other reviews have proposed frameworks to capture the multitudes of AI literacy, including a twelve-faceted taxonomy synthesized from prominent AI concept classifications ([Shiri 2024](#bib.bib114)) and a competency-based framework similar to the work by Ng et al. ([Almatrafi et al. 2024](#bib.bib4)). While these taxonomies are comprehensive, they do not address educators’ radically different interpretations of AI literacy and the resulting implementations. This review’s proposed framework focuses on the conceptualizations of AI literacy, thus yielding insights into the motivations behind different AI literacy approaches.

Lastly, there are two papers that proposed learner-oriented frameworks that categorize AI literacy interventions based on learners’ assumed roles. They categorized learner roles as “the informed prosumer, the skilled user, and the expert creator” (prosumer means an individual who both consumes and produces) ([Schüller et al. 2023](#bib.bib106)) and “consumers, coworkers, collaborators, and creators” ([Faruqe et al. 2022](#bib.bib35)). These frameworks provide insights on how conceptualizing learners in different roles surrounding AI leads to different AI literacy approaches. My work seeks to complement these frameworks by exploring how these learner roles are shaped by interactions between perspectives on AI and perspectives on literacy.

### 2.2. Definitions of AI and Literacy

#### 2.2.1. Theories on AI

Complicating the matter of defining AI literacy, both constituent concepts of AI and literacy are complex and lack consensus definitions. To start with artificial intelligence, the term has shifted to encompass different technologies and paradigms since its conception in the 1950s ([Haenlein and Kaplan 2019](#bib.bib42)). In its technical sense, AI usually refers to machine learning and generative AI technologies in the reviewed studies. Older paradigms in AI, such as knowledge representation and reasoning, are almost never mentioned among the reviewed studies.

However, it is insufficient to understand AI only as a technical field. AI’s has been integrated into society to form sociotechnical systems, with social, cultural, and political implications ([Winner 1985](#bib.bib143)). To capture the full breadth of AI conceptualizations, this review draws from the Dagstuhl Triangle, which was originally developed in Germany to describe the objectives of teaching learners to interact with digital systems in general ([Brinda et al. 2016](#bib.bib15)). It involves three perspectives: the technological perspective of understanding how the digital system functions, the user-oriented perspective of how to use the digital system, and the sociocultural perspective of how the digital system interacts with society ([Michaeli et al. 2023](#bib.bib84)). Similar theoretical frameworks have been applied to AI literacy. For instance, Kong et al. expressed their AI literacy learning objectives in terms of ‘cognitive’, ‘affective’, and ‘sociocultural’ ([Kong et al. 2023b](#bib.bib63)). The Dagstuhl Triangle scaffolds the conceptual framework of this review, as the perspectives effectively capture the prominent ways AI literacy scholars discuss AI.

For the sake of clarity, inspired by the Dagstuhl Triangle, this review uses ‘technical detail perspective’ instead of ‘technological perspective’. The word ‘technological’ can be ambiguous, referring to either the technical details of a technology or its real world applications in technologies. The latter interpretation overlaps with the sociocultural perspective, which also covers the real world applications and implications of technologies. In contrast, the term ‘technical detail perspective’ more clearly emphasizes the underlying technical mechanisms. Similarly, this review uses ‘tool perspective’ instead of ‘user-oriented perspective’, because ‘tool’ concretely describes how users view AI.
Applying these perspectives, a programming course about machine learning follows a technical detail perspective of AI, an activity that teaches students how to use ChatGPT effectively views AI from a tool perspective, and a workshop that highlights the latent biases in facial recognition technologies and the resulting ethical concerns views AI through a sociocultural perspective.

#### 2.2.2. Theories on Literacy

While ‘AI’ is a concrete concept, ‘literacy’ is more abstract. ‘Literacy’ is borrowed from its original context of reading and writing, which adds some confusion. Even in its original meaning, literacy is complex, entailing different objectives and approaches given different perspectives ([Scribner 1984](#bib.bib107)). In her 1984 work, Scribner described literacy in three metaphors, as adaptation—the functional knowledge to perform reading and writing tasks as society requires, as power—being empowered to communicate and organize for community advancement, and as state of grace—self-improvement that signals greater social status, virtue, or intelligence ([Scribner 1984](#bib.bib107)). Scribner’s underlying perspectives on literacy—as functional knowledge, as empowerment and critical thinking, and as indirectly beneficial virtues—are valuable when making sense of the divergent motivations behind promoting AI literacy.

More closely related to AI literacy, there is an extensive body of literature on digital literacy and other technological literacies, such as data literacy ([Gummer and Mandinach 2015](#bib.bib40)) and computational literacy ([diSessa 2018](#bib.bib29)). Echoing Scribner’s three metaphors of literacy, Selber described an influential framework of digital multiliteracies, which includes functional, critical, and rhetorical literacies ([Selber 2004](#bib.bib108)). Selber’s functional literacy and critical literacy share significant similarities with Scribner’s first two metaphors, meaning functional skills of using digital technologies and critical evaluation of digital artifacts respectively ([Selber 2004](#bib.bib108)). Selber’s rhetorical literacy is a combination of functional and critical capabilities that enable individuals to create new digital media to express themselves ([Selber 2004](#bib.bib108)). Other digital literacy frameworks are more focused on listing fine-grained competencies ([Eshet 2004](#bib.bib34)), which reflects some of the aforementioned AI literacy reviews.

## 3. Integrative Review Methodology

### 3.1. Rationale

Since 2019, there has been a significant increase in the number of publications on AI literacy ([Lee and Kwon 2024](#bib.bib73); [Tenório et al. 2023](#bib.bib127)). However, the authors of these studies frequently acknowledge that AI literacy is not clearly defined. They typically adopt Long and Magerko’s definition despite seismic shifts in AI since then ([Almatrafi et al. 2024](#bib.bib4); [Lee and Kwon 2024](#bib.bib73); [Long and Magerko 2020](#bib.bib77)).

The lack of a clear definition and major developments in AI technologies pose several challenges to conducting a literature review on AI literacy. Even AI literacy is traditionally of interest to AI education researchers, the newfound popularity of Large Language Model (LLM) based tools has attracted research interest from other fields. These include human-computer interaction (HCI), computer science education, and learning sciences. There are also both a significant number of intervention studies and theoretical work aimed at defining AI literacy, as opposed to mostly intervention studies based on a theoretical consensus. Lastly, AI literacy intervention studies can have completely different learning objectives, proposed underlying mechanisms, and methodologies and study designs, even when controlling for student populations and school settings.

These factors render some review methodologies unsuitable, such as meta-analysis and realist synthesis, which are used to evaluate the effectiveness of specific interventions given their empirical evidence, or systematic review, which is used to adjudicate on specific research questions([Souza et al. 2010](#bib.bib118); [Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)). In contrast to these review methods, the integrative review method seeks to integrate both theoretical and empirical literature to generate new comprehensive insights of a topic, as opposed to adjudicating established positions ([Whittemore and Knafl 2005](#bib.bib140); [Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)). Integrative reviews build structured conceptual frameworks that capture holistic patterns across different communities of practice, instead of delving into individual findings ([Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)). Since AI literacy as a research field has vaguely defined boundaries, includes a large number of both theoretical and empirical works, and is studied by researchers across several fields, the integrative review method is the most suitable to review studies in the field.

An integrative review ensures rigor by identifying the connected but distinct discourses about a topic, constructing a conceptual structure to organize them, and generating new knowledge from this integration ([Torraco 2005](#bib.bib129); [Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)). Thus, the integrative review methodology is particularly suitable for addressing emerging topics and building new frameworks ([Torraco 2005](#bib.bib129)). This methodology has often been applied in nursing science, mental health research, and organization studies ([Torraco 2005](#bib.bib129)), and it can be used to manage the complexity and diversity of AI literacy studies.

### 3.2. Methodology

#### 3.2.1. Scoping and Problem Identification

Following guidance on conducting integrative reviews ([Whittemore and Knafl 2005](#bib.bib140); [Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)), the process begins with determining the purpose of the review and identifying the problem to be addressed. A purposive search was first conducted, which entails searching for studies to address a question without concerning about the balance or comprehensiveness of the search. To identify prominent recent AI literacy studies, the purposive search focused on studies from high-visibility venues, such as ICER, ITiSCE, and SIGCSE. This search revealed the wide range of conceptualizations of AI literacy and corresponding diverse interventions, from technical machine learning courses to critical evaluation of AI applications, and thus motivated the creation of a conceptual framework.

#### 3.2.2. Literature search

In order to fully integrate literature across different methodologies and fields, the literature search process of an integrative review aims to minimize bias towards any given field and seeks to be complete and balanced ([Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)). As such, the literature search stage applies a systematic and exhaustive search approach. To ensure balanced coverage of the fields relevant to AI literacy, two digital database were used—the Education Resources Information Center (ERIC) and Scopus, which includes literature from various venues affiliated with Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). The search term used covers various different terms associated with AI and literacy respectively, as shown in table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2.2. Literature search ‣ 3.2. Methodology ‣ 3. Integrative Review Methodology ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review"). To complement the results of searching digital databases, a second round of purposive search by tracing citations of the included studies was conducted.

| Category | Search Keywords |
| --- | --- |
| Terms related to AI | machine learning OR ML OR artificial intelligence OR AI OR large language model OR LLM OR ChatGPT |
| Terms related to Literacy | literacy OR competency |
| Logistical terms | published since 2020 AND in English AND in peer-reviewed publications |

The following set of inclusion and exclusion criteria helps determining whether a study is within the scope of this review:

The study should be a peer reviewed publication in journals or conference proceedings.

The study can be theoretical or empirical, including curriculum design, intervention study, developing AI literacy survey instruments, interviewing experts about their AI literacy definition, etc. This is to achieve the flexibility necessary for an integrative review.

The study should be published in English.

The study should be published after 2019.

The study clearly communicates its objectives and motivations for studying AI literacy, since this review focuses on conceptualizations rather than interventions.

The education setting of the study can be across the whole world. AI literacy is garnering interest and active research efforts from around the world, and AI literacy research can have diverse standpoints and approaches by different researchers. Thus, this criteria is to ensure balanced and just representation of their perspectives.

The education stage should be K-12 or undergraduate, thus excluding graduate schools, adult upskilling and reskilling, professional training, etc. Notably, teacher AI literacy is a popular topic among recently published studies and is relevant to the broader discussion of promoting AI literacy among students, but was deemed out of scope for this work.

The study should not involve discipline-specific AI literacy other than Computer Science. This excludes AI literacy specific to healthcare, business, English as a second language (ESL), etc. This criteria does not exclude general AI literacy, such as teaching AI literacy to non-CS major students.

The study should not be about AI-based learning, such as theorizing applications of LLM in education or building and testing AI-based tools. In other words, included literature should be about learning about AI, not learning with AI. As such, educational tools developed to promote AI literacy should be included.

The study should not be only measuring or observing students’ perception of AI, such as surveying student AI-usage behavior or understanding of AI. The study should involve teaching or promoting AI-related skills or awareness, or deriving AI literacy outcomes by consulting with students.

#### 3.2.3. Data Evaluation

![Refer to caption](2503.00079v2/fig_1_lit_search.jpg)

The literature search process is shown in figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.2.3. Data Evaluation ‣ 3.2. Methodology ‣ 3. Integrative Review Methodology ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review"). The initial search term on the digital databases yielded 1559 results on Scopus and 44 on ERIC. After removing duplicate results and reviewing the study titles and abstracts for relevance to the research topic, there remained 153 results from Scopus and 12 from ERIC. Next, studies were evaluated using the inclusion and exclusion criteria to yield 107 sources from Scopus and 9 from ERIC. Note that since the variable of interest for this review is AI literacy definitions and conceptualizations, the quality evaluation focused on whether the researchers properly communicated their study objectives, research questions, and motivations for studying AI literacy. Lastly, eight studies were added from the purposive search. One of them, Touretzky et al.’s Five Big Ideas in AI, was published in 2019, but is highly influential in AI literacy discourse and thus included ([Touretzky et al. 2019](#bib.bib130)).

#### 3.2.4. Data Extraction and Analysis

To address the research questions, the data extraction process focused on each included study’s statements regarding their conceptualization of AI literacy. These included their definition of the term, the studies they cite, their motivations and goals behind researching AI literacy and developing their intervention, and their research questions. The goal of data extraction and analysis of an integrative review is a thematic synthesis to reach a higher level of abstraction ([Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)). To that end, the process began with a bottom-up approach by coding the different themes of how AI and literacy are described and iteratively refined the codes to build a more concise conceptual framework. For instance, some earlier AI conceptualization codes include ‘machine learning’, ‘non-ML technical knowledge’, ‘LLM tools’, and ‘technological applications’. After solidifying the conceptual structure and identifying the theoretical framework of the Dagstuhl Triangle ([Brinda et al. 2016](#bib.bib15)), the data analysis shifted toward a more top-down approach. The theoretical frameworks were used update the codes to better support the abstracted conceptual structure ([Cronin and George 2023](#bib.bib25)).

The finalized codes include three ways to conceptualize literacy—-functional, critical, and indirectly beneficial—and three perspectives on AI—technical detail, tool, and sociocultural. Note that these codes are not mutually exclusive, and a study can conceptualize AI or literacy through multiple perspectives (e.g. a curriculum teaching both machine learning principles and the ethical quandaries of self-driving cars).

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies

| Author | Title | Year | Venue | Citation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Touretzky, D., Gardner-McCune, C., Martin, F., & Seehorn, D. | Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? | 2019 | AAAI | 615 |
| Long D.; Magerko B. | What is AI Literacy? Competencies and Design Considerations | 2020 | CHI | 512 |
| Ng D.T.K.; Leung J.K.L.; Chu S.K.W.; Qiao M.S. | Conceptualizing AI literacy: An exploratory review | 2021 | CAEAI | 239 |
| Zamfirescu-Pereira J.D.; Wong R.Y.; Hartmann B.; Yang Q. | Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts | 2023 | CHI | 157 |
| Lee I.; Ali S.; Zhang H.; Dipaola D.; Breazeal C. | Developing Middle School Students’ AI Literacy | 2021 | SIGCSE | 112 |
| Su J.; Zhong Y.; Ng D.T.K. | A meta-review of literature on educational approaches for teaching AI at the K-12 levels in the Asia-Pacific region | 2022 | CAEAI | 82 |
| Laupichler M.C.; Aster A.; Schirch J.; Raupach T. | Artificial intelligence literacy in higher and adult education: A scoping literature review | 2022 | CAEAI | 80 |
| Ng D.T.K.; Leung J.K.L.; Chu K.W.S.; Qiao M.S. | AI Literacy: Definition, Teaching, Evaluation and Ethical Issues | 2021 | ASIS&T | 78 |
| Kong, S. C., Cheung, W. M. Y., & Zhang, G. | Evaluating an Artificial Intelligence Literacy Programme for Developing University Students’ Conceptual Understanding, Literacy, Empowerment and Ethical Awareness | 2023 | ET&S | 67 |
| Su J.; Ng D.T.K.; Chu S.K.W. | Artificial Intelligence (AI) Literacy in Early Childhood Education: The Challenges and Opportunities | 2023 | CAEAI | 66 |

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies ‣ 4. Analysis ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review") lists the ten most cited studies among the reviewed studies. The two most cited studies by Touretzky et al. and Long & Magerko laid the foundations for defining AI literacy by listing skills and competencies that they deemed central to being AI literate ([Touretzky et al. 2019](#bib.bib130); [Long and Magerko 2020](#bib.bib77)). Five of the studies are literature reviews, covering AI literacy early childhood, K-12, post-secondary, and adult education contexts ([Ng et al. 2021b](#bib.bib87); [Su et al. 2022](#bib.bib124); [Laupichler et al. 2022](#bib.bib69); [Ng et al. 2021a](#bib.bib86); [Su et al. 2023](#bib.bib120)). However, all these reviews were conducted before the rise of generative AI, indicating a need for new reviews to update our understanding of the AI literacy research landscape. Three studies are empirical, discussing ’LLM-and-prompt literacy’ ([Zamfirescu-Pereira et al. 2023](#bib.bib147)), middle school AI literacy curriculum ([Lee et al. 2021](#bib.bib71)), and teaching machine learning to college non-CS major students ([Kong et al. 2023b](#bib.bib63)). The diversity of subject matter in these empirical studies demonstrates the complexity of AI literacy as a concept and highlights the need for a conceptual framework to organize them. The venues where these studies were published are similarly diverse, with both specialized education venues, such as SIGCSE and Computer & Education: Artificial Intelligence (CAEAI), and more general venues, such as CHI and Education Technology & Society (ET&S).

![Refer to caption](2503.00079v2/fig_2_publication.png)
![Refer to caption](2503.00079v2/fig_3_context.png)

Based on the number of reviewed studies published each year, several trends emerge. Note that the paper by Touretzky et al. is not included in the graphs, as it was included during purposive search due to its significant influence on the field, and not within in the main time range of this review. As shown in figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies ‣ 4. Analysis ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review"), there were significant increases every year except between 2021 and 2022. Note that the literature search was conducted in July 2024, so the data for 2024 is not complete. Despite that, the number of AI literacy publications in 2024 by July (48) already exceeded the total amount in 2023 (38). As shown in figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies ‣ 4. Analysis ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review"), while there was a steady increase in the number of AI literacy studies in K-12 contexts, there was a much sharper increase in studies in post-secondary contexts.

![Refer to caption](2503.00079v2/fig_4_framework.jpg)

To further analyze the studies, this review applies the conceptual framework in figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies ‣ 4. Analysis ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review") that includes three conceptualizations of AI—AI technical details, AI tools, and AI sociocultural impact—and three conceptualizations of literacy—functional literacy, critical literacy, and indirectly beneficial literacy. These conceptualizations are not mutually exclusive and can be freely combined. Breaking down the publications along these dimensions surfaces additional trends.

![Refer to caption](2503.00079v2/fig_5_AI.png)
![Refer to caption](2503.00079v2/fig_6_literacy.png)

As shown in figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies ‣ 4. Analysis ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review"), while there were comparable numbers of studies that discuss AI by focusing on its technical details and its sociocultural influences each year, the number of studies that discuss AI as tools increased rapidly since 2023, dwarfing the other perspectives by July of 2024. As this review will later discuss, this trend was driven by the proliferation of AI literacy studies that specifically teach the use of generative AI tools.

As for the literacy perspectives in figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies ‣ 4. Analysis ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review"), there were comparable numbers of studies with a functional literacy perspective and critical literacy perspective over the time range of this review. However, starting in 2023, there was also the emergence of discussing AI literacy in terms of its indirect benefits, such as increasing students’ interest in STEM, improving their computational thinking, or supporting their intrinsic motivation for studying CS.

![Refer to caption](2503.00079v2/fig_7_frequency.png)

Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.1. Overview of Reviewed Studies ‣ 4. Analysis ‣ AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review") shows the number of studies that include each combination of perspectives, which helps demonstrate how frequent different AI literacy approaches are studied. For instance, among the 88 studies that apply the functional literacy perspective, 63 of them also apply the AI technical detail perspective. This suggests that the relative popularity among reviewed studies to teach the technical fundamentals of AI, such as machine learning models, for functional stated goals, such as preparing students to become AI engineers. Other common approaches include pairing AI sociocultural perspective with critical literacy (e.g. teaching AI ethics to promote critical awareness regarding AI) and pairing AI tool perspective with functional literacy (e.g. teaching generative AI tool knowledge to ensure effective use). This graph also reveals notable research gaps. Relatively fewer studies combined AI tool perspective with either critical literacy or AI sociocultural perspective, indicating a need for further research on teaching responsible and critical use of AI tools.

In the following detailed analysis, the reviewed studies are organized along several dimensions. To begin with, studies are sorted based on whether their conceptualizations were established prior to generative AI, or emerged from the influence of generative AI. Note that this is not distinguished based on their publication time, as not all studies published after the public introduction of generative AI involved it. For instance, some studies published in 2024 continue to teach only machine learning curricula that do not mention generative AI (e.g. ([Bilstrup et al. 2024](#bib.bib13); [Lim et al. 2024](#bib.bib74))), while others follow the new trends of teaching ChatGPT usage (e.g. ([Chiu 2024](#bib.bib22))). As such, this review focuses more on identifying established and emerging conceptualizations and approaches in the wake of generative AI, rather than identifying specific watershed moments that distinguish studies published before and after.

Next, studies are sorted based on their educational context. For the purpose of this review, studies are divided broadly based on whether they focus on K-12 or post-secondary contexts. While there are variations in approaches to introduce AI literacy to high school students from those for elementary school students, there are more significant differences between K-12 and higher education that this review highlights.

Lastly, studies within a specific educational context are organized based on their perspectives on AI and literacy. Each category will focus on commonalities of studies with its specific combination of AI literacy perspectives and highlight exemplar papers.

### 4.2. Established AI Literacy Conceptualizations

Several notable conceptualizations of AI literacy studies were established before the introduction of generative AI and have received continued interest since. Studies that adopt these conceptualizations do not involve generative AI, even if they were published since 2023. There are numerous studies that introduced technical AI courses to K-12 settings with the stated objective of promoting AI literacy, even though similar courses in college CS major settings are almost never labeled as AI literacy (e.g. ([Buxton et al. 2024](#bib.bib17); [Baldoni et al. 2021](#bib.bib8); [Zammit et al. 2021](#bib.bib148))). In contrast, other studies specifically focus on raising awareness of AI ethics issues among K-12 students (e.g. ([Domínguez Figaredo and Stoyanovich 2023](#bib.bib30); [Solyst et al. 2023](#bib.bib115); [Schaper et al. 2020](#bib.bib105))). Another group of studies in K-12 settings use more comprehensive curricula that cover AI ethics and sociocultural implications in addition to AI technical details (e.g. ([Lee et al. 2021](#bib.bib71); [Zhang et al. 2023](#bib.bib149); [Williams et al. 2024](#bib.bib141))). Lastly, there are a few AI literacy studies conducted in post-secondary contexts without involving generative AI, but they are relatively rare (e.g. ([Kong et al. 2023b](#bib.bib63); [Aler Tubella et al. 2024](#bib.bib2))).

#### 4.2.1. Machine Learning for K-12

Twelve studies (out of 124, 10%) can be summarized as translating machine learning curricula that are traditionally taught in post-secondary settings to K-12 learners. Their contents are predominantly about machine learning principles and techniques, thus mostly framed from a technical detail perspective of AI. Two of these studies were published in 2020, constituting 50% of the reviewed studies from that year. Four were from 2021 (22% of that year’s studies), one from 2022 (7%), one from 2023 (3%), and four from 2024 by July, when the literature search was conducted (8%). The volume of research in this group remained low but stable.

Six of the studies focuses on functional literacy ([Buxton et al. 2024](#bib.bib17); [Dwivedi 2021](#bib.bib32); [Quiloan et al. 2023](#bib.bib98); [Toivonen et al. 2020](#bib.bib128); [Bilstrup et al. 2024](#bib.bib13); [Sanusi et al. 2024](#bib.bib104)). They extended the traditional perspective on AI as an academic branch of CS and adopted learning objectives that emphasize acquiring the skills and knowledge related to machine learning, such as implementing supervised learning algorithms to perform computer vision tasks ([Buxton et al. 2024](#bib.bib17)). Notably, all reviewed studies that use purely technical machine learning curricula were in K-12 settings, with three studies targeting elementary school students ([Dwivedi 2021](#bib.bib32); [Quiloan et al. 2023](#bib.bib98); [Toivonen et al. 2020](#bib.bib128)), two for middle school students ([Bilstrup et al. 2024](#bib.bib13); [Buxton et al. 2024](#bib.bib17)), and one for a broader age range between 3-13 ([Sanusi et al. 2024](#bib.bib104)). Studies about machine learning curricula in higher education are rarely labeled as AI literacy, likely due to CS major students not fitting the ‘literacy’ framing. In contrast, these reviewed studies typically justify offering machine learning curricula to younger learners by emphasizing the importance of AI in the future.

For instance, in the study by Buxton et al., they developed a curriculum that involved having 7-10 grade students train neural network-based image processing models that were then used to control autonomous robot cars ([Buxton et al. 2024](#bib.bib17)). They piloted the curriculum with twenty-nine students and found all student groups successfully completed the task ([Buxton et al. 2024](#bib.bib17)). When describing their study motivation, they cited how AI technology will transform future careers and K-12 educators need to prepare students for an ‘AI-driven society’ ([Buxton et al. 2024](#bib.bib17)). Note that despite being published in 2024, the authors made no mention of generative AI. The emphasis on adapting learners to potential future careers, along with the technical nature of the curriculum content, suggests a functional perspective on literacy. In other words, ‘literacy’ is taken to mean the ability to work with or work on AI/ML technologies, as opposed to critically evaluate them. Other researchers’ approaches include having children explore image recognition models using Google’s Teachable Machine ([Sanusi et al. 2024](#bib.bib104); [Toivonen et al. 2020](#bib.bib128); [Carney et al. 2020](#bib.bib18)), teaching Q-learning (a reinforcement learning algorithm) using a tool named PlayGrid ([Quiloan et al. 2023](#bib.bib98)), and developing a web-based online machine learning curriculum that teaches machine learning basics ([Bilstrup et al. 2024](#bib.bib13)).

Six additional studies used similar curricula that focused almost entirely on machine learning, but mentioned their motivation to help learners become critical and empowered through their technical knowledge in addition to functional literacy ([Baldoni et al. 2021](#bib.bib8); [Rodríguez-García et al. 2020](#bib.bib101); [Voulgari et al. 2021](#bib.bib136); [Zammit et al. 2021](#bib.bib148); [Sanusi et al. 2022](#bib.bib103); [Zhang et al. 2024b](#bib.bib151)). Several interventions aimed at elementary school learners used game-based learning tools to teach machine learning concepts while also promoting critical awareness of their ethical implications. These included studies that applied an embodied learning approach by include having students program a robot that has image process capabilities using a block-based programming language ([Baldoni et al. 2021](#bib.bib8)) or a game-based learning approach by developing a game where students train ‘ArtBot’ to categorize artworks based on supervised learning principles ([Zammit et al. 2021](#bib.bib148); [Voulgari et al. 2021](#bib.bib136)). An additional study developed an assessment named AI Literacy Concept Inventory Assessment based on the Developing AI Literacy curriculum (DAILy), which primarily tested students’ machine learning knowledge ([Zhang et al. 2024b](#bib.bib151)). While these studies also teach only machine learning concepts, they discuss learning objectives that promote students’ critical literacy regarding AI. For instance, in the most highly cited study in this group, Rodríguez-García et al. developed the LearningML platform that teaches exclusively ML algorithms, but stated their motivation was “to educate
critically thinking citizens able to understand technologies that
have a relevant impact on their lives” ([Rodríguez-García et al. 2020](#bib.bib101)). As another example, a study with Nigerian middle school learners implemented a technical machine learning curriculum, but emphasized bridging the gap between African AI education and the majority of AI literacy resources that are “Eastern and Western-centric” by considering “contextual and cultural values” to empower learners ([Sanusi et al. 2022](#bib.bib103)).

#### 4.2.2. AI Ethics in K-12

Beyond treating AI as a technical field, many scholars highlighted the importance of AI ethics and recognized AI’s sociocultural impact even before the rise of generative AI. While generative AI technologies represent the latest development, other machine learning applications have long been understood to have significant societal impact, such as facial recognition technologies gender and racial biases ([Buolamwini and Gebru 2018](#bib.bib16)), political polarization from social media algorithms ([Cho et al. 2020](#bib.bib23)), and misuses of machine learning models in legal systems and policing ([Angwin et al. 2016](#bib.bib5)). In response, another popular perspective in AI literacy research is viewing AI as sociotechnical systems and teaching learners about its sociocultural influences. Ten reviewed studies were in this category, with one (25% of reviewed studies that year) in 2020, three (20%) in 2022, four (11%) in 2023, and two (4%) in 2024 by July. Even though many of these studies were published after 2022, they do not involve generative AI.

From the sociocultural perspective of AI, researchers focus on educating learners about how AI becomes embedded in society and how they can participate as informed citizens. The majority of these studies adopt the critical literacy perspective. Their learning design approaches include having elementary school students write creative stories about solving real-world problems with AI ([Ng et al. 2022](#bib.bib88)), having students analyze automated decision-making systems and identify stakeholders to highlight accountability and fairness issues ([Domínguez Figaredo and Stoyanovich 2023](#bib.bib30); [Xie et al. 2022](#bib.bib144)), and inviting students to co-design AI technologies to express their visions of an AI-driven society and make them feel empowered ([Lee et al. 2022](#bib.bib70); [Solyst et al. 2023](#bib.bib115)). The emphasis of these studies on identifying AI’s social applications, stakeholders, and intentions behind their designs clearly highlight their sociocultural perspective on AI. There are also some effort at developing lecture-based curricula to teach AI ethics ([Choi et al. 2024](#bib.bib24); [Kong et al. 2024](#bib.bib60); [Krakowski et al. 2022](#bib.bib65)). Given these studies’ sociocultural focus, they usually spend little time on explaining the technical mechanisms of AI, instead often using open-ended discussion activities to engage students to think critically about how AI technologies interact with society. For example, Schaper et al. recruited twenty-three middle school students to a workshop, where they engaged with AI fairness and accountability issues by brainstorming and telling stories about having a robot president ([Schaper et al. 2020](#bib.bib105)). It is also worth noting that all these studies were conducted in K-12 settings, highlighting the gap in developing dedicated sociocultural AI or AI ethics learning activities for post-secondary settings.

Even though a focus on the sociocultural perspective of AI pairs well with critical literacy, one reviewed study adopted the functional literacy perspective, despite focusing on AI as sociotechnical systems. Hammerschmidt and Posegga developed a AI literacy taxonomy that specifically focuses on sociocultural AI, but described their motivation as “sociocultural AI literacy plays a significant role in enabling employees to engage with AI effectively at work” ([Hammerschmidt and Posegga 2021](#bib.bib43)).

#### 4.2.3. Comprehensive K-12 AI Curricula

Without involving generative AI, the most prevalent AI literacy curriculum design was to first introduce AI’s technical aspects, then use them to explain its sociocultural effects. Thirty-four studies (out of 124, 27%) were in this category. In contrast to the previous group adapting machine learning courses for K-12, many of these curricula expanded upon machine learning fundamentals with new learning activities that highlighted AI ethical issues and the sociocultural implications of AI technologies. Within the conceptual framework of this review, these studies have both technical detail and sociocultural perspectives of AI, and almost always included a critical perspective of literacy. args.summary:
This paper presents an integrative review of AI literacy in K-12 and higher education in the wake of generative AI. The study analyzes 124 empirical and theoretical AI literacy studies published between 2020 and 2024 (with searches conducted in July 2024), using the integrative review methodology because it allows for integrating both theoretical and empirical literature to generate new comprehensive insights.

**Key Findings and Framework:**
The review identifies a framework combining three ways to conceptualize literacy—functional, critical, and indirectly beneficial—and three perspectives on AI—technical detail, tool, and sociocultural. These conceptualizations are not mutually exclusive and can be freely combined. Key trends include:
- A significant increase in publications each year (2024 already had 48 by July, exceeding 2023's total of 38)
- Since 2023, studies discussing AI as tools increased rapidly, dwarfing technical detail and sociocultural perspectives
- Starting in 2023, there emerged discussion of AI literacy in terms of indirect benefits (e.g., increasing STEM interest, improving computational thinking)
- Among 88 functional literacy studies, 63 also applied the AI technical detail perspective
- Notable research gaps exist in combining AI tool perspective with critical literacy or sociocultural perspective (teaching responsible/critical use of AI tools)

**Study Background and Context:**
AI literacy remains vaguely defined despite its prominence. The term encompasses widely divergent interventions—from kindergarteners interacting with social robots to CS undergraduates practicing prompt engineering. Foundational works include Touretzky et al.'s 2019 'five big ideas' for AI4K12 and Long and Magerko's 2020 definition of AI literacy as "a set of competencies that enables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies; communicate and collaborate effectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace."

**Methodology:**
The literature search used ERIC and Scopus databases with terms related to AI (machine learning, artificial intelligence, LLM, ChatGPT) and literacy. Initial searches yielded 1,559 results from Scopus and 44 from ERIC; after applying inclusion/exclusion criteria, 107 sources from Scopus and 9 from ERIC were included, plus 8 from purposive search. Inclusion criteria covered peer-reviewed publications since 2020 in English, K-12 or undergraduate settings, and general (non-CS-discipline-specific) AI literacy, excluding AI-based learning (learning with AI rather than about AI).

**Categories of Established Studies:**
1. **Machine Learning for K-12** (12 studies, 10%): Translating ML curricula to K-12 learners, predominantly functional literacy with technical detail perspective (e.g., neural network-based image processing, Google's Teachable Machine, Q-learning with PlayGrid)
2. **AI Ethics in K-12** (10 studies): Focusing on AI's sociocultural impact, critical evaluation of AI's societal effects, fairness, accountability, and stakeholder analysis
3. **Comprehensive K-12 AI Curricula** (34 studies, 27%): The most prevalent design—introducing AI's technical aspects then explaining sociocultural effects, combining technical detail and sociocultural perspectives with critical literacy

**Notable Highlights:**
- All studies using purely technical ML curricula were in K-12 settings (not higher education, where such courses are rarely labeled as AI literacy)
- All AI ethics-focused studies were in K-12 settings, highlighting a gap in post-secondary sociocultural AI literacy
- Key trends driven by generative AI tool usage instruction emerged primarily since 2023

## Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how learning environments are designed and experienced, offering new possibilities for personalization, creativity, and immersive engagement. This systematic review synthesizes 43 empirical studies (Scopus, Web of Science) to examine the training needs and practices of primary and secondary education teachers for effective AI integration and overall professional development (PD). Following PRISMA guidelines, the review gathers teachers’ needs and practices related to AI integration, identifying key themes including training practices, teachers’ perceptions and attitudes, ongoing PD programs, multi-level support, AI literacy, and ethical and responsible use. The findings show that technical training alone is not sufficient, and that successful integration of AI requires a combination of pedagogical knowledge, positive attitudes, organizational support, and continuous training. Based on empirical data, a four-level, process-oriented PD framework is proposed, which bridges research with educational practice and offers practical guidance for the design of AI training interventions. Limitations and future research are discussed.

## 1. Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is already present in educational environments and is influencing the educational landscape, placing teachers at the center of these developments. However, the pivotal role of teachers as mediators and facilitators of interactions between students and AI tools as not been sufficiently explored [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B1-computers-15-00049),[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B2-computers-15-00049)]. Digital literacy in AI is essential for teachers to effectively integrate it into their teaching practices [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B3-computers-15-00049)], and professional development (PD) programs should explicitly link learning theories with the practical implementation of AI to successfully support this integration [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B4-computers-15-00049)]. AI literacy, which is also important for students’ learning, can enhance teachers’ ability to incorporate AI technologies into the learning process, and its development has become a priority in many countries [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B5-computers-15-00049)], following directives from international organizations, such as AI competency frameworks for teachers and students from United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B6-computers-15-00049)]. Building on the conceptualization of knowledge necessary for integrating emerging technologies into education [[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B7-computers-15-00049)], the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework underscores the dynamic interaction among technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge, which is critical for effective technology adoption [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B8-computers-15-00049)]. Recent extensions of this framework, such as Intelligent-TPACK [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B9-computers-15-00049)] and AI-TPACK [[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B10-computers-15-00049)], aim to align teacher competencies with the evolving demands of AI.

Nowadays, teachers are called to participate in AI PD programs, the majority of which focus on the utilization of continuously emerging AI applications. Such PD programs emerge in rapid succession, a phenomenon attributable both to economic incentives and to the growing demand for AI-based tools. Practical training that lacks pedagogical orientation does not ensure that teachers will ultimately integrate AI into classroom practice. Such approaches, unfortunately, do little to support the effective integration of AI into pedagogical design, nor do they contribute to the development of teachers’ pedagogical competence in relation to AI [[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B11-computers-15-00049)]. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, previous systematic reviews do not synthesize empirical evidence for tangible and immediately implementable AI-focused teacher PD. To cover this gap, this systematic review aims to investigate teachers’ views of AI and its implementation in teaching and learning processes by documenting their training needs as shaped by the rapidly evolving technological landscape. Furthermore, the collection of empirical evidence from the papers analyzed in this systematic review will inform the development of a process-oriented PD framework.

This systematic literature review investigates teachers’ training needs for AI use and corresponding PD in primary and secondary education. Training needs are conceptualized as the knowledge, skills, and support required for the pedagogically effective and ethical integration of AI in classroom practice. The focus on primary and secondary education reflects the developmental characteristics of these levels, where learning is structured and AI use is predominantly teacher-driven [[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B12-computers-15-00049)].

The findings of this study could serve the best interests of multiple stakeholders [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B13-computers-15-00049)]: teachers, who strengthen their professional resilience; school leaders, who enhance institutional performance; educational consultants, who organize training programs supporting teachers; and students, who benefit from AI-literate teachers capable of personalizing learning. The necessity of continuous PD for teachers across diverse domains, including AI integration, is well established. Consequently, AI competence should be embedded within PD programs by policymakers and educational leaders through the design of training initiatives that strengthen teachers’ knowledge and skills for the effective use of AI in school settings [[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B14-computers-15-00049)].

## 2. Previous Systematic Literature Reviews

In [Table A3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#table_body_display_computers-15-00049-t0A3), there is a list of previous systematic reviews referenced to in this section, along with their basic findings. Ref. [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B15-computers-15-00049)] systematically reviewed 67 articles related to AI-powered chatbots in education and highlighted enhancements in personalization and feedback, but also the need for PD training for teachers and the demand to implement measures for ethical use and the promotion of awareness among students. ChatGPT’s use in K-12 education was also investigated by ref. [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B16-computers-15-00049)], who synthesized 13 articles and performed strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis, underscoring the importance of thoughtful integration and highlighting the practices of teachers. Ethical and regulatory concerns of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in education were the focus of a systematic review of 53 peer-reviewed articles, which underlined that addressing these challenges can ensure responsible AI use [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B17-computers-15-00049)]. Additionally, on the use of GenAI in K-12 education, ref. [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B18-computers-15-00049)] conducted a systematic review with 197 studies, highlighting gaps in teachers’ PD and demonstrating the potential of AI to transform educational systems, while noting that dependency and ethical concerns need to be addressed. It also stated that teacher training, both pre-service and ongoing, must be collaborative, innovative, inclusive, and transparent to ensure the effectiveness of AI-enhanced education and to improve AI literacy among students [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B18-computers-15-00049)].

Another aspect of teacher education, human–machine dialogic learning, was the focus of ref. [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B19-computers-15-00049)] in their systematic review of 22 studies. They revealed three core elements: pedagogy, technological tools, and learning environment, three types of affordances: teaching skill and practice, learning experience and participation, and teaching interaction and communication, and four key aspects: dialogic purpose, dialogic medium, dialogic mode, and dialogic application [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B19-computers-15-00049)]. This review revolved around pre-service teacher education, but dialogic teaching aids can also be a critical tool for in-service teacher PD, allowing them to engage in collaborative conversations and self-reflection, enhance professional skills, and contribute to their professional growth and development [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B19-computers-15-00049)]. A systematic literature review of 24 papers by ref. [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B20-computers-15-00049)] provided guidance for the application of human-centered AI (HCAI) in policy formulation, teacher training, and the promotion of technology applications, emphasizing data privacy and ethical issues, algorithmic bias, and guidance for teachers to design personalized instruction with ongoing training at a practical level. In addition, ref. [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B21-computers-15-00049)] conducted a systematic review of 40 empirical studies unpacking key characteristics of human-centered AI and identifying essential stakeholders, underscoring the necessity of collaborative efforts to ensure that AI does not dehumanize learning and has sustainable and positive outcomes in education.

Regarding AI literacy, ref. [[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B22-computers-15-00049)], in a systematic review of 25 empirical studies, emphasized the critical construct of AI ethics in AI literacy and underscored the need for more diverse and innovative pedagogies, and the development of an inclusive AI literacy competency framework. Key themes identified in diverse conceptualizations of AI literacy include the development of curricula and literacy frameworks tailored to different educational levels [[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B22-computers-15-00049)]. As highlighted by ref. [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B23-computers-15-00049)] in a systematic review of 87 articles, the integration of AI literacy in K-12 education emerges as a critical priority—one that must cultivate not only technical competencies but also address the ethical dimensions of AI use. A systematic review of 22 studies on AI literacy in K-12 education underscored its absence in the context of teacher education and the research gap for factors influencing AI literacy among students and teachers, for whom AI literacy constitutes a core element of AI-enhanced learning [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B24-computers-15-00049)]. Evidence from in-service teachers indicates generally positive attitudes toward AI and given its critical role in facilitating the integration of AI-driven applications, AI literacy should be prioritized within PD initiatives [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B24-computers-15-00049)].

As for the establishment of clear guidelines and regulatory frameworks, it has been expressed that integrated mechanisms for ongoing assessment are required to balance technological progress and individual rights, through the collaboration of all stakeholders: policymakers, teachers, and technologists [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B17-computers-15-00049)]. Ref. [[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B25-computers-15-00049)] reviewed and classified AI competence frameworks for teachers, emphatically stating the need for both theoretical policy and teacher-driven approaches, while noting challenges such as the avoidance of redundancy with digital competency models. Furthermore, a systematic review of 14 publications on AI and PD emphasized significant gaps in AI PD programs regarding AI tool integration, underscoring the need to promote teachers’ teaching skills with AI rather than limiting PD programs to AI content alone [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B26-computers-15-00049)]. It also highlighted the significance of a guiding framework in AI PD, the need to balance pedagogical, content, and technological knowledge, and the gap in addressing ethical dimensions of AI technologies in teacher PD [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B26-computers-15-00049)]. AI PD features, formats, and active learning approaches should be further explored, while structured feedback and support mechanisms, practical application with specific AI-based tools, balance between technical expertise and pedagogical effectiveness, incorporation of acquired skills and knowledge in daily teaching routines, and the establishment of an evidence-based conceptual framework have a great impact on teacher outcomes, can inform stakeholders in decision-making, and are crucial for the design of AI PD [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B26-computers-15-00049)].

All previous systematic reviews agree on the benefits of AI [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B27-computers-15-00049)] and GenAI [[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B28-computers-15-00049)] such as personalization, accessibility, teaching and learning support, improved learning outcomes, flexibility, and enhanced interaction. They also recognize ethical challenges [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B27-computers-15-00049),[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B28-computers-15-00049)] like algorithmic bias, academic integrity, privacy, digital divide, lack of emotional intelligence, and dependence on technology. Some have proposed human-centered approaches to AI to promote equality and social justice through personalization and call for the integration of AI into curricula, the development of guidelines, and AI literacy. The emphasis is placed on pedagogical dimensions, the obligation for cooperation among the stakeholders involved, and the need for continuous teacher PD. Although they recognize the challenges of AI integration and the need for teacher PD, all these systematic reviews are limited in synthesizing empirical evidence for tangible and immediately implementable guidelines.

### Objective of This Study

According to the previous discussion, the objective of this study is to systematically review empirical studies to identify the training needs and practices of primary and secondary education teachers for efficient AI integration and overall PD.

## 3. Methods

This review adopts a qualitative thematic synthesis rather than an effectiveness-focused meta-analysis. To maintain the integrity of this systematic literature review, the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines ([Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#fig_body_display_computers-15-00049-f001)) [[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B29-computers-15-00049)] were followed. During identification, two of the most robust and rigorously validated databases of research—Scopus and Web of Science—both of which cover only peer-reviewed journals and provide extensive indexing across many disciplines, were used. Because each database includes unique journal content, the utilization of both reduced the potential to omit vital studies. Additionally, their combined search capability enables reproducible queries as per PRISMA standards, thereby enhancing methodological quality. Both databases offer comprehensive coverage within the topic area specific to this review and are globally recognized for containing high-quality scholarly content, thereby capturing a broad body of literature. [Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#table_body_display_computers-15-00049-t001) shows the search string queries performed across all databases in February 2025, targeting online literature produced up to the end of the last day of December 2024. A few articles were published in January 2025 but were already online in late December 2024 and were therefore included. The findings of previous systematic reviews focused on the positive aspects of using AI in the educational process [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B15-computers-15-00049),[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B16-computers-15-00049),[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B19-computers-15-00049)], but they also highlighted many challenges [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B17-computers-15-00049),[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B22-computers-15-00049),[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B23-computers-15-00049)], with most of them emphasizing the significant gap in teacher training, which could mitigate these difficulties [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B18-computers-15-00049),[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B20-computers-15-00049),[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B24-computers-15-00049),[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/1/49#B26-computers-15-00049)]. As a result, the search terms were set after screening the relevant systematic reviews and were similar or synonymous with “teacher training”, “professional development”, and terms related to the teachers’ educational levels that were the focus of our study.
