**Introduction**

India is positioning itself as a global AI powerhouse, with rapid growth across the sector. In 2024, 89% of new startups were AI-powered, and 87% of the enterprises are actively employing AI.  This is just the beginning – the Indian AI market is expected to grow at a rate of 25%-35% through 2027. To support this growth, India, which had an AI talent pool of 600,000-650,000 in 2024, needs over 1.25 million AI professionals by 2027, at a 15% CAGR, according to NASSCOM.

Various initiatives and policies of the government are addressing the monumental shift in the labour market disrupted by AI. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 recognises AI's potential for economic growth, solving educational challenges, enhancing teacher capabilities, and personalising learning – and emphasises the importance of AI-learning across all educational levels. The IndiaAI Mission (launched in March 2024) aims to make India a global AI leader by fostering innovation across government, institutions, startups, private sector, and academia.

Central to this strategy is democratising technology—ensuring AI tools and digital platforms reach remote villages, tribal areas, and underserved communities, bridging the digital divide. This comprehensive approach aligns with the **Viksit Bharat 2047** vision, positioning India as an inclusive global AI leader.

**National Education Policy 2020 on AI**

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image003QO2I.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image003QO2I.jpg)

The NEP acknowledges that AI, big data and machine learning will transform labour markets and drive innovation. To ensure that the youth can cope with these monumental shifts, the NEP emphasises the importance of learning about AI, computer science/data science, along with other subjects for multidisciplinary education.

The policy aims to equip students in these subjects for economic success and greater opportunities.

As education is in the Concurrent List, NEP 2020's recommendations influence both Union and State/Union Territory education policies and support the government's push to position India as a global AI leader.

**AI Initiatives in School Education**

The Ministry of Education has integrated AI into school curricula across India through CBSE and NCERT, starting with grades 9, under National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2023.

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image004PV75.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image004PV75.jpg)

Currently, CBSE offers a 15-hour AI skill module from Class VI onwards and AI as an optional subject in Classes IX-XII.   NCERT has incorporated AI content in Class XI Computer Science and Informatics Practices textbooks and used AI/ML to translate Grade 1-2 textbooks into 22 Indian languages.

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image00543OB.jpg) 

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image00543OB.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image006S6WB.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image006S6WB.jpg)

**AI-Courses for Students and Educators**

**DIKSHA Platform**

DIKSHA (Digital Infrastructure for Knowledge Sharing), a Ministry of Education initiative, uses AI for inclusivity: AI-based keyword search in videos and read-aloud feature for visually impaired students. The DIKSHA mobile app is available for teachers and also for students and parents. The app is loaded with engaging learning material that fits the needs of the prescribed school curriculum.

**SOAR Initiative**

The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship launched SOAR (Skilling for AI Readiness) to build AI awareness and skills for classes 6–12 students and educators. Program includes three 15-hour student modules and one 45-hour "AI for Educators" teacher module.

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image007LP0J.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image007LP0J.jpg)

"AI for Educators" Module:

The module trains teachers to understand AI curriculum and pedagogy, use AI tools effectively in classrooms, promote inclusivity for diverse learners, create educational AI projects, and teach responsible AI ethics.

**SWAYAM Platform**

The Ministry of Education's SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) platform offers 110+ free AI courses from IITs and IISc, with 41.2 lakh+ students enrolled.

**AI in Higher Education**

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image008SEEP.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image008SEEP.jpg)

**University Grants Commission (UGC):** The 2022 undergraduate curriculum includes AI, 3D machining, big data analysis, machine learning, drone technologies, and deep learning with applications in health, environment, and sustainable living.

**All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE):**

**Perplexity Partners with AICTE**

Perplexity, an AI-powered search engine has partnered with AICTE to provide support to 40 million students of 14,000 institutions through digital distribution via AICTE’s various communication channels, faculty training session and pilot launches in Centres of Excellence. There is also student access to the Perplexity website/app through institutional onboarding. The purpose of the project is for students to explore how AI tools can support research, innovation and real-world applications. This project aligns with the NEP’s emphasis on experiential learning.

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image0097U9Z.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image0097U9Z.jpg)

**IIT Madras Bharat Bodhan AI Conclave 2026**

Ministry of Education, Government of India, is inviting participants who have developed credible and research-backed AI solutions with demonstrated measurable outcomes to part in the IIT Madras Bharat Bodhan AI Conclave 2026 which will take place on February 12-13 in New Delhi. The call is open to solution providers, academic and research institutions, government bodies and other stakeholders from across India and abroad.

Submissions are invited across four priority verticals:

1. AI for School Education,

2. AI for Higher Education,

3. AI for Skilling and Workforce Readiness, and

4. AI Research and Deep Technology.

**Research and Development**

The government is supporting research and development in AI through various initiatives or schemes.

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image01054CE.jpg)

![](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/userfiles/image/image01054CE.jpg)

 IndiaAI and Meta established the **Center for Generative AI, Srijan (सृजन****)** at IIT Jodhpur and launched the **YuvAi Initiative** (with MeitY and AICTE) to advance open-source AI in India. The program targets **100,000 students and developers (aged 18-30)** over three years to develop AI solutions for healthcare, education, agriculture, smart cities, and financial inclusion.

**Key Components:**

1. Gen AI Resource Hub (courses, case studies, open datasets)

2. LLM for Young Developers Course (designed by Meta)

3. Master Training Activation Workshops (foundational AI concepts)

4. Unleash LLM Hackathons (mentoring, seed grants, market support for top ideas)

5. AI Innovation Accelerator (supporting 10 student-led startups with incubation and visibility)​.

**IndiaAI Mission’s Educational Goals**

IndiaAI Mission (launched in March 2024) is laying the foundation for India’s AI sector development. The initiative has been allocated a budget of ₹10,371.92 crore over five years. It provides computing infrastructure for developing AI models, creates datasets for training, and develops practical applications across sectors including education.

This PIB (Press Information Bureau) backgrounder, published 03 March 2026, outlines India's comprehensive AI education strategy aimed at building India's talent pipeline for global leadership, aligned with NEP 2020, the IndiaAI Mission, and the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision.

**Key Statistics:**
- In 2024, 89% of new startups were AI-powered and 87% of enterprises actively employ AI.
- Indian AI market expected to grow 25%-35% through 2027.
- India's AI talent pool was 600,000-650,000 in 2024; needs over 1.25 million AI professionals by 2027 (15% CAGR, per NASSCOM).

**Policy Framework:**
- NEP 2020 recognizes AI's potential for economic growth, teacher enhancement, and personalized learning; emphasizes AI-learning across all educational levels.
- IndiaAI Mission (launched March 2024) allocated ₹10,371.92 crore over five years.

**School Education:**
- Ministry of Education integrated AI into curricula via CBSE and NCERT starting Grades 9 (under NEP 2020 and NCF 2023).
- CBSE offers 15-hour AI skill module from Class VI and AI as optional subject in Classes IX-XII.
- NCERT incorporated AI content in Class XI Computer Science and Informatics Practices textbooks and used AI/ML to translate Grade 1-2 textbooks into 22 Indian languages.

**Platforms/Initiatives:**
- DIKSHA platform uses AI for inclusivity (keyword search, read-aloud for visually impaired).
- SOAR (Skilling for AI Readiness) by MSDE: three 15-hour student modules plus 45-hour "AI for Educators" teacher module for classes 6-12.
- SWAYAM platform offers 110+ free AI courses from IITs and IISc with 41.2 lakh+ students enrolled.
- Perplexity partnered with AICTE to support 40 million students across 14,000 institutions.
- IIT Madras Bharat Bodhan AI Conclave 2026 (Feb 12-13, New Delhi) invites submissions across four verticals: AI for School Education, Higher Education, Skilling and Workforce Readiness, and Research/Deep Technology.

**Research & Development:**
- IndiaAI and Meta established Center for Generative AI "Srijan" at IIT Jodhpur; YuvAi Initiative (with MeitY and AICTE) targeting 100,000 students/developers aged 18-30 over three years.
- Key components: Gen AI Resource Hub, LLM for Young Developers Course, Master Training Workshops, Unleash LLM Hackathons, AI Innovation Accelerator (10 student-led startups).
- AI applications for learning disabilities: Readabled (dyslexia), ScreenPlay (autism screening in ages 3-6), Voice Fusion AI, Jiveesha, Special Educator AI.
- DeepFlood project (IIT Delhi) for flood inundation mapping using SAR data and deep learning.
- Responsible AI projects at IIT Jodhpur (Machine Unlearning), IIT Roorkee (Synthetic Data), NIT Raipur (bias mitigation in healthcare), DIAT Pune (explainable/private AI), IIIT Delhi/IIT Dharwad (privacy-preserving models), IIIT Delhi (AI ethical certification), Civic Data Labs (ParakhAI auditing), Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham (Track-LLM governance).

**Skilling Programs (table summary):**
- PMKVY 4.0 (MSDE): 36,584 trained in AI as of June 30, 2025; 45% women; AI Career for Women Initiative (8,000 girls over 2 years).
- SkillSaksham (MSDE + Microsoft, MoU Aug 2024): 200 ITIs, 10,000+ candidates, 1,200 hours AI + 400 hours advanced AI training.
- iGOT Karmayogi Bharat: courses in AI, data analytics for government officials.
- FutureSkills PRIME (Govt + NASSCOM): 16.29 lakh+ enrolled; 500+ courses, 2,000+ digital pathways.
- YUVA AI For All (IndiaAI Mission): Free 4-4.5 hour foundational course, targeting 1 crore citizens.

The strategy extends beyond urban centers to tribal and aspirational districts, democratizing technology access, positioning India as an inclusive global AI leader embodying "Sarvajanam Hitaya, Sarvajanam Sukhaya" (Welfare for All, Happiness for All). Release ID: 2234853.

# **Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into School Curricula**

## **Prioritizing Equity and Literacy in India’s School Education Reforms**

## **Introduction**

As India accelerates toward a technology-driven future, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into school curricula has sparked both enthusiasm and apprehension. A recent opinion article in [The Indian Express](https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns/ai-in-schools-soar-artificial-intelligence-digital-divide-10326205/), titled “AI from Class III: Is India’s emphasis on technology in primary education a leap forward or one too soon?”, critiques the Ministry of Education’s announcement to embed AI education from Class III (ages 7-8) in the 2026-27 academic year. Authored by Professor V. Balakrishnan of Azim Premji University, the article questions the Skilling for AI Readiness (SOAR) initiative – launched in July 2025 and now active in nearly 18,000 CBSE-affiliated schools – which promises to equip young learners for global AI leadership while ostensibly bridging digital divides. Yet, this ambition collides with stark evidence from the [Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024](https://asercentre.org/aser-2024/), which reveals persistent deficits in foundational literacy and numeracy (FLN) among rural and government school students, with only 44.8% of Class V learners achieving basic reading proficiency.

This analysis synthesizes these concerns into a cohesive framework, advocating for a recalibrated approach that places FLN at the forefront before scaling AI. Drawing on developmental psychology, equity imperatives, and policy evaluations, it proposes reforms to Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), India’s cornerstone school education program, to ensure technology enhances rather than erodes inclusivity. Such perspectives resonate with the mission of [Education for All in India](https://educationforallinindia.com/), a dedicated platform illuminating pathways to universal quality education, particularly for marginalized communities (see ASER insights on the site).

## **The Perils of Premature AI Integration: Developmental and Equity Challenges**

Balakrishnan’s critique underscores a fundamental mismatch: introducing AI concepts – such as computer vision, natural language processing, and ethical frameworks – from primary grades presumes cognitive readiness that many children lack. At age eight, learners are typically in Piaget’s preoperational stage, excelling in concrete play but struggling with abstract systems like “AI project cycles” or “reinforcement learning,” as outlined in CBSE’s evolving curriculum. Without experiential anchors, these topics risk devolving into rote exercises, such as quiz questions on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) tied to AI, which demand maturity beyond most middle-schoolers’ grasp.

Compounding this is the digital chasm. SOAR’s rhetoric of “bridging divides” falters in a nation where 70% of rural schools lack functional computers and 40% of households endure unreliable internet, per recent [ICRIER analyses](https://icrier.org/pdf/State_of_India_Digital_Economy_Report_2024.pdf). For students from Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, or economically vulnerable backgrounds – disproportionately in government schools – AI exposure without device access becomes exclusionary theater. Balakrishnan’s mobile phone analogy illuminates this: we prioritize safe usage over engineering internals for children; similarly, AI should begin with ethical navigation, not algorithmic dissection.

ASER 2024 amplifies these inequities, documenting that just 23.4% of Class III government school students read at a Class II level – a modest post-pandemic uptick from 16.3% in 2022, yet woefully inadequate for NEP 2020’s 2026-27 FLN universality goal. In states like Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, where infrastructure lags, AI mandates could accelerate dropouts, as tech-deficient learners disengage further. [Education for All in India](https://educationforallinindia.com/) warns that unaddressed gaps transform innovation into privilege, urging offline proxies like community AI literacy hubs to democratize access.

Teacher preparedness exacerbates the issue. With only 15% of educators AI-fluent, per 2025 surveys, government schools – catering to 70% of enrollees – face a steep uphill. Initiatives like IIT Madras’s 64-hour SWAYAM courses offer promise, but scaling for 9 million teachers could span 2-3 years, amid NEP implementation strains. Partnerships with tech giants, such as IBM’s SkillsBuild for CBSE or OpenAI’s educator licenses via AICTE, skew urban, leaving rural voids unfilled.

## **ASER 2024’s Imperative: Building Literacy Foundations Before AI Horizons**

The ASER 2024 survey, encompassing 649,491 children across 17,997 rural villages, serves as an unflinching diagnostic: arithmetic lags mirror reading woes, with merely 25.5% of Class III students identifying numbers to 9. These foundational shortfalls – rooted in teacher absenteeism, multilingual barriers, and post-COVID disruptions – not only stall progression but sabotage AI’s purported benefits. [UNESCO’s 2025 monitoring report](https://www.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2025/09/ild-2025-factsheet.pdf) posits literacy as the “gateway” to digital agency; without it, AI tools yield biased or incomprehensible outputs, entrenching divides.

Prioritizing FLN is not reactionary but strategic. [NEP 2020](https://www.education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/NEP_Final_English_0.pdf)’s foundational stage (ages 3-8) devotes half its curriculum to play-infused basics, envisioning AI as a later augment – perhaps via adaptive phonics apps in regional languages post-80% proficiency. Recent pilots, like Rajasthan’s AI-tutored math program elevating 400,000 students’ outcomes, succeed precisely because they target post-FLN grades, achieving 96.4% Class X pass rates in select districts. Yet, national rollouts like CISCE’s 2025-26 robotics-AI infusion risk overreach without baselines.

In this light, AI’s 2025 surge – fueled by the Union Budget’s ₹500 crore for an [AI Centre of Excellence](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2181411) (details here) and AICTE’s “Year of AI” with free K-12 tools – demands guardrails. Platforms like Embibe’s adaptive assessments align with hybrid visions but must embed privacy safeguards, especially in data-scarce rural contexts.

## **Policy Reforms: Harmonizing AI with Equity Through Samagra Shiksha**

[Samagra Shiksha](https://samagra.education.gov.in/), buoyed by an estimated  ₹41,000 crore 2025 allocation, anchors these tensions, yet its digital provisions – recently updated for 1.2 lakh ICT labs – require FLN-conditional pivots. The Project Approval Board’s May 2025 revisions nod to AI but overlook sequencing.

### **Proposed Modifications**

* **Annual Planning Reorientation:** Dedicate 60% of SSA’s tech budget to FLN reinforcements (e.g., AI-enhanced vernacular readers), leveraging [UDISE+](https://udiseplus.gov.in) analytics for targeted rural interventions. [NIEPA’s](https://niepa..ac.in) AI dashboards could track progress, ensuring AI modules activate only at 70% district-level FLN thresholds.
* **Funding Innovations:** Carve a 20% AI sub-quota from equity streams, tied to teacher upskilling via SOAR’s 45-hour modules (full SOAR framework). Pilot device-sharing cooperatives in marginalized areas, audited socially as in Delhi’s 2025-26 trials, to preempt elitism.
* **Implementation Timeline:** Phase AI from Class VI upward post-2027 FLN audits, integrating ethics early to foster critical users, not passive consumers.

Expert voices temper optimism: [EY’s 2025 review](https://www.ey.com/en_in/insights/education/how-ai-is-activating-step-changes-in-indian-education) hails AI’s personalization potential but mandates infrastructure audits; [ORF](https://the-fln-hub.webflow.io/about) advocates predictive FLN tools; [UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/india/blog/ai-and-human-agency-indias-role-shaping-future-learning) stresses ethical safeguards. For comprehensive resources, consult the [ASER 2024 full report](https://asercentre.org/aser-2024/) and [Samagra Shiksha guidelines](https://samagra.education.gov.in/).

## **Concluding Observations**

India’s AI odyssey, from SOAR’s schoolroom infusions to budgetary CoEs, embodies visionary zeal – but at what cost to the foundational? Balakrishnan’s plea for “social wisdom” over haste finds echo in ASER’s data-driven clarion: literacy must precede algorithms to forge true equity. By recalibrating Samagra Shiksha toward sequenced, inclusive reforms, policymakers can transmute ambition into attainment, empowering every child – not just the connected few – for an AI-resilient tomorrow. As [Education for All in India](https://educationforallinindia.com/) articulates, sustainable progress blooms from roots nourished by basics, not rushed by trends. Let this be the pivot: foundations fortified, futures unlocked.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

args.summary:
This webpage from Education for All in India (a platform run by Prof. Arun C. Mehta, Ex-Head of EMIS Department, NIEPA) provides an analytical article on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Indian school curricula, specifically critiquing the Ministry of Education's plan to embed AI education from Class III (ages 7-8) starting in the 2026-27 academic year.

**Core Issues Addressed:**
- The article is based on a critical opinion piece by Professor V. Balakrishnan of Azim Premji University published in The Indian Express, which questions the "Skilling for AI Readiness (SOAR)" initiative (launched July 2025, active in ~18,000 CBSE-affiliated schools).
- Key developmental concern: Introducing abstract AI concepts (computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, "AI project cycles") to 8-year-olds who are in Piaget's preoperational stage of cognitive development creates a mismatch that risks devolving into rote exercises.
- Digital divide evidence: 70% of rural schools lack functional computers and 40% of households have unreliable internet (per ICRIER). Students from Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and economically vulnerable backgrounds are disproportionately excluded.
- Teacher preparedness: Only 15% of educators are AI-fluent (2025 surveys); scaling training for 9 million teachers could take 2-3 years.
- ASER 2024 data: Only 44.8% of Class V learners achieve basic reading proficiency; only 23.4% of Class III government school students read at a Class II level (up from 16.3% in 2022); only 25.5% of Class III students can identify numbers to 9. The survey covered 649,491 children across 17,997 rural villages.

**Policy Recommendations (Proposed Modifications to Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan):**
- Dedicate 60% of SSA's tech budget to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) reinforcements, with AI modules activating only at 70% district-level FLN thresholds.
- Carve a 20% AI sub-quota from equity streams tied to teacher upskilling via SOAR's 45-hour modules.
- Phase AI from Class VI upward post-2027 FLN audits, integrating ethics early.

**Key Context:**
- NEP 2020's foundational stage (ages 3-8) envisions AI as a later augment; the 2026-27 FLN universality goal is undermined by current deficits.
- Positive pilots cited: Rajasthan's AI-tutored math program elevated 400,000 students' outcomes (96.4% Class X pass rates in select districts) by targeting post-FLN grades.
- 2025 Union Budget allocated ₹500 crore for an AI Centre of Excellence; AICTE declared "Year of AI" with free K-12 tools.
- Samagra Shiksha has an estimated ₹41,000 crore 2025 allocation with digital provisions updated for 1.2 lakh ICT labs.

The article concludes by advocating for a recalibrated approach that prioritizes foundational literacy before scaling AI, arguing that "literacy must precede algorithms to forge true equity." Expert voices cited include EY, ORF, and UNICEF on ethical safeguards and infrastructure audits.

The page also includes website elements: guestbook testimonials, enrollment ratio data (UDISE+ 2024-25), a Kerala vs. Bihar education comparison dashboard, and contact information for Prof. Arun C. Mehta.

# Using AI to Protect Teaching Time and Improve Learning Quality in Indian Schools

Author : [Arpan Tulsyan](https://www.orfonline.org/people-expert/arpan-tulsyan)

##### [**Issue Briefs**](https://www.orfonline.org/content-type/issue-briefs)Published on **Jul 13, 2026** [Using Ai To Protect Teaching Time And Improve Learning Quality In Indian SchoolsPDF Download](https://www.orfonline.org/public/uploads/posts/pdf/20260714092224.pdf)   [Add as preferred on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=orfonline.org)

![share img](https://www.orfonline.org/public/images/share.png)

* [![Using Ai To Protect Teaching Time And Improve Learning Quality In Indian Schools](https://www.orfonline.org/public/img/twitter-x.png)](https://x.com/intent/post?text=Using+AI+to+Protect+Teaching+Time+and+Improve+Learning+Quality+in+Indian+Schools - https%3A%2F%2Fwww.orfonline.org%2Fresearch%2Fusing-ai-to-protect-teaching-time-and-improve-learning-quality-in-indian-schools&via=orfonline)

![ballistic missiles,Defense,Doctrine,North Korea,Nuclear,PLA,SLBM,Submarines](https://www.orfonline.org/public/uploads/posts/image/thumbnail/1784001135_IB-888.jpg) ![Using Ai To Protect Teaching Time And Improve Learning Quality In Indian Schools](https://www.orfonline.org/public/images/bg-image1.jpg)

# Using AI to Protect Teaching Time and Improve Learning Quality in Indian Schools

Teaching time is the most limited resource in India’s government school system, exacerbated by numerous unfilled vacancies, single-teacher institutions, multilingual classrooms, and a heavy load of administrative and scheme-related duties upon teachers. In addition, reforms under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2023, and the National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy (NIPUN) Bharat Mission have increased expectations from teachers, requiring them to shift towards competency-based, personalised instruction, along with cultivating critical thinking and future-ready skills among their students. This brief argues that a teacher-centric artificial intelligence (AI) support system can offer a pragmatic pathway to reclaim teaching time and improve instructional quality at scale. The analysis highlights key gaps in language coverage, curriculum alignment, system integration, teacher training, infrastructure, and administration. It concludes with a set of policy recommendations on how governments can embed AI into public systems to maximise teaching time, protect teacher agency, and advance equity.

**Attribution:**

Arpan Tulsyan, “Using AI to Protect Teaching Time and Improve Learning Quality in Indian Schools,” *ORF Issue Brief No. 888*, Observer Research Foundation, July 2026.

## Introduction:  India’s Teachers

India has 1.01 crore teachers instructing 24.69 crore students across 14.71 lakh government and private schools.[[1]](#_edn1) While there has been a steady increase in the number of teachers from 94,30,839 in 2018–19 to 1,01,22,420 in 2024–25,  the deficit persists.[[2]](#_edn2),[[3]](#_edn3) A Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education report in 2025 flagged nearly 10 lakh teacher vacancies across government schools, of which about 7.5 lakh are at the primary level.[[4]](#_edn4) Significant teacher vacancies exist in various states (see Figure 1).

**Figure 1: Teacher Vacancies in Schools in Select States**

**Source:** *Prepared by the author using data from NITI Aayog (2026)[[5]](#_edn5)*

Over one lakh schools across the country, catering to over 33 lakh students, continue to function with only one teacher, most of them in remote rural areas.[[6]](#_edn6) For instance, in Jharkhand, over 20 percent of schools have only a single teacher to handle over 50 students across multiple grades.

These structural deficits are compounded by the nature of teachers’ work. Over the past decade, several studies have documented how government schoolteachers devote a large share of their working hours to non-teaching tasks. A time-use analysis estimated that teachers in a typical government school spent about 23 hours per week on non-teaching activities; morning routines, co-curricular management, and mid-day-meal work alone accounted for nearly 14.5 hours.[[7]](#_edn7) Similarly, a study by the National University of Educational Planning and Administration (NUEPA), covering 28 districts across 17 states and Union Territories (UTs), found that teachers spend 33.91 percent of time on teaching-related activities such as planning and preparing lessons, remedial teaching, grading assessments, and supporting sports and co-curricular activities, and only 21.57 percent of the time actually teaching in classrooms. The remaining 44.52 percent of their time is lost in non-academic work.[[8]](#_edn8) Mid-day-meal-related activities alone took up an estimated two and a half to three hours of a teacher’s day.[[9]](#_edn9)

These operational burdens add to already challenging conditions such as large class sizes in several government schools, a multilingual student population, and complex rural–urban and socioeconomic disparities that impact learning outcomes. For instance, while the average pupil–teacher ratio (PTR) remains under 30 students per teacher (in accordance with the National Education Policy [NEP] norm), across all levels, there are pockets of overcrowding, with high classroom strength, especially in urban areas such as Delhi and Chandigarh, along with a parallel prevalence of single-teacher schools handling multiple grades in states like Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.[[10]](#_edn10)

Meanwhile, policy expectations from teachers are rising. Systemic reforms under NEP 2020[[11]](#_edn11) and the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2023[[12]](#_edn12) have asked teachers to shift towards competency-based personalised instruction, along with developing critical thinking and future-ready skills. Guidelines for the National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy (NIPUN) Bharat Mission also mention expanded roles for teachers in continuous assessment, remediation, community engagement, and home–school partnerships in the early grades, raising expectations from teachers already trying to manage with a severe lack of resources.[[13]](#_edn13)

International research indicates that technology could be helpful in such situations. A study on K-12[[a]](#_ftn1) teachers estimated that 20–40 percent of their workload, especially grading, administrative work, and lesson preparation, could be automated using existing tools. This could potentially free up about 13 hours per week for higher-value activities such as feedback, small-group instruction, and one-on-one mentoring.[[14]](#_edn14) However, this global estimate does not take into account India’s grim reality, where digital infrastructure and support are uneven across states and districts, classroom needs are highly context-specific, and many educational tools are not well adapted to multilingual, multi-grade, and low-resource environments. Moreover, AI tools will require careful design and governance to truly support teachers’ needs and reduce their workload, rather than increasing it by creating additional reporting and compliance tasks.

This issue brief addresses a central policy question: how can India strengthen its teacher-facing AI systems and improve their design, deployment, and governance to reduce non-teaching burdens and expand time for instruction, without weakening equity, trust, or teacher autonomy?

With large vacancies unlikely to close quickly, this brief argues that AI can help reduce teachers’ administrative and preparatory burden, freeing more of their limited time for classroom instruction, feedback, and student support. It also contends that teacher-facing AI should be geared towards the key goal of protecting teaching time and enhancing instructional capacity. This would reframe the narrative from AI replacing teachers to AI supporting them. AI can help teachers navigate multilingual instruction, differentiate material for first-generation learners, and maintain educational quality even for large classrooms—while preserving the human touch that remains central to effective learning.[[b]](#_ftn2)

## Why Teacher-Centric AI Is the Right Policy Frame

Global debates on artificial intelligence in education are often shaped by contexts vastly different from India’s. In high-income systems with relatively stable teacher supply, AI is usually discussed in terms of automation, efficiency gains, or even labour substitution. However, in the Indian context, AI’s policy value lies in augmentation: helping teachers manage complexity, reduce routine workload, and focus attention where human judgement matters most.

Framing ‘AI as an ally’ will strengthen local engagement and trust, unlike the resistance when AI tools are perceived as monitoring or job-threatening. Evidence from educational technology (EdTech) adoption studies in low- and middle-income countries demonstrates that teacher buy-in is the single strongest predictor of sustained use and impact.[[15]](#_edn15)

India’s policy framework for school education increasingly recognises the role of digital technologies and AI in improving learning outcomes, administrative efficiency, and system-level governance. NEP 2020 explicitly calls for using  technology to support teaching, learning, planning, assessment, and management across school education. It emphasises digital tools for lesson planning, adaptive learning, formative assessment, and administrative efficiency, while cautioning against technology-driven inequities.[[16]](#_edn16) However, NEP 2020 also underscores that technology must remain a means to empower teachers, not replace them, and that pedagogical judgement and human interaction remain central to schooling.

Positioning AI as teachers’ ally, therefore, reflects a realistic theory of change for Indian contexts, and offers the only scalable pathway consistent with NEP 2020’s human-centred vision of education. Moreover, a teacher-centric framing is also an equity strategy. AI systems that assist with differentiation, translation, and formative assessment can help teachers handle heterogeneous classrooms without lowering expectations. When designed for low-bandwidth environments and Indian languages, such tools can narrow instructional gaps and promote equity.

Despite a strong use case and policy alignment, teacher-centric implementation frameworks, capacity-building programmes, AI governance, and accountability systems are still evolving in India. The next section maps current initiatives and discusses some key challenges to large-scale adoption and deployment of AI as a systemic tool for teacher support.

## Existing Teacher-Facing AI Tools in India’s Schools

Teacher-facing AI in India is fast emerging as a set of tools supported by existing public digital infrastructure, especially Digital Infrastructure for Knowledge Sharing (DIKSHA), National Digital Education Architecture (NDEAR)-aligned registries, and state teacher-support ecosystems. Generative and language AI are beginning to find a place in teachers’ workflows for lesson planning, classroom material creation, multilingual mediation, formative assessment support, and administrative documentation. Table 1 groups existing AI tools for teachers by the core tasks they assist in, along with their salient features**.**

**Table 1: India’s Teacher-Facing AI**

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Category** | **AI Tool Examples** | **Uses for Teachers** | **Features** |
| Lesson Planning and Content Creation | Shiksha Copilot (Karnataka)[[17]](#_edn17); ChatGPT[[18]](#_edn18) (informal usage); TeachBetter.ai Lesson Planner[[19]](#_edn19) | Generates lesson plans, ideas, and learning materials in line with the curriculum. | Auto-drafts lesson outlines; suggests activities, videos, and quizzes; compiles online resources; provides examples in seconds rather than hours. Teachers can edit and adapt the AI-generated plans. |
| Multilingual and Localised Support | Sahayak AI assistant[[20]](#_edn20) (pilot for multi-grade rural classes); Bhashini[[21]](#_edn21) (Government of India’s language AI) | Helps teachers bridge language gaps and tailor content to local context. | Generates localised examples and stories in regional languages; translates or simplifies content into students’ mother tongues; provides text-to-speech or speech-to-text for low-literacy contexts. Culturally relevant analogies and hyper-local content make lessons more relatable. |
| Assessment and Grading Automation | AI quiz/worksheet generators (for example,  TeachBetter Quiz tool); Sahayak’s quiz generator; NIPUN Lakshya App for assessment of foundational learning in children | Reduces manual workload in creating and grading assessments. | Quickly creates multiple-choice quizzes and differentiated worksheets from input material. Some tools can suggest rubrics, check answers, and analyse common errors to give teachers insight into student performance. (High-stakes grading by AI is still nascent; teachers use AI output as drafts and review them for accuracy.) |
| Classroom Instruction Aids | AI teaching assistants (Sahayak’s instant Q&A and visuals); Speech-based tutors (‘Tara’ voice assistant for English reading)[[22]](#_edn22) | Assists in real-time teaching and student engagement. | AI chat interfaces answer teachers’ queries with simple explanations for tough concepts. Visual aid generators produce diagrams or charts that teachers can sketch on the board. Some AI tutors engage students in practice (for example, an English pronunciation bot), allowing the teacher to facilitate group work. These aids help manage multi-level classrooms by providing on-demand support to different learners. |
| Administrative and Routine Tasks | Facial recognition attendance (pilot projects in Karnataka and Bihar);[[23]](#_edn23) AI note-taker; report assistants | Automates non-teaching chores. | AI-based attendance systems can mark student or teacher attendance in seconds via face recognition, eliminating the need for prolonged roll call. Other AI tools can help draft routine documents, such as report cards, parent communication, or exam result summaries, based on data input. This reduces paperwork so that teachers can focus on instruction. |
| Professional Development | Shiksha Copilot’s teacher chatbot (general query mode); online AI training modules (DIKSHA–CIET courses) | Supports teachers’ learning and growth. | Some tools also serve as mentors, e.g., a chatbot that provides pedagogical tips or answers subject questions beyond the immediate lesson. Additionally, platforms like DIKSHA offer AI-in-education courses and certifications to train teachers to use AI effectively. This is an emerging category that aims to personalise teacher training and encourage reflective practice with AI feedback. |

**Source:** *Author's own, using sources as cited.*

Lesson planning and classroom resource generation are the fastest-growing AI use cases, and are being built especially with government-school realities in mind. For example, Shiksha Copilot is a curriculum-ingesting assistant designed to prepare lesson plans and activities, which reduces teachers’ time and effort while allowing them to customise content according to their classroom needs.[[24]](#_edn24) Evaluations show a measurable reduction in the time and effort teachers spend on record-keeping and lesson planning, reducing overall stress for the teacher. While English lesson plans generated by Shiksha Copilot showed particular accuracy, Kannada translations required extensive linguistic edits by teachers. However, they still find the tool useful and time-saving.[[25]](#_edn25)

Multilingual and local-language support apps are becoming more common, often offering language mediation by translating instructions, simplifying text, generating explanations in the students’ mother tongues, and producing bilingual worksheets. They are also growing in scale; for example, Bhashini covers 22 scheduled languages.[[26]](#_edn26)

A smaller but strategically important category is AI that helps teachers manage multi-grade instruction by generating parallel activities for different levels, suggesting sequencing of lesson activities, and proposing structures for group work. An early prototype is Sahayak, which can create a simple worksheet for Grade 3 and an advanced one for Grade 5 from the same textbook page, helping teachers achieve appropriate classroom differentiation with less effort.[[27]](#_edn27)

Teacher-facing AI that includes support for teachers to learn and apply AI responsibly has also been expanded through portals like DIKSHA and National Initiative for School Heads’ and Teachers’ Holistic Advancement (NISHTHA). A study on Delhi government schoolteachers found that over 80 percent of those surveyed had completed at least one NISHTHA module via DIKSHA. This demonstrates the channel’s wide reach, although daily DIKSHA usage remains low.[[28]](#_edn28)

An equally promising aspect is the ease of use, as many teacher-AI solutions are engineered to fit into existing workflows. For example, recognising that many teachers are more comfortable with messaging apps than complex new software, Shiksha Copilot can be accessed through a simple chatbot interface on WhatsApp, Telegram, or through a mobile app.[[29]](#_edn29) Likewise, offline functionality in tools like Sahayak addresses patchy connectivity in rural areas. Content packs and language models can be preloaded onto secure digital (SD) cards or low-cost smartphones, allowing AI features to work without internet. By meeting teachers where they are, be it basic Android phones, or voice inputs for those less comfortable typing, these AI tools increase their practical utility in government schools, which lowers the barrier to their adoption.[[30]](#_edn30),[[31]](#_edn31) Several initiatives also align content with the official curriculum by ingesting NCERT or state textbook portable document format (PDF). This also builds teacher trust since the AI’s suggestions map directly to their teaching curricula.

An emerging strength is the use of AI to support teachers’ own learning.[[32]](#_edn32)  According to the Ministry of Education, 14 lakh teachers directly benefited from DIKSHA e-courses by January 2023.[[33]](#_edn33) Studies have shown that teachers rate DIKSHA positively, with about two-thirds of them reporting improvement in the teaching process due to its engaging content.[[34]](#_edn34) This is particularly helpful for teachers in remote areas who may lack a rich peer network, thus boosting their confidence.[[35]](#_edn35) However, teacher training and preparedness in using such digital platforms vary widely. Deploying these tools, therefore, needs to be accompanied by training workshops and communities of practice. Combining AI with these will facilitate the creation of professional development networks and enhance teaching practices uniformly at scale.[[36]](#_edn36)

While available evidence suggests that teacher-facing AI tools in India show promise in improving efficiency and access to resources, rigorous evaluations of their impact on classroom practice and student learning remain limited. Most tools are still at the pilot stage and lack large-scale, independent assessment. Accordingly, effective adoption is contingent on teachers’ digital capacity, including training in AI-assisted workflows and institutional ‘safe-use’ policies. Moreover, in multi-grade and single-teacher settings, AI tools should support simultaneous planning across grade levels rather than single-grade optimisation. This is discussed in the next section.

## Gaps and Limitations

While teacher-facing AI in India shows potential, several key gaps are preventing current models from fully addressing day-to-day classroom needs.

### Weak Coverage of Regional Languages and Local Dialects

While AI models support widely spoken Indian languages, like Hindi or Kannada, tribal languages or regional dialects are still unsupported. Even in supported languages, generative text may occasionally have errors or contain unnatural phrasing. Research highlights gaps in training data, uneven linguistic representation, and weak coverage of oral and dialectal variants. While national initiatives such as Bhashini and AI4Bharat are expanding multilingual datasets and models, substantial development is needed to ensure that AI systems can reliably support the full linguistic diversity of India’s classrooms.[[37]](#_edn37)

### Hallucinations, Misalignment, and Content Errors

Ensuring that AI-generated content is accurate, grade-appropriate, and aligned with official curriculum remains a challenge. Instances of hallucinations or factual errors in AI outputs are common, especially when prompting for specialised topics.[[38]](#_edn38) In a school setting, this places an additional verification burden on teachers, who must carefully review and edit AI outputs before classroom use. Moreover, if curricula are updated by the state board, the AI’s knowledge might lag behind or not align with prescribed learning outcomes. Early pilot data suggests that when teachers encounter repeated misalignment or errors, trust in the tool declines and usage drops. Sustained adoption, therefore, depends less on generic AI capability and more on robust curriculum governance, regular data updates, and ‘teacher-in-the-loop’ validation[[c]](#_ftn3) mechanisms.

### Gaps in Teacher Training and AI Literacy

Although AI use in education is expanding rapidly, teacher usage capacity has not developed proportionately. A survey by the Centre for Teacher Accreditation (CENTA) shows that although 70 percent of teachers used AI in the classroom and 67 percent of Indian teachers rated themselves as confident in AI, only 57 percent could spot basic AI misconceptions. This demonstrates a critical need for better teacher training.[[39]](#_edn39) This gap leads to some teachers misusing AI tools (for instance, blindly trusting their output) or underutilising them (sticking to the basic features), limiting their impact.

### Limited Integration in School Systems

While AI adoption is increasing, several tools remain at the pilot stage and have not yet been deeply integrated into public education systems or school routines. For example, if a teacher creates a lesson plan with Shiksha Copilot, it is not easily shareable on official platforms, such as teacher portals or content repositories, to receive mentor or peer feedback. Administrative data systems, including management information systems (MIS),  currently do not interface with these AI tools.[[40]](#_edn40) This lack of integration means that AI currently remains a parallel product for enthusiastic teachers rather than a mainstream institutional resource. Scaling AI beyond the pilot stage thus requires an ecosystem approach that integrates AI assistants into existing educational portals, MIS, or workflow apps.[[41]](#_edn41)

### Unequal Access Due to Weak Infrastructure and Poor Maintenance

Even when teacher-facing AI is well designed, its real-world adoption depends on other infrastructure, particularly device availability and stable connectivity. Resource-constrained schools, with a limited number of devices shared among staff, intermittent internet, and weak maintenance support, cannot rely on cloud-heavy AI features. This creates equity risks as better-resourced schools extract more value from AI, while under-resourced schools find it unreliable or unusable.[[42]](#_edn42) Moreover, generative AI can introduce new cost points (such as server/application programming interface (API) costs, usage caps after free trials, procurement and support charges) that are not routinely part of school budgets.

Therefore, AI tools should be designed for offline or low-bandwidth use and included within routine ICT provisioning for schools through subsidised access, device availability, connectivity support, and procurement through existing education technology budgets. If not, they may add another layer of inequality to an already weak infrastructure.

### Privacy, Security, and Ethical Concerns

The introduction of data-driven AI tools raises concerns about privacy and ethics, especially when children’s data, teacher performance data, or biometric data enter the loop. For instance, facial recognition attendance systems, implemented to save teachers’ time, have sparked worries of surveillance and data misuse.[[43]](#_edn43) Teachers and parents may be reluctant to use such tools if student data (performance, personal details) will be uploaded to external AI systems without clear safeguards. Additionally, AI bias is a concern: if models are trained on data that does not adequately represent rural Indian classrooms, their suggestions might not be culturally appropriate or be less helpful to certain student groups.

While India notified rules for personal data protection under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules, 2025,[[44]](#_edn44) implementation is phased. Current deployments rely on rudimentary safeguards (such as basic content filters), and require stronger privacy protection and ethical guidelines.

### Underdeveloped In-Class Use

So far, most of the AI usage by teachers is for backstage tasks, like planning, grading, and preparing worksheets.[[45]](#_edn45) Few tools directly support live classroom instruction, such as real-time multilingual translation, or handling a small study group while the teacher works with another. The interactive classroom dimension therefore remains underdeveloped. Teachers continue to navigate large classes with diverse learning needs and limited one-on-one time for students, problems that intelligent tutoring systems or formative assessment aids could help with, which current Indian tools have barely touched. The next wave of innovation should focus on working with low connectivity and providing in-classroom AI support that operates in real time alongside the teacher. Without this shift, AI may reduce preparation time but will not address the core instructional constraints of large, heterogeneous classrooms.

In summary, while pilots have shown the feasibility of teacher-facing AI assistants, to scale them, language and content quality issues must be overcome, teachers need the necessary skills and infrastructure, and proper safeguards should be introduced.

## Recommendations for Strengthening the Teacher-Facing AIED Ecosystem

Based on the preceding analysis, this section provides seven recommendations to realise AI’s potential as an ally to India’s 10 million teachers, using a strategic and context-sensitive approach.

### Co-Create AI Solutions with Teachers

Teachers from diverse regions (rural/urban, various states) should be consulted through teacher hackathons and pilot feedback loops right from the design and iteration phase of AI tools. Their feedback on lesson relevance, language use, and classroom practicality would be invaluable. This would also help teachers develop ownership and ensure that the solutions reflect classroom realities.

### Ensure Equity and Access Safeguards

The government and its technology partners should ensure access for all teachers, not just those in well-resourced schools. This requires investing in basic infrastructure (hardware devices, power backup, stable internet connection) in schools and providing offline capabilities (downloadable AI packs) where possible. Equity also means supporting local languages and expanding initiatives like Bhashini to improve AI proficiency in local dialects. Moreover, AI pricing models must be affordable or free for government and low-fee schools. Entering public–private partnerships could subsidise AI assistant tools (similar to how DIKSHA content is free) to avoid a digital divide in AI adoption.

### Scale Successful Models in Other States

Proven interventions like Shiksha Copilot should be replicated and adapted beyond their pilot state. The Ministry of Education can facilitate knowledge-sharing between states—for example, Karnataka can share its curriculum-grounding approach and training module with other SCERTs. A ‘National Teacher AI Toolkit’ could be developed, comprising recommended tools for lesson planning, grading, and other such tasks, which states can customise to their curriculum. Crucially, integration with existing platforms is needed: for instance, embedding AI assistants within DIKSHA or state teacher portals so that usage becomes seamless and officially endorsed. Scaling up also requires capacity building at all levels, training not just teachers but school leaders and district officials on how to support and monitor the effective use of AI in teaching.

### Align AI with NEP 2020 Goals

AI initiatives must advance NEP 2020 goals. They should adapt and strengthen content according to learners’ grades and development levels. Besides being multilingual, AI tools should promote experiential and competency-based learning, helping teachers generate project ideas, real-life examples, and higher-order questions to move beyond rote learning.

### Protect Teacher Agency

It is vital to design and communicate AI around the principle that the teacher remains central to the learning system**.** AI should handle routine tasks (such as generating a 50-question quiz) based on the teacher’s prompts, freeing teachers to teach, interact with, and mentor learners, and also focus on their own professional growth. All training programmes and tool designs should emphasise that AI outputs are suggestions to be finalised as per the teacher’s judgement. This preserves the teacher’s autonomy and expertise. Guidelines should mention teacher review/edit of AI-generated content, integrating a ‘human-in-the-loop’ check.

### Establish Ethical AI and Data Governance

Strong data privacy and bias reduction policies in education need to be implemented. The government could develop education-specific protection guidelines to complement the DPDP Act, 2023. AI tools must comply with rules such as content appropriateness, non-discrimination, and explainability, including a clear disclosure when suggestions are AI-generated and that teachers need to review them before use. For example, any automated attendance or surveillance tool should be vetted for privacy protection and have an opt-out provision. The capacity of educational institutions and teachers must be developed to follow these guidelines, identify ethical issues, and take appropriate action.

Proactively addressing these issues will ensure that AI adoption does not inadvertently harm or lose the trust of the very people it is meant to help.

## Conclusion

The main challenge of India’s school education is not teacher motivation or capacity, but structural constraints on teaching time. Persistent vacancies, single-teacher schools, large and heterogeneous classrooms, and the accumulation of non-teaching duties have steadily eroded the time teachers can devote to instruction, feedback, and student engagement. At a time when national educational reforms place more demands on teachers, it is crucial to address the teaching-time bottleneck so that these ambitions are realised.

This brief argued that teacher-facing AI, when framed and governed as an ally rather than a substitute, offers a realistic and scalable pathway to reclaim teaching time. Pilot projects demonstrate that AI can meaningfully reduce lesson-preparation effort, support multilingual mediation, assist with formative assessments, and ease routine documentation—provided the tools are curriculum-aligned, low-bandwidth, and embedded within public digital infrastructure. However, without deliberate policy design, AI risks becoming another layer of compliance, deepening inequities between well-resourced and under-resourced schools, or undermining teacher trust.

The policy imperative, therefore, is not faster but more strategic and well-governed adoption. Teacher-centric AI must be integrated into existing systems, co-created with educators, supported by sustained professional development, and governed by strong privacy and ethical safeguards. In this way, AI can help India’s government schools do what matters most: give teachers more time to teach well and give every child a better chance to learn. AI can, therefore, become not a technological fix, but a strategic enabler of a more humane, equitable, and effective education system.

args.summary:
This ORF Issue Brief No. 888 (published July 2026), authored by Arpan Tulsyan (Senior Fellow, Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, Observer Research Foundation), argues that a teacher-centric artificial intelligence (AI) support system offers a pragmatic pathway to reclaim teaching time and improve instructional quality in India's government schools. 

KEY CONTEXT/STATISTICS:
- India has 1.01 crore (10.1 million) teachers instructing 24.69 crore (246.9 million) students across 14.71 lakh schools.
- A 2025 Parliamentary Standing Committee report flagged nearly 10 lakh teacher vacancies in government schools, ~7.5 lakh at primary level.
- Over one lakh schools (serving over 33 lakh students) function with only one teacher, mostly in remote rural areas; in Jharkhand, over 20% of schools have a single teacher managing 50+ students across grades.
- A time-use study found teachers spend ~23 hours/week on non-teaching activities; morning routines, co-curricular management, and mid-day-meal work alone account for ~14.5 hours.
- A NUEPA study across 28 districts in 17 states found teachers spend only 21.57% of time actually teaching; 33.91% on teaching-related activities; 44.52% lost to non-academic work.
- Mid-day-meal activities take 2.5–3 hours of a teacher's day.
- Education reforms under NEP 2020, NCF 2023, and NIPUN Bharat Mission have raised expectations for competency-based, personalised instruction.

ARGUMENT: With vacancies unlikely to close quickly, AI can reduce teachers' administrative and preparatory burden, freeing time for instruction. AI should be framed as an "ally" (augmentation), not a replacement/surveillance tool, since teacher buy-in is the strongest predictor of sustained EdTech adoption in low/middle-income countries. This reframing is consistent with NEP 2020's human-centred vision.

EXISTING TOOLS (Table 1): Categories include lesson planning/content creation (Shiksha Copilot in Karnataka, ChatGPT informal use, TeachBetter.ai); multilingual/localised support (Sahayak AI, Bhashini covering 22 scheduled languages); assessment/grading automation (TeachBetter quiz tool, NIPUN Lakshya App); classroom instruction aids (Tara voice assistant for English); administrative tasks (facial recognition attendance pilots in Karnataka and Bihar, AI note-takers); and professional development (DIKSHA–CIET courses, Shiksha Copilot chatbot). Tools use accessible interfaces (WhatsApp/Telegram) and offline capabilities for low connectivity.

GAPS LIMITING ADOPTION:
1. Weak coverage of regional languages/dialects (tribal languages unsupported; even supported languages show errors)
2. Hallucinations, misalignment, content errors (curriculum alignment issues; repeated errors erode teacher trust)
3. Gaps in teacher training/AI literacy (CENTA survey: 70% used AI in class, 67% confident, but only 57% could spot basic AI misconceptions)
4. Limited integration with school systems (AI tools not shareable on official portals; MIS doesn't interface with AI tools; mainly pilot-stage)
5. Unequal access due to weak infrastructure (device shortages, intermittent connectivity, equity risks; new cost points from API/cloud)
6. Privacy, security, ethical concerns (facial recognition surveillance worries; AI bias; DPDP Rules 2025 implementation is phased)
7. Underdeveloped in-class use (most usage is "backstage" planning/grading; few tools support real-time classroom instruction)

SEVEN RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Co-create AI solutions with teachers (hackathons, pilot feedback loops)
2. Ensure equity and access safeguards (infrastructure investment, offline capabilities, local language support, subsidised/public-private pricing)
3. Scale successful models in other states (replicate Shiksha Copilot; develop a 'National Teacher AI Toolkit'; integrate with DIKSHA/teacher portals)
4. Align AI with NEP 2020 goals (competency-based, experiential learning; move beyond rote learning)
5. Protect teacher agency ('human-in-the-loop' checks; AI outputs as suggestions finalised by teachers)
6. Establish ethical AI and data governance (education-specific guidelines complementing DPDP Act, 2023; opt-out provisions for surveillance)

CONCLUSION: The core challenge is not teacher motivation/capacity but structural constraints on teaching time. Teacher-facing AI, framed and governed as an ally, can help reclaim teaching time at scale—provided tools are curriculum-aligned, low-bandwidth, embedded in public digital infrastructure, co-created with educators, and governed by strong privacy/ethical safeguards. Author acknowledges use of ChatGPT 5.2 for literature survey and draft outline.

# Leveraging AI for Transforming School Education

![Watermark of CIET LOGO](/images/web/logo-mark.png)

## **Five Hours Online Training Series on**

## "Leveraging AI for Transforming School Education"

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 emphasizes the strategic use of emerging technologies to transform school education by improving **access, equity, quality and learning outcomes.** Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful enabler in this transformation, offering innovative solutions for personalized learning, adaptive instruction, assessment reform, learner support, and data‑informed decision making.   
  
 Aligned with the vision of **NEP 2020** and the perspectives articulated in the **National Curriculum Framework for Foundational Stage (NCF-FS)** and the **National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCF-SE)**, the integration of AI in school education supports competency‑based, learner‑centric and inclusive pedagogical practices. AI-enabled tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment, learning analytics and educational chatbots can assist teachers in addressing diverse learner needs, monitoring progress and enhancing classroom engagement.   
  
 National digital initiatives and platforms particularly **DIKSHA** provide a strong ecosystem for the adoption of AI-enabled educational resources and professional learning opportunities. At the same time, the **ethical and responsible use of AI** with due consideration to data privacy, transparency, fairness and inclusivity remain central to its effective implementation in schools. AI is envisioned as a supportive tool that augments teachers’ pedagogical capabilities rather than replacing the human element of teaching.   
  
 In this context, **CIET‑NCERT** is organising a **five hours online training series titled “Leveraging AI for Transforming School Education”** during 19 - 23 January, 2026 in the English version and 26 - 30 January, 2026 in the Hindi version from 4.00 pm to 5.00 pm. The programme aims to build AI literacy among educators, support policy-driven and pedagogically sound AI integration in schools, enhance personalised and interactive learning through AI and promote ethical and responsible use of AI in education. The sessions will be broadcast live on **NCERT’s YouTube Channel** and simulcast on **PM e‑Vidya DTH TV** Channels (6 to 12) and the **Jio TV mobile app**. Recorded sessions will also be made available through a dedicated YouTube playlist, allowing participants to revisit key concepts and instructional strategies at their convenience.

##### ***Objectives:***

*After completion of the training series, the learner will be able to:*

1. develop foundational understanding of Artificial Intelligence, including its key concepts, components, and working principles, among school educators and academic leaders.
2. familiarise participants with policy frameworks and governance models guiding responsible AI integration in school education.
3. enable the use of AI-driven classroom practices for personalised, adaptive and interactive learning experiences.
4. support effective pedagogical integration of AI through practical strategies aligned with curriculum and learning outcomes.
5. promote ethical, safe and responsible use of AI, ensuring data privacy, fairness, inclusivity and student well-being.

  From the 2025–2026 academic year, the UAE becomes one of the first nations globally to mandate a national AI curriculum across all public schools from kindergarten to Grade 12.

  • $15.7 trillion → PwC estimates AI will add this much to the global economy by 2030.

  • 1,000+ teachers trained to deliver AI education nationwide
  • 1 million students engaged annually
  • Lesson design: biweekly in lower grades, weekly in upper grades
  • 25% ethics-focused, building digital responsibility with technical skills
  • Integrated across computing, innovation, and entrepreneurship
  • National committee oversight to align with global best practices

  • AI Strategy 2031 → Make the UAE a global top-10 AI leader: target 20%+ of non-oil GDP ($96B by 2030) from AI.

  • Centennial 2071 → Anchor a knowledge-driven economy built on innovation and long-term competitiveness.

  Artificial Intelligence Becomes a Core Curriculum in UAE Public Schools
  From the 2025–2026 academic year, the UAE becomes one of the first nations globally to mandate a national AI curriculum across all public schools from kindergarten to Grade 12.
  This is not just an education reform.
  It is a strategic human capital investment designed to future-proof the nation’s economy and sovereignty.
  The Global AI Context
  • $15.7 trillion → PwC estimates AI will add this much to the global economy by 2030.
  • 170 million new jobs → World Economic Forum’s 2025 Jobs Report forecasts AI and automation will create this many roles by 2030.
  • Yet, only a handful of countries have moved to embed AI education at scale.
  The UAE is moving early — not to adapt to AI, but to produce AI-native citizens.
  Global Comparison: Who Else Is Moving?
  • China (Beijing) → Mandatory 8+ hours of AI education per year, starting 2025, covering robotics, algorithms, and ethics.
  • Estonia → AI Leap 2025 will reach 20,000 students & 3,000 teachers in a national pilot.
  • Australia → Introduced a Generative AI framework for responsible classroom use.
  • South Korea → AI-powered digital textbooks in math, English, and computing.
  • Hong Kong → 10–14 hours of AI literacy for junior secondary students.
  • Uzbekistan → Piloted AI adaptive learning tools in 10,000+ schools.
  Among these, the UAE stands out as one of the only nations implementing AI education system-wide (K–12) making its youth “AI-native citizens” from day one.
  The UAE’s Strategy
  • 1,000+ teachers trained to deliver AI education nationwide
  • 1 million students engaged annually
  • Lesson design: biweekly in lower grades, weekly in upper grades
  • 25% ethics-focused, building digital responsibility with technical skills
  • Integrated across computing, innovation, and entrepreneurship
  • National committee oversight to align with global best practices
  Why This Matters for the UAE’s National Vision
  • AI Strategy 2031 → Make the UAE a global top-10 AI leader: target 20%+ of non-oil GDP ($96B by 2030) from AI.
  • UAE Vision 2031 → Build the world’s best education system and an economy powered by talent, technology, and adaptability.
  • Centennial 2071 → Anchor a knowledge-driven economy built on innovation and long-term competitiveness.
  Anticipated Outcomes
  • A generation fluent in AI development, prompt engineering, and digital ethics.
  • Stronger human capital competitiveness — beyond literacy and numeracy, toward adaptive intelligence.
  • A talent pipeline feeding into universities like [MBZUAI (Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence)](https://ae.linkedin.com/school/mbzuai/?trk=public_post_reshare-text), sovereign AI clusters, and global R&D hubs.
  • Consolidation of the UAE’s role as a magnet for AI investment, startups and talent.
  The UAE has once again shown the world:
  Power is not only population or size of economy it is the ability to equip your youth with the tools of the future.
  Should AI literacy now be treated as fundamental as reading and math for every child worldwide?

This LinkedIn page features a viral post by Mahmood Abdulla (Global Emirati Voice and LinkedIn Top Influencer) announcing that the UAE will mandate a national AI curriculum across all public schools from kindergarten to Grade 12, starting in the 2025–2026 academic year. The post frames this as a strategic human capital investment to future-proof the nation's economy and sovereignty, not just an education reform.

Key context cited: PwC estimates AI will add $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030, and the World Economic Forum's 2025 Jobs Report forecasts 170 million new jobs from AI and automation by 2030. The UAE aims to produce "AI-native citizens."

Global comparison details: China (Beijing) mandates 8+ hours of AI education per year starting 2025; Estonia's AI Leap 2025 will reach 20,000 students and 3,000 teachers; Australia introduced a Generative AI framework; South Korea uses AI-powered digital textbooks; Hong Kong has 10–14 hours of AI literacy for junior secondary students; Uzbekistan piloted AI adaptive learning in 10,000+ schools. The UAE is highlighted as one of the only nations implementing AI education system-wide (K–12).

UAE strategy details: 1,000+ teachers trained nationwide, 1 million students engaged annually, biweekly lessons in lower grades and weekly in upper grades, 25% ethics-focused content, integrated across computing, innovation, and entrepreneurship, with national committee oversight.

National vision alignment: AI Strategy 2031 (top-10 global AI leader, 20%+ of non-oil GDP or $96B by 2030 from AI), UAE Vision 2031 (world's best education system), and Centennial 2071 (knowledge-driven economy). Anticipated outcomes include a generation fluent in AI development, prompt engineering, and digital ethics, plus a talent pipeline into MBZUAI and global R&D hubs.

The page also includes multiple associated posts: Haekal Adha Al Giffari notes Indonesia is rolling out AI and coding electives in 59,000 schools from 2025, backed by the National AI Strategy (Stranas KA) 2020–2045, including "unplugged" AI lessons for schools with limited tech. Other commentators discuss implications: Vik S. celebrated the UAE as first in the world; Laura Wojciechowski and Education UAE asked about private school AI preparedness; Gift Egbeiyon warned Africa risks being left behind (by 2030 young Africans projected to make up 42% of world's youth); ALIMAMY KARGBO and Abdulfetah S. Bedru discussed applying similar models in Sierra Leone and Ethiopia. The recurring question posed is whether AI literacy should be treated as fundamental as reading and math for every child worldwide.

<webpage_content>
[Dan Murphy](https://ae.linkedin.com/in/danmurphynews?trk=public_post_feed-actor-name)

* [Report this post](/uas/login?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Fposts%2Fdanmurphynews_the-uae-just-made-a-huge-shift-in-how-future-activity-7325387838873653248-Cse7&trk=public_post_ellipsis-menu-semaphore-sign-in-redirect&guestReportContentType=POST&_f=guest-reporting)

I spoke with UAE Education Minister [Sarah Al Amiri](https://ae.linkedin.com/in/sarah-al-amiri-3515b898?trk=public_post-text) about the UAE’s plan to introduce AI as a core subject across all government schools, starting from kindergarten. We spoke about the impact for the national curriculum, for teachers, and what this strategic investment in human capital means for the economy. [CNBC International](https://uk.linkedin.com/showcase/cnbc-international/?trk=public_post-text) [Ministry of Education – UAE](https://ae.linkedin.com/company/moeuaeofficial?trk=public_post-text)

##### **Transcript**

Dan, as you know, the UAE has been investing quite extensively in artificial intelligence and it makes a lot of sense to start teaching children at a very young age how to use AI and how AI is going to benefit them and how to use it correctly and ethically. Another underlying factor is the following. We studied the advent of technology across the last few decades and we saw that if we don't react appropriately, and that's what we didn't do when it came to social media and didn't. Transformer education process. From there, we were not able to equip students with the right skills to use that tool correctly. So we wanted to make sure that today students are aware of the downfalls of using AI or their limitations, the ethical considerations, the biases that are built into those systems, how to discern them, how to critically approach the utilization of artificial intelligence. Indeed, Minister, and when you think about this more deeply, of course nation states are all looking at how do we incorporate artificial intelligence into their education system. The UAE is a real first mover on this. But how do you balance this ambitious new initiative with your own warning this week that we may not yet be there when it comes to actually having the capacity to use AI wisely and ethically? So that, that's why we looked at this when designing this curriculum. We looked at the factors that we knew about. So the known knowns and what we, what was imperative for us is to focus on AI literacy. This, this curriculum focuses from a very young age. So kindergarten students will be taking role play. They will look at mechanisms to discern what smart machines are, what are robots? How do robots work? How do they react? Who teaches them what to do? Do they have feelings if they make a mistake? Who, who's responsible to fix that mistake and so on. And then you take that and move that forward while progressing, you ensure that students understand how to use it ethically and more importantly for students that are at later grades, those that will go into university, those that we know will definitely use AI, we show them how to prompt engineer. So how do you write the right prompts? How do you analyze the data that comes or the information that you receive from AI? How do you use it avoiding. Plagiarism and how do you ensure that you infuse it across different mechanisms of of their daily work done? What what what I was talking about when referring to a lack of understanding of how to infuse it is how do you use it as a tool to further advance education? And that's why we broke down AI in education into four different fields. One is AI electricity and that's what this curriculum covers We also look at AI as a. Tool to improve personalized learning and to to improve differentiated learning in the classroom as a tool to support teachers and that's something that's currently in development. We are also looking at AI to make school operations more seamless and remove over burdens that are currently on school leadership and also teachers and educators across the across the board and also in terms of analytics and teaching students how to design and develop AI. Indeed, a minister, you also studied computer science yourself, so you know perhaps more about this than most other people. You've said AI is unlike any previous tech shift. I think we're also seeing that play out in the public markets right now as well, just given the huge interest and investment that we're seeing in this space. Talk to me about the end goal here and the translation for the UAE. You see this initiative as a way to also future proof the Emirati workforce against what could be really significant. AI driven disruption. This is not future proofing. This, I'll call it as the first stepping stone towards future proofing our work, our workforce. What we're actually working on is transforming education. The reason I said the AI is a paradigm shift and AI has needs to transform what our education sector is meant to teach. And that's the outcomes today. We are transforming our education system to focus on skills. If we're talking about future proofing our workforce, our students need to graduate. School thinkers, they need to graduate with great resilience. They need to be great communicators. They need to have very strong analytical and creative skills. This means that you've the paradigm shift that we're doing in education today. It's no longer about the knowledge that they acquire in the classroom, it's about how they utilize that knowledge. How do they acquire that knowledge? How do they discern the viability and reliability of that knowledge? How do they use it in their daily lives? How can they use artificial intelligence and any other technological advancement? To move forward done. Our education systems around the world has not done monumental shifts since the inception of Formula K12 education.   The Shift in Higher Education: The Role of General Education Courses in Fostering Graduates Ready for the AI Era The world of higher education is witnessing a profound transformation. Artificial Intelligence is reshaping every discipline, not only in engineering and computer science, but also in business, health, education, law, and the humanities. Universities must therefore prepare all students, not just specialists, to understand and apply AI responsibly, ethically, and innovatively. The foundation for this transformation lies in a modern General Education framework that equips every graduate with the mindset and competencies needed for the AI-driven future. This shift moves to include: (i) Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, (ii) Data Literacy, (iii) Communication Skills, (iv) Ethics in the Age of AI, (v) Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Sustainability, and (vi) UAE Society. Together, the enhanced General Education courses provide a balanced foundation that connects technology with humanity, and knowledge with values. They ensure that every graduate, regardless of major, becomes AI-literate, ethically grounded, and future-ready. This is the essence of the shift in higher education, from knowledge transfer to capability building; from subject expertise to human–AI fluency. Through this renewed role of General Education, universities can lead the way in preparing all graduates to be ready not only for the AI era, but for shaping its future.
