--- SOURCE 20: More Districts Are Training Teachers on Artificial Intelligence: Findings from the American School District Panel | RAND ---
URL: https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA956-31.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This RAND research report (published April 8, 2025) examines the prevalence and nature of artificial intelligence (AI) teacher training across U.S. K–12 public school districts, based on data from the American School District Panel (ASDP), a partnership between RAND and the Center on Reinventing Public Education.

**Key Survey Findings:**
- In fall 2023, 23% of districts reported having provided AI training to teachers. By fall 2024, this rose to 48%—a 25-percentage-point increase. An additional 26% of districts planned AI training during 2024–2025, projecting that about three-quarters of districts will have provided AI training by fall 2025.
- The findings align with a federal survey of principals from December 2024, which found 59% of U.S. schools have trained some or all teachers on AI use.
- A poverty-based training gap persists. By fall 2024, 67% of low-poverty districts had trained teachers on AI, compared with 42% of middle-poverty and 39% of high-poverty districts. Projections suggest almost all low-poverty districts will have trained teachers by the 2025–2026 school year, while only six in ten high-poverty districts will have done so.

**Key Interview Findings (14 district leaders):**
- Nearly all leaders said the primary purpose of AI training was to address teachers' concerns, confusion, and fears about the technology. Thirteen of 14 interviewees encountered teachers with negative views of AI, viewing it as a threat or cheating tool. Leaders aimed to lower anxiety and encourage experimentation.
- Most leaders focused on educator proficiency (e.g., lesson planning, differentiation) before addressing student use of AI. Few engaged in training around student use.
- Training formats varied widely, but virtually all were optional/opt-in; only one district ran mandatory training. Formats ranged from full-day sessions to "bite-sized" newsletter-based learning and peer leadership models.
- Eleven of 14 district leaders took a do-it-yourself approach to developing AI training programs, citing a scarcity of external experts. Half struggled to find qualified outside trainers. Leaders used resources from state school board associations, Digital Promise, ISTE, Google, and OpenAI. Competing professional development priorities and time constraints were cited as barriers.

**Council of the Great City Schools (CGCS) Efforts:**
CGCS developed the K–12 Gen AI Maturity Tool and the K–12 Gen AI Readiness Checklist (with the Consortium for School Networking, funded by Amazon Web Services grant) to assess AI readiness across six domains: Leadership, Operational, Data, Technical, Security, and Legal Risk.

**Implications:**
1. Training organizations should seriously address educator fear and reluctance, designing AI professional development that starts with trust-building and AI fundamentals before practical applications, including hands-on, low-stakes learning and peer-based structures.
2. High-poverty districts need targeted support and funding to close the persistent AI training gap; best practices should be equitably shared through state/federal agencies, philanthropy, and technical assistance.

**Methodology:**
- Fall 2023 survey: 231 of 1,167 invited districts completed (19.8% completion rate; October 12–December 14, 2023).
- Fall 2024 survey: 291 of 8,017 invited districts completed (4% response rate; October 24–December 23, 2024).
- Responses weighted to be representative of all U.S. K–12 public school districts. Poverty levels derived from U.S. Census Bureau's Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates; districts divided into quartiles by family poverty rate of 5–17 year olds (low = 1st quartile, middle = 2nd-3rd, high = 4th).
- 15 qualitative interviews conducted with district leaders between November 2024 and January 2025, lasting 20–40 minutes each, audio recorded and transcribed.
- Research funded by the Gates Foundation.
</summary>

URL: https://livehandbook.org/k-12-education/miscellaneous/k-12-education/school-resources/artificial-intelligence-in-k%E2%80%9312-schools

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the AEFP Live Handbook (last updated August 2026) by Barnard, Fesler, and Loeb examines the state of AI in K-12 education. It argues that the most useful way to evaluate AI is to ask whether tools expand students' access to proven learning experiences—personalized instruction, complex problem-solving, meaningful collaboration, substantive discussion, and sustained relationships with educators.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Thin evidence base:** Of 800+ academic papers on AI in K-12 education, only 20 meet standards for strong causal inference. No high-quality causal studies exist on student-facing AI tools in U.S. K-12 classrooms. Most studies examine short-term performance rather than durable learning.

2. **AI as a mediator of learning experiences:** AI shapes learning through three pathways—student-facing interactions, educator support, and system-level organization. The central evaluative question is whether tools expand access to experiences that research identifies as important for development.

3. **Performance vs. proficiency gap:** A randomized study of high school math students found that those using a general-purpose chatbot performed worse on subsequent closed-book exams than students who practiced with no AI support, despite higher performance during practice. Students using a tutoring-style system (hints and guided reasoning) showed no difference on exams. Similar patterns appear across subjects.

4. **Design choices matter:** Systems that prompt explanation, reflection, and revision reinforce cognitive work for deeper learning. Systems that generate complete answers reduce cognitive work and learning. Guided reasoning tools improve independent problem-solving performance.

5. **Educator capacity:** A randomized experiment found teachers with ChatGPT spent less time preparing lessons while maintaining quality. AI tools that provide instructional feedback to teachers and tutors show early promise, with largest gains for lower-performing tutors.

**Research Priorities:** Long-term studies on durable learning outcomes, equity implications, system-level applications (scheduling, tutoring coordination), and AI-based assessment validity are needed. The article emphasizes that the evidence base is too thin to draw definitive conclusions, especially for U.S. K-12 settings.
</summary>

URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review article published in Frontiers in Education on September 23, 2025, authored by Abdullah Alfarwan from Najran University, Saudi Arabia. The study systematically reviews empirical research on the use of Generative AI (GenAI) in K-12 education, analyzing 30 papers retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and snowballing techniques.

**Key Findings:**
- **Publication Timeline:** Most papers (19 of 30) were published in 2024, with 6 from 2025 and 5 from 2023.
- **Educational Levels:** High school students and pre-service teachers were most represented. In-service teachers, elementary, primary, and vocational education were underrepresented. No studies focused on early childhood education (ECE).
- **Subject Domains:** Mathematics was the most common subject (5 papers), followed by Physics (4). The majority focused on STEM-related subjects. Non-STEM subjects included History, Writing, and English Language.
- **Geographic Representation:** Most studies were conducted in Taiwan and China (4 each), followed by the US and Germany (3 each). No studies from Africa were included.
- **GenAI Tools:** ChatGPT was used in 21 of 30 papers. Other tools included Copilot, DALL-E, Midjourney, and others.
- **Study Design:** Quasi-experimental design was most common (30% of papers), followed by descriptive and mixed-method approaches (20% each).
- **Measures:** Primarily psychological variables (attitudes, self-efficacy, trust, motivation, critical thinking, self-regulated learning). Only two studies examined self-regulated learning specifically. Objective measures (standardized tests) were largely absent.
- **Recommendations:** 90% of papers emphasized the need for teacher professional development for AI-integrated classrooms. Future research should explore longitudinal studies, true experimental designs, objective learning measures, parental involvement, diverse GenAI tools, and under-researched contexts (ECE, special needs, rural settings).

**Limitations:** The search only covered English-language publications and specific GenAI tools (ChatGPT, Google Bard, Copilot, Midjourney). There is a lack of representation from Africa, the Middle East, and South America.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: A Systematic Review of Generative AI in K–12: Mapping Goals, Activities, Roles, and Outcomes via the 3P Model ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2079-8954/13/10/840

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review article published in the journal Systems (2025, Volume 13, Issue 10, article 840, DOI: 10.3390/systems13100840), authored by Xiaoling Lin and Hao Tan from the School of Design, Hunan University, China. The paper presents "A Systematic Review of Generative AI in K–12: Mapping Goals, Activities, Roles, and Outcomes via the 3P Model."

METHODOLOGY: Following the PRISMA framework and appraising quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), the authors synthesized 84 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025 involving learners aged 3–18. The search (conducted May–July 2025) identified 817 records from Scopus (528) and Web of Science (289); after de-duplication and screening, 84 studies with MMAT scores ≥3 were retained. The review integrated Biggs's 3P model (Presage–Process–Product) with the CIMO-Logic framework to code learning objectives, activity designs, AI role paradigms, and outcomes. Four research questions addressed the primary learning goals, learning activities, human–AI role patterns, and reported opportunities/risks in outcomes.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Seven recurring learning objectives emerged: language/literacy; STEM; creativity; socioemotional skills; feedback literacy and self-regulation; motivation; AI literacy.
2. Five dominant activity patterns were identified: AI-facilitated dialogic tutoring; generative iterative co-creation; project-based problem-solving; simulation/game-based learning; and formative feedback with adaptive scaffolding.
3. AI roles shift from AI-directed (learner-as-recipient) to AI-supported/AI-empowered paradigms, re-allocating agency among students, teachers, and caregivers via feedback loops.
4. Reported outcomes span three categories—epistemic, practice, and affective/identity—with opportunities including deeper knowledge, improved practice, and stronger engagement, and risks including hallucinations, reduced originality, over-reliance, motivational loss, and ethical concerns.

CONTEXT AND GAP: The field lacks theoretically grounded accounts linking learning goals, pedagogical activities, and human–AI role configurations to measurable outcomes for 3–18-year-olds. Existing AIEd research is skewed toward higher education, privileges traditional AI, and largely predates powerful LLMs. GenAI enables new space for personalization, learner–AI co-creation, and immersive assessment while raising questions about role allocation, ethical governance, and impact evaluation. Learning is framed through constructivist, situated, and sociocultural perspectives, moving beyond the knowledge-acquisition metaphor toward participation, collaboration, and distributed cognition.

CONTRIBUTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS: The authors contribute a theory-led goal–activity–role–outcome map, a clarified shift toward co-regulated human–AI ensembles, and practice-oriented guidance. They propose a goal–activity–role alignment heuristic for instructional design, plus safeguards around teacher professional development, feedback literacy, and ethics. They call for longitudinal and cross-cultural research to evaluate GenAI impacts in K–12.

The article belongs to the MDPI Systems journal's Special Issue on "Generative AI Transformation in Education: Current Issues and Challenges." Submission dates: received 14 August 2025, revised 13 September 2025, accepted 23 September 2025, published 25 September 2025. The article has received 14,534 views and 8 citations (at the time of capture) and an Altmetric score of 15.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ORF Issue Brief No. 888 (published July 2026), authored by Arpan Tulsyan (Senior Fellow, Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, Observer Research Foundation), argues that a teacher-centric artificial intelligence (AI) support system offers a pragmatic pathway to reclaim teaching time and improve instructional quality in India's government schools. 

KEY CONTEXT/STATISTICS:
- India has 1.01 crore (10.1 million) teachers instructing 24.69 crore (246.9 million) students across 14.71 lakh schools.
- A 2025 Parliamentary Standing Committee report flagged nearly 10 lakh teacher vacancies in government schools, ~7.5 lakh at primary level.
- Over one lakh schools (serving over 33 lakh students) function with only one teacher, mostly in remote rural areas; in Jharkhand, over 20% of schools have a single teacher managing 50+ students across grades.
- A time-use study found teachers spend ~23 hours/week on non-teaching activities; morning routines, co-curricular management, and mid-day-meal work alone account for ~14.5 hours.
- A NUEPA study across 28 districts in 17 states found teachers spend only 21.57% of time actually teaching; 33.91% on teaching-related activities; 44.52% lost to non-academic work.
- Mid-day-meal activities take 2.5–3 hours of a teacher's day.
- Education reforms under NEP 2020, NCF 2023, and NIPUN Bharat Mission have raised expectations for competency-based, personalised instruction.

ARGUMENT: With vacancies unlikely to close quickly, AI can reduce teachers' administrative and preparatory burden, freeing time for instruction. AI should be framed as an "ally" (augmentation), not a replacement/surveillance tool, since teacher buy-in is the strongest predictor of sustained EdTech adoption in low/middle-income countries. This reframing is consistent with NEP 2020's human-centred vision.

EXISTING TOOLS (Table 1): Categories include lesson planning/content creation (Shiksha Copilot in Karnataka, ChatGPT informal use, TeachBetter.ai); multilingual/localised support (Sahayak AI, Bhashini covering 22 scheduled languages); assessment/grading automation (TeachBetter quiz tool, NIPUN Lakshya App); classroom instruction aids (Tara voice assistant for English); administrative tasks (facial recognition attendance pilots in Karnataka and Bihar, AI note-takers); and professional development (DIKSHA–CIET courses, Shiksha Copilot chatbot). Tools use accessible interfaces (WhatsApp/Telegram) and offline capabilities for low connectivity.

GAPS LIMITING ADOPTION:
1. Weak coverage of regional languages/dialects (tribal languages unsupported; even supported languages show errors)
2. Hallucinations, misalignment, content errors (curriculum alignment issues; repeated errors erode teacher trust)
3. Gaps in teacher training/AI literacy (CENTA survey: 70% used AI in class, 67% confident, but only 57% could spot basic AI misconceptions)
4. Limited integration with school systems (AI tools not shareable on official portals; MIS doesn't interface with AI tools; mainly pilot-stage)
5. Unequal access due to weak infrastructure (device shortages, intermittent connectivity, equity risks; new cost points from API/cloud)
6. Privacy, security, ethical concerns (facial recognition surveillance worries; AI bias; DPDP Rules 2025 implementation is phased)
7. Underdeveloped in-class use (most usage is "backstage" planning/grading; few tools support real-time classroom instruction)

SEVEN RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Co-create AI solutions with teachers (hackathons, pilot feedback loops)
2. Ensure equity and access safeguards (infrastructure investment, offline capabilities, local language support, subsidised/public-private pricing)
3. Scale successful models in other states (replicate Shiksha Copilot; develop a 'National Teacher AI Toolkit'; integrate with DIKSHA/teacher portals)
4. Align AI with NEP 2020 goals (competency-based, experiential learning; move beyond rote learning)
5. Protect teacher agency ('human-in-the-loop' checks; AI outputs as suggestions finalised by teachers)
6. Establish ethical AI and data governance (education-specific guidelines complementing DPDP Act, 2023; opt-out provisions for surveillance)

CONCLUSION: The core challenge is not teacher motivation/capacity but structural constraints on teaching time. Teacher-facing AI, framed and governed as an ally, can help reclaim teaching time at scale—provided tools are curriculum-aligned, low-bandwidth, embedded in public digital infrastructure, co-created with educators, and governed by strong privacy/ethical safeguards. Author acknowledges use of ChatGPT 5.2 for literature survey and draft outline.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article examines the initial implementation of generative AI in Japanese schools and its socio-emotional impact, covering the period from hardware infrastructure development (2021) through policy evolution (2023-2025) and actual classroom practices.

**1. GIGA School Foundation:** Japan established the physical infrastructure for AI education through the GIGA School Program, which achieved "one device per student" for compulsory education nearly nationwide by 2021. Approximately 7.4 million tablet devices and laptops (about 28% iPads) were distributed, with 97.6% of planned devices deployed across 1,769 municipalities by March 2021. This digitalization was accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic and reached rural areas, earning Japan a reputation as a country that "already possesses the hardware for Generation AI."

**2. Policy Evolution (2023-2025):** Japan's policy shifted from caution to integration. In July 2023, MEXT issued interim guidelines emphasizing caution and careful experimentation — prohibiting AI for graded assignments, requiring students to verify AI output and cite tool/prompt usage, and mandating that "human judgment is essential at the end of every task." MEXT did not impose a uniform ban but asked boards of education to adjust approaches regionally. --- SOURCE 19: China's AI Education Experiment - by Lily Ottinger ---
URL: https://www.chinatalk.media/p/chinas-ai-education-experiment

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# China's AI Education Experiment

The article explores China's ambitious government-led push to integrate artificial intelligence into its K-12 education system, driven by the Ministry of Education's (MOE) goal to universalize basic AI access in primary and secondary schools by 2030. The MOE's May 2025 white paper on "intelligentizing" education outlines four main use cases: **(1) teacher task reduction** (AI-assisted grading, lesson planning), **(2) improving rural schools** (digital education support, AI literacy lessons), **(3) analyzing student biometrics** (facial expression monitoring, attention tracking, mental health screening), and **(4) helping students with disabilities**.

## Key Motivations
The Party prioritizes AI in education because improving the education system is extremely popular with Chinese families. Chinese households spend an average of 17.1% of annual income on education (vs. 1-2% in US/Japan), and the poorest quartile devotes 56.8% of income. However, only 30.6% of China's population has ever attended high school, and roughly 40% of middle school graduates don't go on to high school. The system is fundamentally zero-sum — universities are overwhelmingly urban, and less than 5% of elite university students come from rural families despite 65% of children having rural hukou.

## Structural Challenges
Rural education faces severe resource depletion: elite schools systematically attract talent from periphery areas, leaving rural schools with teacher shortages (senior teachers are only 6.8% of all teachers in China vs. 26% in the US with 20+ years experience), oversized classrooms (56+ students), and severe funding constraints. Local governments bear ~85% of education spending, and poorer counties have less to spend. A 2025 study found 82% of rural children aged 6-36 months had at least one developmental delay.

## Implementation Barriers
- **Funding**: MOE white papers are unfunded mandates that signal priorities but provide no money. Schools are instructed to "strengthen overall planning of funds" but budgets are already stretched thin.
- **Device access**: Rural areas face a shortfall of 8.5 million computers. Historical scandals (schools forcing families to buy overpriced tablets) and concerns about screen time and addiction have hindered device distribution.
- **Private sector costs**: iFlytek's smart classroom software cost one school ¥1,744,000 (~US$254,000). Even the Bengbu city contract covering 875 schools worked out to roughly ¥800 per student per year.
- **Data privacy**: At least 63% of primary/secondary students have dealt with spam calls from data leaks. Student data protection relies on non-mandatory recommendations. Schools routinely pressure parents to sign expansive data agreements.
- **Teacher incentives**: Rural teachers' careers are centrally managed with forced transfers, reducing motivation to integrate AI. The "County-managed, school-hired" system is widely resented.

## Key Concerns
The article notes that while computer-assisted learning has shown some benefits, AI cannot address root causes of educational inequality — the gaokao system, hukou-based restrictions, centralization of resources, and early childhood developmental delays. The mental health surveillance use case is particularly worrying, as the structure of boarding schooling itself (with 47.3% of boarding students suffering from acute pessimism and 63.8% feeling lonely) is a major source of psychological harm. Meanwhile, wealthy urban students already enjoy AI-guided learning tools, potentially widening rather than narrowing the gap.
</summary>

## Study Overview
This paper presents experimental evidence on the impact of **Mindspark**, a personalized technology-aided after-school instruction program for middle-school students in Delhi, India (Grades 6-9). Conducted by Karthik Muralidharan (UCSD), Abhijeet Singh (Stockholm School of Economics), and Alejandro J. Ganimian (NYU), the study uses a lottery design where 619 students from low-income neighborhoods in five public middle schools were randomly assigned to receive free access to the program.

## Key Results
- **Lottery winners scored 0.37σ higher in math and 0.23σ higher in Hindi** over a 4.5-month period (ITT estimates with 58% average attendance).
- **IV estimates** suggest attending for 90 days would raise math and Hindi scores by 0.6σ and 0.39σ respectively.
- Lottery winners made **over twice the test-score value-added in math** and ~2.4 times in Hindi versus the control group.
- **Absolute gains were similar for all students**, but relative gains were much greater for academically weaker students (because the bottom third of students in the control group showed near-zero academic progress under status quo).
- The program was **cost-effective even at small scale**, with treatment group value-added over 100% greater than control at lower cost per student than public schooling.

## Context and Background
- In India, over 50% of Grade 5 students cannot read at second-grade level despite enrollment rates over 95%.
- The central problem addressed is the **mismatch between classroom instruction level and student learning levels** (“Teaching at the Right Level” / TaRL challenge).
- Average Grade 6 student was 2.5 grade levels behind in math; by Grade 9, this deficit grew to 4.5 grade levels. Students in the same grade span 5-6 grade levels in preparation.

## Mindspark Program Design
- **Software**: Developed by Educational Initiatives (EI); used by 400,000+ students, had 45,000+ test questions, administered over a million questions daily.
- Key features: adaptive content that dynamically personalizes to each student's level, error analysis using millions of student-question observations, interactive engagement (limited instructional videos, constant student interaction).
- **Centers**: 90-minute sessions, 6 days/week; 45 minutes of computer-based instruction + 45 minutes of supervised group study (12-15 students with one locally-hired instructor). Fee was INR 200 (USD 3) per month (subsidized).

## Heterogeneity Findings
- **By subject content**: In math (where students were far behind grade level), gains appeared only on below-grade-level questions. In Hindi (where gaps were smaller), gains appeared on both at- and below-grade-level questions.
- **On school exams**: Significant gains in Hindi (0.19σ) but not math on grade-level annual exams. Top-tercile students scored 0.33σ higher across subjects; bottom two-thirds showed no school exam improvements (consistent with not receiving grade-level content on the platform).

## Methodology Notes
- Tests were independently designed, paper-and-pencil, linked using **Item Response Theory (IRT)** for cross-grade and cross-time comparability.
- Randomization stratified by center-batch preferences; 305 control, 314 treatment; 87% follow-up rate.
- Key methodological insight: relying solely on grade-level assessments would have led to incorrect inference about program impact given wide within-grade variation in learning.

## Broader Contributions
- The study contrasts with prior findings: hardware-focused CAL interventions show no positive impact, pedagogy-focused CAL (reviewing grade-appropriate content at own pace) shows modest 0.1-0.2σ gains, while **personalized CAL interventions deliver the largest gains**.
- The study suggests technology-enabled personalized instruction could scale up TaRL approaches without increasing teacher workload, offering a "leapfrogging" path for human capital accumulation in developing countries—though government-led initiatives will likely be necessary given affordability constraints.

# Generative AI use in college writing classes: An analysis of student chat logs and writing projects

## Authors

* Sarah Madsen Hardy   Boston University | US
* Pary Fassihi   Boston University | US
* Shuang Geng   Boston University | US
* Christopher McVey   Boston University | US
* Matt Parfitt   Boston University | US

## DOI:

 <https://doi.org/10.17239/jowr-2026.17.03.05>

## Keywords:

 generative AI, writing pedagogy, higher education, English as a foreign language

## Abstract

This study contributes to the emerging research on generative AI and writing pedagogy by exploring how college writing students make use of GAI when offered instruction in a range of responsible uses and latitude to integrate it into their writing process as they see fit. We analyzed chat log data and papers from participants recruited from six sections in which students were guided in experimenting with ChatGPT Plus and permitted to use it to produce up to 50% of submitted work. Through a combination of AI and human thematic content analysis of student chat logs, we found that in 18.6% of prompts, students asked ChatGPT to write for them. The rest of the prompts involved work leading up to or in support of the writing process. Human thematic content analysis of papers showed that students used ChatGPT to generate 8.2% of the writing they submitted. The most common rhetorical purpose of the AI-generated text they included was discussion/analysis/synthesis. English as a foreign language students (EFLs) in the sample prompted ChatGPT to clarify understanding less often than non-EFLs and integrated less AI-generated text into their papers, with a particularly notable difference in their use of AI-generated summaries. This unexpected finding merits further research, but it suggests that EFLs may use GAI for somewhat different purposes than non-EFL peers.

args.summary:
This webpage presents a peer-reviewed research article published in the Journal of Writing Research (Vol. 17, No. 3, 2026) examining how college writing students use generative AI (GAI) when offered instruction in responsible uses. The study, conducted at Boston University by authors Sarah Madsen Hardy, Pary Fassihi, Shuang Geng, Christopher McVey, and Matt Parfitt, analyzed chat log data and papers from participants recruited from six course sections where students were guided in experimenting with ChatGPT Plus and permitted to use it for up to 50% of submitted work.

Key findings include: (1) In 18.6% of prompts, students asked ChatGPT to write for them, with the rest involving preparatory or supportive work for the writing process; (2) Students used ChatGPT to generate 8.2% of the writing they submitted; (3) The most common rhetorical purpose of AI-generated text was discussion/analysis/synthesis; (4) English as a foreign language (EFL) students prompted ChatGPT to clarify understanding less often than non-EFLs and integrated less AI-generated text into their papers, particularly noting a difference in their use of AI-generated summaries. The study suggests EFLs may use GAI for somewhat different purposes than non-EFL peers, meriting further research.

The article includes a comprehensive reference list covering related research on ChatGPT in education, AI-assisted writing, GPT detector bias against non-native writers, and human-AI collaboration patterns. The article is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 3.0 Unported License with the DOI: https://doi.org/10.17239/jowr-2026.17.03.05.

## [IJRISS](https://rsisinternational.org/journals/ijriss/)

# Teaching Secondary School Essay Writing Using Generative AI

**Teaching Secondary School Essay Writing Using Generative AI**

**Shirley Ling Jen1, Abdul Rahim Salam2**

**1****Faculty of Educational Sciences & Technology, University Technology Malaysia**

**2****Language Academy, Faculty of Social Sciences & Humanities, University Technology Malaysia**

**DOI:** [**https://dx.doi.org/10.47772/IJRISS.2025.903SEDU0438**](https://dx.doi.org/10.47772/IJRISS.2025.903SEDU0438)

**Received: 28 July 2025; Accepted: 04 August 2025; Published: 27 August 2025**

### ABSTRACT

Artificial intelligence has made a tremendous impact in the education field since the emergence of Generative AI such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot.  Apart from adding a variety to the normal way of teaching, GenAI is able to provide personalised feedback and ideas to writers in a split second.  However, studies regarding the use of generative AI among Malaysian secondary school students are still lacking.  In addition, there are also insufficient training and materials to guide Malaysian secondary school teachers and students in using Generative AI.  Thus, in this study, the researchers had produced their learning aid known as Bard G to guide students in using Google Gemini, a generative AI developed by Google.  Bard G consists of a mobile application, two modules and a rainbow chart.  In this study, 40 Form 4 students were chosen as the respondents for this study.  Students’ responses were analysed qualitatively using thematic approach. Among the problems identified while using generative AI include lack of facilities, insufficient computer knowledge and lack of guidance in using AI.  On the other hand, themes such as personalised learning, differentiation strategy and self-directed learning were identified regarding the usefulness of Gemini.  However, the results of this study were confined to only Form 4 students of a secondary school in Johor Bahru.  It is hoped that in the future, Bard G can be used in teaching with other age group of students and with other language aspects such as Grammar, listening and speaking skills.

**Keywords**— Artificial intelligence, student-centred learning, essay writing, self-directed learning, second language acquisition

### INTRODUCTION

Artificial intelligence has made tremendous remarks in the education field since the emergence of Generative AI such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot [1],[2], [3]-[5].  This is particularly seen in the field of essay writing as it is considered as the co-author for students’ essays.  Most of the time, GenAI has been used in higher learning education and there are still insufficient studies with other age groups of students [6].  Apart from that, one of the main reasons that hinders teachers from using digital tools in teaching students is the lack of guidance and training provided [7],[8].  Thus, in this study, the researchers had produced their own teaching aid known as Bard G to help Malaysian secondary school students to learn essay writing using Gemini.  Bard G is a teaching aid that consists of a mobile application, two modules, and a rainbow chart to teach students the prompts in using Gemini.  Essay writing was chosen for this study as writing is one of the most difficult language skills to acquire because of its complexity in nature and English is a second language or even a foreign language for majority of Malaysian students [9],[10]-[12].  Besides, writing consists of many elements such as word choice, language use and spelling.  The main problems faced by Malaysian students in their essay writing include the inability to form grammatically accurate sentences and generalization of ideas due to poor command of vocabulary and interference from their mother tongue [13].  Due to lack of time, poor facilities and weak command of the English language, the majority of Malaysian English teachers usually employ teacher-centred method in teaching essay writing [14],[15].  Thus, there should be a call for a more creative approach in teaching essay writing such as through the use of Artificial Intelligence [2],[5].

Although AI has long existed since 1950, it has only made tremendous impact in education field since the emergence of ChatGPT.  Similar to ChatGPT, Gemini is able to generalise information from a large corpus of data built in it.  Research shows that Gemini can help with creative tasks, explaining complex topics and generally extracting information from a variety of sources on the internet.  Although studies had been carried out about ChatGPT, there are a few studies on the use of other AI tools such as Gemini and Copilot [6],[12],[16].  Moreover, there is lack of guidance in using AI such as Gemini.  Thus, this has discouraged teachers and students to explore further in the field of AI.

The research objectives for this study are to:

### LITERATURE REVIEW

Gemini is a generative AI developed by Google, one of the largest communication providers in the world [13].  It is even known as one of the best AI in terms of generating high-quality data as it can access information directly from Google, thus making it a reliable source of information compared to other AI [17],[18].  Apart from that, Gemini is safeguarded for kids’ usage and it is also strongly recommended by MOE of Malaysia to be used throughout the country.

The results of the previous study showed that Gemini is perceived as useful by a group of Malaysian secondary school students because of its features such as differentiation strategy, personalized learning, ability to generate high-quality data and safe for students to use [13].  Nevertheless, Gemini is still not widely practised in Malaysian secondary schools due to lack of guidance for Malaysian teachers in using it.  In fact, one of the problems that hindered teachers to use digital tool in ESL classroom is lack of guidance and facilities [7], [19].  Thus, Bard G was developed in this study to provide guidelines to teachers and students in using Gemini AI for essay writing.

### METHODOLOGY

In this study, Bard G is a learning aid in guiding students to use Gemini AI for essay writing.  It consists of a mobile application, two modules and a rainbow chart.  The first book is for beginners.  It consists of explanations and illustrations about Gemini while the second book consists of step-by-step explanation to guide students to use Gemini in all the three stages of essay writing:  Pre-writing, while writing and post-writing.  The second book also consists of translation in Bahasa Melayu to guide the weaker students in using Gemini for essay writing.   In addition, the rainbow chart is developed to guide students to use Gemini more easily and promptly.  It consists of only the prompts used in the three stages of essay writing.

Below is the rainbow chart used in this study.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20571%20444'%3E%3C/svg%3E)![](https://rsisinternational.org/journals/ijriss/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Picture1-19.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20571%20444'%3E%3C/svg%3E)
![](https://rsisinternational.org/journals/ijriss/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Picture1-19.png)

**Fig. 1  Rainbow Chart**

**A.Participants**

40 Form 4 students of a secondary school in Johor Bahru were selected as the respondents for this study.  They were High English Proficiency (HEP) students and a few of them had experience in using digital tools before.  They were purposely chosen for this study as they were not sitting for any public examination that year, and there was a call for more studies on lower secondary school students in Malaysia [20],[21].  This is because most of the studies carried out on Artificial Intelligence have centred on higher learning institutions so far.  Thus, more studies on Artificial Intelligence should be carried out with other age groups of students [13].

**B.Instruments**

In this study, a set of semi-structured interviews, journal entries and participant observation were used to gather the data for this study.  The research instruments used were developed by previous researchers [13],[22].

**C.Procedures**

Respondents were first exposed to the usage of AI such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot in the first essay writing class.  Then, in the second lesson, students were asked to write their essay individually using instructions from Bard G Modules.  Students were asked to complete an essay entitled ‘Review of A Traditional Restaurant’ using Gemini.  Students were asked to submit their essays at the end of the lesson.  In the third essay writing lesson, students were asked to evaluate their essays using Gemini.  For students who could not understand the evaluation, they were taught to translate the evaluation into their own mother tongue.  They were then required to send the evaluation generated by Gemini to teacher’s email.

### FINDINGS

The findings for this study were collected through students’ journal entries, participant observation and interviews.  It was then analysed qualitatively using Atlas.ti and presented using themes identified in the study.

Students’ Problems in Using Gemini

Students were asked to complete a journal entry after using Gemini in the post-writing activity.  Among the problems highlighted by students while using Gemini include lack of facilities, insufficient computer knowledge, lack of guidance in using AI and some commented that the language used by Gemini was too difficult to understand.

**Lack of Facilities**

Although there were sufficient laptops and notebooks for students, students complained that poor internet connection was one of the main problems they faced while using Gemini.  This was because there were too many students using the Wifi connection at the same time.  Due to this, teacher had to use her own Wifi coverage for students’ usage.  The poor connection prevented students to fully utilize the benefits of using Gemini although all of them managed to complete the essay writing tasks using Gemini.  The insufficient facilities and poor internet connection had caused frustration among a few students as they had to struggle connecting using Wifi.

**Lack of Computer Knowledge**

Students also faced problems in terms of using laptops.  Although most of them had experience in using mobile phones, they did not have laptops at home.  Thus, it was their first experience using laptops.  As the features of laptops and mobile phones were different, a few students were struggling in completing tasks such as uploading photos of their essays. Many of them stated that they did not know how to take clear photos of their essays.  Some of the comments received from Gemini regarding their essay were illegible handwriting due to the unclear images taken.

**Lack of Guidance in Using AI**

During the interviews, most of them revealed that it was their first time to use AI.  Although a few of them had heard about AI before, this was the first time for them to experience using AI.  Nevertheless, students expressed that they still depended on the prompts developed by the teacher in their essay writing tasks.  Without the prompts, they were not confident to teach other students in using Gemini.  Thus, teacher plays an important role in teaching students to use AI.  Teacher has taught students using her own AI teaching aid known as Bard G in this research.  The teaching aid was developed to guide students in using Gemini on their own without depending on teacher all the time.  Students were observed to be able to progress on their own using the learning aid without much guidance from teacher.  Compared to previous research carried out by the researchers, students were able to master the skills of using Gemini at the first lesson compared to before this.  It shows that the modules developed by teacher was indeed helpful for students in using Artificial Intelligence such as Gemini.

All 40 students were asked to write down their perceptions regarding the use of Bard G after the essay writing lessons. Below are the students’ responses collected through students’ journal entries.

Student 1

Bard G helps me to write easily.

Student 2

I have no problem to use Gemini if I have Bard G.

Student 3

Gemini is easy to use.

Student 4

I am confident to teach other students to use Gemini with the prompts in Bard G

Student 5

At first, it was difficult to use Gemini.  However, after using    Bard G, I can use Gemini easily.

**Findings from Observation**

Compared to the previous study carried out by the researchers, it was observed that students were struggling initially in using Gemini for essay writing because they had to depend fully on the teacher.  However, the use of Bard G had enabled students to progress further on their own just by following the instructions in the Bard G mobile application and modules.  Before using Bard G, it was observed that students had to spend about an hour for the essay writing task.  However, with the use of Bard G, students could complete the essay writing task within half an hour.  Students were observed to be more confident in doing the essay writing task on their own with the use of Bard G.  As responded during the interviews, the respondents stated that they believed they could teach other students how to write using Google Gemini with the use of Bard G.  Finally, teacher no longer had to spend tremendous amount of time to guide students in using Gemini.

**Findings from Semi-Structured Interview**

The semi-structured interview used in this study was adopted from previous study [22].

During the interview session, students revealed that they could learn on their own using Google Gemini through Bard G as the latter provided responses based on students’ queries. For instance, Google Gemini was able to provide different essays for the prompts ‘Form Three students’ and ‘Primary Three ‘ students. In addition, Google Gemini also provided different evaluations for students’ essays. Gemini was able to analyse students’ strengths and weaknesses in essay writing and provided suitable recommendations for them. This helped students to further improve their essays based on the personalised responses given by Google Gemini. However, students responded that they had to depend on Bard G and prompts developed by the teacher to use Google Gemini.

In addition, students could learn on their own using the ‘drafts’, ‘canvas’ and ‘regenerate’ functions available in Google Gemini as they provide different types of responses based on students’ queries. For the same prompt, Google Gemini is able to generate different types of responses such as easy, difficult, casual and informal. This helps students with different proficiency levels to choose the type of responses based on their needs and proficiency level.  However, students asserted that they need to refer to Bard G to use Google Gemini effectively.

Finally, Google Gemini enables students to learn on their own based on their pace and time. Students who are better can progress on their own using Google Gemini and Bard G while the weaker students can choose a simpler text to learn.

### DISCUSSION

The findings of this study were supported by studies carried out by previous researchers [2],[3]-[5].  They stated that generative AI can provide personalised learning for students as it can give different responses based on the prompts used. In fact, Google Gemini is the best generative AI nowadays [17],[18]. However, there are still many challenges in the implementation of AI based classroom in Malaysia due to factors such as lack of facilities and guidance in using generative AI. In Malaysia, the demand in using technology and the lack of proper guidance in using it have caused tremendous stress among teachers [19]. This phenomenon is termed ‘technostress’. Thus, proper guidance in using generative AI such as the use of Bard G should be encouraged among language teachers.

### CONCLUSION

Although generative AI has made tremendous impacts in our education, there is still lack of proper guidelines for Malaysian educators and teachers in using it.  Hence, learning aid such as Bard G should be used to provide proper guidelines in using generative AI.  The use of Bard G enabled students to use generative AI on their own without depending totally on the teacher as they can refer to the prompts and steps in Bard G to further progress on their own.  However, this study is a case study that was carried out on a group of Form 4 students at a secondary school in Johor Bahru.  Different results might be obtained with different age groups of students and with different language skills.  Hence, it is recommended that in the future, research can be carried out regarding the use of Bard G and Gemini with different age groups of students as well as other language skills.

The article has DOI https://dx.doi.org/10.47772/IJRISS.2025.903SEDU0438, was received 28 July 2025, accepted 04 August 2025, and published 27 August 2025.

PURPOSE & BACKGROUND: The study addresses the lack of studies on generative AI (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) use among Malaysian secondary school students and insufficient training/materials to guide teachers and students. Writing is identified as one of the most difficult language skills for Malaysian students (for whom English is a second/foreign language), with common problems including inability to form grammatically accurate sentences, poor vocabulary command, and mother-tongue interference.

METHOD: The researchers developed a learning aid called "Bard G" (consisting of a mobile application, two modules/books, and a rainbow chart) to guide students in using Google Gemini for essay writing. The first module is for beginners with explanations and illustrations about Gemini; the second provides step-by-step guidance for all three essay writing stages (pre-writing, while writing, post-writing) with Bahasa Melayu translations for weaker students. The rainbow chart contains only the prompts for the three essay writing stages. Participants were 40 Form 4 students (High English Proficiency) from a secondary school in Johor Bahru, chosen because they had no public examinations that year. Data was gathered using semi-structured interviews, journal entries, and participant observation, analyzed qualitatively using thematic approach with Atlas.ti.

PROCEDURE: In the first lesson, students were exposed to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot. In the second lesson, they wrote an essay individually ('Review of A Traditional Restaurant') using Gemini guided by Bard G modules. In the third lesson, students evaluated their essays using Gemini (with translation to mother tongue for those who couldn't understand), and sent evaluations to the teacher's email.

FINDINGS - Problems identified while using Gemini included: (1) lack of facilities/poor internet connection (too many students on Wifi), (2) insufficient computer knowledge (students were used to mobile phones, not laptops, and struggled with uploading clear photos of essays, resulting in illegible handwriting comments), and (3) lack of guidance in using AI (most students' first time using AI; they depended on teacher-developed prompts). Some students found Gemini's language too difficult to understand.

FINDINGS - Usefulness: Themes of personalized learning, differentiation strategy, and self-directed learning were identified. Gemini provided different essays and evaluations based on prompts (e.g., different responses for 'Form Three students' vs 'Primary Three' prompts), analyzed strengths/weaknesses with recommendations, and offered 'drafts', 'canvas', and 'regenerate' functions allowing students of different proficiency levels to choose response types. Students could learn at their own pace. With Bard G, students could complete essay writing tasks within half an hour (compared to about an hour before), were more confident, and could teach others to use Gemini. Student quotes included: "Bard G helps me to write easily", "I am confident to teach other students to use Gemini with the prompts in Bard G", and "At first, it was difficult to use Gemini. However, after using Bard G, I can use Gemini easily."

DISCUSSION & CONCLUSION: Findings align with previous research showing GenAI provides personalized learning. The lack of guidance and facilities in Malaysia has caused "technostress" among teachers. The paper recommends Bard G be used to provide proper guidelines in using generative AI, allowing students to progress independently. Limitations: the study is a case study confined to Form 4 students at one Johor Bahru secondary school; different results may occur with other age groups or language skills. Future research is recommended on Bard G and Gemini with different age groups and other language skills (grammar, listening, speaking).

# The Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools to Enhance University Students’ Academic Writing Skills in English Education

## Authors

* Sofia Dwi Sanzain   Department of English Education, Muhammadiyah Mataram, Indonesia
* Ilham   Department of English Education, Muhammadiyah Mataram, Indonesia
* Rima Rahmaniah   Department of English Education, Muhammadiyah Mataram, Indonesia

## DOI:

 <https://doi.org/10.55885/jerp.v6i1.924>

## Keywords:

 Artificial Intelligence, Academic Writing, Higher Education, Writing Performance, Learner Autonomy

## Abstract

*The rapid advancement of technology has transformed higher education, particularly in the domain of English academic writing, which requires complex cognitive, linguistic, and organizational skills. This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in enhancing university students’ academic writing performance, cognitive engagement, and learner autonomy. Using a quantitative one-group pretest–posttest design, 20 students participated in an AI-assisted writing intervention incorporating grammar checkers, paraphrasing aids, vocabulary enhancers, and automated feedback. Descriptive and non-parametric analyses, including the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test, were conducted to evaluate changes in writing performance, while students’ perceptions were collected via questionnaires. The findings indicate significant improvements in accuracy, coherence, and overall writing quality, with reduced performance gaps among students. Learners reported positive experiences, emphasizing increased confidence, motivation, and autonomy in the writing process. Despite methodological limitations, the results highlight the pedagogical and cognitive benefits of AI integration, suggesting that AI tools can function as effective scaffolds for complex writing tasks. Implications for curriculum design and future research on long-term and diverse applications are also discussed.*

This webpage presents a research article titled "The Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools to Enhance University Students' Academic Writing Skills in English Education," published on May 8, 2026, in the Journal of Education Review Provision (Vol. 6, No. 1, pp. 1-13). The article is authored by Sofia Dwi Sanzain, Ilham, and Rima Rahmaniah from the Department of English Education, Muhammadiyah Mataram, Indonesia. The DOI is https://doi.org/10.55885/jerp.v6i1.924.

The study investigates how AI tools can enhance university students' academic writing performance, cognitive engagement, and learner autonomy in English education. The methodology employed was a quantitative one-group pretest-posttest design with 20 students participating in an AI-assisted writing intervention that incorporated grammar checkers, paraphrasing aids, vocabulary enhancers, and automated feedback. Data analysis used descriptive and non-parametric statistics, including the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test, while student perceptions were collected via questionnaires.

Key findings indicate significant improvements in writing accuracy, coherence, and overall quality, with reduced performance gaps among students. Learners reported positive experiences, emphasizing increased confidence, motivation, and autonomy in the writing process. The results highlight the pedagogical and cognitive benefits of AI integration, suggesting that AI tools can serve as effective scaffolds for complex writing tasks. The study also discusses implications for curriculum design and future research on long-term and diverse applications, while acknowledging methodological limitations.

The article includes an extensive reference list of approximately 70 sources covering topics such as AI in education, writing feedback, EFL/ESL writing instruction, learner engagement, and educational technology. The article is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License and is available for download in PDF format.

# New Research: Majority of High School Students Use Generative AI for Schoolwork

*New research reveals rising adoption among students, growing concerns among educators, and major policy gaps in U.S. high schools*

[College Board

* October 6, 2025](/author/college-board-communications)

In [new research](https://research.collegeboard.org/technology-learning) published today, College Board finds **AI use is more prevalent than ever in America’s high schools**. Recent advancements of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, like ChatGPT, have contributed to the surge in AI’s growing use in high school settings.

Findings from student, parent, and educator responses to College Board surveys administered between June 2024 and June 2025 highlight three emerging trends:

1. **The percentage of high school students who report using GenAI tools for schoolwork is growing, increasing from 79% to 84% between January and May 2025.**  
   Half of high school students are using AI tools for schoolwork to brainstorm ideas, edit or revise essays, and/or conduct research and find sources. ChatGPT is high school students’ GenAI tool of choice. 69% of high school students reported using ChatGPT to help with school assignments and homework in May 2025.
2. **High school students, parents, and educators believe there are benefits to using AI, but they also have concerns.**  
   Students are on the fence. 50% neither agree or disagree that the benefits of using AI are greater than the risks, one-quarter agree, and one-quarter disagree. Among parents of high school students, nearly 6 in 10 agree it’s better for students to use GenAI for schoolwork than not to use it. As for school administrators, more than 85% view students’ learning to use AI tools as part of their high school education as very or somewhat valuable. However, principals, AP coordinators, and teachers still have concerns about AI affecting students’ academic integrity, students’ essential learning skills, and teachers’ technical and professional support needs.
3. **Educators are still finding their way regarding AI, and a minority of schools are establishing official, uniform student GenAI use policies.**  
   55% of principals indicate that their high schools haven’t blocked students or teachers from accessing GenAI tools on the school’s network, while the remaining 45% report at least some level of restrictions around GenAI tool access. As for use, roughly 2 in 5 schools or districts don’t allow students to use GenAI. Approximately 1 in 5 allow such use but have no policy in place. About 13% encourage GenAI use in all classes, while 16% delegate GenAI policy determination to individual teachers, and 12% delegate policy setting to departments or grade levels.

“Many are experimenting with AI in education, but a meaningful impact requires more than experimentation. It requires listening to students, parents, and educators, and grounding solutions in evidence,” said **College Board** **Vice President of Research Jessica Howell, Ph.D.** “Our research-driven approach ensures that schools at every level, including our vast network of K−12 and higher education members, have the clarity and confidence to navigate this shift while keeping authentic student learning at the center.”

The surge in AI’s adoption has been so swift that many educators, including teachers, administrators, and district leaders, are struggling to keep up and provide the support and guidance their students and colleagues need. Until now, little has been known or understood about how students are using AI in high schools for schoolwork and about the perceptions of students, parents, and educators on its impact on learning. This research begins to close that gap and offer clarity on the rapid rise.

As a trusted partner to schools, College Board is focused on ensuring that AI enhances student learning rather than short-circuiting it. That begins with giving educators the tools and [support](https://apcentral.collegeboard.org/exam-administration-ordering-scores/administering-exams/exam-policies/artificial-intelligence-tools) they need to navigate this new reality. At the same time, we’re committed to helping students build and demonstrate the [skills](https://apcentral.collegeboard.org/courses/ap-career-kickstart) that will matter most for their futures.

In 2024, College Board launched the GenAI Studio, an internal incubator dedicated to accelerating generative AI learnings and responsible use of AI across College Board programs. “Our GenAI work is grounded in a commitment to safeguarding authentic student learning, enhancing the student-teacher relationship, and helping students build the skills they will need to thrive in the future,” said **College Board General Manager of GenAI Studio Sophia Romee**.

Uncovering the role of GenAI is a call to action. Research on how key stakeholders in education are navigating this shift is critical in two ways: It supports the implementation of best GenAI practices in the classroom. It helps develop effective GenAI policies to turn this moment of uncertainty into one of opportunity for all students.

---

**College Board Research**

The Research Department generates data and evidence on the impact of educational programs, assessments, and initiatives on students and various education stakeholders. For further information and publications, visit [research.collegeboard.org](https://research.collegeboard.org).

# Discovering how students use generative artificial intelligence tools for academic writing purposes

## Authors

## DOI:

## Keywords:

## Abstract

The aim of this project was to identify ways in which students are using Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) technologies for the planning and researching stage of essay style assignments. The study recruited 30 students from various subject areas and levels of study and with different self-reported levels of confidence in using GAI tools. Each student was given three essay questions to choose from and 50 minutes to research their topic, make notes from sources, and put together an essay plan, using GAI tools if they deemed them useful. Their screens were recorded to facilitate a natural planning process and they were encouraged to narrate to provide insight into their reasoning. Of the 30 participants, 21 (70%) used GAI technologies within their process. ChatGPT 3.5 (Open AI) was the most frequently chosen, with 18 students (60%) using this. The most popular use of GAI was asking for definitions, explanations, or examples; or creating an essay plan or structure. The study also provided insight into students’ searching process, revealing that Google was the most popular starting point (chosen by 30% of students). Journal articles were the most popular source type (used by 80% of participants), and skim reading a section of a source was the most common method used to decide if it was relevant, with 63.3% of students doing this. When examining referencing behaviour, 80% of the students included some form of references in their essay plan, but none of the students created references for any GAI tools they had used.

# A guide to creating AI-powered art in the classroom

AI art tools democratize visual expression in classrooms, helping students visualize complex ideas across subjects through text prompts—building creativity and critical thinking skills.

Nikki Muncey • May 27, 2025

Teacher Workflow & Planning
