# Digital Education

## Digital Education

Digital education is the integration of digital technologies into teaching and learning processes, ranging from the use of devices and platforms in the classroom to the development of digital skills of students and teachers. It goes beyond simple access to computers or the internet: it involves transforming the way teaching and learning take place, preparing young people to participate in an increasingly digitalized economy.

Its importance is strategic for Latin America and the Caribbean, where the digital divide exacerbates existing educational inequalities. According to PISA 2022 data, only 66% of students in the region attended a school with effective online learning platforms, and barely 3 out of 10 students attended a school whose teachers received incentives to integrate technology into their teaching — a figure that does not even reach half the average of OECD countries.

The World Bank Group supports educational digital transformation in the region with a strategy that combines financing, technical assistance, and innovation.

Since 2024, the World Bank has presented the Digital Innovations for Education series, which documents and disseminates successful cases of digitalization in the region, including the use of artificial intelligence for principals, teachers, and students, as well as tools for personalized learning.

## **INVESTING** IN DIGITAL

Digitalization is one of the most powerful development opportunities of our time. Connectivity, data, and digital tools are now essential to how hospitals deliver care, how farmers access markets, how teachers reach students, and how governments serve their citizens. With the right foundations—affordable internet, trusted data systems, and secure digital platforms—developing countries can unlock faster, more inclusive growth.

Artificial intelligence and the broader data revolution are accelerating this shift. They are expanding what institutions can do, improving service delivery, and opening new economic pathways. Yet not everyone is benefiting equally. As of [2025](https://www.itu.int/itu-d/reports/statistics/facts-figures-2025/), over 2 billion people - about a quarter of the world's population - remained offline, and internet use ranged from over 90% in high-income countries to just 23% in low-income countries. Meanwhile, 800 million people still lack official ID, limiting access to digital public services, finance, and healthcare.

At the same time, digitalization is transforming labor markets. New types of jobs are emerging; others are changing, and all require new skills. With nearly 800 million people in low- and middle-income countries at risk of being without work over the next decade, investing in digital skills and workforce readiness is essential for countries to compete and thrive.

The good news is that countries don’t need to wait for large, complex AI systems to start benefiting. Many are already adopting “[small AI](https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/voices/small-ai-big-impact-harnessing-artificial-intelligence-for-development)” approaches—nimble, targeted tools that deliver practical results now. These solutions can support frontline health workers with decision support, help teachers personalize learning, strengthen early-warning systems in agriculture, and improve core government operations. “Small AI” offers a steppingstone toward more advanced AI-enabled transformation by building capacity, trust, and responsible data use along the way.

Ensuring that these digital opportunities translate into real development impact requires strong safeguards and institutions. Data protection, cybersecurity, and interoperable systems are critical to building confidence among users and ensuring that digital platforms remain secure, inclusive, and resilient.

Together, digitalization and AI offer a historic chance to expand opportunity, strengthen public services, and boost economic resilience—if countries can access the tools, skills, and foundations, they need to use them well.

To help countries benefit from today’s digital age, the World Bank Group works to ensure that people, governments, and businesses can get online, use digital and AI tools safely, and tap into new economic and job opportunities.

The World Bank Group’s digital work supports countries as they build the infrastructure, institutions, and skills needed to make the most of digital technologies. It helps expand connectivity, strengthen data systems, grow the private sector, improve digital public services, and use emerging tools like AI in practical, responsible ways. The strategy centers on four core pillars, with a strong emphasis on digital safeguards throughout.

*Access:* The World Bank helps countries expand access to high-quality connectivity, especially in hard-to-reach areas, by supporting governments to create the right conditions for inclusive digital development—facilitating shared infrastructure, cross-border fiber networks, and public-private partnerships that attract private investment and lower deployment costs.

*Affordability:* The World Bank works with governments to make digital access more affordable by reducing the cost of devices and data through demand aggregation, tax reform, local manufacturing, and programs that promote refurbishment and reuse.

*Ecosystems:* The World Bank supports countries in strengthening digital transactions and services through digital public infrastructure—such as digital IDs, payment platforms, and secure data sharing systems—and user-centric digital government. In parallel, it helps build digital skills, foster startup ecosystems, advance regulatory reforms, and attract investment to spur innovation and job creation.

*AI Readiness*: The World Bank helps countries build the foundations for AI innovation and apply practical “small AI” solutions suited to local needs and infrastructure—for example, mobile apps for precision agriculture or personalized education. It also supports stronger data ecosystems, investments in cloud and computing capacity, workforce training, and inclusive national AI strategies.

*Cross-Cutting Digital Safeguards*: Across all areas of engagement, the World Bank emphasizes the importance of building legal and regulatory frameworks that protect data privacy, promote cybersecurity, and ensure responsible technology use.

By working closely with governments, industry, and development partners, the World Bank Group helps countries put proven digital solutions into practice, scale what works, and take advantage of new opportunities for inclusive, sustainable growth.

<webpage_content>
AI Education Copyright © 2019, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence. All rights reserved. ISSN 0738-4602 88 AI MAGAZINE T oday’s children are growing up with artificial intelli-gence (AI). By the time children enter kindergarten, they have likely been conversing with Amazon’s Alexa for years. AI is a disruptive technology, promising social and economic changes our society needs to wrestle with. As cur-rent users of AI and future decision-makers, children must be AI literate to engage in meaningful discourse about its effects. Due to the widespread impacts of AI, we want to foster a diverse population of AI developers. In this context, we need to engage students throughout their education starting as early as kindergarten through high school (K-12) and encourage early consideration of AI-related careers.
There are national efforts under way to make computing a core fixture in K–12 classrooms. While there are national  The time is ripe to consider what 21st-century digital citizens should know about artificial intelligence (AI). Efforts are under way in the USA, China, and many other countries to promote AI education in kindergar-ten through high school (K–12). The past year has seen the release of new curricula and online resources for the K–12 audience, and new professional development opportunities for K–12 teachers to learn the basics of AI. This column surveys the current state of K–12 AI education and introduces the work of the AI4K12 Initiative, which is developing national guidelines for AI education in the USA.
A Year in K–12 AI Education David Touretzky, Christina Gardner-McCune, Cynthia Breazeal, Fred Martin, Deborah Seehorn AI Education WINTER 2019 89 standards for K–12 computing instruction developed by the Computer Science Teachers Association, the 2017 version contains only two sentences about AI (CSTA 2017). A growing number of teachers want more guidance in this area, but this is a significant challenge, given that most K–12 educators do not have a background in computer science or AI.
In May 2018, the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence and the Computer Science Teachers Association launched a joint initiative to develop national guidelines for teaching AI in K–12. The AI4K12 Initiative (AI4K12.org) is a National Sci-ence Foundation-funded project led by a four-person steering committee (Touretzky, Gardner-McCune, Martin, and Seehorn 2019). The AI4K12 Working Group is composed of practicing K–12 teachers and AI subject-matter experts. In its first year, the work-ing group published a list of five big ideas in AI that serve as the organizing framework for the guidelines (figure 1). Each big idea is unpacked into a set of con-cepts and subconcepts that are further expanded for each grade band (K–2, 3–5, 6–8, and 9–12) and then summarized in a progression chart. Completing this progression chart by mid-2020 is currently the major focus of the AI4K12 Working Group. The chief aim of this initiative is to support teachers as they engage students in AI, and to provide guidelines that curric-ulum developers will choose to align their work with.
There are a number of K–12 curriculum develop-ment efforts occurring worldwide in academia, non-profits, and for-profit companies. Some significant milestones in the last year were from Exploring Computer Science, Microsoft TEALS, ReadyAI, AI4All, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and the Finnish Center for Artificial Intelligence. For example, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology recently released an AI + ethics curriculum for middle school students that uses a combination of online and un-plugged activities (Payne 2019). The curriculum not only helps students learn about the technical aspects of AI, but also helps them engage with its social and ethical implications. One activity in the curriculum introduces students to machine learning by having them develop a visual classifier using Google’s Teach­ able Machine and then experiment with bias in train-ing. This activity fosters discussion about sources of bias and the ethical implications of technologies. This curriculum has been accessed over 500 times and is being translated into multiple languages by the broader community.
The range of AI topics students are able to explore is closely tied to the availability of developmentally ap-propriate tools for K–12. Many K–12 AI curricula make use of materials that run the gamut from traditional textbooks to interactive media such as Jupyter note-books and online courseware and project-based learn-ing opportunities that leverage student-friendly coding platforms such as Scratch, App Inventor, and Snap!. A number of these platforms integrate commercial cog-nitive services, AI tools, and datasets developed by university or corporate research laboratories to provide user-friendly tools for K–12 students. Cognimates and Machine Learning for Kids combine IBM Watson’s AI services with Scratch. Teachable Machine by Google’s Creative Lab trains custom visual classifiers. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s App Inven-tor leverages the Amazon Alexa Toolkit to provide con-versational AI tools for mobile app development. In addition to these hands-on computer-based activities, unplugged activities such as Socratic seminar, team-based paper prototyping, and creative writing exer-cises also have value for promoting AI literacy.
Given the impact of AI technologies on different industries and society at large, future AI curricula and tools need to incorporate curricular goals of sci-ence, mathematics, social studies, humanities, and the arts. To ensure that AI instruction is accessible and developmentally appropriate for all students, curriculum and tool development efforts need to be iterative, collaborative processes that involve active participation among all stakeholders, including de-velopers, teachers, and the students themselves.
Since the launch of AI4K12, we are seeing the growth of a new K–12 AI Education Community con-sisting of AI researchers, computer science education researchers, K–12 teachers, and curriculum develop-ers. The biggest factor in the growth of the US K–12 teacher community has been the rollout of a teacher professional development course on AI from the International Society for Technology in Education. Joseph South, International Society for Technology in Education’s chief learning officer, reports that as of September 2019, over 560 K–12 educators have completed the course. We anticipate similar growth globally as we are aware of parallel efforts to develop capabilities in K–12 AI Education in numerous other countries, including China, Finland, the United Kingdom, Canada, Turkey, Portugal, South Korea, and Argentina. We hope to see continued growth of this community and to leverage the expertise of AI researchers in collaboration with teachers to produce much-needed resources for K–12 AI education.
Looking to become involved in K–12 AI educa-tion? Join the AI4K12 mailing list (see AI4K12.org for the subscription link). Develop online tools and demos for making AI concepts accessible to the K–12 audience. Volunteer at your local school to help teachers and students explore AI.

This article, published in AI Magazine (Winter 2019), surveys the state of K-12 artificial intelligence (AI) education and introduces the AI4K12 Initiative. The article argues that children growing up with AI must become AI literate to engage in meaningful discourse about its effects, and that diverse AI developers should be fostered through education starting in kindergarten.

Key developments highlighted include:
- In May 2018, the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI) and the Computer Science Teachers Association (CSTA) launched the AI4K12 Initiative (AI4K12.org), a National Science Foundation-funded project led by a four-person steering committee including David Touretzky, Christina Gardner-McCune, Fred Martin, and Deborah Seehorn.
- The AI4K12 Working Group published "Five Big Ideas in AI" as an organizing framework: (1) Perception, (2) Representation & Reasoning, (3) Learning, (4) Natural Interaction, and (5) Societal Impact. Each is expanded into concepts for grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12, with a progression chart due by mid-2020.
- The 2017 CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards contained only two sentences about AI, highlighting the need for more guidance since most K-12 educators lack CS/AI backgrounds.
- Significant curriculum efforts emerged from Exploring Computer Science, Microsoft TEALS, ReadyAI, AI4All, MIT, and the Finnish Center for Artificial Intelligence.
- MIT released an AI + ethics curriculum for middle school students combining online and unplugged activities, including using Google's Teachable Machine to build visual classifiers and experiment with bias in training. This curriculum was accessed over 500 times and translated into multiple languages.
- Tools supporting K-12 AI education include Cognimates, Machine Learning for Kids (combining IBM Watson with Scratch), Teachable Machine by Google, and MIT's App Inventor with the Amazon Alexa Toolkit, alongside unplugged activities like Socratic seminars and paper prototyping.
- The International Society for Technology in Education (ISTE) rolled out a teacher professional development course; as of September 2019, over 560 K-12 educators had completed it.
- Similar K-12 AI education efforts are underway in China, Finland, the United Kingdom, Canada, Turkey, Portugal, South Korea, and Argentina.

# 5 Tips For Addressing AI in Your Academic Integrity Code

![Carlos Díaz](https://www.carnegielearning.com/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20images/1590967328146.jpg?width=120&height=120&name=1590967328146.jpg)

## What your school can do to prepare for AI in education

As a librarian and Extended Essay coordinator, the emergence of generative [AI in education](https://time.com/6300950/ai-schools-chatgpt-teachers/) sent shivers down my spine. Within two days of playing with it, I called a meeting with my Head of School to warn him about the storm to come.

At the time, I feared what others feared: writing was dead, and there would be no point in asking students to write essays anymore. Now I realize that I was overreacting. People have worried about using calculators, the internet, and other technology in schools, and we’ve adjusted fine.  
  
As AI in education advances, schools need to update their policies to address the challenges and opportunities this new technology brings. Rather than a doomsday device, generative AI—when [used ethically](https://www.carnegielearning.com/blog/is-using-chatgpt-cheating)—can ease the lives of students and teachers.

With a more realistic view of AI in education, I set about updating our school's academic integrity policy to address the role of generative AI in classrooms. 

Here’s what I learned and recommend to educators for updating their academic integrity policies in the age of AI.

## 1. Leverage existing frameworks. Don’t reinvent the wheel!

Organizations like [International Baccalaureate](http://www.ibo.org/programmes/artificial-intelligence-ai-in-learning-teaching-and-assessment/) and [Elsevier](https://www.elsevier.com/about/policies-and-standards/publishing-ethics), universities, and colleges have developed reliable frameworks for using AI in education. Starting from scratch doesn't make sense, so consider their guidance when writing your school's AI policy.

If your school follows the International Baccalaureate or College Board-sanctioned curricula, you must follow their recently updated guidelines. If your school doesn’t use either, you can get directions from the [MLA](https://style.mla.org/citing-generative-ai/) and [APA](https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/how-to-cite-chatgpt) citation guidelines. Quote them in your policy, and rely on the work of reputed organizations.

## 2. Tailor AI policies for your school

When updating your school’s or district’s academic integrity policy to address AI, you’ll want to consider what makes the most sense for your students and teachers.

There is no universally agreed-upon set of hard-and-fast rules for exactly what is and isn’t ethical when using AI in education. One teacher might think using AI to proofread an essay is cheating, while another teacher might fully support it. So, choose what works for your school or district’s needs, values, and goals.

Here are specific areas of ethical ambiguity to consider when crafting your school's policy:

By implementing and adapting these recommendations to your specific context, you can ensure a smooth integration of AI tools that foster ethical learning and empower students to become responsible digital citizens.

## **3. Provide training and support on AI**

As a school community, your administration should [provide workshops](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-survey-less-10-schools-and-universities-have-formal-guidance-ai) and professional learning opportunities about artificial intelligence for staff and students so everybody knows what to expect.

In our school guidelines, we added that students and teachers can anticipate the following: “The school will guide teachers and students in the ethical use of generative AI and assistive technology.”

This reflects our school's commitment to setting up our teachers and students for success with navigating new AI tools and technology. Training and support on ethical AI usage can delve into these specific areas:

**Identifying bias in AI systems and data.** Awareness of potential biases in AI tools and datasets is crucial to ensuring fair and inclusive use. Workshops can equip educators and students with strategies for critically evaluating AI outputs and addressing potential biases.

**Safeguarding privacy and data security.** Generative AI and assistive technology often require access to personal data. Workshops can educate participants on data privacy best practices.

**Integrating AI tools into existing curricula.** Educators can benefit from training on integrating AI tools into lesson plans and assignments across diverse subjects. This includes exploring the pedagogical potential of AI for personalized learning, collaborative activities, and creative expression.

If you provide training and support on using AI, you can foster a culture of responsible use and continuous learning that will empower teachers and students alike.

## **4. Embrace the ever-evolving nature of AI in education**

Make sure your policy is reviewed regularly, at least once per year. If the sudden boom of AI in education has taught us anything, technology is only accelerating. More and more powerful AI tools will emerge in the coming years. Your policy should be ready to adapt to these massive shifts in how we do things.

Here are some specific tips for making your policy more flexible:

**Avoid using specific examples of AI tools or technologies in your policy.** Instead, focus on broad principles that apply to any AI tool.

**Avoid making sweeping generalizations about AI.** Instead, focus on specific concerns that you have about the use of AI in education.

**Be open to feedback from students, teachers, and other stakeholders.**

These tips will help you develop a flexible policy to adapt to AI's [ever-changing landscape](http://www.forbes.com/sites/vickiphillips/2023/06/07/intelligent-classrooms-what-ai-means-for-the-future-of-education/?sh=7285352deffb) in education.

## **5. Shift your focus from AI policing to growth-oriented assessments**

While relying on AI detectors to monitor student behavior might seem tempting, they often prove to be more trouble than they're worth. Inaccurate and intrusive, these technologies are best avoided as a policing tool.  
Instead, let's focus on designing assessments that foster learning and measure progress, not just outcomes.

When we prioritize growth instead of just focusing on results, we develop assessments that are naturally more resistant to academic dishonesty. This approach promotes a more positive learning environment and yields more meaningful insights into student development.

**Adapting academic integrity policies in the AI era**

Updating educational integrity policies to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI is crucial in making sure students use technology ethically in education.

Schools can create robust policies that promote academic integrity while leveraging the benefits of AI in education if they follow the tips outlined in this article, such as leveraging existing frameworks, emphasizing ethics, providing training, acknowledging the variability of the situation, and avoiding detectors.  

As we foster a learning environment that upholds integrity and intellectual honesty, we will prepare students for future success, no matter how AI shapes the world.

*Want to know the state of AI in education? Download our 2024 AI in Education Report and see what nearly 800 educators across the country think about the present and future of artificial intelligence.*

Rather than a doomsday device, generative AI—when used ethically—can ease the lives of students and teachers.

args.summary:
This is an opinion/advice article by Carlos Díaz, a librarian and Extended Essay coordinator, published on Carnegie Learning's website, offering 5 tips for schools updating their academic integrity policies to address generative AI in education. The author initially feared AI would "kill" essay writing but now believes that when used ethically, generative AI can ease the lives of students and teachers.

The five tips are:

1. **Leverage existing frameworks** — Schools should not reinvent the wheel; instead, they should draw on established AI guidance from organizations like the International Baccalaureate, Elsevier, universities/colleges, and citation guidelines from MLA and APA. Schools using IB or College Board curricula must follow their recently updated guidelines.

2. **Tailor AI policies for your school** — There is no universally agreed-upon set of rules for what is ethical AI use; policies should reflect each school's needs, values, and goals. Schools should address specific areas of ethical ambiguity (e.g., whether AI proofreading constitutes cheating).

3. **Provide training and support on AI** — Administrations should offer workshops and professional learning on AI for staff and students. Key training areas include identifying bias in AI systems/data, safeguarding privacy and data security, and integrating AI tools into existing curricula.

4. **Embrace the ever-evolving nature of AI** — Policies should be reviewed at least once per year. Recommendations include avoiding specific AI tool examples (focus on broad principles), avoiding sweeping generalizations about AI, and being open to stakeholder feedback.

5. **Shift focus from AI policing to growth-oriented assessments** — AI detectors are described as "inaccurate and intrusive" and "best avoided as a policing tool." Instead, schools should design assessments that foster learning and measure progress, which are naturally more resistant to academic dishonesty.

The article concludes that schools can create robust policies promoting academic integrity while leveraging AI's benefits by following these tips. It also references Carnegie Learning's 2024 AI in Education Report (surveying nearly 800 educators) and includes a key quote: "Rather than a doomsday device, generative AI—when used ethically—can ease the lives of students and teachers." Related articles on the page cover topics like students using AI to cheat and how educators are using AI.

## Abstract

To open this special issue of The Journal of Educational Research, I have collected a range of research reports on teaching and learning with generative artificial intelligence (GAI). To guide readers in exploring the contents of this special issue, I have provided a summary of each of the included research reports. I have organized the articles by educational context to provide readers with additional context for the articles and enhance the potential for translating the research into practice. I open and conclude my introduction by positioning the adoption of GAI as considering and exploring GAI in K‑12 learning as an educational innovation and the opportunities and limitations for embracing GAI as a tool for learning and teaching.

Keywords:

*   [Educational innovation](https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/Educational+innovation)
*   [generative artificial intelligence](https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/generative+artificial+intelligence)
*   [teaching and learning with technology](https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/teaching+and+learning+with+technology)
*   [international perspectives](https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/international+perspectives)

Previous article[View issue table of contents](https://www.tandfonline.com/toc/vjer20/118/6?nav=tocList)[Next article](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2511229)

## Introduction

We have entered a new era of technological innovation with the rapid popularization of artificial intelligence (AI). The access and integration of both predictive and generative artificial intelligence has become widespread with a broad and expanding range of potential applications. While predictive artificial intelligence (PAI) has been mainstreamed for many years (e.g., spelling check in word processing software), generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has been a relatively recent introduction to the general public. Generative artificial intelligence has a wide range of capabilities, including generating text, pictures, images, sounds, voices, and movies, including animation. The breadth of the potential of GAI continues to expand as the accumulation of extant data into repositories increases. The expansion of data accessible for GAI creations has increased the potential usefulness in a wide diversity of educational settings.

We dedicated this special issue of the Journal of Educational Research to research reports on the potential and current applications of GAI in K-12 educational settings. My introductory chapter is intended to provide a roadmap and synthesis for exploring the reports published in this issue detailing the evidence-based practices that include integrating GAI in K-12 education. For this issue, I have curated a diversity of empirical research reports detailing how students and teachers are using GAI to enhance learning and teaching effectiveness. The range of contexts and locations in which the research took place, as detailed in the included reports in this special issue, are a testament to the global use of GAI in K-12 education. Further, the reports reflect how GAI may be transforming teaching and learning in alignment with the activities of 21st-century societies.

## Teacher GAI adoption and instructional use

As with many other education innovations, the adoption of GAI in K-12 for teaching and learning appears to be aligned with the fundamental principles of diffusion theory (Rogers, [Citation 1995](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). As Nadelson et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) report, there is a wide diversity of justifications and supports for teachers considering (or not considering) GAI for teaching and learning. The association between the adoption and use of GAI with professional development is consistent with the Nadelson and Seifert ([Citation 2016](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) report on teacher embrace and integration of integrated STEM. In their exploration of teacher experiences with GAI, Döğer and Göçen ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined the related issues across 15 countries, finding educators tended to maintain a critical perspective on using GAI for teaching and learning. The research provides a unique baseline for future analysis that may focus on the evolution of teachers’ adoption of GAI.

Embracing a similar framework to Nadelson et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)), Isik ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined teacher adoption of GAI in alignment with other models of technology and innovation adoption. Isik explored the adoption based on tangible indicators such as usefulness and ease of use among a population of teachers engaged in professional development offerings focused on using GAI for teaching and learning. The research provides empirical documentation for the potential professional development may have on teacher integrations of GAI in their teaching and for their student learning

In their exploration of the perceptions and use of AI tools in eTwinning environments, Döğer and Göçen ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) conducted semi-structured interviews of teachers from a range of participating countries. They found that teachers tended to find benefits to using AI, including increased efficiency in lesson planning, assessing student work, and opportunities for collaboration. Their research also revealed a number of common issues, such as ethical concerns, bias, overreliance, and privacy. Döğer and Göçen also raised concerns about the potential for controlled access to and knowledge of AI to exacerbate social problems, such as broadening the digital divide and supporting AI-driven capitalism. They conclude their report by offering recommendations for evidence-based practices and a roadmap for integrating AI effectively and thoughtfully into teaching and learning.

In their exploration of how teachers perceive and use GAI in teaching foreign languages, Drożdż et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) gathered a combination of qualitative and quantitative data, seeking to empirically document the teachers’ practices. The researchers found the teachers perceived the use of AI-based corpora to be helpful in enhancing their teaching effectiveness and their students’ learning. The teachers noted that the personalization offered by GAI to their students in their language learning was highly beneficial and enhanced student understanding and their acquisition of foreign language. However, nearly half of the teachers in the study indicated they were unfamiliar with using AI to learn languages, suggesting a high potential for emerging uses of GAI in foreign language learning.

To explore how teachers may be using GAI to develop curriculum and learning activities, Delaney et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) conducted a case study research on two high school teachers. Through the lens of a co-design partnership, Delaney et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examine how teachers learn and subsequently adopt educational innovations, utilizing technology to enhance their practice. Examining how the two teachers were both learning about GAI resources and applications and applying their GAI knowledge to develop curriculum and instructional materials. The researchers found that there is a benefit for teachers to learn about GAI in the context of teaching and learning rather than in a discipline-specific context. In their conclusion, Delaney et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) recognize the need for more research on teacher-generated curriculum and activities, which may be particularly critical as teachers develop more custom instructional materials using GAI.

## Administrators

As leaders in their schools and districts, educational administrators can significantly influence teacher consideration and adoption of educational innovations (e.g., Hsieh et al., [Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). Given the potential influence, there was high justification for the Göçen and Döğer ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) exploration of how school administrators across 20 countries used GAI in their leadership activities. The adoption of GAI by administrators for their practice will likely influence school policy regarding the use of GAI and teacher integration of GAI into their practice. Furthermore, as Göçen and Döğer discuss, it is also essential to consider the limitations of GAI and maintain a balance with social interactions to achieve effective leadership.

## Elementary education

In their exploration of GAI integration for elementary-level student learning, Tetteh et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) leveraged a culture-techno-contextual approach (CTCA). Students taught using the CTCA method experienced higher learning gains compared to their peers taught using traditional lectures for instruction. Further, the students recognized the affordances of CTCA, which has implications for their use of AI beyond traditional learning conditions. The potential of AI to shift to a more student-centered focus in instruction may be a critical consideration for both research and teaching. As the work of Tetteh et al. suggests, integrating GAI may lead to gains in achieving learning objectives and increased student self-directed learning.

Taking a different approach to using AI-driven vocabulary builders, Temiz and Kafadar ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) compared student gains achieved with the AI software to those obtained using traditional flashcards. The prediction was that using adaptive and generative AI in the computer-based vocabulary builder would enhance student learning in ways superior to using flashcards. The results showed significant short-term gains but no significant differences in the long term as students working with the flashcards performed higher and equivalent on the delayed post-test. The research exemplifies how AI may impact short-term learning compared to traditional methods, but in the long term, some forms of AI-based instruction may not result in significant differences compared to conventional approaches. The research provides a useful model for comparing traditional and AI-based learning and a model for framing AI research in terms of meeting learning objectives rather than achieving superior outcomes.

## Middle school education

As many secondary students have extensive access to the internet (Haidt, [Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) and are likely engaging with GAI for a range of reasons, there is a particular need to explore in depth how secondary students are engaging with GAI in their learning. Adisa and Adefisayo ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored how middle school students conceived and perceived GAI should be integrated and used for learning. The students shared perceptions of the importance of teacher supervision of student GAI use and the need to restrict the use of GAI in assessments. The students had mixed preferences for using GAI compared to collaborating with other students. The students’ perspectives offer a unique insight into how students may consider the limitations and ethical uses of GAI, a line of research in which data is collected from teachers or administrators.

Also focusing on using GAI in middle school, Chen et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored how the use of GAI could be used to shift history teaching from the common pedagogical model of teacher-led, text-based learning to an approach that is more interactive and personalized for students. Their quasi-experimental design revealed the use of GAI was effective in enhancing student historical knowledge and motivation for learning. The outcome suggests that, when used effectively, GAI can lead to significant learning gains, greater student engagement, and increased creative learning experiences.

## High school education

As students develop, a level of sophistication for learning about and with GAI is likely to increase, as reflected by Smyslova et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). In their pilot study, they investigated the development of student AI literacy. Focusing on both predictive and generative AI processes, the researchers found significant gains in understanding predictive AI text generation. However, the research also revealed challenges in transitioning their understanding to generative AI processes, with some misconceptions persisting. Further, their research noted gender differences. The research report highlights the importance of moving beyond the mechanics and ethics of GAI use to exploring the actual processes so that students can develop an appreciation of how GAI uses extant data to assemble seemingly unique outputs.

Using the reflective lens of a researcher-practitioner teaching high school history and literature, Wall et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) gathered data to develop a set of evidence-based principles guiding the use of GAI for teaching and learning. Wall et al. moved beyond the approach of limiting student access and trying to control the presence of GAI to a more proactive approach of enhancing students’ GAI literacy. Their proposed principles focus on educating students about GAI, enhancing students’ critical analysis of GAI input and output, and considering student learning holistically. In alignment with their embrace of evidence-based practices, they demonstrate how GAI can enhance student learning.

Extending the empirical documentation of student GAU use, Bieńkowska et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) gathered data from students of different ages, genders, community structures, and schools. The researchers investigated how students used GAI and the impact of GAI use on various variables, including motivation to learn, relationships with teachers, independent thinking, and time management. Bieńkowska and colleagues also examined the students’ perceptions of the advantages and disadvantages of GAI use for learning. They found the students had moderate engagement with GAI and used GAI for a range of tasks. Their research also revealed differences in engagement and motivation for the use of GAI, which were associated with the student’s age, gender, school type, and the community location of the schools the students attended. The results reveal multiple indicators of potential differences in GAI use based on student demographics and expose an array of possible influences that may catalyze the broadening of the digital divide.

Mixing the research on the instructional use of GAI and elements of AI literacy, Liu et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined the benefits and limitations of integrating GAI into teaching high school geography. Starting with a comparison of GAI systems in China and the United States, Liu et al. proceed to explore issues related to the accuracy of GAI output, student dependence, ethical use of intellectual property, and equitable access. Thus, while GAI holds the potential for enhancing student geography learning, there are notable limitations that need to be recognized and perhaps resolved to consider GAI as a highly valuable instructional tool.

Moving beyond instructional use and learning using GAI, Meşe et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored the critical variable of learning engagement. Using the context of GAI use in learning English, Meşe et al. examined the levels of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement among tenth-grade students who used GAI in a writing course. Their semi-structured interviews revealed evidence of student persistence in seeking feedback and support for correcting errors. The students also engaged in critical thinking, seeking to enhance their writing by identifying and correcting errors in their work. Further, the students’ use reflected elements of curiosity and enjoyment. The research of Meşe et al. underscores the need to move beyond cognitive limitations to include emotional variables as well.

Similar to Meşe et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) focus on English language learners, Woo et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored the use of GAI by high school students learning English. In their research, Woo et al. examined how students crafted GAI prompts to create English-language text as part of their writing assignments. The results indicated that students require specific instructions and practice to develop GAI prompts that result in meaningful and useful outputs. The research by Woo et al. reinforces the need for GAI literacy and instruction focused on strategically generating GAI prompts to garner desired and meaningful outcomes.

## Curriculum integration

In a unique study examining the use of GAI as a mechanism for curriculum integration, Kepceoğlu and Oguz-Hacat ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined how middle school-level students used GAI to complete assignments that required the students to integrate concepts from mathematics and social studies. In their qualitative exploratory study, Kepceoğlu and Oguz-Hacat found support for using GAI as an instructional context for integrating curriculum. The research found the levels of critical thinking skills of the participating students led to differences in the use and reliance on GAI. The outcomes of the study reflect the potential for using GAI to integrate curriculum and the need to consider and attend to students’ critical thinking skills for meaningful GAI input and their critical examination of GAI output.

## Book review

Closing out this special issue on generative artificial intelligence is a book review by Nufninu et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) of _Empowering K-12 Education with AI: Preparing for the Future of Education and Work_ (Chiu, [Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). The review highlights the focus on GAI for learning and teaching, with many of the ideas well-aligned with the research presented in this issue. In their review, Nufninu et al. emphasize Chiu’s ([Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) primary argument for using GAI as a catalyst for substantial change in K-12 education. As I argued at the beginning of this introduction, GAI is a significant educational innovation that has the potential for a profound impact on teaching and learning. However, as Nufninu et al. also highlight, Chui emphasizes preparing students for a workplace where GAI is integrated as an essential workplace tool.

## Conclusion

Teaching and learning are complex processes that may be constrained by the historical schema of school, limiting the potential for integrating educational innovations. Unlike the introduction of past educational innovations, the presence and use of GAI is impacting nearly all facets of society, business, industry, education, social media, entertainment, sports, and general communication. Given the ubiquitous presence, it will be nearly impossible to stop or even limit the presence of GAI in K-12 education. Thus, rather than trying to prevent or restrict the use of GAI, it is wise we continue to explore and research teaching and learning with the innovation so that we may engage in evidence-based decision-making. The research in this special issue provides a strong foundation for future research on K-12 teaching and learning with GAI.

args.summary:
This webpage is the introduction to a special issue of The Journal of Educational Research (Volume 118, Issue 6, 2025) focused on generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in K-12 education. Written by Louis S. Nadelson of the University of Central Arkansas, the introduction provides a roadmap and synthesis of the research reports published in the special issue, organized by educational context. Published online June 5, 2025, the article has 6,370 views and 2 CrossRef citations.

Key content includes:
- The article positions GAI adoption in K-12 as an educational innovation, distinguishing GAI from predictive AI (PAI), and noting GAI's capabilities in generating text, images, sounds, voices, movies, and animation.
- Teacher GAI adoption is aligned with diffusion theory (Rogers, 1995). Research covered includes: Nadelson et al. on teacher adoption justifications; Döğer and Göçen's cross-national study of educators in 15 countries finding critical perspectives on GAI; Isik's examination of teacher adoption based on usefulness and ease of use in professional development contexts; Döğer and Göçen's eTwinning study finding benefits (efficiency in lesson planning, assessment, collaboration) alongside concerns (ethical issues, bias, overreliance, privacy, digital divide); Drożdż et al.'s foreign language teaching study showing teachers found AI corpora helpful but nearly half were unfamiliar with AI for language learning; Delaney et al.'s case study of two high school teachers showing benefits of learning GAI in teaching/learning contexts rather than discipline-specific contexts.
- Administrators: Göçen and Döğer explored how school administrators across 20 countries used GAI in leadership, noting the need to balance GAI with social interactions.
- Elementary education: Tetteh et al. used a culture-techno-contextual approach (CTCA), finding students taught with CTCA experienced higher learning gains; Temiz and Kafadar compared AI vocabulary builders to traditional flashcards, finding significant short-term gains but no long-term differences.
- Middle school education: Adisa and Adefisayo explored student perceptions of GAI integration (students emphasized teacher supervision and restricting GAI in assessments); Chen et al. used a quasi-experimental design showing GAI effectively enhanced historical knowledge and motivation in history teaching.
- High school education: Smyslova et al.'s pilot study on AI literacy found significant gains in predictive AI understanding but persistent misconceptions about generative AI, plus gender differences; Wall et al. developed evidence-based principles for proactive GAI literacy rather than restricting access; Bieńkowska et al. found moderate student GAI engagement with differences tied to age, gender, school type, and community location; Liu et al. examined GAI in geography teaching comparing China and the US, noting accuracy, dependence, IP ethics, and equity concerns; Meşe et al. examined cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement in English writing with GAI; Woo et al. found students need specific instruction and practice in crafting effective GAI prompts.
- Curriculum integration: Kepceoğlu and Oguz-Hacat examined GAI use for integrating math and social studies, finding students' critical thinking levels affected GAI use and reliance.
- Book review: Nufninu et al. reviewed Chiu's "Empowering K-12 Education with AI" (2024), emphasizing GAI as a catalyst for change and preparation for a GAI-integrated workplace.

The conclusion argues that given GAI's ubiquitous presence across society, it is impossible to prevent or limit GAI in K-12 education; therefore, evidence-based research and decision-making on teaching and learning with GAI is the wiser path forward.
args.key_excerpts: "We have entered a new era of technological innovation with the rapid popularization of artificial intelligence (AI).", "As with many other education innovations, the adoption of GAI in K-12 for teaching and learning appears to be aligned with the fundamental principles of diffusion theory (Rogers, 1995).", "Given the ubiquitous presence, it will be nearly impossible to stop or even limit the presence of GAI in K-12 education. Thus, rather than trying to prevent or restrict the use of GAI, it is wise we continue to explore and research teaching and learning with the innovation so that we may engage in evidence-based decision-making.", "The research in this special issue provides a strong foundation for future research on K-12 teaching and learning with GAI.", "The research provides empirical documentation for the potential professional development may have on teacher integrations of GAI in their teaching and for their student learning."

News

# Teaching academic writing in the age of AI

AI has changed the landscape of writing in higher education. Here’s how instructors are adapting

By [Zara Abrams](https://www.apa.org/contributor?contributor=%22Abrams, Zara%22)



Date created: April 1, 2026

11 min read

Vol. 58, No. 3  
Print version: page 65

* [Artificial Intelligence](/topics/artificial-intelligence-machine-learning)
* [Academia](/education-career/development/academia)

[5](javascript:toggleFeedback();)

![APA Style leaf logo](/Content/Images/leaf-icon.png)
Cite This Article in  [APA Style](https://apastyle.apa.org)

Abrams, Z. (2026, April 1). Teaching academic writing in the age of AI. *Monitor on Psychology*, *57*(3). https://www.apa.org/monitor/2026/04-05/academic-writing-ai-higher-education

![professor in classroom](/images/2026-04-05-career-tile_tcm7-348031.jpg)

## Key points

* AI has posed new challenges for higher education instructors and raised questions about learning outcomes and academic integrity.
* Leveraging best practices in writing pedagogy and psychological science can help instructors ensure that student work is original.
* Classroom and institutional AI policies continue to evolve as those in higher education seek to prepare students for a world where AI is quickly becoming ubiquitous.

Nearly all undergraduate students (92%) now report using artificial intelligence for assignments, most often for writing and editing, according to a survey from the Higher Education Policy Institute ([Freeman, J., *Student Generative AI Survey 2025*, Feb. 2025opens in new window](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/HEPI-Kortext-Student-Generative-AI-Survey-2025.pdf)). That has posed a major challenge for instructors, especially those who teach academic writing or courses built around reading and discussing scholarly research.

How instructors handle AI—specifically, generative AI, or tools that create text, images, or other new content—runs the gamut from total bans to head-on adoption. Those decisions are complicated and personal—and must be made as technology and institutional policies continue to evolve. But a growing number of instructors believe it’s important to engage with AI and update assignments and classroom rules accordingly.

“Engaging doesn’t have to mean adopting. But it can mean having conversations with students, having a clear AI policy, and being intentional around this topic,” said Liz Delf, an AI teaching and learning fellow with the [Center for Teaching and Learningopens in new window](https://ctl.oregonstate.edu/) and a senior instructor in the School of Writing, Literature, and Film at Oregon State University.

To that end, Delf and others are exploring how to create assignments that reduce students’ reliance on AI, including by breaking up academic writing into smaller chunks. They’re also finding creative ways to explore AI’s benefits and limitations in the classroom. The goal is to prepare students for a professional world where they will need to decide when using AI is appropriate or helpful and navigate AI-use policies from employers and publishers alike.

“In the long run, we want to be thinking about what students are going to do outside of school, whether that’s psychology or something else,” said David Williamson Shaffer, PhD, a professor of learning analytics and learning sciences at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “What tools will they need to use, and how can we make sure they are prepared to use them?”

## Adapting writing assignments

AI has so rapidly and drastically changed the learning environment that some teachers have taken extreme measures, such as reverting to Scantrons (standardized multiple-choice forms) or blue books, to ensure that student work is original. Others have turned to oral discussions and exams as primary ways to evaluate students, but these approaches are not always possible for high-enrollment or online courses.

Even as some instructors move to sidestep or limit writing assignments in response to AI, “decades of research support writing as an important mode of learning,” Delf said. “My goal is to help students develop critical thinking, inquiry, and rhetorical judgment—and writing remains central to that, even in a world with generative AI.”

That truth has propelled Delf and others to find creative ways to reduce students’ reliance on AI, leaning into established best practices in writing pedagogy. First and foremost: Emphasize process over product by dividing large writing tasks into a series of smaller, scaffolded assignments. Instead of grading students on a polished, 20-page paper, grade their topic proposals, partial drafts, drafts, annotated bibliographies, and peer review.

“Breaking academic writing into chunks can help students feel less overwhelmed,” said Chris Hakala, PhD, director of the [Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning, and Scholarshipopens in new window](https://springfield.edu/academics/center-for-excellence) and a professor of psychology at Springfield College in Massachusetts. “Part of the reason they turn to AI is that academic writing feels like such a daunting process.”

Reducing page length and extending timelines can also help, he said. Easing students’ stress and workload can help make them less likely to turn to AI. Decreasing the length and number of assignments can also help instructors manage the additional workload of multiple rounds of grading.

Providing feedback to students offers another opportunity. For example, giving students feedback face-to-face can help demonstrate in a tangible way that human input matters, Delf said. Hakala gives students both written comments and verbal feedback via video, and then asks them to respond with a written or video message explaining how they intend to address it. Even in larger courses, this approach can be scaled—such as giving a one-sentence response per student, he said.

Group assignments and multimedia assignments are also harder to offload to AI, Delf said, because the final product makes students’ authorship more visible. When students create a podcast or comic strip, they may use AI for brainstorming, but the finished work requires student-produced elements—such as original audio or hand-drawn illustrations—that cannot be outsourced to AI. She also recommends tapping into personal or local knowledge (having students tackle campus problems, for example, rather than national ones), as well as real-audience or real-world purposes.

“Is there a way to give the assignment real value through a natural audience, an opportunity for publication, or a document that students can use later in their careers?” Delf said. “Students are often more invested when the work feels purposeful” and may therefore be less likely to outsource work to AI.

Redesigning assignments around AI may require more up-front work from instructors, but “it also offers an opportunity to clarify the purpose of writing in higher education—and to adapt in ways that ultimately benefit students,” said Chelsea Lee, instructional lead for the APA Style team.

## Strengthening AI literacy

In a growing number of classrooms, teaching students about effective AI use is seen as an essential part of preparing students for the workforce.

During a December 2025 APA webinar on AI in academic writing, 442 participants reported allowing students to use AI in various ways—mostly around the edges of the writing process. A majority allowed students to use AI to generate ideas (72%) or get feedback on writing (59%), while about half allowed its use for research or outlining. Just 9% said students could use AI to generate text, for an introduction, for example.

Delf starts the conversation about AI when the term begins, giving students opportunities both during and outside class to test AI’s capabilities. For example, she asks students to search for scholarly sources using both Google Scholar and an AI tool of their choice, then compare the results and assess whether the AI-generated citations are authentic.

Shaffer teaches a course on AI where students are required to use AI to help complete assignments, such as writing summaries of scientific papers. He does not restrict how students use AI, but he does require them to submit conversation transcripts, as well as a reflection on how the tool helped—or hindered—their work.

“Nobody was actually relying solely on AI to write things and turn them in, because they very quickly realized that AI was not doing as good a job as they could,” Shaffer said.

His students did find other creative ways to use AI to support their work. Several non-native English speakers uploaded an article and discussed its main points with AI in their native language before writing their own English summary to submit. Other students asked AI to create a reading guide to help direct them toward key concepts in an article.

Overreliance on AI has been shown to weaken critical-thinking skills, so teaching students when not to use these tools is an important way to mitigate that risk ([Gerlich, M., *Societies*, Vol. 15, No. 1, 2025opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.3390/soc15010006)). In that vein, some instructors are experimenting with using AI as a questioning partner. Rather than asking AI to generate text, students prompt it to ask higher-order questions—probing assumptions, requesting counterarguments, or testing the strength of an interpretation. Learning science research suggests that generating and responding to such questions supports deeper comprehension and transfer of knowledge. When AI is positioned to challenge students’ thinking rather than replace it, it can function more like a Socratic tutor than a shortcut.

AI also offers opportunities to improve accessibility for students with disabilities. When used as a planning aid, language support, or organizational scaffold, AI can increase independence without replacing learning, much like other assistive technologies.

Hakala has found it helpful to have students complete an assignment with AI, then critique the result to see what works and what falls short. Hakala’s experience has shown that using AI for brainstorming can limit students’ creativity, but he allows students to ask AI for feedback after generating their own ideas.

“I’m a cognitive psychologist by training, so I think about AI in terms of learning outcomes,” Hakala said. “If it helps scaffold learning, I’m open to it. If it impedes or replaces learning, it has no role in the classroom.”

## Crafting and navigating AI policies

In 2025, 45% of institutions had adopted AI policies covering academic integrity, teaching, research, or some combination of these—up from just 20% the year before, according to Inside Higher Ed ([*2025 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers*opens in new window](https://www.insidehighered.com/reports/2025/09/12/2025-survey-college-and-university-chief-academic-officers); [*2024 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers*, Inside Higher Edopens in new window](https://www.insidehighered.com/reports/2024/04/15/2024-survey-college-and-university-chief-academic-officers)).

Such policies generally give broad guidelines and then defer to instructors to choose how to handle AI in their courses. Some institutions mandate the use of custom generative pretrained transformers (GPTs) for privacy reasons, while a growing number require instructors to include an AI policy in their syllabi.

“Classroom policies really run the gamut—a lot of instructors don’t allow for any use of AI, while others actively encourage their students to use it in different ways,” said Samantha Denneny, development manager for the APA Style team.

Given the range of approaches, Delf said it’s important to set clear expectations for students. On her syllabus, she includes a disclosure about her own AI use (for example: “I sometimes use AI to develop examples or course materials, but I do not use it for grading or feedback”), as well as initial guidelines for students.

Delf then works collaboratively with students during class to draft and commit to a classroom AI policy, which usually permits AI use for brainstorming, research, and feedback but not for generating sentences or paragraphs. She then posts the policy or adds it to the syllabus to give students a sense of ownership over their AI use.

“When we’re transparent and have those conversations up front, my hope is that students are more likely to buy in,” Delf said. “I can’t control how they use AI once they leave my classroom, but I want them thinking critically about their choices going forward.”

Some instructors even allow students to create their own personal AI policies. This may involve declining to use AI because of ethical concerns around privacy, bias, environmental burden, and more. In such cases, Delf offers alternative exercises that don’t require the use of AI.

For additional guidance on creating a classroom AI policy, see the [AI Pedagogy Projectopens in new window](https://aipedagogy.org/) and the Harvard Office of Undergraduate Education’s [generative AI guidanceopens in new window](https://oue.fas.harvard.edu/faculty-resources/generative-ai-guidance/), which includes sample syllabus language.

How to detect unauthorized AI use is another ongoing question. Nearly 8 in 10 U.S. faculty members said cheating has increased on their campus since AI tools became widely available, according to a November 2025 survey ([Watson, C. E., & Rainie, L., *The AI Challenge: Faculty Concerns About Generative AI in Higher Education*, American Association of Colleges and Universities, 2025opens in new window](https://www.aacu.org/research/the-ai-challenge)). About half of those who attended APA’s academic writing webinar reported that their institution uses AI detection software, such as Turnitin or GPTZero, but just 1% said they completely trust these tools.

One reason for concern is that AI checkers have been shown to disproportionately flag original work from neurodivergent students and students writing in a second language ([Pindell, N., “The Challenge of AI Checkers,” University of Nebraska–Lincoln Center for Transformative Teaching, 2024opens in new window](https://teaching.unl.edu/ai-exchange/challenge-ai-checkers/)). Research also suggests that instructors may overestimate their abilities to detect AI-generated student essays ([Fleckenstein, J., et al., *Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence*, Vol. 6, 2024opens in new window](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100209)).

“Use of these checkers can lead to false accusations and can create an adversarial relationship with students,” Delf said. “It makes me feel like I’m policing instead of teaching.”

As AI detectors get better at flagging AI-generated content, “humanizer” tools have emerged to help users evade detection. Shaffer describes this as “an arms race that we’re eventually going to lose,” pointing to the long history of failed attempts to ban new technologies in education, including the so-called calculator wars in mathematics.

“What I tell my students is this: Whatever you turn in—whether it came from AI or not—you are responsible for it,” he said. “If the AI plagiarized, you plagiarized. If the AI made a mistake, you made a mistake. Using AI doesn’t change who gets blamed if there is a problem with the work.”

## How to cite AI

While using AI to write academic papers is generally considered unethical, AI can support certain aspects of the writing process in both student and professional scholarly work. Appropriate uses may include translation, brainstorming, editing, and generating figures or code.

“Citing sources, including AI tools, helps make scholarly work transparent so that readers can monitor and understand how authors reached their conclusions,” said Timothy McAdoo, a manager on the APA Style team.

When using AI to support scholarly work, authors are encouraged to save conversation transcripts and either include them as supplementary materials or make them available upon request. Reproducing results may not always be possible with AI, but retaining these records provides a clear account of how outputs were generated.

APA Style’s blog offers guidance on citing AI tools in a reference list or describing how they were used in the body of an academic paper ([APA Style blog, Sept. 9, 2025](https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/cite-generative-ai-references)).

Authors should also review applicable policies, including those from a governing institution, employer, or publisher. For example, APA’s policy on the use of generative AI in scholarly materials applies to any authors submitting manuscripts to APA journals. This policy dictates that:

* AI use must be disclosed and cited.
* AI cannot be named as a coauthor.

This APA Monitor on Psychology article (published April 1, 2026, Vol. 58, No. 3) examines how higher education instructors are adapting their academic writing instruction in response to the rise of generative AI. Key data points: 92% of undergraduate students report using AI for assignments, most often for writing and editing (Higher Education Policy Institute survey, Feb. 2025); 45% of institutions had adopted AI policies by 2025, up from 20% the prior year (Inside Higher Ed); and nearly 8 in 10 U.S. faculty members said cheating has increased since AI tools became widely available (Nov. 2025 AAC&U survey).

The article outlines several strategies instructors are using to reduce student reliance on AI, including: breaking large writing assignments into smaller scaffolded chunks (topic proposals, partial drafts, annotated bibliographies, peer review); reducing page length and extending timelines; providing face-to-face or verbal feedback; using group and multimedia assignments (podcasts, comic strips) that require student-produced elements; and giving assignments real-world audiences or purposes. Expert quotes from Liz Delf (Oregon State University), Chris Hakala (Springfield College), David Williamson Shaffer (University of Wisconsin–Madison), and Chelsea Lee (APA Style team) emphasize that writing remains central to developing critical thinking and rhetorical judgment even with generative AI available.

The article also covers strengthening AI literacy, noting that in a December 2025 APA webinar, 72% of participants allowed students to use AI to generate ideas and 59% allowed AI feedback on writing, but only 9% allowed AI text generation. Instructors teach students to critique AI outputs, use AI as a "questioning partner" (like a Socratic tutor), and recognize when AI helps vs. hinders learning. Research is cited showing overreliance on AI weakens critical-thinking skills (Gerlich, Societies, 2025).

Regarding AI policies, the article discusses the range of classroom approaches, the importance of transparent, collaboratively-created policies, and concerns about AI detection tools. Only 1% of instructors completely trust AI detection software (which disproportionately flags neurodivergent and second-language students' work), and instructors may overestimate their ability to detect AI-generated essays. Shaffer warns about the "arms race" between AI detectors and "humanizer" evasion tools, comparing it to the failed "calculator wars" in mathematics.

The article concludes with APA Style guidance on citing AI: AI use must be disclosed and cited, AI cannot be named as a coauthor, authors are responsible for accuracy, and submitted content may not be entered into AI tools. Authors are encouraged to save conversation transcripts and provide them upon request.
args.key_excerpts: "Engaging doesn't have to mean adopting. But it can mean having conversations with students, having a clear AI policy, and being intentional around this topic," said Liz Delf, an AI teaching and learning fellow with the Center for Teaching and Learning and a senior instructor in the School of Writing, Literature, and Film at Oregon State University.

### AI-Assisted Research Writing: Graduate Students' Experiences, Outcomes and Academic Integrity

#### Abstract

This study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) tool use and writing outcomes among graduate students engaged in thesis writing, grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model. Using a convergent parallel mixed methods design, the study involved 96 graduate students enrolled in thesis writing courses at a government higher education institution in Bulacan, during the first trimester of the 2025–2026 academic year. Qualitative data focused on students' adherence to academic integrity regulations. Quantitative measures assessed perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention to use, and self-reported writing performance. The results indicated that ChatGPT, Grammarly and QuillBot were the most used AI tools. Statistical analysis demonstrated a strong positive relationship between experience with AI tools and writing performance outcomes. The qualitative analysis surfaced themes about AI tool adoption, namely linguistic support, organization of ideas, and cognitive scaffolding and ideation¾alongside themes reflecting ethical awareness, namely selective use and resistance, responsible and transparent authorship, critical evaluation, accountability in AI tool use, and alignment with institutional guidelines. These results show that technological advances are now integral to writing courses and are used in the preparation and oversight of students' research. The study's key implication is that to use AI tools in thesis writing in an ethical manner, institutions must develop clear ethical frameworks that protect scholarly integrity while accepting the changing reality of human–AI collaboration in academic research.

# AI Tool Demo: Making Music With Suno

Assistant Editor Daniel Leonard shows how the AI music-generation tool Suno turns text into a song in any genre—and shares how teachers are using it in the classroom.

February 27, 2025

Your content has been saved!

[Go to My Saved Content.](/account/my-saved-content)

Have you ever thought that a class assignment would be more engaging if music were involved? A new AI music-generation tool, [Suno](https://suno.com/), lets users turn their original writing into a fully realized song in under a minute—complete with vocals and an instrumental backing in a genre of their choice—and there are lots of applications for the classroom.

Across various subject areas and grades, teachers are using Suno to help their students create catchy songs that can serve as mnemonic devices. In an elementary math classroom, for example, students can collectively write lyrics that name and briefly describe the various types of triangles. The teacher can then input these lyrics into Suno (the software is intended for users 13 and up) and have the AI rapidly create an entire song—in any genre—that the class can sing together as a way to commit the material to memory.

In English language arts, meanwhile, teachers are using Suno as a way to breathe life into writing assignments. If an exercise involves students writing poetry, for example, students can use Suno to turn their poems into songs at the end of the assignment. Besides making the activity more engaging, this exercise helps students deepen their understanding of mood and tone; prompting Suno to turn somber lyrics into a song in a disco or pop genre is likely to produce an awkward-sounding result, while blues might be a much better fit.

In this short demo, Edutopia’s assistant editor Daniel Leonard demonstrates how to access and use Suno to create songs, and offers more detail on some of the teacher-tested use cases for AI music generation in the classroom with the tool. For other fun and engaging ways that teachers are deploying AI in their lessons—from AI-powered chats with historical figures to tools that bring student artwork to life—read Leonard’s feature for Edutopia, “[9 Tips for Using AI for Learning (and Fun!)](/article/using-ai-for-learning-fun).”
