[![HEPI: Higher Education Policy Institute](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/wp-content/themes/hepi-2025/assets/images/logo-hepi-full.svg)](/ "HEPI Home")



# Student Generative Artificial Intelligence Survey 2026

[![](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/HEPI_Report_199-Cover-600x822.jpg)](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/HEPI-Report-199-Gen-AI-Survey-2026.pdf) 

HEPI Number:
:   199

Author:
:   Rose Stephenson and Charlotte Armstrong

Published:

Reports:
:   [Read the full report (PDF)](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/HEPI-Report-199-Gen-AI-Survey-2026.pdf)

Supporting Documents:
:   [2026 Student GenAI Data Weighted WOW Tables (XLSX)](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Third-version-of-2026-data-weighted-WOW-tables.xlsx)
:   [2026 Student GenAI Weighted Data (XLSX)](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Third-version-of-2026-weighted-data.xlsx)

**AI use is now ‘near universal’ among undergraduates, but students are divided on its impact, new HEPI survey finds**

In just three years, generative AI has moved from novelty to near universality among undergraduates. The question is no longer whether students use AI, but how well they use it – and how effectively institutions are supporting them to develop the skills to do so responsibly.

The *Student Generative AI Survey 2026* (HEPI Report 199), published by HEPI and sponsored by Kortext, shows a striking contrast in students’ experiences. For some, AI frees up time for deeper learning and critical thinking. For others, it risks becoming a crutch. Higher education providers have a crucial role in ensuring AI enhances learning rather than diminishing it.

Co-authored by Rose Stephenson, HEPI’s Director of Policy and Strategy and Charlotte Armstrong, HEPI’s Policy Manager, the survey was conducted by Savanta in December 2025 and is based on responses from 1,054 full-time UK undergraduates.

This third iteration of the report shows that students have embraced generative AI at an extraordinary speed. The UK has set out a [clear ambition](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-opportunities-action-plan/ai-opportunities-action-plan) to be a global leader in the development and application of AI technologies, and students are already living that ambition in their day-to-day learning. However, what the survey also highlights is that institutional adoption is lagging behind student behaviour. While nearly all students use AI to support their studies, only 36% feel encouraged by their institution to do so, and only 38% say they are provided with AI tools.

## Key findings:

* **AI use is now almost universal.** Some 95% of students report using AI in at least one way and 94% say they use generative AI to help with assessed work. Many of these students will be encouraged or required to use AI in assessments as providers pivot to teaching and assessing AI skills. However, the proportion of students directly including AI-generated text in assessed work has risen to 12%, up from 8% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.
* **Assessment has changed substantially.**Nearly two-thirds (65%) of students say assessment has changed significantly in response to AI. In addition, some students articulate a sense of anxiety about false accusations of misconduct
* **AI improves the student experience for many – but not all.**Almost half (49%) of students believe AI has improved their student experience, particularly by saving time, improving understanding and providing instant support. However, a minority feel AI has worsened their experience, citing concerns about fairness, skill erosion, social isolation and future employment.
* **Students are using AI to support their wellbeing.** Around 15% of students report using AI for companionship, advice or to address loneliness.
* **Students see AI skills as essential, but institutional support lags behind.**While over two-thirds (68%) of students believe AI skills are essential to thrive in today’s world, fewer than half (48%) feel their teaching staff are helping them to develop these skills for their future careers. Arts and Humanities students are particularly likely to feel under-supported.

## A polarised landscape:

There are numerous results from this year’s survey suggesting that in 2026, we have reached a somewhat polarised AI landscape. These results include:

* the proportion of students who agree that their institution encourages AI use (37%) and those who disagree (36%);
* the equal distribution of students who feel that AI makes them feel lonelier (20%) and less lonely (21%); and
* the relatively equal proportion of students that lean towards using traditional sources (33%), using an equal balance of sources (29%) and favouring AI sources (37%).

(Notably, students from Russell Group institutions are most likely to agree that their institutions encourage the use of AI (39%) – this has increased from 26% last year.)

Further, the qualitative results demonstrate that even among students who embrace AI, individual learning experiences vary widely. Two contrasting statements from respondents stand out. One student responded:

> *AI tools allowed me to quickly summarise dense readings and generate drafts or outlines for assignments, saving hours of tedious work and letting me focus on critical analysis and deeper understanding.*

And another said:

> *I’m not using my brain at all.*

There is a striking contrast here between a student who is utilising AI to advance their learning and a student who is outsourcing their learning to AI. It is the role of institutions to develop skills within their student bodies to use AI to their advantage, rather than disadvantage, and to provide the impetus for them to do so.

## Key recommendations

The report urges higher education providers to:

* **Provide structured AI induction and transition support for all students**

* **Consider revamping their curricula to explicitly teach AI knowledge and skills, at both the general and subject-specific levels.**

* **Publish clear, accessible and assessment-specific guidance on AI use.**

* **Ensure that the AI tools necessary or advantageous for course content or assessment are accessible to all students.**

* **Ensure staff have access to AI training – and the time to invest in developing their own skills.**

As part of its work to identify gaps in the current evidence base, the Higher Education Mental Health Implementation Taskforce should:

* **Support research to understand the impact of students using AI for friendship, company, advice or to tackle loneliness.**

Charlotte Armstrong, co-author and Policy Manager at HEPI, said:

> *Students overwhelmingly see AI as essential for their futures, but many do not feel adequately supported to develop the necessary skills. If universities want graduates to feel prepared for the future, then AI literacy and capability must be embedded across the curriculum. These skills cannot be treated as optional.*

Robin Gibson, Director of External Affairs at Kortext, said:

> *Student AI use is changing quickly. Universities are starting to close the gap between student expectations and AI provision and teaching, with more institutions now offering supported access to trusted tools. The provision of AI assistants grounded in educational contexts that enhance teaching, learning and study skills is how providers can safely and effectively empower students to develop the AI skills and capabilities needed in a rapidly changing world. Ensuring that every student can develop confidence and competence with these technologies is essential. This year’s findings show increasing momentum, with a sector preparing to match students’ enthusiasm and expectations in delivering institutional capability – but there is more to do.*

## Comments

* ### Jonathan Alltimes says:

  “Almost half (49%) of students believe AI has improved their student experience, particularly by saving time, improving understanding and providing instant support.”

  This is exactly the true way to summarise and state the responses of the opinion survey, if it were accurate. Students have beliefs about AI which are beyond evidence or proof. You can only judge what AI produces relative to you own experience or that of a group, but may not be able argue its likelihood. Academics should be worried, as AI has the power to damage learning. What did we do before search engines, the Web, software applications, PC databases, electronic files, and the electronic calculator? What did we forget as we used these technologies?

  Reply
* ### Paul Vincent Smith says:

  “AI tools allowed me to quickly summarise dense readings and generate drafts or outlines for assignments, saving hours of tedious work and letting me focus on critical analysis and deeper understanding.

  And another said:

  I’m not using my brain at all.”

  I showed this to a colleague. He said: the first one just sounds like a fancy version of the second. My thoughts entirely. We need to consider the findings of such surveys with a great deal of care.

  Reply

  #### Replies

  + ### Rose Stephenson says:

    This is a good challenge, Paul!

    Reply
  + ### Jo I says:

    The first one sounds like it was AI generated.

    Reply
* ### Denis Blight says:

  I agree that accurate summaries that genuinely reflect the intention of their writer can be helpful- provided they accurately reflect indisputable facts not mere opinions nor sound judgements. Does AI capture both to a necessary degree? As a mature researcher used to making fine judgements in disciplines such as chemistry and history I find the distinction inherent in both extremely difficult. Is there room for ‘on the one hand judgment A and on the other a different judgement?’ Should be.

  Reply

# AI Enters Japan Classrooms

May 05, 2026 | News On Japan

KANAGAWA, May 05, 2026 ([News On Japan](https://newsonjapan.com/)) - The rapid spread of artificial intelligence into classrooms is transforming how students learn and how teachers work, with pilot programs across Japan highlighting that the key lies not in relying entirely on AI but in using it effectively.

At a junior high school in Sagamihara, Kanagawa Prefecture, students present original satirical drawings created with AI, explaining their ideas to classmates in a style that blends creativity with critical thinking, a sharp contrast to the traditional classroom model where students passively listened to lectures.

A second-year student recalled initial confusion when first introduced to AI, saying it felt overwhelming to be suddenly told to use it, but added that over time it has become “almost like a friend.” The student described AI as a “third teacher” or “third textbook,” especially useful when seeking deeper explanations beyond standard lessons.

Sagamihara Municipal Nakano Junior High School is among roughly 30 institutions selected as “generative AI pilot schools,” where efforts are underway to integrate AI into education in a structured way.

The benefits extend beyond students to teachers as well, with one English teacher in his fifth year noting a significant reduction in workload, as AI now assists in tasks such as generating answers for listening tests, saving considerable time while maintaining accuracy.

The use of AI has helped cut down excessive overtime, which previously exceeded 80 hours per month, allowing teachers to focus more on direct interaction with students, including offering guidance and listening to their concerns—areas that remain beyond AI’s capabilities.

Still, educators caution that AI can be a double-edged sword. A third-year student pointed out that while interaction is important, there are times when students simply ask for answers and stop thinking further.

Umeno, a lead teacher overseeing AI integration at the school, emphasized that over-reliance on AI can weaken students’ ability to think independently, warning that handing over all problem-solving to AI may ultimately hinder learning.

He stressed that the crucial factor is “how it is used,” advocating for a balanced approach that encourages students to engage with challenges on their own while leveraging AI as a support tool.

Ben Gomes, a senior executive overseeing education initiatives at Google, noted that while information was once something people simply received, AI now enables interactive engagement with knowledge, allowing for deeper thinking if used correctly.

Gomes added that fostering curiosity—especially the habit of asking “why?”—is the most important skill for students, as tools to support learning are increasingly accessible.

As AI continues to reshape education, the ability to question and think critically may prove more important than ever for the next generation.

## Integrating Generative AI into Japanese Higher Education: Policy Responses, Pedagogical Practices, and Future Directions

2025.10.16 24068

**Introduction**

Japan, known for its long-standing commitment to technological innovation, is now navigating this transformation in its higher education sector. The rise of Generative AI presents both exciting opportunities and pressing challenges for Japanese universities: How can they embrace new technologies to enhance learning, while safeguarding academic integrity and educational quality? How can they prepare students not just to use AI tools, but to think critically about them?

This article reviews the latest developments in national policies, university guidelines, and teaching practices, highlighting The University of Osaka as a case study of its comprehensive approach to AI in education. Drawing on interviews with AI research leaders and university leaders, it also outlines the directions universities are likely to take as they move toward deeper integration of AI.

**Government Policies: A Human-Centered AI Strategy**

In November 2019, Japan released its AI Strategy 2019, which laid out three core principles: human dignity, diversity, and sustainability[1]. The strategy emphasised that AI development must be human-centered, uphold human dignity, and foster broad, sustainable applications of AI across sectors. A critical focus of the strategy is education reform, aimed at cultivating professionals through the establishment of dual-degree programmes that integrate AI and domain-specific studies, and encouraging higher education institutions to incorporate general education courses in data science and AI into their major fields of study.

**NexTech Week Tokyo 2024 Spring Source: AFP.**

In 2021, Japan introduced a certification system for education in mathematics, data science, and AI, led by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT)[2]. This initiative aims to accredit educational programmes that meet established standards and ensure high teaching quality, and to further promote composite human resources with professional knowledge and AI capabilities.

As AI technology advanced further, new challenges emerged. In July 2023, MEXT issued official guidance Policies for Addressing the Use of Generative AI in Universities and Technical Colleges, which aims to help institutions appropriately incorporate Generative AI to enhance education while managing associated risks[3]. The document is concerned about technology-induced issues such as academic misconduct, information security, and copyright infringement, and recommends that institutions establish and update tailored usage guidelines of technology based on the institutional needs. It also stresses the importance of transparency in student use of AI tools, encouraging diversified assessment methods to prevent overreliance on AI-generated content and the significance of content validation and the cultivation of critical thinking.

In parallel with these education-focused initiatives, the Japanese government has since 2023, been actively promoting the development of homegrown Generative AI models. One notable initiative is led by the National Institute of Informatics (NII), which has identified a critical issue: conventional English-centric models tend to lack sufficient understanding of the Japanese language and cultural context. To address this, NII has placed strong emphasis on developing "sovereign AI" trained with extensive Japanese corpora. The result of this effort is the LLM-JP model, designed with the ability to grasp Japan's history, literature, and cultural heritage[4]. In the field of higher education, its application for learning support is also highly anticipated.

**Reimagined ukiyo-e with new technology Source:**[**ET Today News**](https://www.ettoday.net/news/20160224/652478.htm)

**Institutional Generative AI Usage Guidelines**

Since 2023, numerous Japanese universities have introduced policies governing the use of Generative AI. The authors conducted a survey of the 37 universities involved in Japan's Top Global University Project (a national initiative launched by MEXT to enhance the global competitiveness of selected universities) and found that 27 of them had issued guidelines on the use of Generative AI for students and faculty. We subsequently carried out a detailed analysis of the content of these guidelines to examine their scope, focus, and underlying principles[5].

In terms of benefits, 44% of universities cite AI's ability to enhance efficiency and automate tasks, 22% highlight its potential in content creation and editing, 19% emphasise personalised learning support, and 11% discuss its role in fostering creativity and innovation (Figure 1). However, these descriptions are often general, with limited detailed application scenarios.

In contrast, concerns regarding AI risks are more comprehensively addressed: 78% of universities highlight data security issues, 67% raise concerns about copyright, 63% warn against the spread of misinformation, and 41% specifically address academic plagiarism (Figure 2). However, other risks—such as environment risks, AI divide, and control of speech and thought—remain largely unaddressed.

For instance, in response to these challenges, The University of Tokyo recommends that faculty evaluate AI tools prior to classroom use, while Tohoku University offers strategies to reduce inappropriate student use of AI in assignments. Sophia University and Hiroshima University have included AI education in their faculty development programmes to enhance AI literacy among teaching staff.

The survey also reveals that 63% of universities allow instructors to determine the scope and manner of AI use in their classrooms, reflecting an autonomous policy approach. Additionally, 52% regularly revise their policies in response to technological advancements, promoting adaptive course design and pedagogical innovation.

**Figure 1. Percentage of Universities that Address Usefulness in Guidelines**

**Figure 2. Percentage of Universities that Address Risk in Guidelines**

**Case Study: The University of Osaka's Comprehensive Approach to AI in Education**

As one of Japan's leading comprehensive research universities, The University of Osaka (UOsaka) issued Japanese- and English-language guidelines on the use of generative AI for students as early as April 2023[6]. The guidelines recognises the role of generative AI in supporting pre-research for learning, but suggests thatstudents must use it responsibly—remaining mindful of risks such as misinformation, data leaks, and copyright issues—while valuing independent thinking, dialogue, and the overall learning process as the true essence of higher education. Furthermore, UOsaka has adopted a multi-layered, systematic approach to integrating generative AI across undergraduate and graduate education, faculty development, and institutional innovation.

**Undergraduate Education: Building Foundational Literacy and Interdisciplinary Skills**

In alignment with MEXT's AI education initiative, UOsaka structures its undergraduate AI education into two tiers: foundational AI literacy for all students and applied courses tailored to individual disciplines. All undergraduates, regardless of major, engage in hands-on analysis of social data to develop basic competencies in mathematics, data science, and AI. The curriculum combines theoretical knowledge with practical applications, often delivered through industry-collaborative project-based learning, to strengthen students' analytical and problem-solving skills.

**Graduate Education: Deepening AI Integration through Interdisciplinary Learning**

At the graduate level, Institute for Transdisciplinary Graduate Degree Programmes offers interdisciplinary programmes such as "Graduate Minor Programme" and "Graduate Programme for Advanced Interdisciplinary Studies" that incorporate AI into diverse academic fields[7]. The Digital Humanities Programme targets students in the humanities and social sciences, equipping them with the ability to utilise AI tools in their research. Another initiative, the "Programme for Developing Security Human Resources for Secure Data Utilisation" aims to cultivate high-level professionals equipped to address challenges related to data ethics and privacy. These programmes balance technical expertise with societal application, reinforcing AI literacy among advanced learners.

**Faculty Development: Enhancing AI Teaching Competencies**

To support faculty, UOsaka's Center for Education in Liberal Arts and Sciences offers Generative AI Teaching Guide website, which outlines core AI principles, ethical considerations, and practical teaching strategies. As part of its faculty development initiative, the center offers both "introductory" and "advanced" workshops to enhance pedagogical integration of AI. Additionally, educational videos aimed at incoming students are disseminated via platforms like YouTube to foster early engagement and comprehension of AI concepts.

**D3 Center: Building a Data-Driven Institutional Ecosystem**

In October 2024, UOsaka established the D3 Center—focusing on Digital Design, Datability, and Decision Intelligence—to drive institutional transformation through data science. "Digital Design" involves structuring information for analysis, "Datability" emphasises extracting actionable insights from large datasets, and "Decision Intelligence" supports data-informed strategic decision-making. The center builds an integrated framework from data generation to application, accelerating the university's transition into a data-driven organisation and enhancing the role of AI in research and administration.

**ELSI Center: Addressing the Ethical, Legal, and Social Dimensions of AI**

In response to the ethical and societal challenges posed by AI, Ethical, Legal, and Social Issues (ELSI) Center published two research reports on the implications of Generative AI in March 2023 and August 2024. The center aims to identify and address key concerns such as ethical dilemmas, legal accountability, and social equity, promoting a responsible use of technology framework. By integrating expertise from law, ethics, and sociology, the center offers theoretical and policy support for the sustainable development of AI in education and research.

Through these initiatives, UOsaka has developed a structured AI education framework that includes foundational courses, graduate-level training, faculty support, institutional adjustments, and attention to ethical considerations. This approach reflects efforts to build a data-informed, technologically integrated, and ethically aware academic environment.

**Figure 3. AI Education Ecosystem at The University of Osaka (visuals illustrated by the authors)**

**Future Directions: Insights from Japanese Academic Leaders**

|  |
| --- |
| Currently, AI experts in Japan are actively working to promote the adoption and utilisation of generative AI. In February 2025, the Science Council of Japan released a proposal titled Toward the Realisation of a Society that Accepts and Utilises Generative AI[8]. Prof. Sadao Kurohashi, Secretary of the Committee on Informatics at the Science Council of Japan and Director-General of the National Institute of Informatics, emphasised the need for active discussion and utilisation of generative AI across a wide range of fields, including education, healthcare, and industry. In particular, he stressed the importance of dialogue and collaboration between AI and other disciplines, positioning this as essential for society as a whole to advance efforts that take into account the broader impact of generative AI. |
| At The University of Osaka, Senior Executive Vice President, Prof. Toshihiro Tanaka further pointed out that, in an AI-driven society, respect for humanity must serve as the foundation for shaping the future. Building on advances in science and technology, universities should place humanistic values at the center of education and nurture individuals who can move beyond dependence on AI to stay one step ahead. To this end, it is essential to foster a deep understanding of humanity, including ethics, through education that transcends disciplinary boundaries, and to cultivate the ability to create new value beyond AI. Providing such an environment, is the very mission of universities. |

This shared vision highlights Japan's balanced approach toward Generative AI, where technological advancement is pursued in tandem with human-centered values. By emphasising interdisciplinary collaboration, ethical awareness, and the cultivation of creativity beyond machine capabilities, Japanese university leaders underscore that the future of AI should not only drive efficiency and innovation but also reinforce social trust and human dignity. This perspective positions universities and research institutions as critical bridges between technology and society, ensuring that Generative AI contributes to sustainable and inclusive progress.

This webpage, published by UNESCO-ICHEI (International Centre for Higher Education Innovation under the auspices of UNESCO), features an article titled "Integrating Generative AI into Japanese Higher Education: Policy Responses, Pedagogical Practices, and Future Directions" (dated 2025.10.16). The article examines Japan's approach to integrating Generative AI into higher education, covering national policies, university guidelines, and teaching practices, with The University of Osaka as a case study.

KEY GOVERNMENT POLICIES:
- November 2019: Japan released AI Strategy 2019 with three core principles: human dignity, diversity, and sustainability. The strategy emphasized human-centered AI development and education reform, including dual-degree programmes integrating AI with domain-specific studies and general education courses in data science and AI.
- 2021: Japan introduced a certification system for mathematics, data science, and AI education, led by MEXT (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology).
- July 2023: MEXT issued official guidance "Policies for Addressing the Use of Generative AI in Universities and Technical Colleges," addressing academic misconduct, information security, and copyright infringement. It encouraged institutions to establish tailored usage guidelines, transparency in student AI use, diversified assessment methods, and critical thinking cultivation.
- Since 2023, the Japanese government has promoted homegrown "sovereign AI" development. The National Institute of Informatics (NII) developed the LLM-JP model, trained with extensive Japanese corpora to better understand Japanese language and cultural context, with applications anticipated for learning support.

INSTITUTIONAL GUIDELINES SURVEY:
A survey of 37 universities in Japan's Top Global University Project found 27 had issued Generative AI guidelines. Key findings:
- Benefits cited: 44% cited efficiency/automation, 22% content creation, 19% personalised learning support, 11% creativity and innovation.
- Risks addressed: 78% data security, 67% copyright, 63% misinformation, 41% academic plagiarism.
- 63% allow instructors to determine AI use in their classrooms (autonomous policy approach); 52% regularly revise policies.
- The University of Tokyo recommends faculty evaluate AI tools before classroom use; Tohoku University offers strategies to reduce inappropriate student AI use; Sophia University and Hiroshima University include AI education in faculty development programmes.

CASE STUDY - THE UNIVERSITY OF OSAKA (UOsaka):
- Issued Japanese- and English-language generative AI guidelines as early as April 2023, recognizing AI's role in supporting pre-research while emphasizing responsible use and independent thinking.
- Undergraduate education: Two-tier structure (foundational AI literacy for all students + applied discipline-specific courses), including hands-on social data analysis and industry-collaborative project-based learning.
- Graduate education: Institute for Transdisciplinary Graduate Degree Programmes offers interdisciplinary programmes (Graduate Minor Programme, Graduate Programme for Advanced Interdisciplinary Studies, Digital Humanities Programme, and Programme for Developing Security Human Resources for Secure Data Utilisation).
- Faculty development: Center for Education in Liberal Arts and Sciences offers a Generative AI Teaching Guide website, plus introductory and advanced workshops; educational videos for incoming students via YouTube.
- October 2024: Established the D3 Center (Digital Design, Datability, and Decision Intelligence) to drive institutional transformation through data science.
- ELSI Center (Ethical, Legal, and Social Issues) published two research reports on Generative AI implications (March 2023 and August 2024), addressing ethical dilemmas, legal accountability, and social equity.

FUTURE DIRECTIONS:
- February 2025: Science Council of Japan released proposal "Toward the Realisation of a Society that Accepts and Utilises Generative AI." Prof. Sadao Kurohashi (Secretary, Committee on Informatics, Science Council of Japan; Director-General of NII) stressed the need for active discussion and collaboration between AI and other disciplines.
- Prof. Toshihiro Tanaka (Senior Executive Vice President, University of Osaka) emphasized that respect for humanity must serve as the foundation for shaping the future in an AI-driven society, with universities nurturing individuals who can move beyond AI dependence through humanistic values and interdisciplinary education.

The article concludes that Japan's approach balances technological advancement with human-centered values, positioning universities as critical bridges between technology and society to ensure Generative AI contributes to sustainable and inclusive progress.

# AI-powered textbooks fail to make the grade in South Korea

South Korea’s AI learning program was rolled back after just four months following a backlash from teachers, students, and parents, underlining the challenges in embedding the technology in education.

![A girl with a pink backpack stands in front of a large, oversized book that features a cut-out window and colorful tabs, set against a blue background with green ground.](https://fastly.restofworld.org/uploads/2025/10/Ai-education-South-Korea_TEXTURED-scaled.jpg?width=800&dpr=2&crop=16:9)

Ko Ho-dam, a high school junior on South Korea’s Jeju Island, was at first curious to hear that the government [planned to roll out](https://english.moe.go.kr/boardCnts/viewRenewal.do?boardID=254&boardSeq=95291&lev=0&m=0202&opType=N&page=2&s=english) artificial intelligence-powered textbooks. The program would provide personalized learning for students, help prevent dropouts, and reduce the workload of teachers, authorities promised.

The program — a flagship initiative of former President Yoon Suk Yeol — took shape over the last year and a half, with about [a dozen publishers](https://www.newsis.com/view/NISX20241128_0002977168) approved to develop the digital textbooks. When the textbooks were launched at the start of the school year in March for math, English, and computer science, Ko was disappointed, he told *Rest of World*.

“All our classes were delayed because of technical problems with the textbooks,” Ko said. “I also didn’t know how to use them well. Working individually on my laptop, I found it hard to stay focused and keep on track. The textbooks didn’t provide lessons tailored to my level.”

Across the country, students like Ko, as well as teachers and parents, complained that the books had factual inaccuracies, posed data privacy risks, increased screen time for children, and resulted in a heavier workload for teachers and students. After just one semester — four months — the AI textbooks were [stripped](https://english.moe.go.kr/boardCnts/viewRenewal.do?boardID=265&boardSeq=102075&lev=0&searchType=null&statusYN=W&page=1&s=english&m=0201&opType=N) of their official status as textbooks, and classified as “supplementary material,” meaning their adoption is left to each school’s discretion.

South Korea’s experience shows that embedding AI in education is complex, and requires careful handling, Lee Bohm, a doctoral candidate at the Centre of Development Studies at the University of Cambridge, told *Rest of World.*

“AI should first be piloted in homework or practice before being carefully introduced in class,” said Lee, who was previously a policy adviser to the Seoul education office. “The focus should be on how to integrate it into the school curriculum, as that’s the only way AI-based education can be truly effective. In South Korea, attempts to apply it in class were pushed too far.”

![](https://fastly.restofworld.org/uploads/2025/10/aa³aa³aaµaaaao-2025-09-19-aa©aa®-12.59.09-scaled.png?width=800&dpr=2&crop=16:9)

Governments around the world are betting that AI will revolutionize education. Big tech firms including [Meta](https://restofworld.org/2025/colombia-meta-ai-education/), [Google](https://edu.google.com/intl/ALL_us/), and [OpenAI](https://chatgpt.com/for-business/education/) are aggressively promoting initiatives in schools worldwide. Some countries have embraced AI tools to solve [teacher shortages](https://restofworld.org/2025/ai-teaching-tools-kenya-teacher-shortage/) and bridge the gap between urban and rural students. In others, AI chatbots and other tools have [worsened](https://restofworld.org/2025/colombia-meta-ai-education/) student performance and increased the workload for teachers.

South Korea is an early adopter of technology, with [robot chefs](https://restofworld.org/2025/robot-chefs-south-korea-restaurants/) and [robot carers](https://restofworld.org/2025/korea-ai-robot-senior-care-hyodol/) becoming an increasingly common sight. Authorities have long backed edtech, training teachers in the use of AI, and deploying digital tutors to support teachers and students.

The government spent more than [1.2 trillion won](https://news.sbs.co.kr/news/endPage.do?news_id=N1007732476) ($850 million) on the AI textbook program, including on equipment and teacher training. The publishing companies invested around 800 billion won ($567 million) to develop the textbooks.

There were signs of unease early on. In November, the [Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union](https://www.eduhope.net/bbs/board.php?bo_table=maybbs_eduhope_4&wr_id=238713&sfl=wr_subject&stx=ai+%EA%B5%90%EA%B3%BC%EC%84%9C&sop=and&page=2&menu_id=2010), and civic groups such as Political Mamas, which campaigns for the welfare of women and children, [sued](https://www.politicalmamas.kr/post/4378) the then-minister of education for abuse of authority, saying the program was “problematic” because it made the use of AI textbooks mandatory. The groups also said the rollout overlooked potential risks to children, lacked data protection measures, and ignored the inputs of teachers and parents.

“The textbooks worsen learning effectiveness and negatively affect students,” Jang Ha-na, a member of Political Mamas, told *Rest of World*. “Once digital devices like tablets become central in classrooms, screen exposure increases, leading to weaker literacy and communication skills.”

![](https://fastly.restofworld.org/uploads/2025/10/20250918_120354-scaled.jpg?width=800&dpr=2&crop=16:9)

In response to the pushback, the government in January shifted from mandatory adoption to a one-year voluntary trial. Yoon, who had championed the AI textbook project, was impeached by the parliament for his attempt to impose martial law in December, and officially [removed](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz01mjv0v0go) from presidency in April.

Despite the political turmoil, the AI textbooks were introduced as planned in March. Lee Jae Myung, who had promised in his election campaign to rescind the AI textbook policy, was elected president. Lawmakers [revoked](https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20250804008400315) the status of the AI textbooks in August, leaving it up to schools to use them.

The adoption rate for the AI textbooks dropped from 37% in the first semester ending in July to 19% in the current semester that began in September. Only 2,095 schools are signed on now, about half the number earlier in the year, according to data compiled by lawmaker Kang Kyung-sook, who had opposed the program’s rollout.

“Traditional print textbooks take 18 months to develop, nine months for review, and six months for preparation. But the AI textbooks took only 12, three, and three months, respectively. Why was it rushed?” Kang [asked](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u6Qvl6gqPwU) the then-minister of education in parliament in January. “Since they target children, they require careful verification and careful procedures.”

The companies that developed the textbooks say they adhered to the country’s security protocols, and that no personal data of the students was stored. Students are already “hooked” to devices, and the textbooks themselves did not cause screen addiction, Kim Jong-hee, chief digital officer of Dong-A Publishing, one of the textbook developers, told *Rest of World*.

“Using digital devices they are familiar with keeps them more focused, awake, and more willing to participate,” Kim said*.* “The textbooks provide more personalized support for students struggling with lessons. They can also help the growing number of students from multicultural families who aren’t confident in Korean, and make learning more accessible for students with disabilities and those in rural and underserved areas.”

The program failed because everything was rushed; it should have been rolled out gradually after testing its effectiveness.”

Expensive private tuition, or *hagwon*, is the norm in the country. But for AI textbooks to reduce inequality and for students to benefit from them, more hands-on use is needed, Kim said. This is now more difficult, with fewer schools using them. “One key reason [for the program’s setbacks] is that the issue has become overly politicized,” he said.

The Textbook Development Committee, which represents the companies, plans to file a constitutional complaint and a lawsuit for financial damages against the government, Hwang Geun-sik, chair of the committee, told *Rest of World*.

“The companies that trusted the government and invested saw the market suddenly disappear,” Hwang said. “Our business is shrinking, and staff cuts have become unavoidable.”

In classrooms, teachers and students are still divided over the AI textbooks.

“Monitoring students’ learning progress with the books in class was challenging,” Lee Hyun-joon, a high school math teacher in Pyeongtaek city, told *Rest of World*. “The overall quality was poor, and it was clear it had been hastily put together.”

For Kim Cha-myung, an elementary school teacher in Gwangmyeong city near Seoul, the textbooks were convenient, helping save time and support struggling students. Students appreciated the digital features such as earning hearts as prizes for good performance, customizing their avatars, and solving problems in a game-like format, he told *Rest of World*.

“The program failed because everything was rushed; it should have been rolled out gradually after testing its effectiveness,” he said.

The government’s flip-flop has impacted students and teachers beyond just learning, said Kim.

“We no longer trust the government, which I see as the biggest problem.”

![A large crowd gathers at a rally, waving flags, with a group on a platform and buildings in the background](https://fastly.restofworld.org/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-2286830619-scaled.jpg?width=800&dpr=2&crop=16:9)

### The offline messaging apps challenging internet shutdowns

Jack Dorsey’s Bluetooth messaging app surged during India’s internet blackout — and the government’s response suggests a new tech battleground.

![](https://fastly.restofworld.org/uploads/2026/07/QA-AI-VC-Final.jpg?width=800&dpr=2&crop=16:9)

### How one VC burns through hundreds of millions of tokens a day to find the next unicorn

The investor behind a $75-million AI-focused fund explains why reading research papers and testing frontier models has become part of his job.

![A table with three computer monitors and keyboards, facing a display board of new book covers in a library setting](https://fastly.restofworld.org/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-2155295561.jpg?width=800&dpr=2&crop=16:9)

### Growth without work: The human cost of the AI revolution

In an excerpt from his book “The New Divide: Power, Control & the Cost of AI,” writer Jibu Elias examines the technology’s impact on jobs.
</webpage_content>

--- SOURCE 1: Generative artificial intelligence in K-12 education: A systematic review | Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning ---
URL: https://rptel.apsce.net/index.php/RPTEL/article/view/2026-21034

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an academic article titled "Generative artificial intelligence in K-12 education: A systematic review," published in Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning (RPTEL), Vol. 21, 2026. Authored by Tianyu Zhang, Yiu Chi Lai, and Philip Leung Ho Yu (The Education University of Hong Kong), the study systematically reviews 45 studies published between 2020 and 2024 on the application of Generative AI (GenAI) in K-12 education. Key findings include: (1) GenAI tools significantly improve students' academic performance, cognitive abilities, and learning motivation, promoting personalized learning; (2) challenges include misleading or erroneous content generation, difficulty in understanding technology, student dependence on technology, and privacy infringement; (3) educators demonstrate shortcomings in AI literacy, highlighting the need for targeted training; and (4) most existing empirical research focuses on short-term impacts, with future research needing more longitudinal studies to evaluate long-term implications of GenAI in education.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
GenAI tools can significantly improve students' academic performance and cognitive abilities, enhance their learning motivation, and thus promote the development of personalized learning, Using these tools also brings a series of challenges, including misleading or erroneous content generation, difficulty in understanding technology, students' dependence on technology, and privacy infringement, The shortcomings demonstrated by educators in terms of AI literacy emphasize the necessity for relevant educational institutions to organize targeted AI literacy training, Most existing empirical research has focused on the short-term impact of GenAI tools on K-12 education. Future research will incorporate more longitudinal studies to systematically evaluate the long-term and deep implications of GenAI in education
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.thirdrocktechkno.com/blog/ai-in-education-top-use-cases-and-real-examples

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published December 24, 2025, updated August 3, 2026) by Tapan Patel of Third Rock Techkno provides a comprehensive overview of AI in education, covering the nine highest-impact use cases with real-world examples.

**Key Statistics:**
- 86% of education organizations use generative AI (highest adoption rate of any industry, per Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education Report)
- The global AI in education market reached $7.57 billion in 2025, projected to hit $112 billion by 2034
- Teachers using AI tools report reclaiming 5–10 hours per week for instruction
- A 2025 randomized controlled trial in Nature Scientific Reports found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning

**The Nine Core AI in Education Use Cases:**

1. **Personalized Learning** – Adaptive platforms analyze student performance in real-time, adjusting content difficulty and pacing. Example: Sourcebook (built by TRT) turns documents into interactive, adaptive learning experiences.

2. **Automated Content Creation** – Generative AI produces quizzes, lesson plans, and learning modules at scale. Example: Squirrel AI generates tailored textbooks and materials.

3. **Intelligent Tutoring** – AI tutors use NLP to guide students through problem-solving. Example: Khan Academy's Khanmigo (built on GPT-4) asks guiding questions rather than giving answers.

4. **Enhanced Student Engagement** – AI-driven gamification and interactive simulations maintain student interest. Example: Duolingo uses AI to personalize lesson difficulty and spaced-repetition algorithms.

5. **Teacher Assistance & Administrative Automation** – Automated grading, scheduling, and chatbots handle routine tasks. Example: Gradescope uses AI to evaluate handwritten math, coding, and essays.

6. **Language Learning & Translation** – NLP provides personalized vocabulary, grammar practice, and pronunciation feedback. Example: Duolingo's AI optimizes review timing and lesson difficulty.

7. **Predictive Analytics** – ML models identify at-risk students before they fail. Example: IBM Watson Education reported 20% improvements in student performance through early intervention.

8. **Accessibility & Inclusivity** – Text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and translation tools remove barriers. Example: Microsoft Immersive Reader reads aloud, translates, and adjusts formatting for students with dyslexia or visual impairments.

9. **Collaborative Learning** – AI helps form study groups, moderate discussions, and track projects. Example: Kiddom manages virtual study groups and peer collaboration.

**Limitations & Considerations:**
- Student data privacy under FERPA must be protected
- Bias in training data can widen inequities; regular bias testing is essential
- AI should support, not replace, teachers; deep critical thinking still requires human instruction

**Recommendation:** Start with one high-value use case, pilot with real students, and expand based on evidence rather than hype.
</summary>

URL: https://livehandbook.org/k-12-education/miscellaneous/k-12-education/school-resources/artificial-intelligence-in-k%E2%80%9312-schools

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the AEFP Live Handbook (last updated August 2026) by Barnard, Fesler, and Loeb examines the state of AI in K-12 education. It argues that the most useful way to evaluate AI is to ask whether tools expand students' access to proven learning experiences—personalized instruction, complex problem-solving, meaningful collaboration, substantive discussion, and sustained relationships with educators.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Thin evidence base:** Of 800+ academic papers on AI in K-12 education, only 20 meet standards for strong causal inference. No high-quality causal studies exist on student-facing AI tools in U.S. K-12 classrooms. Most studies examine short-term performance rather than durable learning.

2. **AI as a mediator of learning experiences:** AI shapes learning through three pathways—student-facing interactions, educator support, and system-level organization. The central evaluative question is whether tools expand access to experiences that research identifies as important for development.

3. **Performance vs. proficiency gap:** A randomized study of high school math students found that those using a general-purpose chatbot performed worse on subsequent closed-book exams than students who practiced with no AI support, despite higher performance during practice. Students using a tutoring-style system (hints and guided reasoning) showed no difference on exams. Similar patterns appear across subjects.

4. **Design choices matter:** Systems that prompt explanation, reflection, and revision reinforce cognitive work for deeper learning. Systems that generate complete answers reduce cognitive work and learning. Guided reasoning tools improve independent problem-solving performance.

5. **Educator capacity:** A randomized experiment found teachers with ChatGPT spent less time preparing lessons while maintaining quality. AI tools that provide instructional feedback to teachers and tutors show early promise, with largest gains for lower-performing tutors.

**Research Priorities:** Long-term studies on durable learning outcomes, equity implications, system-level applications (scheduling, tutoring coordination), and AI-based assessment validity are needed. The article emphasizes that the evidence base is too thin to draw definitive conclusions, especially for U.S. K-12 settings.
</summary>

This policy paper, published on April 27, 2026, by CODIT, argues that South Korea's K-12 education system must shift from an infrastructure-driven, technology-adoption model to an outcome-based learning architecture for the AI era. **Structural Gaps Identified:**
1. **Fragmented Policy Design:** Korea's "AI for All" initiative and National AI Action Plan focus on input-based metrics (pilot schools, device distribution) rather than fundamentally redesigning instruction, assessment, and curricula around outcomes. 2. **Teacher Capacity Gaps:** According to TALIS 2024, Korean teachers show low adaptive instruction levels (below OECD average), only 12% of new teachers have mentors (OECD avg: 26%), and teachers report lower autonomy in curriculum implementation. Training is institution-centered and misaligned with classroom needs.
3. **Content Sustainability Issues:** Private-sector-driven content is sensitive to policy changes; subscription models constrain school use; accessibility features for special education (120,735 students) and multicultural students (202,208 students) are delayed or partial; standardized content fails to support diverse learning types.
4. **Infrastructure-Use Gap:** Device-to-student ratios have improved significantly (primary: 0.25→0.62, middle: 0.22→0.84, high: 0.30→0.70 over 4 years), but actual classroom use remains limited to specific subjects. Issues include device specs misaligned with classroom needs, maintenance challenges, and security/control circumvention concerns.

**Policy Recommendations:**
1. **National Governance & Public-Private Collaboration:** Establish a central coordinating body (building on the AI Talent Development Task Force) to align curriculum, instruction, assessment, and learning records. Cites Estonia's "AI Leap 2025" as a benchmark (public-private partnership with OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.).
2. **Teacher Community-Based Capacity Building:** Move beyond training toward collaborative ecosystems with lead teacher groups, time-based incentives (reduced teaching loads), and formal recognition mechanisms. Support teacher autonomy in instructional design.
3. **Accessible & Sustainable Content:** Ensure accessibility features (voice support, text conversion, input assistance) from development stage; combine OS-level capabilities with content solutions; create public-private ecosystem for flexible content integration.
4. **Operational Infrastructure for Learning Flow & Safety:** Shift from centralized management to flexible classroom-level operations; evolve MDM systems beyond control-oriented approaches; embed Privacy by Design throughout service lifecycle.

- **What GenAI is**: A range of tools trained on large datasets to create new content, becoming widely available in free and paid forms.

- **Considerations when using AI**: Check outputs for accuracy as AI can produce plausible but incorrect content; avoid using personal data as free tools use prompts for training; be aware of cultural bias (models are weak on mātauranga Māori, te reo Māori, and Pacific languages); read terms and conditions carefully.

- **School policy**: Schools should discuss AI use and develop policies covering purpose, principles, risk mitigation, professional development, data privacy, and review. Schools with consent to assess NCEA standards must have an authenticity policy including acceptable GenAI use.

- **Teachers using AI**: Human teachers must remain central and responsible for student learning. AI marking tools should support, not replace, teacher professional judgement. A principles-based approach is promoted with human oversight.

- **Students using AI**: GenAI can enhance learning but must be restricted to ensure students' work is their own. Age restrictions apply (e.g., ChatGPT requires age 13+ with parental permission for under 18). Never input personal information of anyone under 13.

- **GenAI in NCEA**: Schools must have a GenAI policy. Authenticity requires students to demonstrate their own knowledge. GenAI is not permitted in NCEA external assessments. For internal assessments, teachers must be aware of specific standard requirements.

- **Resources**: Links to Tāhūrangi curriculum materials, Netsafe guidance, Privacy Commissioner guidelines, NZQA AI guidance, and downloadable PDFs including case studies from Aotea College and Hobsonville Point Secondary School.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review article published in Frontiers in Education on September 23, 2025, authored by Abdullah Alfarwan from Najran University, Saudi Arabia. The study systematically reviews empirical research on the use of Generative AI (GenAI) in K-12 education, analyzing 30 papers retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and snowballing techniques.

**Key Findings:**
- **Publication Timeline:** Most papers (19 of 30) were published in 2024, with 6 from 2025 and 5 from 2023.
- **Educational Levels:** High school students and pre-service teachers were most represented. In-service teachers, elementary, primary, and vocational education were underrepresented. No studies focused on early childhood education (ECE).
- **Subject Domains:** Mathematics was the most common subject (5 papers), followed by Physics (4). The majority focused on STEM-related subjects. Non-STEM subjects included History, Writing, and English Language.
- **Geographic Representation:** Most studies were conducted in Taiwan and China (4 each), followed by the US and Germany (3 each). No studies from Africa were included.
- **GenAI Tools:** ChatGPT was used in 21 of 30 papers. Other tools included Copilot, DALL-E, Midjourney, and others.
- **Study Design:** Quasi-experimental design was most common (30% of papers), followed by descriptive and mixed-method approaches (20% each).
- **Measures:** Primarily psychological variables (attitudes, self-efficacy, trust, motivation, critical thinking, self-regulated learning). Only two studies examined self-regulated learning specifically. Objective measures (standardized tests) were largely absent.
- **Recommendations:** 90% of papers emphasized the need for teacher professional development for AI-integrated classrooms. Future research should explore longitudinal studies, true experimental designs, objective learning measures, parental involvement, diverse GenAI tools, and under-researched contexts (ECE, special needs, rural settings).

**Limitations:** The search only covered English-language publications and specific GenAI tools (ChatGPT, Google Bard, Copilot, Midjourney). There is a lack of representation from Africa, the Middle East, and South America.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: A Systematic Review of Generative AI in K–12: Mapping Goals, Activities, Roles, and Outcomes via the 3P Model ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2079-8954/13/10/840

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review article published in the journal Systems (2025, Volume 13, Issue 10, article 840, DOI: 10.3390/systems13100840), authored by Xiaoling Lin and Hao Tan from the School of Design, Hunan University, China. The paper presents "A Systematic Review of Generative AI in K–12: Mapping Goals, Activities, Roles, and Outcomes via the 3P Model."

METHODOLOGY: Following the PRISMA framework and appraising quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), the authors synthesized 84 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025 involving learners aged 3–18. The search (conducted May–July 2025) identified 817 records from Scopus (528) and Web of Science (289); after de-duplication and screening, 84 studies with MMAT scores ≥3 were retained. The review integrated Biggs's 3P model (Presage–Process–Product) with the CIMO-Logic framework to code learning objectives, activity designs, AI role paradigms, and outcomes. Four research questions addressed the primary learning goals, learning activities, human–AI role patterns, and reported opportunities/risks in outcomes.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Seven recurring learning objectives emerged: language/literacy; STEM; creativity; socioemotional skills; feedback literacy and self-regulation; motivation; AI literacy.
2. Five dominant activity patterns were identified: AI-facilitated dialogic tutoring; generative iterative co-creation; project-based problem-solving; simulation/game-based learning; and formative feedback with adaptive scaffolding.
3. AI roles shift from AI-directed (learner-as-recipient) to AI-supported/AI-empowered paradigms, re-allocating agency among students, teachers, and caregivers via feedback loops.
4. Reported outcomes span three categories—epistemic, practice, and affective/identity—with opportunities including deeper knowledge, improved practice, and stronger engagement, and risks including hallucinations, reduced originality, over-reliance, motivational loss, and ethical concerns.

CONTEXT AND GAP: The field lacks theoretically grounded accounts linking learning goals, pedagogical activities, and human–AI role configurations to measurable outcomes for 3–18-year-olds. Existing AIEd research is skewed toward higher education, privileges traditional AI, and largely predates powerful LLMs. GenAI enables new space for personalization, learner–AI co-creation, and immersive assessment while raising questions about role allocation, ethical governance, and impact evaluation. Learning is framed through constructivist, situated, and sociocultural perspectives, moving beyond the knowledge-acquisition metaphor toward participation, collaboration, and distributed cognition.

CONTRIBUTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS: The authors contribute a theory-led goal–activity–role–outcome map, a clarified shift toward co-regulated human–AI ensembles, and practice-oriented guidance. They propose a goal–activity–role alignment heuristic for instructional design, plus safeguards around teacher professional development, feedback literacy, and ethics. They call for longitudinal and cross-cultural research to evaluate GenAI impacts in K–12.

The article belongs to the MDPI Systems journal's Special Issue on "Generative AI Transformation in Education: Current Issues and Challenges." Submission dates: received 14 August 2025, revised 13 September 2025, accepted 23 September 2025, published 25 September 2025. The article has received 14,534 views and 8 citations (at the time of capture) and an Altmetric score of 15.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from FifthRow Blog (published April 9, 2026) provides a comprehensive overview of AI integration in K-12 education globally since 2025. It covers regulatory developments, empirical evidence, risks, stakeholder perspectives, and best practices.

**Regulatory Landscape:** In the U.S., an April 2025 executive order established a national K-12 AI literacy strategy; by early 2026, over half of U.S. states had enacted AI policy guidance. China leads with a mandatory national AI curriculum. South Korea rolled out AI-enabled tutors. Europe's EU AI Act is still being debated with unclear practical impacts. Iceland launched a first-of-its-kind national AI pilot with Anthropic. No national bans on AI in K-12 education have been enacted since 2025.

**Empirical Evidence:** 85% of U.S. K-12 teachers and students report using AI, primarily for lesson planning, feedback, and data analysis. Two-thirds endorse AI's benefits for personalized learning and administrative tasks. Up to 75% of students report higher motivation in AI-enhanced settings. Academic improvements of 15–35% have been recorded in some studies. However, no long-term longitudinal studies exist on sustained impacts on higher-order cognitive skills. Most evidence comes from short-term interventions.

**Key Risks:** Privacy and security concerns are significant—only 11% of U.S. districts rigorously vet AI tools for data privacy. AI-generated deepfakes and false cheating accusations have caused harm. 72% of students would use generative AI for assignments, but only 17–22% receive instruction on responsible use. The digital divide persists, with AI adoption below 15% in most African and Latin American systems.

**Stakeholder Views:** Teacher attitudes are polarized—25% believe AI causes more harm than good, while 6% see clear net gains. Student enthusiasm (39%) lags behind teacher enthusiasm. Parent engagement is growing but under-researched.

**Best Practices:** Recommendations include targeted ongoing professional development, ethical/privacy guidelines that evolve with technology, digital infrastructure investment in under-resourced regions, institutional oversight on procurement, and maintaining human-in-the-loop approaches for high-stakes decisions.

- Education reforms under NEP 2020, NCF 2023, and NIPUN Bharat Mission have raised expectations for competency-based, personalised instruction.

ARGUMENT: With vacancies unlikely to close quickly, AI can reduce teachers' administrative and preparatory burden, freeing time for instruction. AI should be framed as an "ally" (augmentation), not a replacement/surveillance tool, since teacher buy-in is the strongest predictor of sustained EdTech adoption in low/middle-income countries. This reframing is consistent with NEP 2020's human-centred vision.

EXISTING TOOLS (Table 1): Categories include lesson planning/content creation (Shiksha Copilot in Karnataka, ChatGPT informal use, TeachBetter.ai); multilingual/localised support (Sahayak AI, Bhashini covering 22 scheduled languages); assessment/grading automation (TeachBetter quiz tool, NIPUN Lakshya App); classroom instruction aids (Tara voice assistant for English); administrative tasks (facial recognition attendance pilots in Karnataka and Bihar, AI note-takers); and professional development (DIKSHA–CIET courses, Shiksha Copilot chatbot). Tools use accessible interfaces (WhatsApp/Telegram) and offline capabilities for low connectivity.

GAPS LIMITING ADOPTION:
1. Weak coverage of regional languages/dialects (tribal languages unsupported; even supported languages show errors)
2. Hallucinations, misalignment, content errors (curriculum alignment issues; repeated errors erode teacher trust)
3. Gaps in teacher training/AI literacy (CENTA survey: 70% used AI in class, 67% confident, but only 57% could spot basic AI misconceptions)
4. Limited integration with school systems (AI tools not shareable on official portals; MIS doesn't interface with AI tools; mainly pilot-stage)
5. Unequal access due to weak infrastructure (device shortages, intermittent connectivity, equity risks; new cost points from API/cloud)
6. Privacy, security, ethical concerns (facial recognition surveillance worries; AI bias; DPDP Rules 2025 implementation is phased)
7. Underdeveloped in-class use (most usage is "backstage" planning/grading; few tools support real-time classroom instruction)

SEVEN RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Co-create AI solutions with teachers (hackathons, pilot feedback loops)
2. Ensure equity and access safeguards (infrastructure investment, offline capabilities, local language support, subsidised/public-private pricing)
3. Scale successful models in other states (replicate Shiksha Copilot; develop a 'National Teacher AI Toolkit'; integrate with DIKSHA/teacher portals)
4. Align AI with NEP 2020 goals (competency-based, experiential learning; move beyond rote learning)
5. Protect teacher agency ('human-in-the-loop' checks; AI outputs as suggestions finalised by teachers)
6. Establish ethical AI and data governance (education-specific guidelines complementing DPDP Act, 2023; opt-out provisions for surveillance)

CONCLUSION: The core challenge is not teacher motivation/capacity but structural constraints on teaching time. Teacher-facing AI, framed and governed as an ally, can help reclaim teaching time at scale—provided tools are curriculum-aligned, low-bandwidth, embedded in public digital infrastructure, co-created with educators, and governed by strong privacy/ethical safeguards. --- SOURCE 2: Generative AI in Japanese Schools: Initial Implementation and Socio-Emotional Impact｜Hafnium ---
URL: https://note.com/hafnium/n/n5721c8198e03?hl=en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article examines the initial implementation of generative AI in Japanese schools and its socio-emotional impact, covering the period from hardware infrastructure development (2021) through policy evolution (2023-2025) and actual classroom practices.

**1. GIGA School Foundation:** Japan established the physical infrastructure for AI education through the GIGA School Program, which achieved "one device per student" for compulsory education nearly nationwide by 2021. Approximately 7.4 million tablet devices and laptops (about 28% iPads) were distributed, with 97.6% of planned devices deployed across 1,769 municipalities by March 2021. This digitalization was accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic and reached rural areas, earning Japan a reputation as a country that "already possesses the hardware for Generation AI."

**2. Policy Evolution (2023-2025):** Japan's policy shifted from caution to integration. In July 2023, MEXT issued interim guidelines emphasizing caution and careful experimentation — prohibiting AI for graded assignments, requiring students to verify AI output and cite tool/prompt usage, and mandating that "human judgment is essential at the end of every task." MEXT did not impose a uniform ban but asked boards of education to adjust approaches regionally. By December 2024, updated guidelines (Ver. 2.0) expanded AI's scope, framing it as potentially beneficial based on usage while emphasizing human-centered use. Use cases like AI chatbots as English conversation partners were cited, with particularly cautious operation recommended at the elementary level. The policy's tone shifted from treating AI primarily as a risk to "an innovative educational tool to be used with caution."

**3. Classroom Practices (2024-2025):** MEXT selected 52 designated schools as "testbeds" for AI verification in the 2023-2024 fiscal year. Key applications include:
- **Teacher-side use:** Reducing workload via AI-drafted lesson plans, handouts, parent documents, administrative documents, and quiz questions. Benesse developed an automatic test-question generation tool; Nagoya piloted a "grading AI" for multiple-choice tests.
- **Student language learning:** AI chatbots serve as English conversation partners, allowing anxious students to practice speaking "without the fear of being judged" under teacher supervision.
- **Inquiry-based learning:** AI acts as a "capable peer" or 24/7 research assistant when fields fall outside teacher expertise.
- **Creativity:** Image-generation AI helps students visualize story ideas; ChatGPT acts as a "story editor" and "idea coach" in art, music, writing, and manga production classes. Teachers note AI "does not take away student creativity, but rather expands it."
- **Guided AI platforms:** "Chattomo Sync" launched at end of 2024 (after pilot in ~100 schools), operating on closed networks with content filtering and usage monitoring. Osaka introduced three AI types with different difficulty levels for self-paced learning, plus a "Learning Companion AI" for truant students and those needing Japanese language instruction.
- **Municipal-level implementation:** The Tokyo Metropolitan Government announced it would introduce 'Tokyo Metropolitan AI' to all 256 metropolitan schools starting May 2025, indicating a shift toward system-wide implementation. A pilot history lesson explored counterfactual scenarios (e.g., "What if World War I had not happened?").
- **Cram schools (juku):** Benesse's 'Shinken Zemi' provides specialized tablets with Naver's Clova AI assistant for individually optimized learning plans.

**Expected Benefits and Risks:** Benefits include reduced teacher workload, personalized learning, and inclusion. Risks include "yes-bot" behavior, excessive convenience undermining creativity and critical thinking, and disparities by region, school type, and family background. Success will depend on teacher training, equitable dissemination, and incorporating SEL-related perspectives.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Ethical, Legal, and Social Issues in the Use of Generative ... ---
URL: https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/itel/5/1/5_5.1.Inv.p002/_pdf/-char/ja

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper by Atsuo Kishimoto (University of Osaka) examines ethical, legal, and social issues (ELSI) arising from integrating generative AI into educational settings in Japan. Following ChatGPT's emergence in late 2022, Japanese schools began pilot programs with generative AI, supported by MEXT's 'Generative AI Pilot Schools' initiative starting in 2023. The key distinction is that unlike traditional predictive/classification AI where students were only subjects of analysis, generative AI makes students active users, expanding potential risks and benefits.

Key ELSI concerns identified include: bias amplification in training data (which marginalizes minority information/cultures), hallucination (AI outputs sounding plausible but being false), privacy violations, copyright infringement (illustrators and news publishers opposing unauthorized use of their works), prompt injection attacks, information leaks from careless prompt input, and environmental impacts (CO2 emissions and water consumption from computing resources). NIST-identified risks listed include CBRN information, confabulation, harmful bias, data privacy, intellectual property issues, and information integrity concerns.

The paper presents multilevel response strategies:
1. AI company engagement through procurement guidelines (Japan's Digital Agency published procurement/contract checklists in May 2025), pledge systems (like the discontinued Student Privacy Pledge of 2014), and whitelist certification methods (as used in Swedish municipalities)
2. Institutional policy development, including AI policies, ethics curricula, and faculty training at universities
3. Enhanced AI literacy training for both educators and students

The paper engages with fundamental questions about teaching, learning, and schools, drawing on OECD's Learning Compass (2019) and Teaching Compass (2025) frameworks. The Teaching Compass explicitly positions AI agents (assistants, avatars, and tutors/co-pilots) as targets of co-agency alongside traditional teacher-student collaboration. MEXT's updated guidelines (Version 2.0, December 2024) outline five key perspectives: safety considerations, information security, protection of personal information/privacy/copyright, ensuring fairness, and transparency/accountability to stakeholders.

The paper concludes that responsible implementation requires balancing innovation with ethical considerations to maintain trusting relationships essential in education. The author acknowledges funding from JST's RInCA program (Grant JPMJRS22J1).
</summary>

To maintain this trust, both students and teachers must practice responsible use of generative AI.", "In an era where knowledge can be learned through AI and digital materials, schools are becoming increasingly important as communities, where people can meet diverse individuals and refine their values, rather than just physical classrooms."

Key points from the Guidelines:
- Generative AI is evaluated as capable of producing useful output that, depending on usage, can assist, extend, and expand human capabilities and possibilities.
- Students need to deepen their understanding of generative AI and acquire appropriate usage methods at the school level, anticipating its future role in everyday life.
- Generative AI carries inherent risks including erroneous output (hallucination) and the regeneration of biases such as prejudice and discrimination.
- Teachers are asked to utilize generative AI while accounting for these risks and to instruct students to use AI output only as a reference, ultimately exercising their own judgment.

The article also references pilot programs: Since 2023, generative AI pilot schools were designated, with end-of-year questionnaire results published. 2023 academic year results showed students may enhance motivation and creativity through experimentation, but also revealed cases where students blindly accepted AI answers or struggled to appropriately select when to use it—raising the need for appropriate teacher guidance and a supportive environment.

Key points for AI use in schools highlighted in the Guidelines:
(1) Appropriate use with safety in mind
(2) Ensuring information security
(3) Protection of personal information, privacy, and copyrights
(4) Ensuring fairness

The Guidelines recommend that teachers gain hands-on understanding of both the conveniences and concerns of generative AI, and call on boards of education to support classroom practice by developing an Education Information Security Policy and organizing training.

The article was published on February 28, 2025, by the EN-ICHI Editorial Team (with additions/revisions in the February 2025 issue of "EN-ICHI FORUM"), and falls under the Education field and Issue briefs and Researches category.

However, only 30.6% of China's population has ever attended high school, and roughly 40% of middle school graduates don't go on to high school. The system is fundamentally zero-sum — universities are overwhelmingly urban, and less than 5% of elite university students come from rural families despite 65% of children having rural hukou.

## Structural Challenges
Rural education faces severe resource depletion: elite schools systematically attract talent from periphery areas, leaving rural schools with teacher shortages (senior teachers are only 6.8% of all teachers in China vs. 26% in the US with 20+ years experience), oversized classrooms (56+ students), and severe funding constraints. Local governments bear ~85% of education spending, and poorer counties have less to spend. A 2025 study found 82% of rural children aged 6-36 months had at least one developmental delay.

## Implementation Barriers
- **Funding**: MOE white papers are unfunded mandates that signal priorities but provide no money. Schools are instructed to "strengthen overall planning of funds" but budgets are already stretched thin.
- **Device access**: Rural areas face a shortfall of 8.5 million computers. Historical scandals (schools forcing families to buy overpriced tablets) and concerns about screen time and addiction have hindered device distribution.
- **Private sector costs**: iFlytek's smart classroom software cost one school ¥1,744,000 (~US$254,000). Even the Bengbu city contract covering 875 schools worked out to roughly ¥800 per student per year.
- **Data privacy**: At least 63% of primary/secondary students have dealt with spam calls from data leaks. Student data protection relies on non-mandatory recommendations. Schools routinely pressure parents to sign expansive data agreements.
- **Teacher incentives**: Rural teachers' careers are centrally managed with forced transfers, reducing motivation to integrate AI. The "County-managed, school-hired" system is widely resented.

## Key Concerns
The article notes that while computer-assisted learning has shown some benefits, AI cannot address root causes of educational inequality — the gaokao system, hukou-based restrictions, centralization of resources, and early childhood developmental delays. The mental health surveillance use case is particularly worrying, as the structure of boarding schooling itself (with 47.3% of boarding students suffering from acute pessimism and 63.8% feeling lonely) is a major source of psychological harm. Meanwhile, wealthy urban students already enjoy AI-guided learning tools, potentially widening rather than narrowing the gap.
</summary>
