#### The AI Digital Textbook Rollout and Reversal

**UNESCO GEM Report / World Education Blog (January 3, 2025)** [75][76]: AI textbooks use generative AI to create customized content, adjust pace/difficulty, provide real-time data for teacher feedback. Nearly USD 70 million invested in digital infrastructure. Concerns from educators led to delays—Korean and home economics textbooks held back, social studies and science rollout delayed until 2027. Government committed $760 million over three years for teacher training. The National Assembly reclassified AI digital textbooks as supplementary (not mandatory) materials, leaving usage to school principals' discretion—a move the education minister warned would cause "significant confusion."

**Rollout Failure Analysis** [77][78][101][102][103]:
- **PHI Learning (November 15, 2025)** [78]: The initiative was downgraded from "official textbooks" to "supplementary material" within just four months. Student Ko Ho-dam (high school junior on Jeju Island) reported class delays, poor focus from solo laptop work, and lessons not tailored to his level. Researcher Lee Bohm (Cambridge): "AI should first be piloted in homework or practice before being introduced in class... South Korea pushed too far, too fast."
- **Rest of World (2025)** [102][103]: Launched March 2025 under President Yoon Suk Yeol; stripped of official textbook status after four months. Government spent over 1.2 trillion won ($850 million); publishers invested about 800 billion won ($567 million). Complaints: factual inaccuracies, data privacy risks, increased screen time, heavier workloads, poor-quality content. Development timeline: traditional textbooks take 18 months development/9 months review/6 months preparation; AI textbooks took 12/3/3 months. A lawsuit from the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union and civic group Political Mamas. After Yoon's impeachment and removal, newly elected President Lee Jae Myung followed through on a campaign promise to rescind the policy. Adoption rates dropped from 37% to 19% between semesters, with only 2,095 schools remaining. Developers like Dong-A Publishing defend the textbooks citing personalized support, accessibility for multicultural families and students with disabilities. "The program failed because everything was rushed; it should have been rolled out gradually after testing its effectiveness. We no longer trust the government, which I see as the biggest problem." — Kim Cha-myung, elementary school teacher.
- **Friedrich Naumann Foundation** [101]: As of March 2025, fewer than 30% of elementary schools adopted the AI textbooks, with usage rates between 23.8% and 29.1% across subjects. A parental petition gathered 56,505 signatures citing screen time, data privacy, and over-dependence concerns. A teacher survey found 98.5% of 2,626 respondents considered training insufficient. Political polarization: in conservative Daegu, AI textbook usage is 98%; in liberal Sejong, only 8%. With progressive President Lee Jae-myung taking office June 4, 2026, significant policy changes expected.
- **Yoonseo Choi (Geumcheon-Gu High School)** [77]: Concerns include: 40.1% of Korean teenagers (ages 10-19) at risk of smartphone over-reliance (Ministry of Science and ICT); Swedish students' literacy skills dropped 11 points per PIRLS following digital education implementation; Sweden and Norway reverting to paper books; 86.6% of 106,448 parents and teachers oppose AI textbooks as substitutes (Educational Policy Design Institute research).
- **YouTube analysis** [104]: A survey of teachers who participated in digital textbook training more than once showed 94% opposed the rollout. Over 50,000 parents signed a petition calling for postponement. South Chungcheong Province Superintendent Kim Ji-won cautioned the country might be rushing.
- **Springer Chapter (August 11, 2026)** [100]: 6-3-3-4 education structure; 93.5% of 25-64-year-olds have high school diploma (OECD highest); 71% of 25-34-year-olds have tertiary degree. AI digital textbooks address basic digital skills, equal opportunities/inclusion, personalization. Planned investments: ~$69.3M for digital classrooms, $43.2M for 6,000 schools by 2026. Six development phases: basic development (1995-2010), piloting (2011-2017), national expansion with AI (2018 onward), pandemic innovation (2020-2022), legal anchoring/rollout (2023-2025), course adjustments (August 2025 onward). On August 4, 2025, the National Assembly decided to introduce digital textbooks as optional rather than mandatory learning resources. TOUCH teacher group: 400+ teachers selected for intensive 2-year digital training.

**CODIT Policy Paper (April 27, 2026)** [17]: Argues Korea must shift from infrastructure-driven technology adoption to outcome-based learning architecture. Structural gaps: (1) fragmented policy design—"AI for All" initiative and National AI Action Plan focus on input-based metrics; the 7-year curriculum revision cycle cannot keep pace; (2) teacher capacity gaps—per TALIS 2024, Korean teachers show low adaptive instruction levels (below OECD average), only 12% of new teachers have mentors (OECD avg: 26%); (3) content sustainability issues—accessibility features for special education (120,735 students) and multicultural students (202,208 students) delayed or partial; (4) infrastructure-use gap—device-to-student ratios improved (primary: 0.25→0.62, middle: 0.22→0.84, high: 0.30→0.70 over 4 years) but actual classroom use remains limited. Cites Daejeon Metropolitan Office of Education case study showing a 36.25% increase in creative learning when teachers integrate digital devices into instructional flow. Cites Estonia's "AI Leap 2025" as a benchmark (public-private partnership with OpenAI, Anthropic).

#### Classroom Case Studies and Evidence

**Mindspark RCT (Delhi)** [24]: Experimental study by Karthik Muralidharan (UCSD), Abhijeet Singh (Stockholm School of Economics), Alejandro J. Ganimian (NYU). 619 students from low-income neighborhoods in five public middle schools randomly assigned to receive free access to Mindspark (Grades 6-9). Key results:
- Lottery winners scored 0.37σ higher in math and 0.23σ higher in Hindi over a 4.5-month period (ITT estimates with 58% average attendance).
- IV estimates: attending for 90 days would raise math and Hindi scores by 0.6σ and 0.39σ respectively.
- Lottery winners made over twice the test-score value-added in math and ~2.4 times in Hindi versus control.
- Absolute gains similar for all students, but relative gains much greater for academically weaker students.
- Cost-effective even at small scale.
- Context: over 50% of Grade 5 students cannot read at second-grade level; average Grade 6 student was 2.5 grade levels behind in math, growing to 4.5 by Grade 9.
- Program design: 90-minute sessions, 6 days/week; 45 minutes computer-based instruction + 45 minutes supervised group study; fee INR 200 (USD 3) per month (subsidized).
- Key insight: personalized CAL interventions deliver the largest gains (contrasting with hardware-focused and pedagogy-focused CAL).

**Rajasthan "Padhai with AI" (Tonk)** [21]: AI-based program led by Tonk Collector Shri Saumya Jha providing personalized learning, practice tools, and remedial support for government school students in tough subjects like maths, resulting in 95% of Class 10 students passing. The Better India reports Tonk's AI program went from poor math scores to a 96.4% pass rate in six weeks.

**Rajasthan BCG/Playpower Labs/Dell Foundation Partnership** [22]: IAS officer Gaurav Agrawal announced that partnering with Boston Consulting Group, Playpower Labs, and the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation India, Rajasthan brought 400,000 government school students out of "learning poverty" over two years. Rajasthan has ~72,000 schools with ~8 million students; 50-70% were behind grade level. The program designed an AI-based assessment system where teachers photograph students' answer sheets, and AI conducts backend analytics. Results: student learning assessment time dropped from 6-7 minutes per child to 30 seconds; learning outcomes improved by 8-10% across subject-grade combinations.

**Smart Paper AI (Jodhpur)** [23]: Developed by Nirmal Patel (co-founder of EdOptimize, Chief Data Scientist at Playpower Labs, two-time Tools Competition Prize winner). In a proof of concept in Jodhpur District, more than 10,000 handwritten exams from 2,500 students were graded by the platform for 300 teachers across 55 government schools. AI not only scores but analyzes student reasoning—when 1,000 students solve the same algebra equation incorrectly, Smart Paper's large language model clusters answers, identifies common misconceptions, and generates targeted lesson plans. Currently used across 65,000 middle schools for multiple-choice grading. "You're reading the thoughts of students at scale. That's never been possible before." Earlier prototypes digitized multiple-choice worksheets using computer vision that works on low-end phones; over three years collected data on 5 million students. Related LinkedIn report: AI was used for the first time in India to check handwritten subjective exam answers via Smart Paper, evaluating 3,200 students from classes 6-8 across 55 government schools in just two minutes [21].

**Gumla, Jharkhand** [21]: Teachers being trained to bring AI into lessons with support of District Commissioner Prerna Dixit, led by Wisme AI.

**Shikshak App (Rajasthan)** [21]: Teacher-facing app, part of state partnership with BCG and Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, lifted nearly 4 lakh students out of learning poverty; UP's Nipun Assessment Test uses AI for foundational skills of children in grades 1-8.

**Indonesia Case Study (relevant regional context)** [3]: "ChatGPT in Secondary Education: A Multi-Theoretical Case Study from a Developing Country" (Educational Alternatives journal, 2026) by Sanggam Pardede, Dearlina Sinaga, Stevani Simamora — qualitative instrumental case study in a public secondary school in Indonesia. **Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools** [23]: Government-endorsed policy document guiding responsible and ethical use of generative AI in school education. In June 2025, Education Ministers endorsed the 2024 Framework Review, undertaken by the National AI in Schools Taskforce in consultation with all jurisdictions, school sectors, and national agencies. The framework was released in December 2023 and outlines principles including privacy and security standards, equity and accessibility; requires schools to engage students on how AI tools work, including limitations and biases, and requires student work to outline how AI tools should or should not be used [60].

**National AI Plan (December 2025)** [13]: 37-page plan released by the Department of Industry, Science and Resources under the Albanese Government; goals: capturing opportunities, spreading benefits, keeping Australians safe. Key items: NBN expansion, $10 billion data centre investment in 2024; regional vs metro AI adoption divide (29% regional vs 40% metropolitan); GovAI (secure government AI hosting service government schools may access); over $362 million in research grants; $47 million Next Generation Graduates Program; National AI Centre's Guidance for AI Adoption (October 2025); First Nations Digital Support Hub; Framework for Governance of Indigenous Data; "Responsible AI microcredential" with 150,000+ enrolments; AI Safety Institute; online safety reforms criminalizing non-consensual deepfake material; copyright decisions ruling out text and data mining exception; Privacy Act 1988 modernisation. Department of Education commits to "ensure a strong pipeline of AI-ready school leavers and graduates." The Plan states "in education, AI offers opportunities to reduce teacher workloads and improve student outcomes."

**APPI Participatory Research** [22]: Multi-university team (University of Sydney, UTS, University of Bergen) led by Professor Kalervo Gulson tested participatory methods within the NSW EdTech ecosystem. Policy opportunities: operationalising local engagement to identify AI risks and benefits, establishing a permanent Advisory Council for AI in Education, strengthening equity and inclusion in EdTech procurement. "With the global AI education market forecasted to reach US$22 billion by 2028, proactive governance and policy tools to ensure safety and equity have become more critical."

**SotaTek ANZ Guide (September 30, 2025)** [21]: 65% of educators see AI as critical for improving student outcomes; educators could save up to 13 hours per week through AI-assisted automation. Australia follows the *Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Schools*; both Australia and NZ "stress transparency, explainability, and human oversight. Schools are expected to keep records of how AI systems are used, make decision processes understandable to students and families, and provide alternatives when AI-generated outcomes are disputed."

#### Classroom Case Studies

**South Australia EdChat Trial** [59][11]: First trial of its kind in Australia (announced July 5, 2023), in eight public high schools (later 16 schools per Guardian [60]). "EdChat" is an AI chatbot similar to ChatGPT but designed specifically for educational use, developed by the state's education department and Microsoft. Unlike ChatGPT, EdChat does not simply answer student questions; it provides hints, suggestions, or counter-questions like a good tutor, available 24/7. It doesn't save students' input or use it to learn from. South Australia is the only state that has not banned generative AI tools in public schools. A June 2023 YouthInsight survey found 70% of Australians aged 14–17 have used ChatGPT—59% for schoolwork or study, 42% for completing school assignments. South Australia's minister for education Blair Boyer: schools would be doing young people an "incredible disservice" if it didn't educate students about appropriate AI use: "AI will be a part of our work and lives in the future." A two-year trial program was subsequently announced [63].

**NSW EduChat** [13][62]: In New South Wales, 50 public schools are trialing "EduChat," a department-designed AI chatbot restricted to the state syllabus. "The use of individual free-to-use generative AI tools other than NSWEduChat is neither endorsed nor recommended by the department" [13]. All Year 5-12 NSW public school students can access it. At Plumpton High in Western Sydney, year 11 students use it to draft essays (on Shakespeare's Othello), learning prompt engineering. The chatbot refuses to write essays for students and instead prompts deeper thinking; "it has improved writing dramatically—students now generate 1,000-1,500 words in 40 minutes compared to 800 words previously." Student quote: "Students aren't getting their thinking replaced, but rather they're getting a tool that can assist them. So, it's in no way like taking over our thinking, but rather pushing us to improve literacy skills." The department acknowledges the system "hallucinates" and confirms there are "absolutely no plans" to replace teachers with AI [62].

**Chuttwood Primary (multilingual Year 5)** [62]: Students use EduChat as a last resort for translating tricky words after dictionaries. Assistant principal Isabelle McGloin reminds students AI cannot understand human contexts like whether a child missed breakfast.

**Westbourne Grammar School (Victoria)** [62]: Principal Adrian created an AI chatbot avatar of himself on the school's website that speaks multiple languages. The school embraced AI after Victoria and other states initially banned ChatGPT in late 2022. The school uses programs with AI audiences for public speaking feedback, AI art generation, and video game creation. Principal quote: "I don't think banning is ever the solution... we need to be educating our young people about the safe, effective, and ethical uses." UNSW senior lecturer Jake Renzella warns of "over-reliance"—early studies show students' ability to recall what went into an essay is "heavily reduced" when they use AI tools: "The real concern here is that are we outsourcing the learning when we ask students to do work with these tools."

**Queensland Cerego Trial** [60]: Queensland completed a trial of the AI learning tool Cerego among 500 students, released to all state schools in 2024.

**History of State Bans** [60]: Most Australian states and territories initially moved to ban or restrict ChatGPT in public schools in 2023 due to privacy and plagiarism concerns, though some private schools adopted it. Western Australia lifted its AI ban for teachers in May 2023. Victoria lifted its restriction in term two of last year. Education Minister Jason Clare launched an inquiry into generative AI use: "If we get this right, generative AI can help personalise education and make learning more compelling and effective." UTS academic Leslie Loble: "A lot of students still aren't getting the basics of computers and wifi," pointing to funding gaps between government and independent schools; "that divide is deeply troubling and will lead to a learning gap getting even worse."

**Day of AI Australia** [20][5]: Free, country-specific AI literacy programs tailored to local curricula, available from March 9; delivered in partnership with UNSW Sydney, backed by Microsoft, Rokt, Commonwealth Bank. Reaching 340,000+ students since 2022; 2026 program includes new educational games (Inky's Great Experiment, Pyramid Puzzle), classroom incursions for disadvantaged schools, a Student Challenge aligned with UN SDGs culminating in a "Dolphin Tank" showcase. Statistics: in Australia, 84% of young people aged 15-24 have used generative AI, yet only 27% say they have an "excellent" or "very good" understanding of it (Year13, 2025); 69% of Australian high school students want more training on using AI responsibly and effectively (Elevate Education, 2025).

### IX. NEW ZEALAND / AOTEAROA

#### National Policy Context

**Ministry of Education Generative AI Guidance (updated May 22, 2026)** [24]: Key points:
- Considerations when using AI: check outputs for accuracy (AI can produce plausible but incorrect content); avoid using personal data as free tools use prompts for training; cultural bias—"AI models are likely to be weak on mātauranga and te reo Māori, as well as Pacific languages and Polynesian cultures"; read terms and conditions carefully.
- School policy: schools should discuss AI use and develop policies covering purpose, principles, risk mitigation, professional development, data privacy, and review. Schools with consent to assess NCEA standards must have an authenticity policy including acceptable GenAI use.
- Teachers: "Human teachers must remain central in students' education and take responsibility for students' learning." AI marking tools should support, not replace, teacher professional judgement. Principles-based approach centred on teacher responsibility and professional judgement, human oversight, appropriate use cases.
- Students: age restrictions apply (e.g., ChatGPT requires age 13+ with parental permission for under 18); never input personal information of anyone under 13.
- NCEA: "The use of GenAI is not permitted in NCEA external assessment." "Valid assessment evidence must be the student's own work. Similarly to plagiarism or over-scaffolding, if GenAI is used to produce evidence that is assessed as the student's work, then the assessment is invalid."
- Resources include case studies from Aotea College and Hobsonville Point Secondary School (downloadable PDFs).

**NZCER Primary Schools Survey** [80][81]: Report on generative AI use in Aotearoa New Zealand primary schools (Years 5-8):
- Study: 266 teachers (from over 200 schools) disproportionately interested in AI; 147 students across four case study schools.
- 79% of sample teachers used generative AI at least monthly, compared to ~46% of the general primary teacher population.
- Most common teacher uses: lesson planning, designing assessments, personalizing learning, research for teaching.
- 18% of teachers' schools provided premium AI versions; 27% paid for AI tools themselves (mostly Twinkl and ChatGPT).
- Only 8% of schools had a teacher-use AI policy; 14% had a student-use policy.
- Only 39% felt adequately supported to incorporate AI into teaching.
- ~Half of teachers encountered problems with AI tools not being customized for the Aotearoa New Zealand context; 60% agreed AI tools don't always provide accurate information about Māori.
- Students reported higher AI use than teachers estimated; students used AI more outside school than for school work; high use of chatbots, art/image generation, and "talking to AI like it's a friend" (19% among year 5s, up to ~1/3 among years 7-8); most students agreed using AI too much makes it hard to learn and can feel like cheating; most students didn't recall an adult telling them when they could use AI.
- Recommendations: premium AI tools for teachers; Ministry-supported policy development; professional development; iterative inclusion of AI criticality in curriculum; work with toolmakers to create customized Aotearoa New Zealand content; look to peer countries (UK, Australia); avoid risks of shadow practice, privacy failures, exacerbating inequalities.

**SchoolNews (June 3, 2025)** [96]: Ministry of Education and NZQA provided official guidelines in 2023. NZQA recommends education programs on academic integrity, referencing, warnings about AI bias; assessment authenticity strategies include regular milestones, observing progress, follow-up conversations, using AI detectors cautiously (mindful of false positives), authenticity declarations. The refreshed NZC technology learning area (including AI teaching—its whakapapa, processes, bias potential, risks, benefits, ethics) will be compulsory by 2027. One Auckland English teacher reported one in five students misusing AI for assignments. Jannat Maqbool (Executive Director, AI Researchers Association) envisions personalized learning, language and cultural inclusion, ethical data use, and teachers becoming facilitators.

**Day of AI Aotearoa New Zealand** [20][5]: First nationally designed AI literacy program for New Zealand's school context, targeting Years 5-10; piloted with 10 schools in 2025; incorporates Māori concepts such as whakapapa, data sovereignty, tikanga, and kaitiakitanga; developed with MIT's RAISE initiative, EPIT, TENZ, and NZCER. Pilot results: 92% of students were already using AI, but understanding rose from 20% to 64% after the pilot; students moved from viewing AI as a "magic helper" to critically evaluating it; teachers reported greater confidence. Seeking partners to expand to Years 11-13. Coordinator Susana Tomaz: "In the absence of a formal national framework for generative AI in schools, many schools recognize the urgency of AI literacy but lack clear, coherent guidance."

**Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology Case Study (2025)** [79]: Learner-centred case study by Cindy de Villiers and Ruth Thomas on GenAI in Applied Professional Studies (Scope: Learning & Teaching 15, 2025, DOI: 10.34074/scop.4015002). 16 postgraduate students (15 experienced teachers, 1 social work professional) using generative AI across two courses. Findings: 66.7% increase in GenAI "awareness" and 55% increase in "readiness for GenAI adoption" between pre- and post-questionnaires (62.5% overall growth); 50% rise in "equitable access" positive responses; 62.5% increase in concerns about academic integrity, ethics, and privacy; students reported increased confidence, better time management, reduced study stress—especially beneficial for international students. Tools included ChatGPT, Canva, Cogniti, Elicit, Gemini, Grammarly, LinkedIn Learning, Otter.ai, Quillbot, Zotero.

### X. CROSS-CUTTING EVIDENCE (non-country-specific but relevant)

**Tutor CoPilot RCT (Stanford)** [25]: First randomized controlled trial of a human-AI tutoring system, built on OpenAI's GPT-4, examining about 1,000 students helped by about 900 tutors. Students with AI-assisted tutors were four percentage points more likely to master a math topic; students working with lower-rated tutors saw performance jump by nine percentage points (pass rate rose from 56% to 65%, nearly matching the 66% pass rate for higher-rated tutors' students). Cost: about $20 per student per year. Lead researcher Rose E. Wang: "The big dream is to be able to enhance humans." Susanna Loeb (Stanford): "AI is best used to augment, not replace, tutors since people are better at caring, motivating, and engaging."

**Japan's Ministry of Education "Generative AI Pilot Schools"** [51]: Following ChatGPT's emergence in late 2022, Japanese schools began pilot programs supported by MEXT's 'Generative AI Pilot Schools' initiative starting 2023.

**OECD TALIS 2024 (referenced via UAE)**: About 75% of UAE teachers use AI tools (far above global average of 33%, matched only by Singapore) [12].

**Leon Furze Analysis (December 2025)** [13]: Advice for schools includes monitoring NSWEduChat and South Australia's EdChat; avoiding long-term commitments to commercial AI platforms; implementing three-dimensional professional development; respecting First Nations data sovereignty; encouraging girls into AI/tech subjects.

---

### Notes on Coverage Gaps (for transparency)

- The researcher gathered strong policy-level and case-study evidence for China, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, India, UAE, Australia, and New Zealand.
- No school-level case study from Japan's Tokyo Metropolitan AI rollout results (beyond the announcement) was retrieved; the Sagamihara Nakano Junior High School pilot case study provides the most detailed classroom-level Japanese evidence.
- No standalone school-level case study from the UAE (beyond Dubai British School Jumeirah Park and Swiss International Scientific School Dubai traffic-light/teaching examples) was retrieved.
- New Zealand's Aotea College and Hobsonville Point Secondary School case studies are referenced by the NZ Ministry of Education as downloadable PDFs on the GenAI guidance page but their full text was not retrieved.
- Some statistics (e.g., "1 million students" vs. "400,000 learners" for UAE curriculum) vary across sources and are reported as stated by each source.
- The OECD Japan workplace source was a navigation directory page with low direct relevance and is retained only for completeness.

messages.content:
**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

Four Tavily web-search batches were conducted (each containing multiple simultaneous queries), yielding 70+ sources. Queries included:

1. **Frameworks & teacher training batch**: "AIGC AI-generated content K-12 education implementation frameworks taxonomy 2024 2025"; "UNESCO AI education framework K-12 2024"; "ISTE AI Explorations teacher training program outcomes"; "TPACK-AI framework teacher competencies AI education"
2. **Future trends batch**: "agentic AI education 2025 2026 trends OECD multimodal AI personalized learning pathways"; "OECD Digital Education Outlook 2025 artificial intelligence K-12 report"; "EDUCAUSE Horizon Report 2025 AI education trends predictions"; "Khanmigo AI tutor pilot efficacy results K-12 2025"
3. **Implementation & infrastructure batch**: "SAMR model AI education taxonomy teacher professional development hours cost District AI pilot evaluation criteria academic integrity policy"; "CoSN K-12 AI infrastructure bandwidth devices cost equity digital divide report 2025"; "U.S. Department of Education AI guidance 2025 TeachAI toolkit K-12 roadmap"; "teacher AI professional development outcomes time commitment study hours training effectiveness"
4. **Global/equity & policy batch**: "UNESCO Guidance for generative AI in education 2023 human-centred principles equity"; "World Bank artificial intelligence K-12 education report developing countries digital divide"; "AI4K12 five big ideas artificial intelligence curriculum guidelines K-12"; "school district AI use policy template academic integrity student responsible use 2025"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Implementation Frameworks and Taxonomies

### 1.1 UNESCO AI Competency Frameworks

**UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students** (published August 8, 2024; last updated January 16, 2026; authors: Miao, Fengchun; Shiohira, Kelly; Lao, Natalie) is "an international reference that sets out the importance of integrating AI learning objectives into school curricula." [6][7][8] It:
- Outlines **12 competencies across four dimensions**: (1) Human-centred mindset, (2) Ethics of AI, (3) AI techniques and applications, and (4) AI system design [6][7][8]
- Spans **three progression levels: Understanding, Applying, and Creating with AI** [6][7][8]
- Is "tool-agnostic" and "keeps the focus on human rights, ethics, sustainability and inclusion and aims to support students to become responsible users and active co-creators of AI, rather than passive consumers" [6]
- "Details curricular goals and domain-specific pedagogical methodologies" and is "grounded in the vision of students as AI co-creators and responsible citizens" [8]
- Is available in Arabic, English, French, Portuguese, Spanish, and Vietnamese [8]

**UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers** (published August 8, 2024; last updated January 16, 2026; authors: Fengchun Miao and Mutlu Cukurova) "defines the knowledge, skills, and values teachers must master in the age of AI" and addresses the shift from traditional teacher-student relationships to teacher-AI-student dynamics. [10] It:
- Outlines **15 competencies across five dimensions**: (1) Human-centred mindset, (2) Ethics of AI, (3) AI foundations and applications, (4) AI pedagogy, and (5) AI for professional learning [10]
- Is organized into **three progression levels: Acquire, Deepen, and Create** [10]
- "Serves as a global reference tool to guide the development of national AI competency frameworks, inform teacher training programmes, and help design assessment parameters" [10]
- Was "developed with principles of protecting teachers' rights, enhancing human agency, and promoting sustainability" [10]

**UNESCO Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research** (first global guidance, published September 7, 2023; authors: Fengchun Miao and Wayne Holmes; 44 pages; ISBN 978-92-3-100612-8; DOI: https://doi.org/10.54675/EWZM9535; CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO; available in 14 languages) [59][60][62][63]:
- Aims "to support countries to implement immediate actions, plan long-term policies and develop human capacity to ensure a human-centred vision of these new technologies" [59]
- Notes that "the absence of national regulations on GenAI in most countries leaves the data privacy of users unprotected and educational institutions largely unprepared to validate the tools" [59][60]
- "Proposes key steps to the regulation of GenAI tool, including mandating the protection of data privacy, and setting an age limit for the independent conversations with GenAI platforms" [59][60]
- "Proposes a human-agent and age-appropriate approach to the ethical validation and pedagogical design processes" [59]
- Assesses "potential risks GenAI could pose to core humanistic values that promote human agency, inclusion, equity, gender equality, and linguistic and cultural diversities" [62]
- "Outlines requirements for GenAI providers to enable their ethical and effective use in education" [62]

**UNESCO digital competencies project for G77+China**: UNESCO launched a project focused on developing digital competencies for teachers and school students in the 134 Member States of the Group of 77 and China, stating "Digital competencies of teachers and school students are the most important human cornerstone to underpin the success of the digital transformation of education." The project "will guide efforts of Member States in the formulation of national frameworks and institutional programmes on digital and AI competencies through the UNESCO AI competency frameworks for teachers and for students, released during Digital Learning Week, in September 2024." [9]

### 1.2 TPACK and AI-TPACK Frameworks

**Base TPACK framework**: "Created by researchers Punya Mishra and Matthew Koehler in 2006, [the TPACK framework] explains what it takes for educators to use technology effectively in their practice." It has seven components: Content Knowledge (CK), Pedagogical Knowledge (PK), Technology Knowledge (TK), Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Content Knowledge (TCK), Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK), and central TPACK. A more recent addition, Contextual Knowledge (XK), "recognizes that integration is shaped by district policies, resources, and student needs." [20]

**AI-TPACK framework** (based on Celik, 2023, also called Intelligent-TPACK): "consists of five fundamental components, namely AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK), AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK), AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK), and Ethics." [16] Celik (2023) "proposed the Intelligent-TPACK framework, which incorporates five interconnected dimensions: Intelligent Technological Knowledge (Intelligent-TK), Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (Intelligent-TPK), Technological Content Knowledge (Intelligent-TCK), integrated TPACK, and AI Ethics." [18]

**Empirical AI-TPACK studies**:
- **Hava & Babayiğit** (Springer, Education and Information Technologies, Vol 30, pp. 3491–3508, 2025; published Aug 19, 2024): Correlational survey of **401 teachers in Turkey**. Findings: "teachers' AI-TPACK competencies were below average" (mean = 3.33 on a 7-point scale; lowest in AI-TPACK at 3.22, highest in AI-TCK at 3.51 and AI-TPK at 3.47); digital proficiency above average (mean = 4.93); "a significant relationship between teachers' AI-TPACK and digital proficiency levels was identified, with digital proficiency as a significant predictor of AI-TPACK competencies." [16]
- **Ning et al.** (Sustainability, 2024, Vol 16, Issue 3, Article 978; East China Normal University, Guangxi Normal University, Beijing Normal University): Proposed a **seven-component AI-TPACK framework** (PK, CK, AI-TK, PCK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, AI-TPACK). Survey of **366 valid respondents** (teachers with educational technology coursework and systematic AI training, July–September 2023). EFA showed KMO = 0.939, seven factors extracted, cumulative variance 75.91%. Key findings: "the influence of core knowledge elements (PK, CK, and AI-TK) on AI-TPACK is indirect, mediated by composite knowledge elements (PCK, AI-TCK, and AI-TPK)"; "non-technical knowledge elements have significantly lower explanatory power... compared to knowledge elements related to technology"; "content knowledge (C) diminishes the explanatory power of PCK and AI-TCK." [19]
- **Setiyawan et al.** (Computers and Education Open, Vol 9, December 2025, 100319): Adapted and validated the AI-TPACK scale for vocational education with **460 pre-service and in-service vocational teachers from Indonesia**. The instrument "encompasses seven constructs, including AI Pedagogical Knowledge, AI Content Knowledge, AI Technological Knowledge, and their intersections, culminating in a comprehensive AI-TPACK construct." CFA confirmed strong model fit; "These findings affirm the adapted AI-TPACK scale as a reliable and valid tool for assessing AI-integrated pedagogical competencies specifically within vocational education contexts." [17]
- **Antonio** (Journal of Technology and Science Education, Vol 15, No 3, 2025; Bulacan State University, Philippines): Pre-experimental study of **84 preservice science teachers** through a 14-week AI-focused pedagogical learning course. "Wilcoxon Signed-Ranks Test revealed statistically significant improvements across all dimensions of AI-TPACK... (z = -6.900, p < .001, r = 0.76), indicating a large effect size." Cronbach's alpha = 0.889. Course topics (8 core topics over 14 weeks): TPACK Framework, SAMR Model, Integrating AI Tools in Science Education, Community of Inquiry Framework, Inquiry-Based Learning, Universal Design for Learning, Revised K to 12 Science Curriculum, and Developing Science Lesson Exemplars. Course design grounded in four principles: instructional, experiential, collaborative, and reflective (Antonio & Prudente, 2025). [18]

### 1.3 SAMR Model Applied to AI

**SAMR model** (developed by Dr. Ruben Puentedura) has four levels: **Substitution** (technology replaces traditional tools with no functional change), **Augmentation** (adds functional improvements), **Modification** (allows significant task redesign), and **Redefinition** (highest level, enabling tasks previously impossible). [40][42]

**State applications of SAMR to AI**:
- **Delaware**: "Uses the SAMR model for AI integration, with version tracking for updates" [1]
- **Louisiana** (Fall 2024): "Four-tiered approach (AI-Empowered, Enhanced, Assisted, Prohibited) aligned with the SAMR model" [1]

**SAMR + AI Matrix** (EDUCAUSE Review, April 30, 2026, by Alyshia Keys-Harris, Harvard University): Combines SAMR with Bloom's Taxonomy for instructional design. Five-step process: (1) Reflect on current practices; (2) Select one instructional component; (3) Identify the component's Bloom's level; (4) Integrate AI using the SAMR + AI Matrix; (5) Ensure active cognitive engagement. Key premise: "The ability of AI tools to generate outputs that mirror these processes poses a significant challenge to maintaining academic rigor," but GenAI errors create opportunities for higher-order thinking. Recommends starting with a single instructional component rather than overhauling courses. [42]

**Edutopia PD use of SAMR**: "Our initial discussions focused on how AI was not a substitute (the S in the SAMR framework) for teachers, but a way to augment (A), modify (M), and redefine (R) learning when presented strategically." [44]

### 1.4 AI4K12 Five Big Ideas Taxonomy

**AI4K12 Initiative** (jointly sponsored by AAAI and CSTA; NSF Grant No. DRL-1846073; launched May 2018 by David Touretzky, Christina Gardner-McCune, Fred Martin, and Deborah Seehorn) has three goals: national guidelines, curated resource directory, and community building. [72][73] Its organizing framework is the **"Five Big Ideas in AI"**: (1) **Perception**, (2) **Representation & Reasoning**, (3) **Learning**, (4) **Natural Interaction**, and (5) **Societal Impact**. Guidelines are presented as grade band progression charts (K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12), currently open for public comment. [69][72] The 2017 CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards "contained only two sentences about AI," which motivated the initiative. [71]

The team advocates a **"glass-box approach"** to teaching AI—showing inner workings—rather than an "opaque-box approach." [71] Tools supporting K-12 AI education include Cognimates, Machine Learning for Kids (IBM Watson + Scratch), Google's Teachable Machine, MIT's App Inventor with the Amazon Alexa Toolkit, plus unplugged activities. MIT released an AI + ethics curriculum for middle school combining online and unplugged activities, accessed 500+ times and translated into multiple languages. [70]

**CSTA & AI4K12 "AI Learning Priorities for All K-12 Students"** (2025): "All students must learn about artificial intelligence (AI) as part of a foundational computer science (CS) education in order to be prepared for a world powered by computing." Key findings: "Eight out of ten CS teachers believe that learning about and using AI should be part of a foundational CS learning experience"; "Over two-thirds of CS teachers stated they covered AI specifically, despite the lack of explicit definition in most CS standards." Outcomes are organized by grade band across **five categories**: (1) Humans & AI; (2) Representation & Reasoning; (3) Machine Learning; (4) Ethical AI System Design & Programming; (5) Societal Impacts of AI. "Even the youngest elementary school students can learn... that, for example, a decision tree can be used to show the process by which decisions are made." Tools include Google's Teachable Machine, MIT RAISE Playground, Neuron Sandbox, and TensorFlow Playground. [5]

### 1.5 SREB Four-Pillar Framework

**SREB "Guidance for the Use of AI in the K-12 Classroom"** (Southern Regional Education Board, April 2025) provides four pillars: [2]
- **Pillar #1: Use AI to develop more cognitively demanding tasks** — AI as a tool to enhance student engagement, not a final product; use for lesson planning partner, project-based learning, interactive simulations, exploring counter perspectives. Cautions: AI bias, ensuring mastery of underlying concepts first. [2]
- **Pillar #2: Use AI to streamline teacher administrative and planning work** — planning partner, assignment improvement, grading/feedback, drafting communications, behavioral insights, ELL support. Cautions: never input personally identifiable information; avoid over-reliance; continuous teacher training needed. [2]
- **Pillar #3: Use AI to support personalized learning** — individualized experiences, special needs support (text-to-speech, speech recognition), intelligent tutoring systems, predictive analytics, automated feedback, adaptive platforms. Cautions: FERPA compliance, algorithmic bias, digital divide, screen time balance. [2]
- **Pillar #4: Develop students as ethical and proficient AI users** — ethics (data privacy, bias, transparency, academic integrity), brainstorming/outlining, critical media literacy, cross-disciplinary learning, student-led AI ethics committees. Cautions: cheating, deepfakes, hallucinations, data security. [2]
- Key quotes: "AI must become seen as a tool rather than the final product"; "AI is a partner, not a replacement for a teacher." Appendix includes an **Artificial Intelligence Literacy for Educators** framework and **Hess' Cognitive Rigor Matrix**. [2]

### 1.6 ILO Group District-Wide Framework

**ILO Group "Framework for Implementing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in K-12 Education Version 1.0"** divides guidance into: [3]
- **Part 1: District-Wide AI Areas of Consideration** across four pillars: [3]
  - **Political**: AI policy document with ethical guidelines; district-wide AI steering committee; systems for detecting/responding to fake AI incidents; proactive caregiver engagement; AI for community polls/surveys; legal consultation on caregiver consent. [3]
  - **Operational**: District-wide AI introductory training; equitable student access; AI purchasing sign-off and integration roadmap; revise digital literacy curriculum to include AI basics, ethics, safe online behaviors. [3]
  - **Technical**: Technology audit; third-party vendor contract review; AI-specific IT support and feedback loops; data-integrity checks; validation tests for predictive analytics. [3]
  - **Fiscal**: Specific AI budget (hardware, software, licensing, infrastructure, training, legal guidance, compliance); ROI analysis. [3]
- **Part 2: Department-Specific AI Applications** across eight departments: Curriculum & Instruction; Special Education (IEP writing support, accessibility tools); Student Support Services (predictive analytics for at-risk students, course advising); Family & Community Engagement (chatbots, translation); Enrollment; Human Resources; Facilities & Operations (predictive maintenance, transportation routing); Information & Technology Management. [3]
- **Risk Profiles** across five categories: Inaccurate Communication, Bias and Privacy, Technological and Operational, Educational and Pedagogical, Legal and Compliance. [3]
- Key guidance: "Given how rapidly AI is changing you may want to avoid complex policies that are difficult to refine as the technology evolves and focus on principles"; "Families are going to turn to their child's classroom teacher and school principal when they have questions or concerns about AI in the classroom." [3]

### 1.7 OECD Taxonomy: Three Modes of Human-AI Collaboration

The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 "introduces three modes of human-AI collaboration": [28]
- **Replacement**: "AI performs tasks traditionally requiring instructional judgment, risking erosion of teacher-student interaction and professional expertise." [28]
- **Complementarity**: "AI handles repetitive/administrative tasks while teachers retain responsibility for final decisions (reduces workload but doesn't reshape instructional judgment)." [28]
- **Augmentation**: "AI actively re-stimulates and extends teachers' professional judgment—teachers critically examine, revise, and recontextualise AI outputs within their instructional goals, prompting deeper reflection." [28]

### 1.8 State-Level Frameworks and Taxonomies (U.S.)

As of October 28, 2025, **34 states (plus Puerto Rico)** have issued official guidance or policy on AI use in K12 schools. [1] Highlights:
- **Alabama** (June 2024): AI Policy Template emphasizing human oversight, data privacy, and an AI Governance Committee. [1]
- **Alaska**: Framework addressing remote/rural connectivity challenges, cultural responsiveness, and digital equity. [1]
- **Arizona**: Human agency, AI literacy, ethical considerations (bias, misinformation, IP, data privacy, equitable access). [1]
- **California**: Integration with computer science standards and the "5 Big Ideas of AI" framework. [1]
- **Colorado**: Roadmap emphasizing local control, student voices, "If and How Checklist." [1]
- **Connecticut**: Instructional best practices, risks, policy considerations, social/emotional risks. [1]
- **Delaware**: SAMR model for AI integration with version tracking. [1]
- **Georgia** (January 2025): "Traffic Light" system (Red/Yellow/Green) for AI use, comprehensive evaluation rubric, June 2025 addendum on ethical principles. [1]
- **Hawaii**: Avoiding AI detection tools; citing AI use. [1]
- **Indiana**: AI literacy integrated with computer science. [1]
- **Kentucky**: "Policy-in-Action Spotlights," three paradigms for AI learning. [1]
- **Louisiana** (Fall 2024): Four-tiered approach (AI-Empowered, Enhanced, Assisted, Prohibited) aligned with SAMR. [1]
- **Maine**: "KEEP THE HUMAN IN AI" principle; "Maine DOE explicitly rejects technology prohibitions, stating that 'technology prohibitions prevent students from learning critical skills to function in today's technology-enriched society and do not prepare them for the reality they will face.'" [1]
- **Massachusetts**: Distinguishes teaching ABOUT vs. WITH AI; addresses three digital divides; "Explicit guidance against AI detection tools due to unreliability and punitive effects, recommending instead trust-based, transparency-focused approaches to academic integrity." [1]
- **Michigan**: Three-stage maturity framework (Investigating → Implementing → Innovating) across eight domains. [1]
- **Minnesota**: Centering people in decision-making; advancing equity. [1]
- **Missouri**: Prompt engineering "Five S" model; cyclical seven-step policy development process. [1]
- **Montana**: Rural-centered design with tribal sovereignty and Indigenous Education for All (IEFA) integration; biannual review cycles. [1]
- **Nevada**: STELLAR principles (Security, Transparency, Empowerment, Learning, Leadership, Achievement, Responsible Use) integrated with Personalized Competency-Based Learning. [1]
- **New Mexico** (May 2025): M.A.Z.E. framework (Monitor, Assess, Zero-in, Evaluate), five-level AI Assessment Scale, emphasis on digital equity. [1]
- **North Carolina**: Implementation roadmap based on AI for Education's work; CRAFT and EVERY frameworks. [1]
- **North Dakota**: Implementation roadmap and checklist with grade-level-specific considerations. [1]

### 1.9 Published Taxonomy Specific to AIGC in K-12 Classrooms

The **Frontiers in Education systematic review** (Alfarwan, September 23, 2025) analyzed 30 empirical papers on GenAI in K-12: most (19 of 30) published in 2024; high school students and pre-service teachers most represented; no studies on early childhood education; mathematics most common subject (5 papers) followed by physics (4); most studies from Taiwan and China (4 each), then US and Germany (3 each); no studies from Africa; **ChatGPT used in 21 of 30 papers**; quasi-experimental design most common (30%); measures primarily psychological (attitudes, self-efficacy, trust, motivation, critical thinking, self-regulated learning); "Nearly all the reviewed papers (90%) emphasize the need for teachers' professional development for AI-integrated classrooms." [4]

---

## 2. Teacher Training and Professional Development

### 2.1 ISTE Programs

**ISTE AI Explorations** (funded by General Motors for 6+ years; "served over 2,000 educators and education leaders in the US and internationally") is "an ISTE professional learning program... that cultivates future AI programmers and provides professional learning for educators to support student-driven AI explorations." Its Hands-On AI Projects for the Classroom guides (elementary, secondary, elective, CS educators) were revised January 2024; 5 free guides available in English, Spanish, and Arabic. A Dec 3, 2024 webinar "Using Gen AI to Understand Shakespeare" demonstrated students ethically leveraging GenAI to create a movie version of Macbeth. [12]

**ISTE AI Explorations for Educator Preparation Programs (EPPs) Fellowship** (announced June 25, 2023): "the first of its kind in higher education," an "eight-month learning and development opportunity designed to enhance faculty understanding of AI best practices in education." Seven fellows: Dr. Amy Eguchi (UC San Diego), Dr. Elizabeth Langran (Marymount University), Dr. J. Camille Dempsey (Pennsylvania Western University), Dr. Lucretia M. Fraga (University of the Incarnate Word), Dr. Nicol R. Howard (University of Redlands), Dr. Stacy George (University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa), Dr. Stein Brunvand (University of Michigan-Dearborn). ISTE CEO Richard Culatta: "This creation of this program reflects ISTE's commitment to support teacher education faculty in preparing future teachers to thrive in today's digital learning environments." [11]

**ISTE+ASCD "AI Deep Dive for Educators" course**: "a 15-hour, self-paced, instructor-led course that provides a complete introduction to artificial intelligence (AI) in education... No previous knowledge of AI or experience coding is required." Fees: $186 members / $249 non-members. Target audience: PK-12 teachers, instructional and curriculum designers, technology/instructional coaches, technology directors. "This course replaces the previous AI Explorations for Educators course with all new, updated content." Graduate credit available through Dominican University of California. [13]

**ISTE+ASCD broader AI offerings**: GenerationAI (coalition for K-12 AI education), AI Innovator program, Educator AI Community on Connect, **StretchAI ("the first AI coach specifically for educators")**, Google AI Educator Series for K-12 and Higher Ed, **"Profile of an AI-Ready Graduate"** (competencies students need in an AI-shaped world), downloadable AI lessons in English/Spanish/Arabic, free PDF guide for school leaders on safe/responsible AI use, and custom AI training for schools/districts/states. [14]

### 2.2 RAND National Survey Data on AI Teacher Training

**RAND report "More Districts Are Training Teachers on Artificial Intelligence"** (American School District Panel, published April 8, 2025; funded by Gates Foundation): [58]
- "In fall 2023, 23% of districts reported having provided AI training to teachers. By fall 2024, this rose to 48%—a 25-percentage-point increase. An additional 26% of districts planned AI training during 2024–2025, projecting that about three-quarters of districts will have provided AI training by fall 2025." [58]
- "As of fall 2024, 47 percent of teachers said that they had received at least some training on AI." Aligns with a federal survey of principals (December 2024) finding "59% of U.S. schools have trained some or all teachers on AI use." [58]
- **Poverty-based gap**: "By fall 2024, 67% of low-poverty districts had trained teachers on AI, compared with 42% of middle-poverty and 39% of high-poverty districts. Projections suggest almost all low-poverty districts will have trained teachers by the 2025–2026 school year, while only six in ten high-poverty districts will have done so." [58]
- **Interview findings** (14 district leaders): primary purpose was addressing teachers' concerns/confusion/fears; 13 of 14 encountered teachers with negative views; most focused on educator proficiency before student use; "virtually all were optional/opt-in; only one district ran mandatory training"; 11 of 14 took a DIY approach due to scarcity of external experts; half struggled to find qualified outside trainers. Resources used: state school board associations, Digital Promise, ISTE, Google, OpenAI. [58]
- **CGCS efforts**: Council of the Great City Schools developed the **K-12 Gen AI Maturity Tool** and **K-12 Gen AI Readiness Checklist** (with CoSN, funded by AWS grant) assessing readiness across six domains: Leadership, Operational, Data, Technical, Security, and Legal Risk. [58]
- **Implications**: training should start with trust-building and AI fundamentals, include hands-on low-stakes learning and peer structures; high-poverty districts need targeted support and funding. [58]

### 2.3 Gallup / Walton Family Foundation Survey

**Gallup and Walton Family Foundation survey** (June 25, 2025): [55]
- "Teachers who use AI weekly save an average of **5.9 hours per week** (equivalent to six extra weeks per school year)." [55]
- "During the 2024-25 school year, 60% of teachers reported using an AI tool, with usage highest among high school teachers (66%) and early-career educators (69%)." [55]
- "64% report better quality in materials modified to meet student needs, 61% generate higher-quality insights on student learning data, and 57% say AI improves grading and student feedback quality." [55]
- "40% of teachers favor AI versus 28% opposing it." [55]
- "Most teachers (68%) received no formal AI training from their school or district, with teachers more likely to self-teach (52%) than receive school training (31%)." [55]
- "Teachers in schools with AI policies save 26% more time per week, yet only 19% work at schools with an AI policy." [55]
- AI users see strong potential for real-time student feedback (62%), more engaging materials (58%), and improved accessibility for students with disabilities (57%; rising to 65% among special education teachers). [55]

### 2.4 Preservice Teacher Training Evidence

The JOTSE study (Antonio, 2025) demonstrated that a **14-week AI-focused pedagogical course** significantly improved preservice science teachers' AI-TPACK (large effect size, z = -6.900, p < .001, r = 0.76), identifying affordances (enhanced pedagogical design, improved AI literacy, increased student engagement) and constraints (tool limitations, ethical dilemmas, contextual barriers). "The study contributes empirical evidence and pedagogical insights for advancing AI integration in pre- and in-service teacher training, reinforcing the need for intentional design, policy alignment, and continued research on equitable and context-sensitive AI adaption." [18]

### 2.5 Professional Development Models and Approaches

**Edutopia four-pronged approach** (Lockhart, July 8, 2024), using SAMR as guiding model: (1) Creating an AI professional learning community (PLC) supported through Google Spaces; (2) Facilitating PD sessions and creating interactive posters exposing teachers to tools like Eduaide and MagicSchool; (3) Highlighting teacher leaders who experimented with tools like Diffit; (4) Digital communication strategies including a newsletter ("AI in the Humanities") and hallway conversations. Emphasizes evaluating tools for privacy issues (FERPA, COPPA) and alignment with school mission. Success story: a new teacher used MagicSchool's student chatbots for research paper feedback and student-composed AI disclosure statements. [44]

**MobileMind "6 Risks of Neglecting AI Professional Development"**: (1) Inadequate foundational understanding; (2) K-12 implications (age-appropriate tools, alignment with instructional goals); (3) Data privacy and confidentiality (free third-party apps collecting student data); (4) Data-driven decision making (misinterpreting AI insights); (5) AI integration strategies (need concrete use cases); (6) Duty to students (preparing them for careers that don't yet exist). Notes "AI is feared by many educators due to the current lack of understanding regarding what AI even is and how it will impact them in their roles." [57]

**Fordham Institute / Rivet Education** (Morrison, Nov 14, 2023): "We spend nearly $18 billion a year on professional learning in this country, yet... only one in three teachers find the professional learning they receive to be useful. That means nearly $11 billion spent on professional learning is wasted; this is equivalent to giving every teacher in the U.S. a stipend of $3,000." Proposes using AI to review training materials and live training transcripts; notes Rivet's PLPG evaluation process takes "upwards of 500 hours per review cycle." [56]

**UNESCO G77+China project**: five organized seminars to provide resources and knowledge exchange on digital/AI competencies for educators and students in G77+China countries, "a particularly urgent need in the 134 countries of the Group of 77 and China." [9]

### 2.6 Required Teacher Competencies and Skills

The SREB appendix **"Artificial Intelligence Literacy for Educators"** framework outlines skills and aptitudes for teachers and school/district leaders. [2] The UNESCO Teacher framework defines 15 competencies across 5 dimensions (see §1.1). [10] Panorama notes teachers need "a working understanding of how AI generates answers, where it may be inaccurate, and how bias or hallucinations can appear," and that "Studies show that teachers' AI-TPACK competencies are still below average, largely because AI is new and fast-moving." [20] 48% of teachers now use AI tools weekly. [20]

OECD teacher preparation implications: "Teacher preparation must cultivate pedagogical judgment—helping preservice teachers recognize when AI use undermines learning and develop professional criteria for adjusting those patterns. Teachers are framed not as managers permitting/prohibiting AI use, but as professional decision-makers guiding students to use AI as a tool to support thinking." [28]

## 3. Infrastructure Requirements

### 3.1 AI Readiness and Network Infrastructure

**CoSN 2025 State of EdTech District Leadership Report** (12th annual survey, released May 6, 2025, with AASA, CDW Education, Lightspeed Systems, MCH Strategic Data, Sogolytics): [47]
- A 2025 CoSN report found **only 16 percent of K-12 schools were fully ready for AI**, and **61 percent had dirty and/or siloed data not operationalizable by AI**. [46][47]
- "94% of EdTech leaders see AI as having a positive impact, with productivity as the top benefit. Gen AI is the top technology priority (80% of districts have initiatives), and only 1% of districts have completely banned it. 57% of districts use or are exploring AI-detection tools for student work." [47]
- "If the Supreme Court rules the E-Rate program's structure is unconstitutional, the impact will be major or catastrophic for 74% of districts, affecting students in all settings — rural, town, suburban and urban" — with 48% of city districts describing it as catastrophic. "Only 7% of districts report all students have adequate home bandwidth. Off-campus broadband support has dropped from 74% in 2023 to just 66%." [47]
- Cybersecurity: "61% of districts rely on general funds for cybersecurity (no dedicated funding), and 78% invest in monitoring, detection, and response. Phishing is the top threat (27% high risk), followed by data breaches and ransomware (13% each)." [47]
- Interoperability: "Approved app lists have grown from 42% (2023) to 59% adoption." [47]
- EdTech leader demographics: female respondents dropped to 29% (from 37% in 2024); professional backgrounds shifted from education (58% in 2015) to technology (52% in 2025); "61% of female respondents aged 50+ versus 52% of male respondents under 50." [47]

**GovTech infrastructure analysis** (May 11, 2026, by Julia Gilban-Cohen): District technology leaders report schools are NOT facing a sudden AI bandwidth crisis, but AI is "steadily transforming school network architecture, devices, cybersecurity, and budgets by accelerating existing pressures such as aging devices, cloud dependency, cybersecurity threats, and staffing shortages." [45]
- **Key infrastructure components** (per CoSN board member Tom Ryan): foundational systems, policies, protocols and facilities; wireless connectivity capable of handling "microbursts" ("when everybody turns the computer on in the morning, you get these microbursts that shoot way up beyond your capacity"); guardrails for privacy, security, and legal compliance before wide-scale deployment. [45]
- **Hardware**: Jason Neiffer (Montana Digital Academy) noted that if AI workloads shift from cloud back to local devices, districts will save cloud costs but need "more girthy hardware," questioning the longevity of low-cost devices like **Chromebooks with only 2-4 GB of RAM** that provide poor user experiences. [45]
- **Bandwidth**: No major AI-specific bandwidth crises yet, but "however much bandwidth you have today, you will need 200 percent more in five years." [45]
- **Funding**: Kris Hagel (CIO, Peninsula School District, WA): "there's nowhere near enough funding in K-12 education," with many districts facing bankruptcy-level conditions. "The federal E-rate program covers broadband subsidies but not AI operational costs. Districts increasingly pay 'per-token costs' to providers like AWS or Microsoft Azure." [45]
- **"Human bandwidth"**: staff needed to triage AI-flagged student safety/mental health interactions. [45]
- **Rural disparities**: In remote areas like the Navajo Nation or southeast New Mexico, "there's not available bandwidth in the community"—some communities lack basic electricity. Rural Montana districts struggle with bandwidth and lack internal tech departments or full-time CIOs. [45]

**CoSN "Driving K-12 Innovation" 2025 report** (Feb 2025): Hurdles = attracting/retaining educators and IT professionals (4th consecutive year), evolution of teaching and learning, digital equity (digital foundations, conditions for learning, meaningful learning opportunities). Accelerators = learner agency, building human capacity of leaders, changing attitudes toward demonstrating learning. Tech Enablers = **generative AI (top tech enabler for 2025, a "transformative force")**, analytics and adaptive technologies, untethered broadband and connectivity. [49]

### 3.2 Global Equity and the Digital Divide

**World Bank data**: [63][67]
- "As of 2025, over 2 billion people (about a quarter of the world's population) remained offline; internet use ranges from over 90% in high-income countries to just 23% in low-income countries." [67]
- "Visits to ChatGPT per internet user is 50 times greater in high-income countries than in low-income countries, as of May 2025." [63]
- "In low-income countries, a data-only 5GB mobile package would take up nearly half of a household's remaining budget after food consumption." [63]
- "5% of the population of low-income countries had basic digital skills in 2023." [63]
- "As of late 2022, only 11 countries (mostly high-income) had officially endorsed K-12 AI curricula." [64]
- "Up to 94% of teachers in parts of Africa report insufficient STEM materials and infrastructure." [64]

**World Bank approach to Digital Technologies in Education**: "AI presents a unique opportunity: If supported by foundational digital skills and connectivity, AI could help address the global learning crisis—particularly in communities with teacher shortages and high dropout rates." As of 2025, over 94% of World Bank education projects include an EdTech component. The **Global EdTech Readiness Index (ETRI)** evaluates countries across six pillars: school management, teachers, students, devices, connectivity, and digital resources. [65]

**World Bank "small AI" concept**: "Countries don't need to wait for large, complex AI systems. Many are adopting 'small AI' approaches—nimble, targeted tools that support frontline health workers with decision support, help teachers personalize learning... These offer a steppingstone toward more advanced AI-enabled transformation by building capacity, trust, and responsible data use." [67]

**LAC region** (World Bank): PISA 2022 shows only 66% of students in Latin America/Caribbean attended schools with effective online learning platforms; only 3 in 10 students attended schools whose teachers received incentives to integrate technology. [66]

**Developing countries STEM paper** (Discover Education, April 9, 2026): AI applications in developing-country biology/STEM education include virtual labs and simulations, AI tutors (e.g., ADvLEARN in South Africa; uLesson in Nigeria which works offline via SD cards), enhanced data analysis, and language translation/inclusive tools (including Kenyan Sign Language translation and text-to-speech for visually impaired learners). Country examples: China piloted AI courses in 40 high schools in 2018; South Korea integrated AI into high school curriculum in 2021; the UK announced a £187 million program in 2025; India introduced AI as optional secondary subject in 2019; UAE made AI education compulsory from kindergarten; RobotsMali produced 180+ culturally relevant children's books in Bambara within a year. Conclusion: "AI is not a panacea but can serve as a 'force multiplier' when deployed thoughtfully within existing educational ecosystems" and "Ensuring that students in developing countries are not left behind in the AI era is not only a practical necessity but a moral imperative." [64]

### 3.3 Cost Analysis

- **AI agent development costs**: "typically ranges from $50,000-$250,000+, with ongoing run costs of $4,000–$25,000+ per month depending on scale, complexity, and governance requirements." [20]

- **Khanmigo**: free to all U.S. K-12 teachers via Microsoft partnership (late 2024); serves 400,000+ educators across 50+ countries. [34][20]
- **BrainFreeze pricing**: "completely free for individual teachers and just $0.50 per user per month at the district level." [74]
- **PL cost context**: $18B/year spent on professional learning in the U.S., ~$11B considered wasted. [56]
- **AI TA economics** (higher ed example): "$3,200/semester vs. $40,000 for human TAs (92% savings)." [21]
