**E.2. EEF Teacher Choices Trial – ChatGPT for KS3 Science Lesson Preparation**

- The Education Endowment Foundation (EEF), co-funded by the Hg Foundation and independently evaluated by NFER, conducted a randomized controlled trial involving 259 teachers of Year 7 and/or Year 8 science from 68 state-funded secondary schools in England during the 2024 summer term. Teachers used ChatGPT (supported by an online guide at teachingwithchatgpt.org.uk) for approximately 10 weeks, recording their lesson planning time weekly in an online diary [28][29][30].
- Teachers in the ChatGPT group saved approximately 25 minutes per week on average (56.2 minutes vs. 81.5 minutes for the comparison group), a 31% reduction in lesson planning time compared to the non-GenAI group, with a high security rating. The time saving increased for teachers who used ChatGPT more frequently and scored highly on a knowledge quiz about effective use [28][29][30].
- There was no difference in the quality of resources produced between groups, based on a blind review by a panel of five science teachers (three experienced teachers with over 20 years of teaching and management responsibilities, and two earlier-career teachers). Lessons were scored out of five in four areas: clarity of lesson resources; activities engaging students with learning and checking understanding; appropriateness for age and ability; and quality and accuracy of science content [28][29][30].
- Three-quarters of the ChatGPT group reported a positive impact on their teaching, and 78% said they would continue using ChatGPT for lesson preparation in the future, though typically only for some lessons. During the trial, the proportion of ChatGPT teachers who felt they spent 'too much time' on lesson preparation dropped from 49% to 26% [28][29][30].
- Common uses of ChatGPT included generating ideas for teaching and quizzes, tailoring lessons for different classes, and adapting existing resources for cover lessons. Teachers who were more confident with technology and those less confident in their subject matter saved more time, though the latter need to check AI outputs for accuracy [28].
- Limitations: privacy concerns (data entered into ChatGPT may be used to train models, so personal details should not be entered), limitations in image generation, and the need for all outputs to be checked for accuracy due to potential hallucination. Schools in the trial had a slight over-representation from London, the South East, and Outstanding Ofsted ratings, with free school meal eligibility close to the national average [28][29].
- EEF research into ChatGPT use found a potential 31 percent reduction in lesson planning time for users, while also highlighting the need for more research on using AI to support teachers without lowering quality [25].
- The guide was designed by Bain & Company's Social Impact practice with input from schools and education charities, and funded by The Hg Foundation. Most teachers in the ChatGPT group were positive about the guide, agreeing it was easy to understand and relevant [30].
- Trial registry details (ISRCTN13420346): Sponsor: National Foundation for Educational Research; Funders: Education Endowment Foundation and Hg Foundation. Study period: December 2023 to July 2024; Completion date: 31/07/2024. Target sample size at registration: 174; total final enrolment: 258. The primary outcome was total hours spent in lesson/resource preparation over the second five-week period. Secondary outcomes included preparation time in the first five-week period, quality of lesson materials (rated by an independent teacher panel), proportion of lessons using ChatGPT, and guide consultation rates. Eligibility: Any English state secondary school with at least one Year 7/8 science teacher completing the baseline survey. Teachers included non-specialists and Early Career Teachers [30].

**E.3. UK Government Policy and Initiatives**

- The UK Government's Education Hub blog post (June 2025) explains: Teachers are permitted to use AI for lesson planning, creating resources, marking work, giving feedback, and administrative tasks. However, they must apply professional judgement and verify AI output for accuracy—final responsibility rests with teachers and their institutions. Schools can set their own rules subject to data protection, child safety, and intellectual property legal requirements [27].
- "Teachers are irreplaceable, and AI could never be a substitute for teachers' professional judgement and the personal relationships they have with their students." The government states emphatically that teachers will NOT be replaced by AI [27].
- Schools decide whether students can use AI, but must implement safeguards including close supervision, safety and filtering features, and age restrictions (many tools are 18+). Schools must consider effects on learning and update homework policies [27].
- Government initiatives: Launched the AI Tools for Education competition (August 2024) with £1 million in Innovate UK funding awarded to 16 innovators, plus an additional £1 million to accelerate development; Created a content store: a £3 million data library funded by the Department for Science and Technology providing high-quality educational information (curriculums, mark schemes) for AI models; Invested up to £2 million in Oak National Academy, which launched the AI-powered lesson assistant "Aila"—teachers report saving 3-4 hours per week in lesson planning; Developed training and guidance packages for teachers and school leaders on safe AI use [27].
- Digital connectivity: Investing £45 million to enhance digital connectivity in schools, including £25 million for wireless network improvements and £20 million for fibre upgrades. A consultation was launched on a long-term strategy for narrowing the digital divide and establishing new digital and technology standards [27].

**F. FINLAND CASE STUDIES**

**F.1. Generation AI Research Programme (University of Eastern Finland, University of Helsinki, University of Oulu, Code School Finland)**

- Finland's Generation AI research programme has been named Europe's best AI literacy initiative for education, winning in the Digital Skills for Education category (90 entries) out of 220 total competition entries. The project is a multidisciplinary, multi-university research programme funded by the Strategic Research Council (SRC) within the Research Council of Finland [28].
- The programme develops research-based educational technologies, learning materials, and learning packages to strengthen AI literacy among children and young people, helping them understand AI operating principles and critically assess ethical and societal impacts. The tools allow pupils to build classifiers or their own language models, examine social media algorithms, and investigate algorithmic bias without needing programming skills [28].
- Key tools developed include the Generation AI Teachable Machine, Social Media Machine, Breaking Machine, and Small Language Machine. The solutions prioritize data protection, safety, and children's rights—tools run locally in browsers, do not track users, comply with GDPR, and do not transfer data outside the classroom [28].
- The tools have been used more than 200,000 times in over 50 countries and have been introduced internationally across Asia, Europe, Egypt, and Mexico. The Generation AI community also won the 2025 national Open Educational Resource of the Year award and received awards at IEEE ICALT 2024, ACM Koli Calling 2025, and AACE EdMedia 2025 and 2026 conferences [28].
- Principal investigator Professor Matti Tedre of the University of Eastern Finland: "We want to help children and young people understand how AI systems work and how they affect, for example, what they see online, how they are profiled and the ways in which decisions concerning them are made." University Researcher Henriikka Vartiainen: "We have also worked closely with teachers and pupils to ensure that the tools and materials we produce genuinely serve the needs of teaching and learning." Professor Teemu Roos of the University of Helsinki: "Especially at a time like this, when our sense of control is disappearing and the AI narrative emphasises the claim that there are no alternatives, it is important to support young people's own thinking and agency, meaning their opportunity to shape technology in ways that reflect who they are." University Lecturer Milka Sormunen: "From the perspective of children's rights, it is essential that children understand how AI systems work and that learning involves children as active participants." Head of Pedagogy Jussi Koivisto of Code School Finland: "The tools and learning materials have been praised specifically for promoting AI literacy and critical thinking" [28].
- Key collaborators include Henriikka Vartiainen, Kati Mäkitalo, Teemu Roos, Milka Sormunen, Jari Laru, and Jussi Koivisto [28].

**F.2. Finnish National AI in Education Guidelines**

- The Finnish National Agency for Education and the Ministry of Education and Culture published "Artificial intelligence in education – legislation and recommendations" in 2025 (in Finnish, Swedish, and English). The material was developed collaboratively with education sector professionals, researchers, and experts. It supports early childhood education, general education, and vocational education and training providers in utilizing AI while promoting responsible, safe, and innovative use. The document consists of two parts: obligations and recommendations, plus supporting background materials. It is part of the implementation of Finland's Digital Compass [28].
- The background material section covers: what is artificial intelligence, AI bias and misinterpretation, the Artificial Intelligence Act, data protection and privacy, copyright in the educational use and development of AI, the potential of AI in supporting teaching and studying, AI in the assessment of learning and competence, AI literacy, AI and sustainable development, and ethical principles [28].
- Implementation support materials include a video series (published under CC BY-NC-ND license) and an extensive PowerPoint slide deck resource bank (published under CC BY-SA 4.0 license) [28].
- According to CEDEFOP, the Ministry of Education and Culture and the Finnish National Agency for Education (EDUFI) prepared the AI guidelines in collaboration with education providers, scholars and experts, drawing on existing work such as UNESCO's AI competency framework for teachers and the EU's Digital Education Action Plan. In spring 2024, preparation began with webinars and discussion forums. In March 2025, national recommendations were published. The initiative spans 2024 (Design phase) to 2025 (Completed) [28].
- The comparative study in the Journal of Science and Technology Policy Management (Kundu A and Bej T, 2025) found Finland and Singapore demonstrate strong ethical and human-centered policies, while China and the USA lean toward innovation and workforce development. Implementation remains challenged by equity gaps, teacher readiness, and contextual mismatches [28].

**F.3. Finnish Teacher and Student AI Use Data**

- A Nordic survey ("Generative AI, education and copyright – A Nordic joint survey," conducted in March 2025 by Kantar) found that in Finland, 62% of teachers (pre-school to university) have at least some knowledge of AI tools. About 8% of Finnish teachers use AI tools daily or weekly to produce teaching content, while 42% have never used them. 6% of Finnish teachers use AI to produce videos/music at least a few times a month (double the rate in other Nordic countries). 58% of Finnish teachers believe they will use AI more within a year, while only 2% expect to use it less [40].
- Thirty percent of Finnish teachers believe at least half of published material will be replaced by AI-generated material in the future. Between 15–33% of Finnish teachers had uploaded material created by others into AI tools in the past month. Around 68% of Finnish teachers (vs. 61% in other Nordic countries) believe creative professionals should be compensated for use of their work to train AI [40].
- Finnish teachers rated student AI use lower than their Nordic counterparts: 53% of primary/lower secondary teachers in Finland reported no students regularly using AI for learning (vs. 41% in Norway). 43% of Finnish teachers believe AI will have a negative impact on students' education, while just under 18% see it as positive [40].
- Kirsi Salmela, Director of Legal Affairs and Research at Kopiosto: "Finland needs to wake up to the expanding use of AI in education and ensure that copyright is protected also in the era of AI. This is an important message to both policymakers and education providers. The survey shows that the Nordic countries are on the threshold of a new era of education" [40].
- A CNA "Asia First" interview (November 28, 2025) with Finland's Minister of Education Anders Adlercreutz: Finland is the most media literate country in Europe, with media literacy part of the national school curriculum from primary through secondary school, with early exposure for preschoolers through experimentation and play. Nearly 2/3 of Finnish teachers have some knowledge of AI tools, 8% use them regularly for teaching, nearly half never use them, but the majority believe they will use AI more soon. Finland issued general ethical guidelines for teachers' use of AI in early childhood, primary, and secondary education. The school system is highly decentralized, with significant teacher autonomy. All teachers hold master's degrees [28].
- Adlercreutz emphasized AI literacy as a central democratic skill, particularly given Russian hybrid pressure and disinformation campaigns. Media literacy teaching has been done since the 1990s; it evolves from exposure and analysis in early childhood to students learning to question sources, and even high school students setting up troll farms to understand how easily people are swayed. On regulation, Adlercreutz noted technical difficulties in regulating digital access, calling for greater accountability and transparency from platform providers. Education budget: Ministry of Education has the second biggest budget in government (after healthcare), but schools are run by municipalities. Finland-Singapore collaboration: Adlercreutz was the fifth Finnish minister to visit Singapore this year; areas of collaboration include AI, technology use, teacher training, and student exchanges [28].
- OECD data shows Asia-Pacific teachers dominate AI use: Singapore leads with UAE (75% of teachers), followed by New Zealand and Australia [28].

**G. GERMANY**

**G.1. Policy and Market Context**

- In October 2024, the Conference of the Ministers of Education of the Länder (Bildungsministerkonferenz) in Germany adopted a "Recommendation for action for the education administration on the use of artificial intelligence in school education processes" ("Handlungsempfehlung für die Bildungsverwaltung zum Umgang mit Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) in schulischen Bildungsprozessen"). The recommendation covers five key topics: 1) Influence of AI on learning and didactics: AI applications should support teachers and create a personalised learning environment addressing individual student needs; 2) Changing the examination culture: Adapting examination formats to account for AI skills and making performance assessment transparent and fair; 3) Professionalisation of teachers: Teacher training and professional development should systematically integrate AI use; 4) Regulation and legal framework: Clear legal requirements to protect students' personal rights while promoting AI use in schools; 5) Equal opportunities: All learners should develop AI skills [27].
- The recommendation builds on the 2021 supplementary recommendation "Teaching and Learning in the Digital World" and the 2016 strategy "Education in the Digital World," as well as a 2024 impulse paper on Large Language Models and their potential in the education system from the Standing Scientific Commission [27].
- Approximately 29% of German schools and universities have integrated AI for personalized learning, administrative automation, and student performance analytics (IU, 2023). Germany has made substantial government investments: the ~$6 billion "DigitalPakt Schule" initiative (2019-2024), followed by "DigitalPakt 2.0" (running until 2030 with ~$5.86 billion planned investment over five years), and Germany's AI Strategy (backed by ~$3.3 billion through 2025). The Federal Government plans to allocate a total of five billion euros by 2025 to support the AI strategy implementation (BMBF, 2023) [27].
- The EU AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024, and becomes fully applicable in August 2026; many education AI applications are expected to fall under its "high-risk" category. AI systems in education must comply with GDPR and the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG) [27].
- Key challenges include data privacy concerns, lack of AI expertise among teachers, and digital infrastructure gaps in rural areas. In the JRC exploratory study, Germany had guidelines in 7 of 16 federal states [27][31].
- German institutions at the forefront include the Technical University of Munich, RWTH Aachen University, German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI), and University of Freiburg (investing ~EUR 600,000 in AI teaching projects) [27].
- A CHE Centre for Higher Education study (survey of 23,288 students at 171 German and Austrian universities, winter semester 2024/25) found 25% of students use AI tools (like ChatGPT) daily, and an additional 40% use them at least weekly. Only 1 in 16 students report never using AI in their studies. AI usage frequency varies by subject — over 75% of mechatronics students use AI regularly, while only about half of Civil and Environmental Engineering students do. AI is most commonly used as a "sparring partner" for general research and brainstorming, while about a third of students have never used AI for text generation (ghostwriting). Students rate existing university programs for acquiring AI skills at only 2.7 out of 5 stars [28].
- Study authors recommend anchoring AI skills in curricula and integrating AI use into scientific methodology. The study, "DatenCHECK – Künstliche Intelligenz im Studium," was authored by Marc Hüsch and Nina Horstmann (CHE) and Andreas Breiter (University of Bremen) [28].

**H. FRANCE**

**H.1. Lalilo (Adaptive Reading Platform)**

- Lalilo (France) is an adaptive reading platform for primary school that adjusts phonics and comprehension exercises based on student performance. Teachers receive dashboards to monitor progress. A 2023 experimental study found significant reading fluency improvements, especially for students needing the most support [28].
- Lalilo was identified as one of the best practices in the European Commission study "Good Practice in AI for Education: Spotlight on EU Case Studies and Insights" (commissioned by the Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture, DG EAC), which identified 209 practices using AI ethically in education (through document reviews, surveys, and interviews conducted between January and October 2025), and selected 14 for in-depth analysis [28].

**H.2. French National AI in Education Framework and Policy**

- The IGESR Report on AI in Schools (May 2025) (General Inspectorate for Education, Sport and Research) identified "areas for rapid action" (the word "rapid" appears 35 times). Key findings: Lack of training is a major obstacle across all stakeholders (students, teachers, managers); AI governance remains "too scattered" with duplication between central administration and local actors; Recommendations include massive training plans for managers, face-to-face teacher training, an AI training curriculum for students, and better coordination bodies; Questions remain about sustainable business models for EdTech tools and sovereign AI tools [29].
- The AI in Education Framework (published June 14, 2025, by the Ministry of Education following consultation from January to May 2025): AI must support (not replace) learning and be supervised by teachers; First-grade students learn about AI basics but don't directly use generative AI; Teachers cannot have students manipulate generative AI before 4th grade (CM1); Use of AI to complete school assignments without teacher authorization and personal work constitutes fraud; AI use must comply with RGPD, SREN law, and European AI regulation [29].
- Critics warn that the framework "appears helpless" against students using AI to offload work. The Education Numérique Raisonnée collective argues that relying on AI-generated results threatens creativity and requires critical thinking skills students haven't developed [29].
- Digital use supervision measures: Minister Élisabeth Borne's back-to-school circular (2025) mandates generalization of "Portable en pause" (laptop on break) system in middle schools; Digital workspaces and school life software updates suspended from 8pm-7am on weekdays and weekends. However, only 8.5% of secondary schools actually implemented the "Portable en pause" scheme two weeks after classes resumed; 67% of school heads do not intend to apply it (SNPDEN-UNSA survey) [29].
- The Cour des Comptes Report on Primary Education (2025) found "numerous shortcomings" in digital deployment in primary education, noting €115 million in France Relance funding and €200 million for "Territoires numériques éducatifs" failed to produce a coherent strategy. Calls for equipment more closely geared to educational needs and better teacher training [29].
- A group of 60 researchers and professionals called for promoting "graduated education in and through digital technology," arguing schools are not "hyper-digitized" and that digital content can support learning, especially for students with special needs [29].

**I. SPAIN**

- Spain's 2025 AI-in-education drive pairs €1.5B (plus €600M previously mobilized) strategy funding with concrete education measures. Key investments include a €90M MareNostrum supercomputer upgrade, the ALIA language model (designed to include >20% Spanish and co-official language data vs. under 5% in many current models), €160M for scholarships/training/talent, €300M Kit Consulting, and €350M Digital Kit expansion. The strategy has three axes: capacity (supercomputing/models), practical adoption (Kit Consulting, Digital Kit), and ethics/oversight via AESIA [44].
- Legal Framework (Royal Decree 69/2025, published February 2025): Rewrites Spain's vocational training playbook by creating state digital registers, adding a new AI & data VET sector branch (total 27 branches), and standardizing modular catalogues aligned with EU levels. The broader package includes over €6.5 billion investment and 376,000 new VET places [44].
- Key Statistics (2024-25): AI has attracted over €2 billion investment since 2020; the digital economy reached 26% of GDP (€414 billion) in 2024; a government-funded AI math platform reportedly helped 85% of users improve final math grades [44].
- Practical classroom uses per the Ministry's Guide on Use of AI in Education: personalized learning pathways, virtual assistants for real-time Q&A, and automated routine assessment. Pilots include University of Alicante's "Help Me See" app (computer vision for visually impaired students) and VAMOS Academy's adaptive language learning [44].
- Teacher training: INTEF provides ethics decalogue and practical classroom examples; the School of Computational Thinking and AI (EPCIA, 2018-2022) ran modular courses (unplugged, Scratch, Python, AI, robotics) reaching ~884 teachers in one cohort and ~900 teachers/17,000 students across editions. Digital Competence Framework (2022), SELFIE, and Procomún OER support progression [44].
- Ethics and privacy: Spain's draft law bans hidden manipulative techniques, exploitative targeting of vulnerable groups, discriminatory classifications, and social scoring, treating some school uses as high-risk. AEPD has clarified authority to enforce the EU AI Act with DPIA templates and privacy-by-design toolkits [44].
- Around 35% of Spanish secondary teachers report using AI in their work. Among non-users, three out of four cite lack of training as the main reason [43].
- At EMINENT 2025 (held in Madrid, Spain on 11-12 December 2025, organized by European Schoolnet in collaboration with Spain's Ministry of Education, Vocational Training and Sports, supported by EU-funded projects Agile EDU and EmpowerED), Mónica Domínguez García (Spain) stated "AI should strengthen public education, not replace it," highlighting Spain's investment in critical digital literacy and teacher training [38].
- The International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research published a study on AI use by undergraduate students of Social Education in Spain and Portugal (Martínez-Carrera, Educ. Sci. 2025, 15, 390, cited by 11) [44].

**J. NORDIC COUNTRIES (SWEDEN, NORWAY, DENMARK, ICELAND)**

**J.1. Google Partnerships in Nordic Classrooms**

- Google is partnering with Nordic school districts in Iceland, Norway, and Sweden to transform classrooms through responsible AI adoption [42].
- Iceland: Building on widespread Google Classroom adoption, Google partnered with the Ministry of Education to launch a pilot with 300 teachers. By integrating Gemini for Education and NotebookLM, the program aims to enhance personalized learning, boost AI literacy, identify resources for ethical AI use, upskill teachers in administrative tasks, and pinpoint student learning gaps [42].
- Sweden: Through partnerships with school districts, Google brought Gemini for Education to nearly 30,000 students and faculty. Teachers use Gemini to create tailored, high-quality materials, which educators describe as "revolutionary." Districts hosted workshops to empower educators and foster dialogue with older students about using Guided Learning mode as a study aid, emphasizing that AI literacy is a shared responsibility. According to Johan Kellén, teacher & ICT Coordinator at Linköping Municipality, "it takes so long to produce good teaching material — you usually have to construct it yourself and ensure it is up to date and current, and adapted to each class and sometimes each student. This is where Gemini is able to help" [42].
- Norway: Norway completed a national Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) that greenlighted the use of Google Workspace for Education and ChromeOS in schools. This was a collaborative effort between Google Cloud and the Norwegian Association of Local and Regional Authorities (KS). By conducting a centrally driven DPIA, KS eliminated the need for every municipality to conduct complex assessments individually, demonstrating that Google tools meet stringent GDPR requirements and freeing local resources for innovation rather than administrative compliance [42].

**J.2. GAIYA Project (NordForsk)**

- The GAIYA project (Generative AI in Education for Young Adults: A Gender-Inclusive Nordic-Baltic Perspective) is a NordForsk-funded project running from 2026 to 2030. The project investigates how students and teachers in Denmark, Sweden, and Norway use generative AI (G-AI) tools, focusing on digital literacy and gender equality, particularly in majority language subjects (Danish, Swedish, Norwegian). It also examines media and AI literacy policies across five countries: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia [42].
- GAIYA addresses two key challenges: the rapid integration of AI in upper secondary education and a persistent gender adoption gap where female students engage less with G-AI than male peers, which risks reinforcing digital inequalities. The project emphasizes playful learning, digital pedagogy, and inclusive design [42].
- Data is gathered through focus groups, interviews, surveys, and policy analysis. Long-term goals include influencing educational policy, providing open-access resources, and establishing a Nordic-Baltic think tank on G-AI in education. Contact persons are Bodil Aurstad and Mathias Hamberg [42].

**J.3. Swedish Physics Lab Study (University of Gothenburg)**

- A research article published in Physical Review Physics Education Research (Vol. 21, 020119, August 27, 2025) titled "Generative AI as a lab partner: A case study" by Sebastian Kilde-Westberg, Andreas Johansson, and Jonas Enger (Department of Physics, University of Gothenburg, Sweden) examines how high school students use ChatGPT during a physics laboratory session (acoustic levitation and the speed of sound in air). It uses variation theory as a theoretical lens [45].
- Key findings: The study demonstrates various ways high school students use ChatGPT during lab work. Although generative AI tools can handle some relevant questions and problems during laboratory work, the teacher still plays a crucial role in identifying students' needs and capabilities for understanding the potential and limitations of generative AI. Students need support and training to efficiently utilize generative AI to further their physics learning [45].
- The complete chat histories of each student group with ChatGPT during the lab sessions are provided as Supplemental Material. Received December 18, 2024; Accepted August 8, 2025; Published August 27, 2025. Cited by 8 subsequent articles [45].

**J.4. Nordic Youth AI Use**

- The "Nordic Media Literacy Survey" found relatively equal AI usage across Nordic countries, though Finns and Icelanders are more likely to test AI technology, while Swedes, Norwegians, and Danes use it more for assignment writing. There is significant concern across the Nordics that AI is developing too fast and that its consequences are difficult to anticipate. Many worry AI will make it harder to distinguish real from false information. Overall, there is limited trust that AI provides accurate and reliable information or contributes positively to democracy, with more scepticism in Sweden, Finland, and particularly Iceland [41].
- Anders Adlercreutz, Finland's Minister of Education and Nordic Cooperation: "Media literacy is an important part of the Nordic countries' resilience. By educating both children and adults to be source critical and by giving them tools to detect attempts at influence and fake news, we strengthen our resilience and our democracy" [41].

- DigiHavel was identified as one of the best practices in the European Commission study "Good Practice in AI for Education." "DigiHavel is a modern deductive tool for civic education teachers. It's actually an application based on artificial intelligence. You can..." [28][46].

**M. ITALY**

- An Italian pilot involves virtual assistants providing personalized feedback in STEM subjects and Italian language learning in secondary/vocational schools. Emphasized teacher training. **N. NETHERLANDS**

- NOLAI Laboratory (Netherlands) develops AI projects based on teacher-identified problems rather than tech company ideas. **O. EUROPEAN UNION POLICY AND FRAMEWORKS**

- The JRC exploratory study (2025) examined the use and perceptions of generative AI (GenAI) in secondary education among early adopters across five EU Member States: Ireland, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, and Spain. Based on qualitative interviews and focus groups with 121 participants (policymakers, teacher educators, school leaders, teachers, and students), conducted during 2024 and co-funded by the JRC and DG EAC [31].
- Key findings from the JRC study: Educators and students saw GenAI as a tool to enhance learning, but raised concerns about academic integrity, bias, and over-reliance on the technology. The importance of human agency was highlighted. Critical reactions focused on data protection, algorithmic biases, critical thinking development, and academic dishonesty, while broader concerns (environmental impact, copyright issues, digital sovereignty) were largely overlooked. Policies and guidelines in education were largely regarded as insufficient at that time; teachers needed specialized support and training. GenAI was seen as a time-saver for teachers (simplifying concepts, personalizing feedback) but also required extra effort to use effectively and ethically. Students valued presential teaching, human interaction, and personal feedback, and worried that GenAI over-reliance could diminish these learning experiences. Educators used GenAI to generate lesson plans, design personalized learning, analyze student data, and design assessments; students may use GenAI more intensively than teachers [31].
- Policy context: The EU is shaping AI through the AI Act (in force August 2024), the AI Continent Action Plan, and the Apply AI Strategy. Key instruments include the Digital Education Action Plan 2021-2027, the Ethical Guidelines on AI in Teaching and Learning (updated guidelines expected early 2026), the AI Literacy Framework (AILit) developed with OECD, and DigComp 3.0. National actions varied: Finland published digitalization policies through 2027; Germany had guidelines in 7 of 16 federal states; Ireland updated its AI strategy and developed guidance; Luxembourg integrated AI into its Digital Decade Roadmap and updated its AI Strategy; Spain issued a Guide on AI Use in Education [31].
- The "Empowering Learners for the Age of AI: An AI Literacy Framework for Primary and Secondary Education" (AILit Framework) is a joint initiative of the European Commission and the OECD, approved by the PISA Governing Board on 8 April 2026, and contributing to the PISA 2029 Media & Artificial Intelligence (MAIL) Literacy assessment. It aligns with the European Commission's Digital Education Action Plan 2021-2027, the 2023 Council Recommendations on digital education, and the EU AI Act (whose Article 4 requires providers and deployers of AI systems to ensure adequate AI literacy) [39].
- The framework defines AI literacy as "the technical knowledge, durable skills and future-ready attitudes required to thrive in a world influenced by AI. It enables learners to engage, create with, manage and shape AI, while critically evaluating its benefits, risks and ethical implications." AI literacy is distinguished from simple AI tool use [39].
- Framework structure — Four Domains of AI Literacy (22 competences total): 1) Engaging with AI: Using AI as a tool to access content, evaluate accuracy/relevance of outputs; 2) Creating with AI: Collaborating with AI in creative/problem-solving processes, guiding outputs via prompts and feedback, addressing ownership/attribution/ethics; 3) Managing AI: Intentionally choosing how AI supports human work, delegating structured tasks while humans focus on creativity, empathy, and judgment; 4) Designing AI: Understanding how AI works and shaping its function, examining how data and design choices affect fairness and impact. The framework organizes competences into four sequential domains: Engage with AI (foundational domain for critical thinking about AI's role in daily life), Create with AI (using AI as a creative partner while maintaining human agency), Manage AI (dividing work intentionally between humans and AI), Shape AI (improving AI systems to reflect human values, culminating domain) [39].
- The framework sections cover Knowledge (facts about the nature of AI, human choices in AI, AI capabilities/limitations, and AI's societal role), Skills (critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, computational thinking, problem solving, communication, self and social awareness), and Attitudes (reflective, responsible, curious, innovative, adaptable, empathetic). Seven Skills: Critical Thinking, Creativity, Computational Thinking, Self and Social Awareness, Collaboration, Communication, Problem Solving. Five Attitudes: Responsible, Curious, Innovative, Adaptable, Empathetic [39].
- Learner personas: four example personas (Sofia, 10; Jun, 13; Omar, 15; Anika, 18) illustrating AI literacy in action [39].
- Following a May 2025 draft launch, over 2,000 individuals from 100+ countries provided feedback through surveys and focus groups. Teacher responses comprised 41% of survey respondents. The framework builds on existing frameworks including DigComp 3.0, UNESCO AI Competencies Frameworks, AI4K12's 5 Big Ideas, and Digital Promise's AI Literacy Framework [39].
- Key issues addressed: misconceptions that AI is human (noting AI lacks awareness, understanding, and intent), the environmental impact of AI requiring significant energy/water resources, inherent bias in AI systems reflecting human choices, and concerns about "metacognitive laziness" and diminished critical thinking from AI overreliance [39].
- European Schoolnet launched a report on AI in school education at EMINENT 2025 covering 23 European education systems, revealing fragmented approaches, uneven readiness, and persistent questions around data governance, assessment, teacher capacity, and student wellbeing [38].
- Key quotes from EMINENT 2025: Marc Durando (Executive Director of European Schoolnet): "Technology alone does not transform education. What matters is identifying where it truly makes a difference, and under which conditions." Olli-Pekka Heinonen (Director General, International Baccalaureate Organisation) keynoted on moving beyond binary thinking about AI, arguing its most profound impacts may be indirect. Prof. Francisco Bella (University of Coruña) addressed explainable AI (XAI), asking "Can we trust AI if we don't know how it works?" Quentin Vidal (OECD) warned that improved performance doesn't automatically translate into improved learning with AI tools, noting "We need to distinguish carefully between doing better on a task and actually learning better." Lidija Kralj (European Schoolnet) described data as "the oxygen of AI." National perspectives from Estonia (teacher-first approach, Kristina Kallas), Luxembourg ("pedagogy must come before technology," Daniela Hau), and Slovakia (short adaptive strategies, Michal Rybár) showed diverse yet converging approaches. A teacher-focused roundtable emphasized educator empowerment beyond technical skills, with warnings about deskilling if AI is adopted uncritically [38].
- The Council of Europe believes AI systems in education have transformative potential—through personalized learning pathways, real-time feedback, and innovative teaching methodologies—to make education accessible, inclusive, and equitable for all. Key publications include: "Regulating the use of Artificial Intelligence systems in education - Preparatory study on the development of a legal instrument" (2024); "The state of artificial intelligence and education across Europe – Results of a survey of Council of Europe member states" (2024); 2nd Working Conference "Regulating the use of AI systems in education" - Conference report (2025) [38].
- UNESCO promotes human-centered, ethical, and equitable technologies in education by design and in use. Global convening scheduled: 8–11 September 2026 at UNESCO Headquarters, Paris. Key facts: 74% of the world population (5.9 billion people) were using the internet in 2025; some report using AI tools, but only 23.6% feel very confident using them [38].
- AI for Education's page reports that 34 states (plus Puerto Rico) have issued official guidance or policy on AI use in K-12 education [16].

**P. AIGC TOOLS FOR SPECIFIC SUBJECT AREAS**

**P.1. Language Arts / Writing**

- Students using guided AI tutors scored dramatically higher on practice problems without harming performance on real tests [5][23].
- A study at Boston University (Journal of Writing Research, Vol. 17, No. 3, 2026, by Sarah Madsen Hardy, Pary Fassihi, Shuang Geng, Christopher McVey, and Matt Parfitt) analyzed college writing students' use of ChatGPT: In 18.6% of prompts, students asked ChatGPT to write for them, with the rest involving preparatory or supportive work for the writing process. Students used ChatGPT to generate 8.2% of the writing they submitted. The most common rhetorical purpose of AI-generated text was discussion/analysis/synthesis. English as a foreign language (EFL) students prompted ChatGPT to clarify understanding less often than non-EFLs and integrated less AI-generated text into their papers [45].
- A study in IJRISS ("Teaching Secondary School Essay Writing Using Generative AI" by Shirley Ling Jen and Abdul Rahim Salam, University Technology Malaysia, published August 27, 2025) developed a learning aid called "Bard G" (mobile application, two modules/books, and a rainbow chart) to guide 40 Form 4 students in using Google Gemini for essay writing. Problems identified while using Gemini included: lack of facilities/poor internet connection, insufficient computer knowledge, and lack of guidance in using AI. Usefulness themes: personalized learning, differentiation strategy, and self-directed learning. With Bard G, students could complete essay writing tasks within half an hour (compared to about an hour before), were more confident, and could teach others to use Gemini [45].
- A Journal of Learning Development in Higher Education study (Heather Johnston and Bryony N. Parsons, University of Liverpool) recruited 30 university students: 21 of 30 participants (70%) used GAI technologies in their process. ChatGPT 3.5 (Open AI) was the most frequently chosen tool, used by 18 students (60%). The most popular uses of GAI were: asking for definitions, explanations, or examples; and creating an essay plan or structure. 80% of students included some form of references in their essay plan, but NONE of the students created references for any GAI tools they had used [45].
- APA Monitor on Psychology (April 1, 2026, Vol. 58, No. 3) outlines strategies instructors are using to reduce student reliance on AI: breaking large writing assignments into smaller scaffolded chunks (topic proposals, partial drafts, annotated bibliographies, peer review); reducing page length and extending timelines; providing face-to-face or verbal feedback; using group and multimedia assignments (podcasts, comic strips) that require student-produced elements; and giving assignments real-world audiences or purposes. Instructors teach students to critique AI outputs, use AI as a "questioning partner" (like a Socratic tutor), and recognize when AI helps vs. hinders learning. Research is cited showing overreliance on AI weakens critical-thinking skills (Gerlich, Societies, 2025). APA Style guidance on citing AI: AI use must be disclosed and cited, AI cannot be named as a coauthor, authors are responsible for accuracy, and submitted content may not be entered into AI tools [33].
- A study in the Journal of Education Review Provision (May 8, 2026) investigated AI tools (grammar checkers, paraphrasing aids, vocabulary enhancers, automated feedback) enhancing university students' academic writing performance with a pretest-posttest design with 20 students. Key findings indicate significant improvements in writing accuracy, coherence, and overall quality, with reduced performance gaps among students. Learners reported positive experiences, emphasizing increased confidence, motivation, and autonomy [45].
- An IJLTER study (DOI: 10.26803/ijlter.25.5.8) examined AI tool use and writing outcomes among 96 graduate students in thesis writing. ChatGPT, Grammarly, and QuillBot were the most used AI tools. Statistical analysis demonstrated a strong positive relationship between experience with AI tools and writing performance outcomes. Qualitative themes: linguistic support, organization of ideas, and cognitive scaffolding and ideation. Ethical awareness themes included: selective use and resistance, responsible and transparent authorship, critical evaluation, accountability in AI tool use, and alignment with institutional guidelines [45].
- A study in the Journal of Educational Research special issue examined cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement in English writing with GAI (Meşe et al.). Woo et al. found students need specific instruction and practice in crafting effective GAI prompts [34].
- The CITE Journal study (Volume 25, Issue 3, 2025, by Torrey Trust, Robert Maloy, Chenyang Xu, and Kael Pelletier, University of Massachusetts Amherst) examined 310 AI-generated lesson plans containing 2,230 learning activities, created by three GenAI chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot) for all 53 content standards in the Massachusetts eighth-grade United States and Massachusetts Government and Civic Life curriculum. Only 213 of 2,230 activities (10%) promoted higher order thinking (analyze, evaluate, create). 90% of activities were coded at lower levels: remember (45%, n=1,010), apply (24%, n=545), understand (21%, n=462). Analyze: 4% (85 activities), Evaluate: 2% (31 activities), Create: 4% (98 activities). AI lesson plans were formulaic, following nearly identical structures regardless of content topic. Gemini had the most higher-order thinking activities; ChatGPT had more apply-level activities. AI-generated plans rarely introduced diverse perspectives; only 144 of 2,230 activities received a Banks' code. Gemini declined to generate plans for 7 standards (including elections and political protests) due to election-related restrictions. The authors caution that "uncritical use of AI carries with it the danger of slipping into problematic discourses" [46].
- A Frontiers in Education study (Paulo Brazão, Universidade da Madeira, Portugal and Luís Tinoca, University of Lisbon) examined critical questioning in dialogic relationships between AI chatbots and 25 first-year undergraduate students over a 15-week semester. Critical Engagement Questions (CEQ) were the most frequent at 30% of all questions, followed by SQ (24%), AQ (22%), GDQ (19%), and IQ (only 5%). Results revealed four emerging dimensions of critical thinking: (A) Levels of Cognitive Engagement, (B) Research and Conceptual Understanding, (C) Analytical Approaches and Thought Structures, (D) Individual and Group Dynamics in Critical Thinking [46].

**P.2. Mathematics**

- A 2024 University of Toronto RCT (Oreopoulos et al., 10,979 students) found only grades 3-6 students who used Khan Academy ~35 min/week saw math gains (0.12-0.17 SD). Grades 7-8 averaged ~10 min/week with no significant improvement. Usage dropped sharply without teacher/parental encouragement [10].
- Khan Academy's 2024 efficacy report (350,000 students) found that only ~9% of students met the recommended dosage of 18+ hours/year (~30 min/week). Those who did saw ~20% greater-than-expected MAP Growth gains (0.36 SD), but the vast majority didn't engage enough [10].
- A 2016 UC Berkeley RCT (103 middle schoolers) explicitly tested parental encouragement and found that without it, students' usage plummeted, and short-term score gains (10-16%) vanished within a week. Conclusion: engagement often depends on external nudging, not the platform itself [10].
- Stanford's TutorCoPilot study showed AI guidance improved math performance by 4 percentage points with 1,800 students [9].
- A study of high school math students found that those using a general-purpose chatbot performed worse on a subsequent closed-book exam than students who practiced with no AI support, despite having higher practice performance [3][5][20].

**P.3. Science (Lab Reports, Data Analysis)**

- The University of Gothenburg study ("Generative AI as a lab partner: A case study," Physical Review Physics Education Research) demonstrates various ways high school students use ChatGPT during physics lab work (acoustic levitation and speed of sound in air). The teacher still plays a crucial role in identifying students' needs and capabilities for understanding the potential and limitations of generative AI. Students need support and training to efficiently utilize generative AI to further their physics learning [45].

Liu et al. examined GAI in geography teaching comparing China and the US, noting accuracy, dependence, IP ethics, and equity concerns [34].

**P.5. Arts (Visual Art Creation, Music Composition)**

- Edutopia article by Vicki Davis (February 29, 2024) discusses incorporating AI art generation tools into K-12 classrooms. AI art tools include Midjourney, Dall-E (in ChatGPT), Microsoft Copilot, Canva AI, Adobe Firefly, and Adobe Photoshop. Key points: AI Art Vocabulary is Essential (there's a big difference between asking for "guitar music" vs. "Spanish guitar in the style of Govi"); Human Supervision is Required; Bias Awareness is Critical; Students should learn locations/periods of art creation, well-known artists and artifacts, art styles, mediums, and visual elements. Caution: Midjourney is NOT recommended for K-12 schools because it uses public Discord servers where the author doesn't want students "hanging out." Diffusion models: Dream Studio, Dall-E, Midjourney Stable Diffusion, and CF Spark. "While some artists may feel threatened in many ways by AI art generation, true handcrafted art may become more appreciated and valued than ever before because more people will become educated about art" [45].
- Edutopia article (February 27, 2025) showcases the AI music-generation tool Suno, which converts text into fully realized songs with vocals and instrumental backing in any genre in under a minute. Classroom applications include: Elementary math: Students collectively write lyrics describing types of triangles, which the teacher inputs into Suno to create a mnemonic song; English language arts: Students turn their poetry into songs, which deepens their understanding of mood and tone. The software is intended for users 13 and up [45].
- SchoolAI blog guide (May 27, 2025) on AI-powered art creation: AI art tools democratize visual expression by allowing students to create compelling visual content through text prompts. Compares DALL-E (photorealism and image editing, free tier available, suitable for high school and above), Midjourney (stylized outputs, subscription-based with educational discounts), and Stable Diffusion (open-source, customizable, can run locally, requires careful oversight). Seven key student benefits: enhanced creativity and critical thinking, increased motivation (citing Lehigh University research on higher engagement with Midjourney), digital literacy, personalized learning (including the Ecole des Beaux-Arts "Artique" AI tutor in France), improved accessibility for non-verbal students, cross-cultural understanding, and building metacognition. Ethical considerations around copyright and attribution, citing the National Art Education Association's (NAEA) recommendation to use public domain or Creative Commons-licensed imagery [45].
- A research article in Transactions of the International Society for Music Information Retrieval (TISMIR, Vol. 9, Issue 1, 2026) analyzed 101,953 songs generated from May to October 2024 by 60,342 users of Suno and Udio. English is most prevalent (71.39% Udio, 46.75% Suno), followed by German, Russian, Spanish, and Portuguese. Lyrics macro-categories included love (largest group with 2182 songs), fantasy (893), weather/seasons (949), religion (854), technology (899), animals (708), food (784), and meme-related content. The largest individual cluster was worship songs. Udio replaces 703 unique real artist names with generic descriptors. Most replaced artists include XXXTentacion (26 times), Drake (19), Taylor Swift (18), Foo Fighters (18), and The Beatles (17). Common metatags in lyrics include verse (88,270), chorus (65,342), bridge (22,491), outro (8,549), and pre-chorus (6,639) [45].
- ETCJ article (August 5, 2025) on AI disrupting fine arts: Musicians use AI for composition, songwriting, production/sound design, live performance (AI holograms/avatars like Hatsune Miku and Grimes), voice cloning/synthetic vocals, and fan engagement. Anyone can create an AI "supergroup" of cloned musician voices without playing instruments or reading music, using tools like Suno, Udio, and Soundraw—though with cautions about voice ownership and copyright. AI is reshaping film (e.g., Runway Gen-2), musical theater, ballet, opera, animation, classical music (e.g., an AI-assisted completion of Mahler's Symphony No. 10 in Germany), and dance (tools: Move.ai, DeepMotion, Kinetix, MetaHuman Animator). Leading institutions embracing AI in creative arts include NYU Tisch School of the Arts, USC Institute for Creative Technologies, MIT Media Lab, Royal College of Art (London), University of the Arts Helsinki, Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD), and Bezalel Academy (Israel). K-12/youth programs include AI4ALL and Design Tech High School (California). "You do not need to play any instruments, read music, or have formal training to create full, high-quality songs using AI tools today. That's one of the most revolutionary things about this moment in music" [45].

**Q. TEACHER-FACING TOOLS AND WORKLOAD**

- Eduaide.Ai blog post (ahead of 2024-2025 school year) reviews five AI tools: 1) Eduaide.Ai - A workspace for lesson planning, resource generation, and instructional design, useful for creating differentiated materials that build on prior knowledge; 2) Curipod - An interactive presentation tool that fosters active learning through real-time student participation and collaboration; 3) Perplexity - An AI-powered research and conversational search engine (using GPT-4 and Claude 3) supporting inquiry-based learning projects; 4) Flint - An AI-powered tutoring platform that personalizes learning by providing targeted practice and feedback based on individual student needs; 5) Quizizz - An interactive quiz platform that gamifies learning and supports spaced retrieval practice through regular low-stakes formative assessments. "AI tools are not a substitute for thoughtful teaching and careful planning. They are aids that, when used judiciously, can support the critical work of helping students learn" [12].
- Top 15 best AI tools for teachers in 2026 (Third Rock Techkno): MagicSchool AI (lesson planning, free for teachers), Gradescope (grading, up to 80% reduction in grading time), and Gamma AI (presentations). Free tiers from ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Canva, and Diffit cover most daily needs. For UK and GCC schools, tools prioritized include MagicSchool AI, Diffit (for EAL students), Twee (for ESL), and Canva (Arabic text support). Critical warnings: never input student names into general AI tools, review all AI-generated grades, check for hallucinated content, and avoid over-reliance on AI. "AI is strong on structured, right-or-wrong answers and weaker on nuanced essays. Review every grade before it is final." "AI should remove busywork, not replace your subject expertise or your relationships with pupils" [14].
- An Open Praxis study (Volume 18, Issue 1, 2026) investigated factors influencing 433 preschool teachers' continuous intention to use AIGC in education, integrating TAM, ECM, and Flow Theory. Confirmation had the strongest effect on perceived usefulness (β=0.505) and satisfaction (β=0.349). Perceived usefulness strongly influenced attitude (β=0.530) and satisfaction (β=0.309). Flow experience positively impacted continuous intention (β=0.223) and attitude (β=0.220). Satisfaction (β=0.280) and attitude (β=0.262) also significantly predicted continuance intention. The model explains 51.8% of variance in continuance intention. "The stronger influence of flow experience and satisfaction over perceived usefulness challenges the rational evaluation assumption of classic technology adoption models. This underscores that affective engagement, not rational utility, plays the critical role in shaping long-term adoption" [2].
- AI can reclaim 20-40% of teachers' administrative time (about 13 hours weekly) per McKinsey estimates [32].

**R. RISKS, CHALLENGES, AND CONCERNS**

- A University of Pennsylvania study found that unguided AI access harmed learning outcomes in high school mathematics [1].
- Over 30% of students risk becoming overly dependent on AI tools. 68%+ of urban teachers have received no AI training [1].
- Equity gaps persist as under-resourced schools struggle to implement AI effectively [1].
- Research indicates that over-reliance on AI during practice can reduce performance in exams taken without assistance [6].
- The #1 failure pattern: institutions adopt AI tools without intentional design, which can harm learning outcomes rather than improve them [1].
- Only 11% in the U.S. follow rigorous evaluation measures for AI privacy compliance. AI-generated deepfakes targeting students have emerged in Australia [4].
- Algorithmic bias: Wisconsin's early warning system was wrong ~75% of the time and disproportionately misidentified Black and Hispanic students [9].
- Georgia State University reduced summer melt from 19% to 9% using an AI chatbot [1].
- The MIT study noted that users who relied on AI tools "may unintentionally hinder deep cognitive processing, retention, and authentic engagement with written material" [7].
- 53% of participating teachers reported a positive experience with the AI tool in Indiana's pilot, and even after the grant ended, some schools chose to continue. The AI essentially helped novice tutors mimic expert questioning strategies, increasing overall effectiveness [9].
- Challenges in Newark: student privacy (facial recognition, cloud storage), equity concerns (surveillance disproportionately affecting students of color), evidence gaps, and infrastructure delays in century-old buildings [32].
- The JRC study noted broader concerns (environmental impact, copyright issues, digital sovereignty) were largely overlooked by educators and students [31].
- A comparative study on China, Singapore, Finland, and the USA (Journal of Science and Technology Policy Management) found implementation remains challenged by equity gaps, teacher readiness, and contextual mismatches [28].
- The Nordic survey found teachers expressed concerns about ethical aspects and climate impacts of AI [40].
- A research article on pre-service teacher education found TCs expressed an inclination to use AI as teachers but held negative views toward their students' use of AI [19].
- The CITE Journal study notes GenAI tools can produce "fake, false, and flat out wrong" information, harmful stereotypes, and biased outputs based on race, gender, language, and disability [46].
- The "arms race" between AI detectors and "humanizer" evasion tools was compared to the failed "calculator wars" in mathematics [33].
- 45% of educators and 52% of students still lack AI training [30].

# AIGC (AI-Generated Content) in K-12 Education: Asia and Australia Case Studies — Cleaned Research Findings

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. **Tavily search 1**: "AIGC AI-generated content K-12 education Asia Australia 2024 2025 2026 case studies", "China AI in education policy K-12 schools 2024 2025 2026", "Singapore AI education Smart Nation schools 2024 2025 2026", "South Korea AI education roadmap K-12 2024 2025 2026", "Australia New Zealand AI in schools education policy 2024 2025 2026"
2. **Tavily search 2**: "Japan K-12 schools ChatGPT generative AI education GIGA school 2024 2025 2026 case study", "India AI in education schools NEP 2020 DIKSHA AI for All K-12 2024 2025 2026", "UAE AI strategy education schools K-12 2024 2025 2026 generative AI", "Squirrel AI China adaptive learning school outcomes evidence study", "iFLYTEK Ernie Bot schools China classroom implementation AI tutors"
3. **Tavily search 3**: "Japan schools ChatGPT pilot classroom case study 2024 2025 MEXT guidelines elementary junior high", "Singapore Student Learning Space AI tutor SLS schools ChatGPT pilot 2025 case study", "Australia schools ChatGPT classroom trial case study 2024 2025 NSW Victoria", "China Ernie Bot Wenxin Yiyan classroom schools case study 2024 2025", "India Rajasthan AI math tutoring program schools results study", "South Korea AI digital textbook pilot schools 2025 teachers experience English math"
4. **Tavily search 4**: "New Zealand school generative AI case study Aotea College Hobsonville 2025 classroom", "Singapore SLS generative AI LLM 2025 2026 MOE announcement new features schools", "China 184 AI education pilot schools outcomes Beijing Shanghai 2025 results", "Japan MEXT generative AI schools survey results prefecture trial 2025 ChatGPT usage"
5. **Tavily search 5**: "Aotea College Hobsonville Point Secondary School generative AI case study New Zealand NCEA", "Tokyo metropolitan AI schools 2025 2026 rollout results Japan generative AI secondary", "South Korea AI digital textbook 2026 status update results challenges", "China AI pilot school outcomes 2025 Beijing English math results study"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### I. GLOBAL / CROSS-COUNTRY CONTEXT

#### Systematic Reviews of GenAI in K-12 Education

**RPTEL Systematic Review (2026)** [1]: A systematic review published in *Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning* (Vol. 21, 2026) by Tianyu Zhang, Yiu Chi Lai, and Philip Leung Ho Yu (The Education University of Hong Kong) reviewed 45 studies published 2020–2024 on GenAI in K-12 education. Key findings: (1) GenAI tools significantly improve students' academic performance, cognitive abilities, and learning motivation, promoting personalized learning; (2) challenges include misleading or erroneous content generation, difficulty in understanding technology, student dependence on technology, and privacy infringement; (3) educators demonstrate shortcomings in AI literacy, highlighting the need for targeted training; (4) most existing empirical research focuses on short-term impacts, with future research needing more longitudinal studies. Verbatim: "GenAI tools can significantly improve students' academic performance and cognitive abilities, enhance their learning motivation, and thus promote the development of personalized learning," "Using these tools also brings a series of challenges, including misleading or erroneous content generation, difficulty in understanding technology, students' dependence on technology, and privacy infringement," "The shortcomings demonstrated by educators in terms of AI literacy emphasize the necessity for relevant educational institutions to organize targeted AI literacy training," "Most existing empirical research has focused on the short-term impact of GenAI tools on K-12 education. Future research will incorporate more longitudinal studies to systematically evaluate the long-term and deep implications of GenAI in education."

**Frontiers Systematic Review (2025)** [25]: Abdullah Alfarwan (Najran University, Saudi Arabia) published a systematic review in *Frontiers in Education* (September 23, 2025) analyzing 30 empirical papers from Scopus, Web of Science, and snowballing. Key findings:
- Publication timeline: Most papers (19 of 30) published in 2024, 6 from 2025, 5 from 2023.
- Educational levels: High school students and pre-service teachers most represented; in-service teachers, elementary, primary, and vocational education underrepresented; no studies on early childhood education.
- Subject domains: Mathematics most common (5 papers), followed by Physics (4); majority STEM-focused; non-STEM included History, Writing, English Language.
- Geographic representation: Most studies from Taiwan and China (4 each), followed by US and Germany (3 each); no studies from Africa.
- GenAI tools: ChatGPT used in 21 of 30 papers; other tools included Copilot, DALL-E, Midjourney.
- Study design: Quasi-experimental most common (30%), followed by descriptive and mixed-method (20% each).
- Measures: Primarily psychological variables (attitudes, self-efficacy, trust, motivation, critical thinking, self-regulated learning); only two studies examined self-regulated learning; objective measures (standardized tests) largely absent.
- Recommendations: 90% of papers emphasized the need for teacher professional development for AI-integrated classrooms. Future research should explore longitudinal studies, true experimental designs, objective learning measures, parental involvement, diverse GenAI tools, and under-researched contexts (ECE, special needs, rural settings).

**MDPI Systems Systematic Review via 3P Model (2025)** [26]: Xiaoling Lin and Hao Tan (School of Design, Hunan University) published "A Systematic Review of Generative AI in K–12: Mapping Goals, Activities, Roles, and Outcomes via the 3P Model" in *Systems* (2025, Vol. 13, Issue 10, article 840, DOI: 10.3390/systems13100840). Using PRISMA and MMAT, they synthesized 84 peer-reviewed empirical studies (2020–2025) involving learners aged 3–18, from 817 records (Scopus 528, Web of Science 289). Key findings:
- Seven recurring learning objectives: language/literacy; STEM; creativity; socioemotional skills; feedback literacy and self-regulation; motivation; AI literacy.
- Five dominant activity patterns: AI-facilitated dialogic tutoring; generative iterative co-creation; project-based problem-solving; simulation/game-based learning; and formative feedback with adaptive scaffolding.
- AI roles shift from AI-directed (learner-as-recipient) to AI-supported/AI-empowered paradigms, re-allocating agency among students, teachers, and caregivers via feedback loops.
- Reported outcomes span three categories—epistemic, practice, and affective/identity—with opportunities including deeper knowledge, improved practice, and stronger engagement, and risks including hallucinations, reduced originality, over-reliance, motivational loss, and ethical concerns.
- The field lacks theoretically grounded accounts linking learning goals, pedagogical activities, and human–AI role configurations to measurable outcomes for 3–18-year-olds.

#### Global Adoption Statistics and Evidence

**Third Rock Techkno (2026)** [2]: Article by Tapan Patel (published December 24, 2025, updated August 3, 2026) covering nine AI in education use cases:
- Key statistics: 86% of education organizations use generative AI (highest adoption rate of any industry, per Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education Report); global AI in education market reached $7.57 billion in 2025, projected to hit $112 billion by 2034; teachers using AI tools report reclaiming 5–10 hours per week for instruction; a 2025 randomized controlled trial in *Nature Scientific Reports* found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning.
- Nine core use cases: (1) Personalized Learning (e.g., Sourcebook); (2) Automated Content Creation (e.g., Squirrel AI generates tailored textbooks and materials); (3) Intelligent Tutoring (e.g., Khan Academy's Khanmigo built on GPT-4 asks guiding questions rather than giving answers); (4) Enhanced Student Engagement (e.g., Duolingo personalizes lesson difficulty with spaced-repetition algorithms); (5) Teacher Assistance & Administrative Automation (e.g., Gradescope evaluates handwritten math, coding, essays); (6) Language Learning & Translation (e.g., Duolingo's AI optimizes review timing); (7) Predictive Analytics (e.g., IBM Watson Education reported 20% improvements in student performance through early intervention); (8) Accessibility & Inclusivity (e.g., Microsoft Immersive Reader for dyslexia/visual impairments); (9) Collaborative Learning (e.g., Kiddom manages virtual study groups).
- Limitations: student data privacy under FERPA; bias in training data; AI should support, not replace, teachers.

**FifthRow Blog (April 9, 2026)** [5]: "AI in K-12 Education: Global Policies, Outcomes, and Actionable Best Practices":
- Regulatory landscape: US April 2025 executive order established a national K-12 AI literacy strategy; by early 2026 over half of US states enacted AI policy guidance; China leads with a mandatory national AI curriculum; South Korea rolled out AI-enabled tutors; Iceland launched a first-of-its-kind national AI pilot with Anthropic; no national bans on AI in K-12 education enacted since 2025.
- Empirical evidence: 85% of K-12 teachers and students report using AI, primarily for lesson planning, feedback, and data analysis; two-thirds endorse AI's benefits for personalized learning and administrative tasks; up to 75% of students report higher motivation in AI-enhanced settings; academic improvements of 15–35% recorded in some studies; no long-term longitudinal studies exist on sustained impacts on higher-order cognitive skills.
- Key risks: only 11% of US districts rigorously vet AI tools for data privacy; AI-generated deepfakes and false cheating accusations have caused harm; 72% of students would use generative AI for assignments, but only 17–22% receive instruction on responsible use; AI adoption below 15% in most African and Latin American systems.
- Stakeholder views: teacher attitudes polarized—25% believe AI causes more harm than good, while 6% see clear net gains; student enthusiasm (39%) lags behind teacher enthusiasm.
- Best practices: targeted ongoing professional development, ethical/privacy guidelines that evolve with technology, digital infrastructure investment, institutional oversight on procurement, human-in-the-loop approaches for high-stakes decisions.

**AEFP Live Handbook (August 2026)** [3]: Barnard, Fesler, and Loeb analyze AI in K-12 education:
- Thin evidence base: of 800+ academic papers on AI in K-12 education, only 20 meet standards for strong causal inference; no high-quality causal studies exist on student-facing AI tools in US K-12 classrooms.
- Performance vs. proficiency gap: a randomized study of high school math students found those using a general-purpose chatbot performed worse on subsequent closed-book exams than students who practiced with no AI support, despite higher performance during practice. Students using a tutoring-style system (hints and guided reasoning) showed no difference on exams.
- Design choices matter: "Systems that generate complete answers tend to reduce cognitive work and learning." Guided reasoning tools improve independent problem-solving performance.
- Educator capacity: a randomized experiment found teachers with ChatGPT spent less time preparing lessons while maintaining quality; AI tools providing instructional feedback show largest gains for lower-performing tutors.

**Beijing High School English Reading Case Study (Frontiers, May 2025)** [65][16]: Yuxin Liu and Chengche Qiao (Beijing Jiaotong University) published an AI-driven teaching model for Chinese high school English reading instruction grounded in deep learning theory. The study involved 16 students from an 11th-grade class at a foreign language school in Beijing (average IELTS reading score of 6). Using the "Science Fiction" unit from the People's Education Press curriculum, an 8-period teaching design was implemented for the short story "Satisfaction Guaranteed (Adapted)" with five sessions: lead-in (using Midjourney for AIGC visuals), knowledge acquisition (using ERNIE Bot/Markmap for mind maps), comprehension and internalization (comparative charts), deep learning (group discussions with generative AIs like Chat-GPT, Deepseek, Doubao AI), and summary/review (retelling competitions and Youdao Writing for automated grading). Key findings: Chinese researchers and China-based funding bodies are the most prominent in ERNIE Bot-related research; top research themes include 'Natural Language Model', 'Semantics', and 'Human'; ERNIE Bot's application in education attracted notable attention with 22.4% of analyzed studies focusing on this area, highlighting potential in personalized learning and human-computer interaction; ERNIE Bot's Chinese origin is framed as a symbol of contextual leadership and a key player in China's technological competition with global models like ChatGPT; ERNIE Bot's strengths in Chinese language processing are highlighted; however, ERNIE Bot lags global counterparts in overall competitiveness, with limitations in data diversity, political censorship, and accessibility restricting global applicability.

The school also uses robots to analyze student health and engagement, uniform chips to track locations, and surveillance cameras monitoring phone use and yawning. Concerns: boarding schools research found 47.3% of boarding students suffered from acute pessimism, 63.8% felt lonely, 17.6% suffered from depression, 8.4% exhibited suicidal tendencies; wealthy urban students already enjoy AI-guided learning tools, potentially widening rather than narrowing the gap.

### IV. JAPAN

#### National Policy Context

**MEXT Guidelines** [49][50][51][52]:
- July 2023: MEXT issued interim guidelines emphasizing caution—prohibiting AI for graded assignments, requiring students to verify AI output and cite tool/prompt usage, mandating that "human judgment is essential at the end of every task." MEXT did not impose a uniform ban but asked boards of education to adjust approaches regionally [50].
- December 2024: Updated guidelines (Ver. 2.0) expanded AI's scope, framing it as potentially beneficial based on usage. Key points: generative AI "is capable of producing useful output and, depending on how it is used, can be a tool that assists, extends, and expands human capabilities and possibilities"; students need to deepen their understanding of generative AI and acquire appropriate usage methods; risks include erroneous output (hallucination) and regeneration of biases; teachers should instruct students to use AI output only as a reference and ultimately make their own judgments. Four key points: (1) appropriate use with safety in mind, (2) ensuring information security, (3) protection of personal information, privacy, and copyrights, (4) ensuring fairness. Boards of education should develop an Education Information Security Policy and organize training [52].
- MEXT selected 52 designated schools as "testbeds" for AI verification in the 2023-2024 fiscal year [50].
- 2023 academic year pilot results: "students may be enhancing their motivation and creativity by experimenting and trying to obtain the intended output from the generative AI. On the other hand, it was also observed that there were cases where students blindly accepted the generative AI's answers or were unable to appropriately select when to use it" [52].

**AI Promotion Act (May 28, 2025)** [53]: Japan's 2025 AI strategy is anchored by the AI Promotion Act, establishing an "innovation-first" framework with five core principles (promotion, transparency, alignment, comprehensive advancement, international leadership). The AI Education Accelerator Program trained roughly 50,000 educators by 2025 through public-private partnerships (including SoftBank Robotics). A 2022 survey found 58% of teachers felt underprepared for AI.

Achieved near-nationwide device coverage for compulsory education by 2021: approximately 7.4 million tablet devices and laptops (about 28% iPads) distributed, with 97.6% of planned devices deployed across 1,769 municipalities by March 2021. Research by Sri Dewi Adriani (Binus University, published March 26, 2025 in Daengku Journal, DOI 10.35877/454RI.daengku3797) concluded the program "successfully reduced the gaps in accessing distance education while creating a new, modern civilization in the teaching process in educational environments in Japan" [28].

#### Student Usage Data and Risks

**Nippon.com Survey (January 2026)** [91]: Survey of 1,200 junior high and high school students by Kankō Gakuseifuku found nearly 80% use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini "frequently" or "occasionally." 46.8% of girls use AI "frequently" (vs. 36.0% of boys). More than 70% said the main reason was checking information for schoolwork. A Carnegie Mellon University and University of Oxford study (April) tested about 1,000 adults: the AI-assisted group initially scored higher, but when AI assistance was removed, accuracy fell below the non-AI group, rate of giving up nearly doubled, and 60% sought "the correct answer itself" rather than hints. An MIT study (June 2025) used EEG measurements showing participants using generative AI to write essays had lower brain activity; those who used AI first did not recover brain activity, motivation, or concentration even when later relying only on their own minds. Key distinction: "For predictive, recognition, and classification types of AI, children and students were primarily 'the analyzed side.' However, for generative AI, children and students can become users." ELSI concerns: bias amplification, hallucination, privacy violations, copyright infringement, prompt injection attacks, information leaks, environmental impacts. Multilevel responses: AI company engagement (Japan's Digital Agency published procurement/contract checklists in May 2025), institutional policy development, enhanced AI literacy training. Primary uses: business efficiency/document creation (43.5%), professional knowledge research (30.5%), text proofreading/summarization (28.0%), language learning (25.6%).
